title: PETA asks rock band 'Cage the Elephant' to temporarily change its name
text:
PETA asks rock band 'Cage the Elephant' to temporarily change its name
Animal rights organization PETA has asked the rock band "Cage the Elephant" to change its name — at least temporarily.
PETA asked the band from Kentucky to go by "Free the Elephant" on its social media accounts for a week in an effort to help an elephant that has reportedly spent decades in captivity.
The elephant, named Okha, is in her late 50s, and the organization says she has spent more than five decades performing in circuses. Okha was taken from the wild in India as a baby and has been transported around in trailers and forced to perform under the threat of punishment, according to PETA.
"Cage the Elephant" is scheduled to perform at the NFL Munich Halftime Show during the New England Patriots and Detroit Lions game on Sunday.
PETA says a temporary name change could help draw attention to animal abuse in circuses and its efforts to rescue Okha.
"Will you help us come a little closer to ending animal abuse in circuses by helping us rescue sweet little Okha?" the letter read.
It is unclear whether "Cage the Elephant" will accept PETA's request.

title: Remember When Maine Had 13 Friendly’s? Here’s What They Look Like Now
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Used to Have 13 Friendly’s Restaurants. What Happened to Them?
Maine has only one Friendly's restaurant as of today, but that wasn't always the case.
Travel back in time to, say, the year 2000, and you'd find there were a bunch more locations in the state serving up classic burgers and a variety of ice creams. (Always had to save room for the Mint Cookie Crunch!)
Ever wonder what happened to them all? You might have even driven past a former Friendly's and not even realized it. I was able to find 13 of them from back in the day and what's in their spots now.
Friendly’s Started in Massachusetts and Once Had Over 850 Restaurants in the US
Friendly first opened in Massachusetts in 1935 (I didn't know it didn't get its apostrophe until 1989), over 90 years ago, according to its website. By 1951, there were 10 locations total in Massachusetts and Connecticut.
The Washington Times reported that by the mid-'90s, Friendly's had reached its peak number of restaurants across the country at about 850.
The First Friendly's in the Portland Area Opened in 1970
I couldn't confirm the first Friendly's location in Maine, but through the Portland Public Library Special Collections & Archives, I was able to find a photo of the grand opening of the first one in the Portland area.
That would be in South Portland at 581 Main Street in 1970, which is now the site of a Dunkin'. Classic.
Another photo from the Portland Public Library Digital Commons indicated that another South Portland location opened in 1974, and that was right inside the Maine Mall. I always remembered just the one at 210 Maine Mall Road, but that clearly was a new spot to replace the Maine Mall one. Still, it must have been wild to do a little shopping in the mall and just walk on over for some Friendly's.
All of that said, it got me thinking about how the popular restaurant felt like it was everywhere back in the day, and so I took to the Wayback Machine, an internet archive of websites, to check out where and when 13 Friendly's locations existed and what they've become today.
Let's take a trip to the past!
Then and Now: 13 Places in Maine Where Friendly's Restaurants Used to Be
Gallery Credit: Sean McKenna
READ MORE: There's a New Year-Round Ice Cream Shop That Just Opened in Maine
It's interesting to see the variety of transformations. You've got a few Five Guys spots, a dentist, a bank, and various other restaurants.
And when you see the side-by-side of some of these places, it's wild to view the transformation from the past to the present. Some spots still have that unmistakable Friendly's building design, too.
While the Washington Times revealed that there are only about 80 or so Friendly's locations left in the U.S. in 2026, Maine still has one Friendly's left.
That would be the Maine Mall Road location in South Portland, and it's still going strong.
Hopefully, it stands the test of time, and remains that iconic New England spot well into the future. Makes me want to go get some ice cream...

title: Old Orchard Surges Past Boothbay in Regional Final
text:
The Boothbay football team lost to undefeated Old Orchard Beach 46-8 in an 8-Man League Small School South Division championship game in the rain on Saturday, Nov 7 in Old Orchard Beach.
The top seed Old Orchard Beach won their fifth straight South Division title and improved to 10 0. The Seagulls will face North Division champion Orono in the state championship game on Saturday, Nov. 11 at Edward Little High School in Auburn.
For the second time this season, the underdog Seahawks gave the Seagulls a scare. The teams met earlier in the regular season on Oct. 2, with Boothbay leading 14-6 halfway through the second quarter before Old Orchard Beach came from behind to win 50-26.
This time, Boothbay took an early lead in the rematch when Miles Murray connected with Thomas Hennessy on a 35-yard touchdown pass in the first quarter. Peyton Barter ran the ball into the end zone on the 2-point conversion attempt to boost the Boothbay lead to 8-0. The Seahawks would not reach the end zone again.
Old Orchard regrouped and their offense responded with three touchdown runs by Brayden Koelker of five, 17, and six yards to claim a 22-8 lead heading into the halftime break.
Koelker bolted for a 45-yard touchdown run in the third quarter, his fourth TD of the contest, to extend the advantage to 30-8. Matthew Charron ran the ball 45 yards for a Seagulls touchdown on the last play of the third quarter. Old Orchard running back Tate Graham scored on a 36-yard touchdown run to provide the final score of 46-8.
The No. 2 seed Seahawks ended their season with a 6-3 record.

title: Skowhegan moves ahead with changing clerk, treasurer to appointed posts
text:
SKOWHEGAN — Town officials are moving ahead with a proposal to give them authority to appoint the town clerk and town treasurer, rather than have voters elect someone to the posts.
Officials also want to change the two jobs, traditionally held by one person, to separate full-time posts.
Skowhegan voters are expected to have their say on the changes at some point in the next two months.
The select board Tuesday evening unanimously authorized Town Manager Aaron Miller to move forward with drafting warrant articles for a special town meeting, in consultation with legal counsel. It is not yet clear how exactly the two separate issues — elective versus appointive and one combined position versus two separate ones — will be presented to voters.
The board scheduled a formal public hearing for 6 p.m. Dec. 8 at the Skowhegan Municipal Building and set a Jan. 15, 2027, deadline for holding the special town meeting.
The Jan. 15 target gives the town some extra time, Miller said. Under state law, the vote would have to happen at least 90 days before the annual town meeting, typically in early June, officials have said.
Voters have been asked to change the clerk and treasurer offices to appointive ones before.
A similar proposal overwhelmingly failed in 2016, and two other times in the decade prior, according to past Morning Sentinel reports. More recently, a proposal to change the town’s road commissioner to an appointed post failed in 2023.
The latest effort began as Gail Pelotte announced she plans to retire at the end of her term in June 2027 and does not plan to run for reelection. Pelotte, a town employee of more than three decades, has been clerk and treasurer since 2009.
Pelotte has told the select board the two jobs require specialized skills. They also require a lot of extra hours: She has said she regularly takes work home and comes in to the office on weekends.
As clerk, Pelotte oversees elections; the front office where residents come to pay tax bills, register vehicles and ask questions; vital records; and administrative aspects of the town’s cemeteries. As treasurer, Pelotte is responsible for managing and safeguarding the town’s funds. In recent years, amid turnover in the town manager position, Pelotte has also taken on some tax collector duties.
Meanwhile, the town remains several years behind on its financial audits, a responsibility that involves the treasurer but also includes other officials. Miller said at Tuesday’s meeting he is meeting regularly with the town’s auditor and finance staff to get the town back on track.
Now, and traditionally, Skowhegan has budgeted the clerk and treasurer positions as half-time, according to Pelotte.
That means someone could run just for one of the posts, as they are two separate offices listed on the ballot. But the person would get only a part-time job, she said.
The current budget lists one combined position with a salary of $93,344.

title: Eddington woman previously charged with infant overdose wanted on new charges
text:
EDDINGTON, Maine (WABI) - An Eddington woman who is out on bail in an infant overdose case is once again wanted by authorities.
During a traffic stop Sunday, authorities say they seized illegal drugs and stopped Brittany Wood, 36, from destroying potential evidence.
In the two days since, officials with the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office say they tried several times to get Wood to surrender voluntarily, but she did not.
Wood faces charges of unlawful possession of scheduled drugs, falsifying physical evidence and violating conditions of release.
Earlier case
The Sheriff’s Office was searching for Wood in July on separate charges connected to an infant overdose. Wood was taken into custody several days later while leaving a home in Eddington.
Her attorney said in court that Wood had been on vacation and did not know about the warrant until she saw news reports online. The defense also said Wood was on her way to turn herself in when she was arrested.
Officials said Wood’s 9-month-old child overdosed in May, with Wood and the baby testing positive for cocaine and fentanyl. A grand jury indicted Wood in October on charges related to the incident.
Wood is a member of the RSU 63 School Board, representing Eddington.
Town Manager Shawna Hinkley said earlier this year that there is no recall process for RSU 63 school board members. Under an absenteeism policy, a member who misses three consecutive meetings is removed from the board.
Wood missed two consecutive meetings after the July warrant. She was released on bail in time to attend the third and kept her seat.
WABI reached out to RSU 63 School Board chair Rachel Downs for comment. She confirmed Wood is still an elected member of the board. “The district will continue to follow applicable district policies and Maine law, including 20-A M.R.S. § 1474 which outlines the circumstances under which a vacancy on a regional school unit board may be declared," Downs said. “Since this is a matter involving an elected official and pending law enforcement matters, the School Board does not have further comments at this time.”
We have contacted the town of Eddington for more information.
Anyone with information about Wood’s whereabouts is asked to call the Sheriff’s Office at 947-4585.

title: 3 dead after car crashes into people outside Los Angeles metro station during rush hour
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The driver of a minivan that crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station, killing three women and critically injuring two more, was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence and three counts of murder, police said Wednesday.
Authorities said the driver was able to talk but appeared to be in shock after Tuesday’s crash, which hit pedestrians and food vendors at a busy intersection in the North Hollywood neighborhood during the height of the evening commute.
Police identified the driver as Ihor Demianenko, 61, who lives in the Valley Village neighborhood. Demianenko was booked early Wednesday and his bail was set at a little over $6 million, records show. He was treated for minor injuries at a hospital, police said.
It wasn’t immediately clear if Demianenko had a lawyer who might speak on his behalf. In California, drivers under the influence of drugs or alcohol can be charged with murder under certain circumstances.
The case had not been presented to the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office as of Wednesday afternoon, spokesperson Venusse Dunn said in an email.
The white Toyota Sienna was traveling at an “unsafe speed” at around 6 p.m. when it veered to the right, ran off the road and collided with a light, Los Angeles police said in a news release Wednesday. It came to rest under a food vendor’s tent.
The force of the collision threw victims in different directions, according to the news release. The driver was trapped in the vehicle until rescuers arrived.
Luis Luna-Guzman was working at a nearby burger stand when he heard a loud boom and saw people on the ground along with food and cups. People started running toward the crash.
Luna-Guzman said he found an injured woman lying near some bike racks, her face, arms and legs bloody. Her eyes were closed as she moaned in pain.
The three women who died were between the ages of 40 and 60, according to the police news release. Authorities haven’t released their names. The two injured women are in their 50s.
The minivan was still on the sidewalk Tuesday night under the food vendor’s tent, its driver’s-side door open and an air bag deployed. Fire engines and emergency crews worked nearby as a helicopter flew overhead.
Investigators will go through video of the crash frame by frame, Police Chief Jim McDonnell said.
The California Supreme Court ruled in 1981 that drivers who kill someone with a vehicle can be charged with second-degree murder if they are found to have acted with “wantonness and a conscious disregard for life” that could support a finding of implied malice. The court upheld a prosecutor’s decision to file murder charges against a driver who was determined to be legally intoxicated at the time of a fatal crash and drove at high speeds, ran a red light and had a near miss right before.
___
Thanawala reported from Atlanta.

title: Medomak Valley Athletic Trainer Settling In
text:
With the fall sports season behind him, Christopher Wight is looking forward to what the rest of the athletic seasons have to bring. In August, Wight began his new job as the first in-house athletic trainer for Medomak Valley High School and Medomak Middle School.
The South China native and Erskine Academy graduate is a full-on sports enthusiast who earned an undergraduate degree in exercise science at Husson University in 2022 and a master’s degree in athletic training in 2025 at the University of Southern Maine. Wight’s first job as a certified and licensed athletic trainer was during the 2025-2026 academic year at Bates College as part of their Transition to Practice program.
“During my tenure at Bates, my primary assignment was working with the Bates football program in the fall,” said Wight. “In the spring, I worked in the outpatient office of St Mary’s Orthopedics as an athletic trainer and performed other sports assignments at Bates College on an as-needed basis.”
According to Athletic Director Matt Lash, Medomak Valley used to contract for athletic trainer services with Pen Bay Sports Medicine, now known as MaineHealth Orthopedics and Sports Medicine-Rockport. About five years ago, the organization informed Lash it was phasing out athletic trainer positions.
After the contract ended, RSU 40 began hiring a patchwork of athletic trainers, including Megan Day, of Lincoln Academy, and Mary Britt, of Oceanside High School, to cover sports events on a per diem basis. Lash noted Waldoboro EMS Chief Derek Booker and the service’s crew did a solid job at filling in at almost every home event over the last three years.
“We decided that our best option was to create our own athletic trainer position, and the school board supported it and put it in the budget” said Lash. “While Megan and Mary have been extremely helpful providing support, not having a full-time athletic trainer here every day to help athletes work through injuries and minor ailments was deeply missed. Having Chris on board has benefited the student athletes for sure.”
Most fans that watch sports are not familiar with the full range of duties for a sports trainer professional like Wight.
“Some see us as glorified water boys rather than the licensed, allied healthcare professionals that we are,” said Wight. “Some of the things I work on behind the scenes that most people don’t see are the countless hours spent on administrative work such as creating and implementing injury prevention programs, creating rehab plans for the athletes, filling out documentation for injury evaluations, speaking with parents and guardians, and fulfilling continuing education requirements.”
Lash agrees that the athletic trainer services that fans see during sports games are only one aspect of what they do on a regular basis.
“Chris’s first duties for us were helping to establish athletic training protocols and policies, and helping to update the athletics emergency action plan,” said Lash. “Chris provides event and practice coverage, refers student athletes to other health care professionals and communicates with parents and staff regarding injuries. He is also involved in the recovery process, assisting them to get back to action.”
Wight said he was had a pair of role models that inspired him toward his career as an athletic trainer. “My uncle John Ryan has been an inspiration and mentor for me,” said Wight of the former certified athletic trainer at Bangor High, who is currently the athletic trainer at South Portland High School.
“The second role model I looked up to was Chris Sementelli, my high school athletic trainer, who I not only got to observe during my time as a student at Erskine Academy but also when I returned as a student during a clinical rotation for my master’s degree.”
Wight’s other inspiration is his passion for sports of all kinds.
“Growing up, I was actively involved in numerous sports all the way through middle and high school including soccer, basketball, baseball, and track and field,” said Wight. “My family avidly watched all the New England pro sports teams including the Red Sox, Bruins, Celtics, and Patriots.”
In terms of credentials, Wight has a master’s degree, is board certified, is a licensed athletic trainer in the state of Maine, and is orthopedic physician extender certified.
“My official signature that I use is pretty long and contains a lot of the alphabet,” said Wight. “It is Christopher Wight MS LAT ATC OPE-C.”
Wight’s tenure at Medomak Valley has gotten off to a good start as the sports community – adjusts to the benefits and opportunities, as well as the protocols and requirements, involved with having a full-time athletic trainer continuously monitoring the well being of the athletes.
“Chris has brought a strong work ethic and desire to get to know our school, community and people,” said Lash. “There has been an adjustment period for everyone in our program, including student athletes and parents. Without a trainer, they have not been used to many of the procedures and expectations that come with having a person in that position. Chris has managed that well.”
Wight cherishes his work in the field of athletics, including seeing the patients from on-field injuries through rehabilitation and eventual return to play. He has been pleasantly surprised by how much he has enjoyed getting to know the Medomak student athletes as people instead of just patients.
“Being able to build relationships with the student athletes and getting to see them as they progress through their lives, succeeding not only athletically but academically and personally, has been very rewarding,” said Wight. “It is also pretty special to be with them from their lowest moments, such as a serious injury, through the rehabilitation process and then to see them step on that field or court again playing the sports they love.”
Wight said it is hard to pick a favorite moment during the Medomak fall sports season.
“If I had to choose one memory from my time at Medomak so far it would have to be the Class C quarterfinal volleyball game that we hosted,” said Wight. “The atmosphere was electric and to see the students leave it all on the court was very endearing to watch.”
There is one sport, according to Wight, that stands out as the busiest and most challenging for an athletic trainer to cover for Medomak Valley so far. “Football as a sport has so many moving components, so it presents unique challenges for athletic trainers when compared to other sports,” said Wight.
With one full sports season at Medomak now complete, Wight said he is looking forward to the upcoming winter season.
“I am most looking forward to being able to continue working with the athletes and building rapport with them,” said Wight. “It is rewarding that some of the athletes have said that it is nice to have an athletic trainer.”
When he is not working, Wight enjoys spending time with friends and family and pursuing hobbies including hiking, fishing, and camping.

title: Maine Turnpike Authority adds veterans-only parking at service plazas
text:
Maine Turnpike Authority adds veterans-only parking at service plazas
The Maine Turnpike Authority has added parking spaces reserved for veterans at all five of its service plazas and at its headquarters in Portland, just in time for Veterans Day.
Maine Turnpike Authority adds veterans-only parking at service plazas
The Maine Turnpike Authority has added parking spaces reserved for veterans at all five of its service plazas and at its headquarters in Portland, just in time for Veterans Day.
Officials unveiled the spaces and new signs on Tuesday at the Kennebunk Northbound Service Plaza. Executive Director Andre Briere attended with active-duty and veteran service members representing all branches of the U.S. military, along with members of American Legion posts in Kennebunk and Kennebunkport.
The Maine Turnpike Authority said its Veterans Group selected the design, which was created in-house.
The MTA also announced a partnership with SkillBridge, a program that gives eligible service members transitioning out of the military hands-on civilian work experience.
"MTA is proud to honor those who have served and to help build a future where their contributions continue to make an impact," officials with the MTA wrote in a Facebook post. "To all who have served, from all of us at the Maine Turnpike Authority: Thank you."

title: Police arrest son of actors Antonio Sabàto Jr., Virginia Madsen in fatal hit-and-run
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - Police in Alaska arrested a 32-year-old Anchorage man in connection with a deadly hit-and-run crash on Monday morning.
Crash details
Charging documents state that 32-year-old Jack Sabàto was driving a white Chevrolet Tahoe when he hit a pedestrian near the intersection of Airport Heights Drive and DeBarr Road at 5:35 a.m. Monday.
The pedestrian was identified as Carl Simmonds, according to charging documents.
Simmonds was the ninth pedestrian hit and killed by a vehicle in Anchorage this year.
Suspect’s family
Sabàto is the son of Antonio Sabàto Jr., a “General Hospital” actor, and Virginia Madsen, an actress known for her roles in movies like “Candyman,” “Sideways” and “A Prairie Home Companion.”
Madsen’s brother Michael Madsen was also an actor whose film credits included “Reservoir Dogs” and “Kill Bill: Volume 2.”
How police identified the vehicle
Police responded to the scene of Monday’s hit-and-run around 5:48 a.m.
Police recovered video of the collision from the Blood Bank of Alaska and were able to identify the car. They traced the vehicle registration to Sabàto’s home address, where a neighbor confirmed his place of work.
At 12:45 p.m., police located a Tahoe parked at the workplace that had “fresh damage to the right front corner that was consistent with a pedestrian strike,” according to the charging document. After obtaining a warrant, police seized the car.
Statement to police
At 2:46 p.m., Sabàto called police saying he hit an animal with his Tahoe and wanted to talk to officers, according to the charging documents. He told officers that he was on his way home after “doing late night Door Dashing” when he turned onto the road by the hospital. He said that “’something’ suddenly appeared in the road” and his headlights went out.
The charging documents state that Sabàto knew he hit “something” but didn’t want to check because he was scared that he did not have insurance. He also allegedly told police he called them because he “knew the worst.”
Charges and court
Sabàto was arrested and sent to the Anchorage Correctional Complex on charges of leaving the scene of an accident without assisting the injured and leaving the scene of an accident that resulted in injury or death.
Sabàto was arraigned in court Tuesday afternoon at the Anchorage Jail Courtroom.

title: POTENTIALLY UNNECESSARY REMINDERS
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Despite a deceptive stretch of temperatures in the high 60s, sunshine, and frostless cars in the morning, November marks a quickly impending winter and colder days ahead.
The change of the seasons is just clockwork to most Mainers. But The Lincoln County News has a few reporters from out of state, including one who never before saw leaves change colors and another who was forced to Google “heating oil.”
For their benefit, other newcomers, new adults whose parents aren’t in charge of these things any more, and folks who might forget with their autopilot habits, here are some important reminders for the upcoming chilly season.
Don’t forget hunter orange. A great gift for new Mainers, the otherwise un-vogue fluorescent shade will keep hikers and dog walkers (and dogs themselves!) safe during a waltz in the woods. This is perhaps the most important instance to endorse function over fashion.
Make sure to update the car inventory. Upon discovery of their from-away-ness by town officers and residents, LCN reporters are typically asked what car they drive, followed by recommendations for what they should keep in it. This list contains items like a shovel, scraper, flashlight, headlamp, first aid kit, extra jacket, extra socks, extra shoes, and hand warmers. The general sentiment expressed is “Stock your car like you’ll get stuck in it,” followed by a knock on wood.
And speaking of wood, no Mainer needs to be made more aware of record-high fuel prices this year. The Maine Department of Energy Resources surveyed the statewide average price of heating oil as $6.05 on Oct. 26, a record-high for the state. Locally, fuel assistance can be found through the Community Housing Improvement Project Inc. and the Community Energy Fund of Lincoln County, among other organizations.
For better or for worse – but favored by LCN reporters from sunny California and Florida – winter this year is forecasted to be warmer, but stormier, on account of the El Niño system brewing on the other coast. Alongside reincorporating your typical winter habits, perhaps preparing for the rainy season early may be useful, too. One LCN reporter needs to remember to buy rain boots for the first time in her life and stop forgetting umbrellas outside of cafes (she has proper rain and winter coats, at least).
Of course, winter isn’t all just chores and extra spending. There are also holiday discounts and nostalgic movies, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, family gatherings and town traditions, and, importantly, an appropriate temperature for a warm cup of coffee or soup. This is also a reminder that there are things to look forward to.

title: Maine Girls Should Use Their Voices, The Best Asset They Have
text:
Deciding what I wanted to say at a Girl Scout conference over the weekend made me think about what I wish I'd known early in my personal and professional journey.
In a World Where Women are Often Overlooked, Maine Women Need to Speak Up
On Saturday, I sat on a panel with two intelligent young women at the Transforming Leadership conference at the University of Maine in Orono.
We talked about how we got to where we are now, and how we overcame the personal challenges we faced.
For me, that was self-confidence.
READ MORE: Maine's Job Market Named 7th Best in the Nation
I was a painfully shy kid who often avoided personal interactions because I was afraid the other person wouldn't like me.
I never raised my hand in class, even when I knew the right answer.
Oh, if I could have known then how much richer my life would be with less self-doubt.
Maine Girls Can Grow Into Strong Women Who Can Do Anything
When I began working in radio, I had to grow into an extrovert who loved interacting with people and talking in front of crowds.
I found that people care about what I have to say, and that being wrong once in a while is just a new opportunity to learn.
Radio is a male-dominated field, and the 'girl announcers,' as we were known in my early days, were often quietly pushed to the side.
My advice to young women? Don't let this happen to you.
Maine Girls: Learn to Use Your Voice Because It's Your Best Asset
Speak up when you feel ignored and make them listen, because what you say matters.
Don't be afraid to say hello, answer a question in class, or share what you're thinking, because your opinion is as valid as everyone else's.
Fear will creep in, as it still does for me, and that's okay.
Speaking in front of a group of Girl Scouts was intimidating, and part of me wanted to run, but I'm glad I overcame those doubts and got to share some of what I've learned.
Don't let fear stop you from doing what you want in life.
Be confident, stand tall, and let the world see you.
Use your voice. It's the best asset you have.

title: WOMB TOMB: Cradle Casket: Community discussions on the bookends of life
text:
In June, the Vassalboro Grange hosted two presentations followed by community discussions covering the bookends of life: Birth & Death.
The first, held on June 11, took place on a very hot evening in the second floor hall. Four panelists introduced themselves and their involvement in the death space. The panel consisted of: a hospice nurse, an end-of-life conversationalist, a home funeral educator, and a board member from Kennebec Land Trust’s conservation cemetery, in Fayette, Baldwin Hill Cemetery.
Speakers covered topics from diagnosis to burial, and after introductions and some discussion, audience members came forward with questions. People wondered about ways to prepare for dying at home, resources Hospice offers, and what various alternatives to body disposition options (hint, there are many more than just burial and flame cremation!). Others asked about the logistics of preparing a deceased loved one’s body at home and organizing a home funeral. Another topic of discussion was green burials: what they are, how they differ from conventional burials, and requirements of a green or conservation cemetery. Audience members also asked about how to create a family cemetery on private land and what constitutes a ‘fence’ per the state of Maine law.
One of the panelists was Chuck Lakin, a Waterville native. Chuck has been teaching about green burials and home funerals for over 40 years. He got into this work after his father died, and shares his story with anyone who asks. “My dad died at home. Our family called the local funeral director and his body was promptly whisked away. About four days later we received a small box containing his ashes…I hated that.” Shaking his head, Chuck then goes on to describe his dad’s funeral. “After the service for dad, a bunch of his friends and relatives came over to our house. They brought food and drinks and started telling stories about Dad that I’d never heard before…soon as you know it we were all laughing and crying together. This went on for hours!” Chuck explains how the acute stage of the grieving process was able to take place in that communion setting. The sharing memories and food with loved ones served as incredible balm to fully integrate the loss of his father.
That experience began Chuck’s journey into learning about the history of the funeral industry, home funerals, and alternatives to flame cremation like green burial. Being a woodworker he also started building pine box coffins. “Eighty percent of caskets manufactured in the U.S. contain some type of metal,” Chuck explains. “A conventional burial is an embalmed body inside a metal coffin set in a concrete vault in a manicured cemetery. None of that keeps the body from deteriorating.” Green burial offers a solution in alignment with the natural way of things, where bodies and all they are buried with can fully decompose, without adding plastics or other pollutants to the ground.
The second discussion that month followed a book club and power point presentation given by Mount Desert resident Linda Orvell. After 23 years as a nurse midwife at the hospital in Bar Harbor, Linda decided to take a break. She was fed up with an increasingly surgical approach to birth happening before her eyes and decided to take a year ‘sabbitical’ to volunteer with MSF, or Doctors Without Borders.
Linda found herself placed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) after a decade of brutal civil war. MSF brings aid where other world welfare groups dare not go: places in the middle of, or recovering from serious – and in this case highly dangerous – crisis. During her time in the DRC, Linda was encouraged to write home each Sunday. Years later she expanded these written recordings into a book. Sunday Morning Shamwana recounts the daily rhythm of life, Linda’s personal trials and tribulations, and other incredible challenges and triumphs over the year as a volunteer midwife in the late 1980s.
“We were given the task of setting up medical clinics in small, remote villages after a decade of brutal civil war. Women there typically give birth at home. One way we incentivized women to come to our clinic to birth was by offering them a bar of soap to take home to their family.” She shakes her head, remembering. “It was completely silent when we first arrived. Villagers were camped out in the bush for ten years hunting and eating everything they could find. There wasn’t a single bird and hardly even crickets – rat stew was a delicacy. I remember the first songbird I heard after several months there!” As the refugees slowly came out of hiding more permanent structures were able to go up.
Linda showed photos of thatched roof buildings with smoke billowing out of them. “The first building to be built was a church. The second, a school.” The next photo showed a woman with smoke streaming up, off of her head, Linda laughs, finding the photo remarkable. “Repairing and rebuilding meant planting. No one maintained crops during the war. When villagers went to work in a field it’s not like they brought a sandwich for lunch! This woman is carrying hot coals [in a wrap on her head] to start a fire next to the field where she worked. That way they could cook what they found!” The audience met her with impressed laughter. She moves to another photo, of a bicycle leaning against a tree.
The women who came to the clinic for help were those who would have complications during pregnancy or labor. In this culture most women simply have their babies at home, often supported by a midwife. This bike was the available emergency transportation for mothers needing medical aid during labor. The pregnant mother in a semi-reclined position on the bicycle seat would be scooted along by her family members, walking next to the bike.
“Sometimes the journey would take days. If the mother died on the way they would bury her there, on the side of the road.” Life expectancy of these women was less than 40 years old with infant mortality so high we in the U.S. would hardly believe it. A mother might come to them pregnant for the seventh time yet having only two living children.
Fast forward to today, where all across Maine, hospitals are closing their maternity departments. “Maternal healthcare is a basic human right! I will never get off this soapbox. Study after study after STUDY proves that midwife-assisted births have better outcomes for mother AND baby than strictly obstetrical births.” The solution is simple: Train more midwives!” In 2016 she gave a TedX talk on this topic, sharing stories from her time in the DRC. Here in Maine our sole midwifery school recently closed. Now anyone wishing to become a midwife must seek out-of-state certification, creating significant obstacles. Undeterred, Linda continues to speak, present, and write on this topic, spreading her message with clarity and urgency.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Veterans tour Washington war memorials using AI glasses
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A group of veterans from across the country toured the nation’s war memorials in Washington on Tuesday, using special sets of AI glasses to help them find fallen service members.
The group was flown into the capital as part of an honor flight trip that was sponsored by Meta.
Many of the veterans that were on the three-day trip, were blind or visually impaired. And each of them were given a pair of the Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to help them navigate the war memorials that were built in their honor.
“We were able to work with the veterans, who are able to use their glasses to, even those who are blind or low vision... explain to them what they’re looking at, and tell them more information about the memorials,” said John Bockstanz, an Innovation Policy Manager at Meta, who is also an Iraq War veteran.
The glasses use built-in cameras, microphones and AI to perceive wearers’ surroundings then can describe them.
Victor Dunham, a Vietnam veteran from Texas, said he used the glasses to try to find out more about a friend named Anthony, or Tony as he knew him, who died while serving alongside him.
“I was trying to to locate him, and I kept coming up with a major that died on that day,” Dunham said. “Well, when I came here, I had an opportunity to use my Meta glasses and learn a little bit further, and we explored the possibility of trying to find this guy.”
The glasses helped Dunham find Anthony on the Vietnam Memorial wall.
“I didn’t know him well, but I felt like I did, and I was with him obviously, when he died,” Dunham said. “But I closed that loop today.”
Bockstanz said Meta has committed to donating 130,000 pairs of the glasses to visually impaired and blinded veterans across the nation.
“They’re already sharing how these AI glasses are transforming their daily lives,” he said. “Restoring their independence, helping them navigate busy airports, read menus at restaurants, or even matching clothing. And that’s why Meta is supporting our veterans. It is not just a single flight. It’s an ongoing, year-round commitment to giving back.”
Dunham said the the trip was incredible for him and his son Mark, an Iraq War veteran, who also came.
“This experience here has been wonderful for me, and I appreciate it beyond belief,” he said.
The trip was also moving for Bockstanz.
“It’s the most meaningful thing I’ve ever done at this company,” he said.

title: Candidate leading supervisor race two months after his death
text:
CALAVERAS COUNTY (KCRA) - Bruce Giudici, who died in August while campaigning for Calaveras County supervisor, is leading Clyde Clapp in the race for the District 5 seat as ballots continue to be counted.
Giudici died after falling on a steep driveway while campaigning. His name remained on the ballot, and his campaign continued.
“Our campaign team kept door knocking. We texted people,” said Carrie Biggs-Adams, a campaign volunteer.
Biggs-Adams said the decision to continue was complicated and emotional.
“We felt very strongly that Bruce had wanted to do this, and that was his mission. And our goal was to finish his mission,” she said.
What happens next
The campaign is confident Giudici will win, Biggs-Adams said, although more ballots remain to be counted.
“There are a few hundred ballots left to process, but it is unlikely that the outcome of the race will change,” she said.
Biggs-Adams said the governor’s office would appoint a replacement from people who volunteer to run. She thanked voters for their support and said the campaign would help ensure someone is selected.
District 5 includes Milton, Jenny Lind, Rancho Calaveras and Salt Spring Valley.

title: Maine Fire Chiefs’ Association president responds to Robbins Lumber investigation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LIBERTY, Maine (WABI) - Liberty Fire Chief Bill Gillespie, president of the Maine Fire Chiefs Association, said he views the state’s investigation of the Robbins Lumber response much like an after-action review: an opportunity to learn what could be done better.
The Maine Bureau of Labor Standards cited six area fire departments for lacking an effective firefighter tracking system during the response in May.
Tracking firefighters
Gillespie said Liberty Fire and Rescue, which was not part of the investigation, is looking at the same accountability program many other departments are adopting.
He said tracking responders at a scene like Searsmont would have been difficult no matter the system. According to the Fire Marshal’s Office, he said, nearly 300 firefighters from about 46 departments responded.
“With all the volunteer departments that were there, the accountability portion would have been a challenge from the beginning, just based on the fact that we had three fire trucks that were burning. And a lot of times the accountability tags are put on the side of the fire trucks to associate that they’re there with that company,” Gillespie said.
Support for volunteer departments
Gillespie said the Maine Fire Chiefs Association is working on legislative proposals to help volunteer departments.
Those efforts include funding for firefighter certifications and the construction of new training facilities across the state.

title: Supreme Court weighs whether government can fine farm without trial
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. Supreme Court is considering whether the Trump administration can fine a New Jersey farm, Sun Valley Orchards, over alleged poor working conditions for workers on visas - without holding a jury trial.
The court does not need to decide whether Sun Valley Orchards provided unsafe working conditions. Justices are determining whether the administration can fine the farm, citing immigration policy, without a jury trial.
The Trump administration says the workers are in the U.S. as part of an immigration work program and the Labor Department should have the authority to regulate it.
“Immigration. Everyone agrees that it includes admission and exclusion of aliens. I don’t think there is any way to conceive of that right that would not also include the fact that, once someone is admitted, they can also be removed, or ruled ineligible to remain based on conditions where the government prescribes,” said Sarah Harris, U.S. principal deputy solicitor general.
Justices appeared somewhat skeptical of the government claiming immigration authority on issues far removed from entering the country.
“Once you get past entry, you’re still faced with this broad array of requirements and conditions that make it look more like a condition of employment than entry,” Justice Neil Gorsuch said.
Some justices signaled the administration could run into problems imposing penalties on U.S. companies over alleged working conditions without allowing the matter to go to court.
“Let’s just posit for now, I agree that Sun Valley could be kicked out of the program. Out of the H-2A program, and I think we agree that the aliens could be removed pursuant to our tradition without an Article 3 court. But the fines, I’m wondering if they’re different,” Justice Amy Coney Barrett said.
Justices said the court has allowed the executive branch to operate outside the court system on certain matters of public interest in the past. They also pointed out that the goal of the visa policy is to keep companies from being able to undercut the domestic labor force.
“It’s a scheme that has nothing to do with contract rights. It’s a scheme that has to do with setting up minimum standards, and setting up a parity requirement in order to protect domestic workers,” Justice Elena Kagan said.
The Supreme Court is likely to release its decision by the end of June 2027.

title: Here's Why Maine Ranks Among the 5 Worst States for Drivers
text:
Here’s Why Maine Ranks Among the 5 Worst States for Drivers in The Nation
If you've ever driven down I95, sat behind someone doing 45 in the passing lane, or watched somebody try a three-point turn in the middle of an intersection, you might not be surprised by this one.
I feel like both of those things happened just last week for me.. But I may have been the one doing the 3 point turn because I forgot my airpods at home. Whoops.
But listen to this, Maine has officially ended up among the states with the worst drivers in America, according to a new LendingTree study. And before anyone gets defensive, we have the numbers to back it up.
Maine has now sadly ranked 5th worst in the country, with 42.3 driving incidents per 1,000 drivers.
Maine's Drivers Have Been Ranked for 2026
The study looked at accidents, DUIs, speeding-related incidents and other driving citations between January and August 2026.
This is what got me, Maine ranked 4th in the country for accidents, with 28 crashes per 1,000 drivers. Massachusetts came in third, which means our sweet and very friendly drivers next door aren't exactly helping our reputation either.
New Jersey took the unfortunate crown as the state with the worst drivers overall, while Michigan had the best driving record in the study.
Now, I'm not saying every Maine driver is bad. Some of us are super lovely and responsible people who use our blinkers and understand how rotaries work.
But, we all know that ONE person, who does treat there blinker like an accessory. And let's talk about winter driving. I know, right? We haven't even gotten through another Maine winter yet! But still, put that ONE person with ice, and snow and you've got an issue.
Read More: Christmas Car in Augusta, Maine Spreads Holiday Cheer
So, the next time somebody cuts you off, just remember: apparently, we've got a national reputation to maintain. Yikes.
What do you think, Maine? Are we really that bad behind the wheel, or is this study completely missing the mark?

title: Former NFL coach Rex Ryan accused of hitting 2 people with his truck, running over their feet, police say
text:
NASHVILLE (WSMV/Gray News) - Former NFL coach Rex Ryan is accused of running over the feet of two pedestrians while driving a pickup truck in Nashville.
Police said the 63-year-old former Jets coach was driving just before midnight last Thursday when he made a right turn and ran over the feet of two people crossing the street, according to a press release.
The pedestrians told police Ryan allegedly kept driving, but they caught up to him at a red light. After an argument, Ryan got out of his vehicle.
The pedestrians told police Ryan left without exchanging information, but they took a photo of his license plate.
Police issued a warrant for Ryan’s arrest.
He faces two counts each of leaving the scene of an accident, failing to provide information or render aid and failing to obey traffic signals.
Ryan’s bond was set at $6,000.

title: Man accused of raping three women in New York’s Central Park; video shows his arrest in Miami
text:
Man accused of raping three women in New York’s Central Park; video shows his arrest in Miami
A man accused of raping three women in New York’s Central Park over the span of five years has been arrested in Florida, police announced Tuesday.
Dereck Rivera-Deleon, 30, was taken into custody with the support of the U.S. Marshals while working at a Burger King in Miami, the New York Police Department said in a post on X.
He is accused of raping a woman in Central Park on Oct. 24, 2026, and will also be charged with two rapes that occurred in the popular park in 2023 and 2021, police said.
Video below shows New York City rape suspect being arrested in Miami:
DNA evidence and positive identification from victims connected Rivera-Deleon to the crimes, Miami Beach Police said in a news release. Detectives determined he had recently arrived in South Florida, police said.
DNA was recovered in the 2021 Central Park sexual assault, but it didn’t match anyone in the system at that time, and the attacker was unknown to the victim, according to NYPD sources.
No DNA was recovered in the 2023 assault, but the attacker and the victim had previously spoken, and the victim knew part of his name, the sources said.
DNA recovered in the latest attack matched DNA from the 2021 case, leading investigators to reexamine other sexual assaults in Central Park, including the 2023 case, the sources said.
The 2023 victim identified the man linked to the 2021 and October attacks as her attacker, NYPD sources said.
After that identification, special victims investigators enlisted the help of the Regional Fugitive Task Force to track down Rivera-Deleon, who appeared to move around frequently. Investigators learned he was in Miami Beach and tracked him to his job, according to NYPD sources.
Rivera-Deleon is being held in Miami-Dade County and is scheduled for an extradition hearing on Thursday, officials there said.
NYPD Crime Stoppers previously asked for help identifying the man following last month’s attack, saying he displayed a knife and sexually assaulted a 39-year-old woman before fleeing on foot. Rivera-Deleon allegedly forced the victim into a wooded area before assaulting her, Miami Beach police said.
This was the fifth reported rape in Central Park this year, according to the NYPD. Crime has been trending down overall in the city, but reported rapes increased 3.7% year to date, according to the NYPD.
The scenic park, popular among New Yorkers and tourists alike, was also the site of a homicide earlier this year: A 63-year-old woman was found dead with trauma to her head on the morning of Sept. 27. A 36-year-old man was arrested and charged with murder the following day, police said.

title: LIVE: Firefighters dig through rubble after NYC building collapse kills 1, traps people
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-story building in Brooklyn after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site Wednesday afternoon, killing at least two people and trapping others beneath the wreckage.
Scores of firefighters and police officers wielding pickaxes and power saws clambered over the rubble pile for hours, punching holes through the ruins to pull dust-covered people from beneath piles of twisted wood and brick.
At least 17 people were hospitalized with injuries, including four in critical condition, officials during a news conference. New York City Fire Department officials said their search and rescue operations would continue into the night. It was unclear whether people might still be trapped.
“This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. “This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for.”
The cause of the collapse was under investigation, but New York City’s buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, noted that when the building fell, construction workers were excavating an empty lot next door for a new building.
Much of the rubble from the collapsed building — a mixed-use structure with apartments sitting atop ground-floor commercial space — wound up in a huge pile inside the construction pit. Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.
About 250 firefighters were working the scene, Mamdani said.
At around 6:30 p.m., firefighters pulled a woman — still alive and moving — out of a hole they had dug into the rubble pile, hoisting her up on a stretcher and rushing to a waiting ambulance.
Additional people were pulled from beneath the pile as the night went on. Seven of the casualties were children, authorities said, without specifying whether any were among the dead.
A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked.
FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the rescue teams were performing “dangerous and perilous” work. “Every move is choreographed,” she said.
One firefighter sustained minor injuries, fire officials said.
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.
One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, told the New York Post he was at work when his wife called and said she and their two kids, ages 7 and 2, were trapped in the wreckage.
“She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her. She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off,” he said.
Velez said he later learned that his family had been pulled from the rubble alive.

title: Read the poem ‘Lemon Lemon’ by Hope St. John
text:
This week’s poem, by Hope St. John, gives a brightly refreshing take on the dual meanings of “lemon” — one being the kind you don’t want to experience buying a used automobile. I love this poem’s light touch, its zesty imagery and rhymes, and how it channels potential frustration into a kind of poetic lemonade (A “dicot” is the type of plant a lemon plant is considered to be).
Hope St. John is a previously unpublished college student from Bangor, currently studying business. Creative writing is an outlet for her personal pursuit of the humanities.
Poets, please note that submissions to Deep Water are open now and through the end of the year. Deep Water is especially eager to share poems by Black writers, writers of color, indigenous writers, LGBTQ+ writers, and other underrepresented voices. Submit your credits at mainewriters.org/deep-water.
Lemon Lemon
Sour fresh and bright
Lemon law or fruited tree
Watch the faulty lights
Growing upward, greater heights
Yellow yield for thee
Sour fresh and bright
Naïveté, the amateur’s plight
Used, like new! Buy from me
Watch the faulty lights
Juice and rind, zest and bite
Colors of balm and bee
Sour fresh and bright
Swindled for the higher price
Dicot, not of three
Soured and with blight
Watch the oversight.
Megan Grumbling is a poet and writer who lives in Portland. title: Susan Collins was not owed our votes
text:
Jody Telfair of Bristol has a Ph.D. in clinical counseling and has spent 45 years in private practice.
Sen. Susan Collins has served in the U.S. Senate for 30 years. When her constituents voted her out of office last week, one would expect her to give a gracious speech thanking Mainers for giving her the opportunity to serve them for 30 years. Instead, she gave an angry interview with the New York Times berating those constituents for being too angry.
So it’s all right for her to be angry at us, but we have no right to be angry at her?
Sen. Collins is showing her true colors in defeat. I witnessed a shocking level of control and entitlement back in the early 2000s when myself and three friends scheduled an appointment to meet with her. We were told by a staff person that we could only speak with her about two issues and asked to express no emotion.
Susan Collins does not engage with constituents except under very controlled circumstances. She has not held a town hall for at least 25 years. She seems to feel that she was entitled to reelection because she works hard and had brought money and various projects to Maine. But that is what she was elected to do.
Engaging with the people of Maine and listening to their concerns and issues, even when she disagrees, is also part of her job, and Collins failed at that aspect of serving the people of Maine.
Even though I am angry at Collins, I abhor attacks and threats on her or any other elected official. I voted for Troy Jackson, not because I am angry with Collins, but because his policies and values, such as universal healthcare, ending the war in Iran, standing up to Donald Trump and working to bring down prices for working people align with my own.
In her interview with the New York Times, Collins sounds like she feels betrayed. Well, many of us Mainers have felt betrayed by her for years — her vote for Brett Kavanaugh (and others) and taking no responsibility for the overturn of Roe v. Wade; the way she has fallen in line with Trump; voting to cut Medicaid and health subsidies in the so-called “big, beautiful bill” while giving huge tax benefits to the wealthy; voting for Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to lead the Department of Health and Human Services; Kristi Noem to head the Department of Homeland Security and Pam Bondi as attorney general.
And she has voted to support the war in Iran. In the debates with Jackson, Collins was unable to point out a single time she voted against Trump when her vote mattered. Finally, I was appalled at the elitist comment from one of her leading supporters, Bill Green, calling Jackson a “bumpkin.”
Sen. Collins seems to have forgotten in her 30-year run as a senator that she serves the
people of Maine at our pleasure. We owe her respect, but not our vote.

title: Mainers join Americans nationwide in rejecting Trump and Trumpism
text:
Like many observers, I thought Susan Collins would ultimately win her Senate race against Troy Jackson. I was wrong. Jackson won handily (by seven-plus points), joining the national blue wave, although “tsunami” is a better term.
I wish for her sake and Maine’s sake that Collins had not elected to run. By the same token, Joe Biden shouldn’t have run in 2024 against Donald Trump. Neither of them had anything left to prove in their political careers.
Try as she might, Collins couldn’t distance herself from Trump. She had voted with the Trump agenda 96% of the time. Moreover, she never crossed the president when it really mattered. She voted to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, which led to the defeat of Roe v. Wade. She often expressed “concern” about this or that issue, but she never demonstrated the courage of the legendary Maine Sen. Margaret Chase Smith.
In her famous “Declaration of Conscience” speech on the floor of the Senate in 1950, Smith said, “It is high time we all stopped being tools and victims of totalitarian techniques — techniques that, if continued here unchecked, will surely end what we have come to cherish as the American way of life.” Now that is courage; that is leadership. Sadly, Collins lacked the spine of her predecessor, preferring to tout her perfect voting record rather than risk Trump’s wrath. She ultimately paid the price.
Collins’ defeat was just one telling example of the lessons learned from the midterms which were, make no mistake, a referendum on Trump and Trumpism. Americans proclaimed in a bold loud voice, “Enough!”
Enough of Trump’s constant lies and bullying. Enough of this shameless grifter who uses the presidency as a way to enrich himself, his family and his wealthy cronies, rather than advance the common good. Enough of a president who would rather roll out the red carpet for Vladimir Putin and Russia than stand up for Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukraine.
As the returns poured in with victory after victory for the Democrats, it became clear that Americans had had enough of the “Only-white-Christian-men-need-apply” message conveyed by Trump’s testosterone-laced, faux Christian administrative team.
As reported in Robert Hubbell’s newsletter, “Democrats elected the following: a Latino governor in California (Xavier Becerra); the first Latino governor in Texas (Gina Hinojosa); the first Black governor and the first Black female governor in U.S. history (Keisha Lance Bottoms); the first Muslim senator in U.S. history (Abdul El-Sayed); the first Native American woman in the U.S. Senate (Peggy Flanagan); and the first out gay man to the U.S. Senate (Chris Pappas).”
The midterms converted Texas to blue, at least for the moment, with Sen. Ted Cruz, hardly a model of decency and restraint, as the only Republican left standing in the GOP delegation. Imagine a future where the Democrats start out with Texas’ 40 electoral college votes in their column.
Incidentally, James Talarico is an authentic Christian who doesn’t need to wear a cross around his neck to show his spiritual bona fides. Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist minister, became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas since 1932 and the Rev. Sarah Trone Garriott won her house race in Iowa. The midterms delivered the white Christian nationalist faction a stunning rebuke.
Some midterm lessons: Black Americans stood up against the Republican attempt to make it harder to vote. Latinos stood up against the outrageous racist attacks by masked ICE agents. Young voters landed squarely on the Democrats side of the ledger, convinced that geriatric politicians didn’t give a damn about the next generation.
Americans signaled that they’re tired of the meanness and bullying so prevalent among Trump and his enablers.
Elon Musk learned that his billions can’t touch hearts or buy votes.
Where does Congress go from here? That will be the topic of next week’s column. Meanwhile, fasten your seatbelts.

title: 4 costly health insurance mistakes to avoid when choosing a 2027 plan
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
4 costly health insurance mistakes to avoid when choosing a 2027 plan
From hidden costs to coverage gaps, avoid these health insurance mistakes in 2027.
4 costly health insurance mistakes to avoid when choosing a 2027 plan
From hidden costs to coverage gaps, avoid these health insurance mistakes in 2027.
Millions of Americans are about to pick their health insurance for 2027. Whether your coverage comes through an employer, the ACA Marketplace or Medicare, the choice involves more than comparing monthly prices. A few wrong assumptions could leave you paying more or without the coverage you expected.
Louise Norris, a health policy analyst who creates guides to help consumers navigate their coverage options, shares four things to consider before you enroll.
1. Check that your doctor is in the plan's network
Having the same insurance company doesn't guarantee your doctor takes the specific plan you're choosing.
"You shouldn't assume that just because your doctor was in-network with company XYZ when you had employer-sponsored coverage that they will be with individual market coverage, because they might not," Norris said.
This catches many people leaving job-based coverage, such as those retiring early or becoming self-employed. Employer networks can be broader, sometimes nationwide. Norris says there's often a learning curve, so check your doctors every year.
Look beyond the monthly premium, too. Compare the deductible, the out-of-pocket maximum and other coverage costs. Most people need some care, but not enough to hit their out-of-pocket maximum.
2. Account for changes to your household or income
Marketplace subsidies are tied to a benchmark plan in your area. When that plan's premium changes, so does your subsidy, so your net premium will almost certainly change for 2027. It could go up or down depending on where you live and your income.
Your own circumstances matter, too.
"Maybe you've had a kid who's aged off of your plan, and so now your household is smaller. That affects your subsidy amount. Maybe your income has changed or you're projecting an income change for 2027," Norris said. "All these factors will change how much you're paying."
Don't assume your plan will stay the same, even if you're happy with it. If it's being discontinued, the Marketplace may choose a replacement for you, but Norris says it's not in your best interest to rely on that. Comparison shop every year.
There is some good news. Despite the sticker shock many felt for 2026, most Marketplace enrollees still qualify for a subsidy that covers most of the premium. Some states also offer their own subsidies on top of the federal ones, which you get by applying through the Marketplace.
3. Don't assume you earn too much for financial help
ACA subsidy eligibility is based on a specific calculation of your household income called modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). Certain eligible contributions and deductions can lower that amount and potentially help you qualify for financial assistance, including:
- The self-employed health insurance deduction, for the portion you pay yourself
- Pre-tax retirement contributions, including traditional IRAs, solo 401(k)s and SEP IRAs
- Health savings account (HSA) contributions
All Bronze plans in the Marketplace are HSA-compatible. In 2027, someone with family coverage can put up to $9,000 into an HSA, which comes off their income dollar for dollar.
That matters most if you're just over the line. Subsidies generally end above 400% of the federal poverty level, and if you're far above it, there isn't much you can do. 
"A pre-tax retirement account or a health savings account will reduce your income, and depending on how old you are and where you live that could translate into thousands of dollars in subsidies that you get," Norris said.
But if you're close to the limit, ask a tax advisor whether those contributions could help you qualify.
HSAs aren't for everyone. Contributions can offer tax advantages, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free, but you need to be able to afford to fund the account. They're "certainly not a magic bullet," says Norris.
4. Get qualified help before you enroll
Whether you're researching an employer plan, an ACA Marketplace plan or Medicare, get help before you sign up. Navigators can explain terminology and how plans work. State-licensed insurance agents and brokers can compare and recommend plans, depending on their licensing and insurer appointments.
Their services are generally free to consumers, although brokers may receive commissions from insurance companies.
"You are not saving any money by not getting help," Norris said. "And getting help can be the thing that really helps you end up in a plan that better meets your needs."
Don't wait until the last minute, since help can get backed up as deadlines approach.
Questions to ask before you choose a plan
Before enrolling, bring these questions to an advisor, navigator, insurance broker or your employer's benefits team. The right questions can help you understand what you're paying for and avoid unexpected expenses.
For any plan
- Are my preferred doctors, specialists and hospital in the plan's network? How can I confirm that?
- Are my prescriptions covered, and at what cost?
- Beyond the premium, what will I pay in deductible, copays, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum?
- What happens if I need care out-of-network or out-of-state?
- What changed in this plan from last year?
For Employer-Sponsored Insurance Plans
- Of the plans my employer offers, which one provides the best overall value based on my healthcare needs and expected expenses?
- If I anticipate needing surgery, ongoing treatment or frequent prescriptions, which plan would leave me with the lowest overall costs?
- Would a high-deductible health plan paired with a Health Savings Account (HSA) make financial sense for me? Does my employer contribute to the account?
- If I'm covering a spouse or dependents, should I compare the cost of covering everyone under one plan versus having different coverage options?
For the ACA Marketplace
- How are my household size and expected 2027 income affecting my eligibility for subsidies?
- Could HSA or pre-tax retirement contributions lower my income and raise my subsidy?
- Am I eligible for premium tax credits or other financial assistance, and how much will I actually pay each month after those subsidies are applied?
- If my current insurer is leaving the Marketplace or my plan is being discontinued, what other plans are available to me?
- Are my current doctors, specialists and preferred hospitals in-network for the 2027 plan I'm considering?
- Are my prescription medications covered? If so, how much will I pay for them under this plan?
- What will my total financial exposure be if I have a major medical expense, including my deductible, coinsurance, and annual out-of-pocket maximum?
- Would a different metal-tier plan (Bronze, Silver or Gold) actually save me money based on my healthcare needs?
For Medicare
- Based on my healthcare needs and budget, would I be better off with Original Medicare and a Medigap policy, or Medicare Advantage?
- What will my total annual costs look like, including premiums, deductibles, copays, coinsurance and potential out-of-pocket expenses?
- Are my current doctors, specialists and preferred hospitals included in the Medicare Advantage plan's network? Can I access providers outside that network?
- Are my prescription medications covered, what will they cost, and which pharmacies can I use?
- If I choose Original Medicare, should I purchase a separate Part D prescription drug plan and Medigap coverage?
- What services require prior authorization or referrals, and are there restrictions on where I can receive care?
- Are there programs such as Extra Help or Medicare Savings Programs that could reduce my premiums, prescription costs or other expenses?
For your tax advisor before enrolling
- How will my estimated annual household income affect my eligibility for ACA premium tax credits?
- Which sources of income count when calculating my ACA Marketplace income, including bonuses, freelance income, investment income and retirement distributions?
- If my income changes during the year, how could that affect my subsidy, and what should I do to avoid owing money at tax time?
- Should I take my premium tax credit in advance to lower my monthly premiums or wait and claim it when I file my taxes?
- How does my tax filing status, including whether I file jointly or separately, affect my eligibility for subsidies?
- If I receive more premium tax credits than I'm ultimately eligible for, will I have to repay the difference when I file my federal tax return?
- Are there any tax implications if I switch from employer-sponsored insurance to an ACA Marketplace plan during the year?
- If I'm self-employed, are there additional tax deductions or considerations I should understand when choosing health coverage?
- If I contribute to a Health Savings Account (HSA), when should I stop contributing before enrolling in Medicare?
- If I delay Medicare because I have employer-sponsored coverage, are there any tax or enrollment consequences I should plan for?
Mark these dates
Marketplace open enrollment generally runs through mid-January in most states, but December 15 is the key deadline for coverage beginning January 1. Check your state's Marketplace for its specific deadlines.
Waiting can have financial consequences. If you select a new plan in January, an automatically renewed plan may already have started January 1, while your new selection generally won't take effect until February. That could mean paying toward two separate deductibles or out-of-pocket maximums in one calendar year because those accumulators generally reset when new coverage takes effect.
Medicare open enrollment runs October 15 through December 7.
Free resources to help you enroll
- Employer plans: Start with your HR or benefits department, which can walk you through your options and deadlines.
- ACA Marketplace: HealthCare.gov lists navigators, certified application counselors and licensed brokers near you through its Find Local Help tool at localhelp.healthcare.gov. The Marketplace Call Center, 1-800-318-2596, is open 24/7 and can also help you apply.
- Medicare: Your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) offers free one-on-one counseling from people who don't sell insurance. Find yours at shiphelp.org or call 1-877-839-2675. Medicare.gov has a free Plan Finder to compare plans by ZIP code and drugs, and 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) answers questions around the clock.
- Medicare Rights Center: This nonprofit runs a free helpline at 1-800-333-4114.
- Local help: Your Area Agency on Aging, reachable through eldercare.acl.gov or 1-800-677-1116, can connect you to benefits counseling.
