title: Jimmy Carter's family farm to be preserved and opened to the public
text:
Jimmy Carter's family farm to be preserved and opened to the public
The family farm where President Jimmy Carter tended peanuts, corn and sugarcane as a boy and later returned throughout his life will be preserved and opened to the public.
Related video above: A look back at the life of President Jimmy Carter
Preservation group The Conservation Fund said Monday that it has acquired the farm as part of a 2,458-acre purchase. The farm is just outside Plains, Georgia, the 39th president's hometown. Carter spent his youth exploring the woods around the farm and returned many times as an adult to walk with his wife Rosalynn and hunt, the fund said.
Near the end of his life, Carter, who died in 2024 at 100, returned to the farm for one final fishing trip to its pond. Rosalynn Carter died in 2023.
"For our family, this land was always about more than a farm. It was home — a place my grandparents treasured. We're grateful to The Conservation Fund and to everyone working to make sure it's protected for generations to come," Jason Carter, a grandson of the Carters, said in a statement.
The farm should be open to the public for hunting, fishing and outdoor recreation as soon as next year, The Conservation Fund said. The fund said it plans to transfer the land to the Georgia Department of Natural Resources the following year. The purchase price was $8.5 million, according to a report from The Washington Post.
The family kept a stand of mature longleaf pines at the farm at Carter's request, The Conservation Fund said. One of his final decisions about the property was to replant much of it with young longleaf pines, the fund said.
The replanting effort means the property is a natural fit to expand Georgia's Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area, which will grow to almost 7,000 acres, the fund said. The Plains area is also home to Jimmy Carter National Historical Park, which includes Carter's boyhood home.
"Long before Jimmy Carter protected millions of acres across America, he was a boy working the fields and roaming the woods of southwest Georgia," said Stacy Funderburke, vice president of the central Southeast region at The Conservation Fund. "This land shaped him and his legacy, and he never stopped coming home to it. We're honored to help ensure this land remains healthy habitat for wildlife, and we look forward to the day it is open to everyone who wants to experience it."

title: A Gorham school keeps evacuating due to gas leaks. How are officials planning to fix it?
text:
Gorham School District officials outlined a plan this week to investigate a series of recent gas leaks and gas odors detected at Narragansett Elementary School, and shared the precautions it is taking to protect students.
The investigation comes after the school closed for the third time in a year due to issues with its natural gas-fired heating system. Some leaks were detected late last year, followed by a cluster last month and gas odor last week that turned out not to be a leak.
At a meeting for families Monday, Superintendent Heather Perry, school facilities staff, Gorham Fire Department leaders, and representatives from mechanical contractor Johnson & Jordan, and natural gas provider Unitil, shared their next steps to tackle the issue and address parent concerns.
Since the three recent leaks resulted from gas regulator failures, staff are looking into whether some of those mechanisms are faulty, Perry said. While the district’s two other elementary schools have only about six regulators combined, Narragansett has more than 40 because of modular classrooms that were added as part of an expansion. As a result, there is more opportunity for error at Narragansett, she said.
The district will replace the regulators if it confirms they are the problem, at a cost of about $150,000. Perry said that money could be found in the current school budget, but that a more significant issue is time, since the installation would need to happen during a 10-day span with no students in the building.
Another idea, Perry said, is to add filters to new regulators to prevent particles from traveling through the natural gas pipes and cause them to vent gas outside. The leak in November 2025 was caused by a wood chip in the system.
If the school needs an entirely new heating system, it would likely cost several million dollars and require a ballot question asking voters to borrow money, Perry said.
Another long-term consideration is the potential consolidation of Narragansett Elementary School and Village Elementary School into a new building or expansion of another building. Perry said that move would likely happen in 15 to 20 years.
While staff look into the issue, the school will install six sensors to better monitor gas, and staff from Johnson & Jordan are conducting daily morning inspections to ensure it is safe.
Perry and Gorham Assistant Fire Chief Phil MacCallum emphasized that there is a large difference in risk from the point at which gas odor is detectable to when it poses a danger of explosion or harmful exposure.
“When we smell gas, we have a level of concern,” MacCallum said. “Very rarely when we smell gas do we have a level of risk.”
Principal Erin Eppler said students are now placing their coats on the backs of their chairs, rather than on hooks, so they can stay warm outside if they have to evacuate. Perry said the district is looking into alternative plans in the event school has to be canceled again, such as busing students to other elementary schools or sending them to neighboring St. Anne’s Catholic Church to continue learning.
Parents at the meeting Monday asked for more information about the health effects of natural gas exposure on children, and Perry said she would request research from the state.
Jane Suchecki, who has children in kindergarten and third grade at Narragansett, said after the meeting that she is concerned about how long some of potential solutions would take.
“We want to know that there’s resolution in sight, and that dependent on whatever the actual cause may be, that the district has laid out exactly the steps that they’ll take,” Suchecki said. “I don’t want to create habits where (my kids) ever have anxiety about school.”
Perry said she will send an update to parents every Thursday about where the district is in the investigation.
“We are doing everything possible and we are reacting to keep everybody safe,” Perry said. “That’s going to be our job every single time.”

title: Republicans, Democrats select leaders for new Congress
text:
Republicans, Democrats select next leaders for new Congress
Republicans and Democrats are choosing their party leaders ahead of the new Congress
Republicans, Democrats select next leaders for new Congress
Republicans and Democrats are choosing their party leaders ahead of the new Congress
Lawmakers on Capitol Hill are selecting their party leaders ahead of the new session of Congress. Those elected will help set the direction of their party's agendas for the next two years.
In a secret ballot vote Monday, House Republicans elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan as their new House minority leader, while South Dakota's Sen. John Thune will continue to lead Republicans as Senate Minority Leader.
Jordan will replace current House Speaker Mike Johnson, who elected to step aside when the new Congress convenes. Jordan will inherit a historically small Republican conference in the House following steep losses in the midterm elections.
But attention now turns to Democrats, where some members have voiced hope for a new generation of leadership, despite current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries expressing confidence that he will go on to become the next House speaker.
In the Senate, incoming Majority Leader Chuck Schumer is facing opposition from many progressives demanding change.
"I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer," Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, said in a news conference. "But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck."
Schumer responded to questions on his leadership.
"I'm confident I will be elected," he said to reporters. "We have great unity in our caucus, and I will be proud to lead it as our majority leader."
House Democrats are expected to hold their party elections next week, while Senate Democrats will make their leadership pick in early December.
The elections signal the potential policy priorities and directions in which each party is headed when the new Congress takes over, including possibly impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
On Monday, House Republicans successfully blocked an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. While the current vote to impeach Hegseth may be dead for now, many Democrats have signaled plans to try again when they take control of Congress in January.
If Democrats pursue impeachment, they will need a majority vote in the House to proceed. The process would then move to the Senate for a trial, requiring a two-thirds majority vote in the chamber to convict.

title: Tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee sentenced
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee was sentenced in San Francisco on Tuesday to 16 years to life to prison.
A jury in December 2024 found Nima Momeni guilty of second-degree murder, rejecting the defendant’s claim that he had acted in self-defense. He has remained in custody since his arrest nine days after the April 4, 2023, killing.
Before imposing the sentence, San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon rejected Momeni’s request for a new trial. His attorneys have said they plan to appeal.
Members of Lee’s family addressed the court on Tuesday, including his 18-year-old daughter, Scout Lee, who spoke directly to Momeni.
“You did not just end his life, you ended an entire future built around a man,” she told Momeni, according to media reports.
Momeni, wearing an orange jail jumpsuit, maintained that he acted in self-defense. He told Lee’s family that he understood their loss.
“Unfortunately, we have completely different understandings of what transpired,” Momeni said.
Lee, a renowned tech mogul, was found staggering on a deserted downtown street, dripping a trail of blood and calling for help. Lee, 43, later died at a hospital.
Prosecutors said Momeni planned the attack on Lee, driving him to an isolated spot under the Bay Bridge and stabbing him three times, including once to the heart, with a knife he took from his sister’s kitchen. They said Momeni was angry with Lee for introducing his younger sister to a drug dealer she says gave her GHB and other drugs and then sexually assaulted her.
But Momeni testified on the stand that Lee was the one who attacked him with a knife, angry after the tech consultant chided him about spending more time with his family instead of searching for a strip club that night. Momeni, who studies martial arts, said he didn’t realize he had fatally wounded Lee or that Lee was even hurt.
Lee had created mobile payment service Cash App and was the chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin when he died. He had recently moved to Miami from the San Francisco Bay Area, where his ex-wife Krista Lee lives with their two children, and had returned to California for a visit.
Jurors in the end rejected a charge of murder in the first degree, which required prosecutors prove that Momeni acted deliberately, willfully and with premeditation. Murder in the second degree does not require premeditation.

title: Irma P. Hall, ‘Soul Food’ and ‘The Ladykillers’ actor who found fame at 60, dies at 91
text:
(AP) - Irma P. Hall, the veteran actor who brought warmth and authority to matriarchal roles in “Soul Food” and “The Ladykillers,” and whose acting career took off after decades as a teacher, died Tuesday in Dallas. She was 91.
Her family announced her death Wednesday. No cause was given.
Hall was best known to many viewers as Big Mama, the family’s steadying force in the 1997 film “Soul Food.” The role earned her an NAACP Image Award and led to a return as the character in the television series based on the film.
She received a Cannes Film Festival Jury Prize for her performance as Marva Munson, a Bible-reading landlady opposite Tom Hanks in the Coen brothers’ 2004 comedy “The Ladykillers.” Hall also appeared in “A Family Thing,” “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil,” “Beloved,” “Patch Adams,” “Collateral” and Tyler Perry’s “Meet the Browns.”
Hall was 60 when “A Family Thing” brought her a major film role. She played Aunt T., a blind woman whose counsel helps guide two half brothers, played by James Earl Jones and Robert Duvall. The part drew attention to an actor who had spent years developing her craft onstage and in smaller screen roles.
“I was just concentrating on developing this craft,” Hall said in a 1996 interview with The Associated Press. “I guess you really never know where you are, you probably think you are on a lower rung than you really are.”
Hall had not set out to become an actor. Born Irma Dolores Player on June 3, 1935, in Beaumont, Texas, she was raised in Chicago and later returned to Texas for college. She taught English and foreign languages in Dallas public schools for more than two decades.
Her path to the screen began when actor and director Raymond St. Jacques heard her recite poetry in Dallas and cast her in his 1973 film “Book of Numbers.” Hall continued teaching as she took acting roles, then made performance her full-time work in the 1980s. She also helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre and remained involved in developing young artists.
Hall’s career included theater, television and film. Her credits ranged from the 1997 Clint Eastwood drama “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil” to the 1998 films “Beloved” and “Patch Adams.” She also voiced Great Aunt T. in the 2001 “Rugrats” Kwanzaa special.
In 2004, Hall was recovering from serious injuries suffered in a car crash, including open-heart surgery, a broken arm and a crushed ankle, when she traveled from a Chicago convalescent center to attend a private screening of “The Ladykillers.”
“I loved the whole thing,” she told The Associated Press. “You never really know until you see it on the screen.”
Hall said she had heard from Hanks and the Coen brothers while recuperating. They had signed her pillow, she said. “Whenever I miss them, I hug it.”
In Dallas, Hall was also a longtime member and Church Mother at Inspiring Body of Christ Church. Her family remembered her as a woman of faith who read to children at the church’s school and stayed active in its theater ministry.
“She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said in the family’s announcement.

title: 106-year-old WWII veteran reflects on his service and provides life advice
text:
106-year-old WWII veteran reflects on his service and provides life advice
At 106 years old, Ralph Conte has lived through history.
From the battlefields of World War II to taking photographs across the world, the South Carolina-based veteran has spent more than a century collecting stories and experiences.
Conte was drafted into the U.S. Army in 1942, serving with the 94th Infantry Division through 1945.
"Everything changes," he said. "You're kind of scared. 'Will I ever get home?'"
He landed on Utah Beach in France 95 days after D-Day. Just 10 days later, he was wounded by shrapnel while serving on the front lines.
"But they put me back on again," he said. "Just keep going."
In 1945, Conte said he and another soldier captured 18 German troops and helped secure a supply route for Allied forces.
His service earned him several honors, including the Purple Heart, Bronze Star and France's National Order of the Legion of Honor.
After the war, Conte turned his attention to another passion: photography.
He built a career as a photographer, traveling throughout Europe. He said his favorite place he visited was Italy.
"I would've loved to have gone back again," he said.
Now living in South Carolina, Conte says he's been surprised by the recognition and honors he's received later in life.
"The first 50 years of my life, nobody knew I existed," he said. "But once I moved to South Carolina, it was different. I've been honored so many times I just can't believe it."
When asked what advice he would give younger generations, Conte said to keep exploring.
"When you're young, you should go out. I didn't know there was so many things to see in this country. You always have to improve yourself."

title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state’s first Black US senator since Reconstruction
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any U.S. state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.
“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”
The Associated Press called the race in Colom’s favor after local officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch.
Hyde-Smith, 67, called Colom late Wednesday afternoon to concede and released a concession speech online shortly afterward.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society, and he repeated that pledge after his victory.
“My commitment to you, each and every one of you, is that first I’m going to treat your children like I want my children to be treated,” Colom said. “I’m going to treat your parents the way I want my parents to be treated. I’m gonna treat your future the way I want my future to be” and “work to make every Mississippian’s life better.”
National Democrats, activists and Mississippians celebrate
Party leaders hailed the senator-elect’s triumph, with nods to the South’s emerging status as a political battleground after other victories from North Carolina and South Carolina to Georgia and Texas.
“Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online.
Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won “because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back.”
Vera Finley was among those supporters.
“I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields,” Finley said ahead of Colom’s victory speech. “Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great-grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history.”
Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state’s voters, most notably Black voters, “made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out” in a state that has seen “some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights.”
A race Washington once viewed as a long shot
The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, finally drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia’s Raphael Warnock and Maryland’s Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see it as winnable.
The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom produced one of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October to rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited to enter. He introduced himself and asked about their concerns.
Later, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said only nine words in six seconds before stepping away: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”
Colom’s appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war that drove up gas prices and tariffs that caused headaches for Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state accustomed to long-serving, powerful senators.
There is some irony in Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
Colom called on Mississippi’s history
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist.
Colom told the story of Evers’ military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction. “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”
At the lectern Wednesday night, Colom said it was appropriate that the race be called on Veterans Day, as he again paid tribute to Evers.
“He served his country, came home to Mississippi, and they wouldn’t let him vote,” Colom said. “But he had faith that Mississippi could make progress.”
Despite Republicans’ domination, the path was always there
Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican discontent and an uptick in Democrats’ usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who’d also been Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of his candidacy but said he cares more about what it means for others.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”
__
Barrow reported from Atlanta and Washington.

Every day, thousands of Mainers are faced with the hardest choices: buy food or pay for a prescription; drive far for medical care or risk going without; toil to afford child care or stop working; go to a homeless shelter or sleep in a tent.
Across the state, many households fall either below the federal poverty line or just above that threshold, where people struggle to afford basic expenses, but don’t always qualify for assistance.

title: At least 1 dead and several others injured after 3-story NYC building collapses, officials say
text:
Death toll rises to 8 in Brooklyn building collapse as rescuers dig through rubble
At least eight people died after a three-story building in Brooklyn collapsed at the edge of a construction site, New York City’s mayor said Thursday, as emergency workers searched for others still trapped.
Search crews peered into crevices in the rubble, pulling out victims and at least one survivor through the overnight hours. At least 17 people were injured, including three firefighters, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. It's not clear how many more people might remain trapped.
The building gave way Wednesday afternoon while construction workers were digging at a neighboring lot, a city official said. The cause was still under investigation.
“We heard the boom and we all rushed outside and saw smoke and dust everywhere,” said Brigitte Anama, a hairstylist at a salon across the street.
Customers and stylists jumped up and ran onto the sidewalk that was engulfed in dust. Anama saw emergency workers pulling people from the site, including what appeared to be a child. “People were saying ‘Pray for the baby, pray for the baby,’” she said.
Video below: Pregnant woman rescued from Brooklyn building collapse
Two deaths were announced Wednesday and the others were confirmed Thursday. Authorities said late Wednesday that at least seven children were among the injured or dead.
“There are no words for a loss of this magnitude,” Mamdani posted on X. “My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.”
This was the second high-profile structural problem with a building in New York in the past five months. In July, several buildings in Manhattan were evacuated after support columns buckled inside a skyscraper that was formerly the headquarters of Pfizer.
Rescuers with dogs searched through the night
Flatbush Avenue, a busy thoroughfare in Brooklyn, remained at a standstill Thursday morning as firefighters picked through the rubble.
Hundreds of firefighters and police officers wielding pickaxes and power saws worked through the night, clambering over the rubble, punching holes in the ruins to pull out dust-covered survivors.
Rescue dogs sniffed piles of twisted wood and brick that were dotted with brightly colored clothing and vinyl record albums. Two excavators removed large chunks of debris. Firefighters filled buckets with debris, passing them down a line.
Heavy rain was forecast for Thursday afternoon, and Fire Department Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore cautioned that could hinder search-and-rescue operations.
“It'll turn to mud,” she told WNYW-TV, vowing firefighters would work through the rain if necessary.
Much of the collapsed building, comprising apartments sitting atop ground-floor commercial space, wound up in a huge pile inside the adjacent construction pit. Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with shoes and clothing.
On Wednesday night, firefighters pulled a pregnant woman from the rubble, hoisted her up on a stretcher and rushed her to a waiting ambulance. Other survivors were rescued as the night wore on.
Bonsignore said the rescue teams were performing “dangerous and perilous” work. “Every move is choreographed,” she said.
Man identifies his brother as one of those killed
Jose Luis Caguana, 26, who was working at the construction site, died in the collapse, his brother told WNBC-TV.
He was an immigrant from Ecuador who had been in the U.S. for about six years, Carlos Caguana said. He had a pregnant wife and a young child.
“Her husband has passed away; he was the sole provider for the family. Now that he’s gone, she is going through an immense amount of pain. She is in a very bad state right now — she’s completely overwhelmed and can’t even find the words to speak,” Caguana said.
The surrounding blocks are tightly packed with mostly older brick buildings and a few newly built apartment complexes. A mix of Caribbean and Mexican restaurants reflects the diversity of the neighborhood.
Novella Spence, who lives across the street, said the screams of her children woke her up from a nap as the building collapsed. They rushed to a window in time to see a wall crumple into the construction pit.
“It came down like boom, boom!” she said. “I was like ‘Oh my God. What happened. How could this happen?’”
City found violations at the construction site earlier this year
The city Department of Buildings is investigating the cause. New York City’s buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, said Wednesday that construction workers were excavating the empty lot next door when the building buckled.
The architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records have not responded to phone and email messages seeking comment.
City officials said a stop work order was issued in March after inspectors concluded the building next door was being demolished without adequate overhead protection such as netting to shield neighboring buildings, the department said in an emailed statement.
In April, inspectors found that the demolition work had resumed in violation of the stop work order, the department said. Work was allowed to continue in May after the problems were corrected, it said.
The project has active permits for excavation and foundation work.

title: Couple who disliked sex offenders arrested in man’s killing, police say
text:
BULLHEAD CITY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) — An Arizona couple who “expressed distaste” for sex offenders was arrested after a man they knew was found dead in the desert over the weekend, police said.
Jacob Dylan Middlebrook, 35, and Layne Justine McIntosh, 36, were arrested Saturday in the death of 29-year-old Arron Christopher Warren, according to the Bullhead City Police Department.
Body found along Silver Creek Road
Police said Warren, a registered Level 2 sex offender experiencing homelessness, was found stabbed to death in a desert area along Silver Creek Road, about a mile east of Bullhead Parkway.
Middlebrook and McIntosh, who were also experiencing homelessness, had known Warren for the past few months and disliked sex offenders, according to police.
The couple reportedly chose the desert location ahead of time and planned to leave Warren’s body there. Police said the couple also measured furniture along the side of the road that could be large enough to cover his body.
Arrests in Nevada
Hours after the body was discovered Saturday, Las Vegas Metropolitan Police officers found Warren’s stolen vehicle at a casino in Laughlin, just across the state line into Nevada.
Officers arrested Middlebrook and McIntosh. They were booked into the Clark County Detention Center in Las Vegas and are awaiting extradition to Mohave County.
Once they return to Arizona, they will likely face first-degree murder charges.
Police chief addresses sex offender notifications
Bullhead City Police Chief Paul George said in a written statement that the department shares information about Level 2 and Level 3 sex offenders as a public service when they move into the area or change addresses.
Required notifications are mailed to residents within about 1,000 feet of an offender’s registered address. The department also shares them on social media to reach a broader audience.
“Our goal is to provide information, not create fear or alarm. We believe an informed community is a safer community,” George said. “However, we want to be clear that we will not tolerate anyone using this information as a reason to threaten, intimidate, harass or harm another person.”
Police can decide when to release the addresses of Level 1 offenders, who are in the lowest risk classification. State law requires notifications about Level 2 and Level 3 offenders, who are classified as more likely to reoffend than Level 1 offenders.
George also said the department’s Bureau of Criminal Investigations conducts monthly address verification checks to make sure sex offenders are following registration requirements.

title: 11-month-old boy chokes to death on balloon while celebrating Halloween
text:
KENOSHA, Wis. (WISN) - An 11-month-old Wisconsin boy died after swallowing and choking on a balloon on the way home from a Halloween event. Now, his mother is sharing an important warning for parents.
Kisha Avitia-Wilson took her 11-month-old son, Don’vyaire Avitia-Mays, to an Oct. 24 trunk-or-treat event in Racine. On their drive home, she heard a loud sound coming from the back seat.
“Two of the balloons had just popped, and one of them had came undone,” Avitia-Wilson said.
Within seconds, Don’vyaire swallowed a piece of the balloon. His mother immediately pulled over, called police and then desperately tried to save him.
“I looked at him. He was blue. I tried to dig my fingers down his throat. I tried to do CPR. I tried to do everything that I could,” Avitia-Wilson said.
Kenosha Police say officers responded to the scene in minutes. Emergency crews tried to save Don’vyaire, but it was too late.
“I lost my baby boy in a matter of five seconds. There was nothing that I could have done to save his life,” said Avitia-Wilson through tears.
Avitia-Wilson, who was 31 weeks pregnant at the time, says the stress caused her to go into labor early.
“It was just very heavy on me, and I contracted that whole day, just trying to fight through it because I wanted to make it to my baby boy’s funeral,” she said.
She brought one son into the world on a Wednesday then buried a son on Friday.
Don’vyaire never made it to his first birthday. His mother wants to share her story as a warning for all parents.
“I just want all mothers to know balloons are dangerous. This can happen to anyone’s child, and I just want my son to make it the last child,” Avitia-Wilson said.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help support the family.

title: Cheverus softball star Addison DeRoche signs with Florida State
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
PORTLAND — Addison DeRoche signed the paper on the table, stood in front of a room full of supporters — family, friends and coaches, many clad in garnet and gold — and raised both fists.
“Go ‘Noles!” she said.
DeRoche, the standout pitcher for the Cheverus softball team, officially made Maine history by signing with Florida State on Wednesday, becoming the state’s first player to join an NCAA Division I power conference school.
DeRoche committed to Florida State in the fall, but said her future of playing big-time softball “got way more real” with the signing, which she and her family celebrated with a gathering at Bruno’s Restaurant and Tavern.
“I really have dreamed of this moment forever, ever since I was a little girl,” the Cheverus senior and Westbrook resident said. “Just sitting at home watching TV, determined to be there one day. … I’m overwhelmingly grateful.”
The room was decorated with Florida State colors, and one wall had jerseys from the four teams DeRoche has played for: New England Elite, Rhode Island Thunder, Mojo and finally Cheverus, where she’s played three years, won three Gatorade and Varsity Maine Player of the Year awards, and become the nation’s No. 5 ranked recruit in the Class of 2027 while compiling 647 strikeouts in 272 innings with a 0.26 ERA.
John Eisenhart, who coached DeRoche at Cheverus all three years before stepping down after taking a new job, was on hand for the celebration.
“It’s so great to see all of her hard work come to fruition and pay off,” he said. “She’s so talented and driven. We all knew this day would come. … I’m so excited to see what she’s going to do in the future.”
DeRoche, the 2025-26 Varsity Maine Female Athlete of the Year, has been on the fast track for the upper reaches of Division I since her freshman year at Cheverus, when she led the Stags to the Class A title while playing a busy national schedule of showcases and tournaments with her Mojo team.
Those busy days haven’t eased up: She played in Illinois, California and Georgia earlier this fall, and is turning around Thursday to play in Clearwater, Florida, before heading to El Salvador for the Pan-American Games.
During one of the few opportunities DeRoche has had to sit still, all the focus was still on where she’ll be going — a place where she’s wanted to play well before making her plans official.
“I think I always pictured myself in the garnet and gold,” she said. “When I was growing up (the Seminoles) were like a dynasty, they were there every year. (I’m excited) to be there and compete at the highest level.”
And a level no Maine player has reached.
“This is my opportunity and I get to share it with everybody else,” she said. “They can follow my lead as well. It’s pretty awesome.”
NEW LEADER ON BOARD
DeRoche’s signing capped a busy few days for the defending state champion Stags. Cheverus also announced the hiring of Grace McGouldrick, who will take over for Eisenhart as the head softball coach.
McGouldrick, 26, was the Miss Maine Softball winner at Gorham in 2018 before going on to play at the University of Maine. But even during her playing days, she knew coaching would eventually be her calling.
“I just really enjoyed doing all those Little League clinics with our high school team, so I kind of figured out at that point that I was really into coaching and helping out the younger kids,” she said. “To help them find the love for it that I still have is No. 1. … I love seeing an individual or an entire team have a light bulb (go off) and really go and execute something.”
McGouldrick, who has coached travel teams from 10U to 18U at the Edge Academy for the past 2 1/2 years, said the Stags, who have reached the regional final each of the past three seasons and won two state championships, are a match for her approach to the sport.
“They take it really seriously, which I really appreciate. I’m a very naturally competitive person, so I appreciate when the teams that I coach align with me in that way,” she said. “At the end of the day it’s a game. It’s fun. … But I want to go win, and I know the girls want to go win.”
McGouldrick will inherit a team that brings back emerging standouts in Cameron Gagnon, Abby Kelly, Maddie Brow and Temperance Lovejoy, but the key piece is DeRoche, who alone will make the Stags favorites again.
“It’s been so fun to listen to all the younger girls go and talk about how awesome it is to have someone show that just because you’re from Maine, it doesn’t mean you can’t go to high places,” McGouldrick said. “She’s brought so much more light to the game of softball in the state of Maine.”
DeRoche said she was “heartbroken” to hear about Eisenhart’s departure, but said she’s eager to play for McGouldrick, whom she’s come to know during practice sessions at the Edge Academy.
“She’s a role model,” DeRoche said. “She’s going to be really fun to play for. … I’m really excited to take the field.”

title: Supreme Court weighs whether government can fine farm without trial
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. Supreme Court is considering whether the Trump administration can fine a New Jersey farm, Sun Valley Orchards, over alleged poor working conditions for workers on visas - without holding a jury trial.
The court does not need to decide whether Sun Valley Orchards provided unsafe working conditions. Justices are determining whether the administration can fine the farm, citing immigration policy, without a jury trial.
The Trump administration says the workers are in the U.S. as part of an immigration work program and the Labor Department should have the authority to regulate it.
“Immigration. Everyone agrees that it includes admission and exclusion of aliens. I don’t think there is any way to conceive of that right that would not also include the fact that, once someone is admitted, they can also be removed, or ruled ineligible to remain based on conditions where the government prescribes,” said Sarah Harris, U.S. principal deputy solicitor general.
Justices appeared somewhat skeptical of the government claiming immigration authority on issues far removed from entering the country.
“Once you get past entry, you’re still faced with this broad array of requirements and conditions that make it look more like a condition of employment than entry,” Justice Neil Gorsuch said.
Some justices signaled the administration could run into problems imposing penalties on U.S. companies over alleged working conditions without allowing the matter to go to court.
“Let’s just posit for now, I agree that Sun Valley could be kicked out of the program. Out of the H-2A program, and I think we agree that the aliens could be removed pursuant to our tradition without an Article 3 court. But the fines, I’m wondering if they’re different,” Justice Amy Coney Barrett said.
Justices said the court has allowed the executive branch to operate outside the court system on certain matters of public interest in the past. They also pointed out that the goal of the visa policy is to keep companies from being able to undercut the domestic labor force.
“It’s a scheme that has nothing to do with contract rights. It’s a scheme that has to do with setting up minimum standards, and setting up a parity requirement in order to protect domestic workers,” Justice Elena Kagan said.
The Supreme Court is likely to release its decision by the end of June 2027.

title: Waterville holds Veterans Day parade, ceremony
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) -Waterville honored veterans Wednesday morning with a parade and ceremony recognizing those who have served.
Parade route
The parade began at Head of Falls Park and circled downtown. Community groups, local law enforcement and residents took part.
Waterville Boy and Girl Scouts marched in the parade. Scouts from Troop 445, Lorelei, Jude and Reese, said marching for veterans made them happy.
“Veterans work hard, so it’s okay to celebrate them,” Jude said.
“We have to celebrate them so that they know we support them for Veterans Day,” Reese said.
“I think it’s very important to be celebrated,” Lorelei said.
“I just want to honor everybody that has ever, and I mean ever, served in the military,” said Fox, of Troop 433.
“I like to honor the people who serve in our country, those living and dead, and thank them for protecting our country,” said Freddie, of Troop 433.
Ceremony at Castonguay Square
The parade ended at Castonguay Square, where Waterville Legion Post Commander Craig Bailey hosted a ceremony. The ceremony included the national anthem, a prayer and moments of silence.
“Each time new people put on the uniform, they carry on the legacy of the professionalism, the integrity, and the means to which we go around the world, with good or bad, to help spread that freedom,” Bailey said.

title: Searsmont EMS chief to be released from hospital next week
text:
SEARSMONT, Maine (WABI) - A first responder severely injured in the Searsmont fire and explosion is being released from the hospital next week.
A welcome home celebration is being planned for Searsmont EMS Chief Sarah Tompkins. Tompkins will come home Wednesday, Nov. 18, according to a post on the Town of Searsmont’s Facebook page.
An escort will start in Augusta and end with a Welcome Home Gathering at the Searsmont Fire/Rescue Station. Times have yet to be announced.
The town’s post invited community members, friends and fellow first responders to attend.

title: Handwritten note leads Florida police to children hiding inside home
text:
Handwritten note leads Florida police to children hiding inside home
A handwritten note reading "HELP US" helped Kissimmee police find children hiding inside a home during a domestic disturbance.
Kissimmee Police Department officers responded to a domestic disturbance involving Andre Janard Smithson on Oct. 26.
Family members told police that children were inside the residence and feared for their safety.
Related video above: Racine gold scam suspects among 10 indicted in federal case
Officers used a drone to search the home and located the children hiding in a room.
During the search, one child held a handwritten note against a window that read "HELP US," according to Kissimmee police.
Police said the children safely left the residence while Smithson was distracted.
Smithson eventually surrendered peacefully, police said.
Kissimmee police said he is facing charges of false imprisonment and an outstanding active warrant.

title: Ted Turner's son says his Western art collection reflects the media mogul's passion for 'big'
text:
BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — Ted Turner didn’t do small.
Whether racing sailboats, building CNN into a global news organization or buying up ranches across the U.S. West to become one of the largest landowners in the nation, the media mogul turned conservationist had a passion for big, his son, Teddy Turner, said in an interview.
And so it was with the art lining the log walls of Turner’s sprawling Flying D Ranch in south central Montana: Paintings by American masters Thomas Moran and Albert Bierstadt capture the grandeur and beauty of the early Western landscape when it was still largely untouched by European settlers.
Over Turner’s imposing stone fireplace was a painting of Yosemite Valley. Elsewhere in his home were images of the Grand Canyon, Oregon’s Mount Jefferson and a Bierstadt work titled “Buffalo at Sunset,” depicting a group of bison near a pool of water that reflects a glaring sun.
Turner died in May and a collection of the paintings from his Montana ranch are due to be auctioned on Jan. 20 by Christie’s in New York. The proceeds will go to the Turner Foundation to further its work preserving natural habitats across large landscapes and helping restore species like the bison that graze on the 178-square-mile (460-square-kilometer) Montana ranch.
What Turner saw in the pieces being auctioned, his son said, was perfection — versions of a bygone West not yet marred by human industry. Turner had similar aspirations for his ranch, where he sought to turn back the clock to an era when bison roamed freely and in immense herds that were hounded by packs of wild wolves.
Turner’s son described him as a person of action — not one to “just sit around staring at his paintings.”
“He loved a professional and if he didn’t deem you an expert, he had no time for you,” Teddy Turner said. “Everything that he wanted to surround himself with was perfection. And he saw perfection in these paintings.”
Ted Turner was born in Cincinnati and made his fortune in cities including Atlanta, where he founded CNN. But the West captivated him, and in the 1980s, Turner started buying up properties in Montana and elsewhere, Teddy Turner said. He restored the sites including with bison herds that now number some 45,000 across his properties, according to Ted Turner Enterprises, which manages his holdings.
Teddy Turner said he would have liked to continue looking at the art for the rest of his life “but that was not his plan.”
“They were always in the great rooms, in the center of our lives for so long,” Teddy Turner said. “So they will definitely be sorely missed. It’s hard to replace a Bierstadt over the mantel. I think maybe some Pulp Fiction posters? Probably not going to get it done.”

title: Hampden Planning Board approves wastewater system expansion at Pine Tree Landfill
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - The Hampden Planning Board voted Tuesday night to approve a request to expand a wastewater management system at the Pine Tree Landfill.
Request tied to Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion
New England Waste Systems of Maine, a subsidiary of Casella Waste Management, made the request as part of a broader effort to expand the state-owned Juniper Ridge Landfill in West Old Town.
State conditions required the company to have a licensed, operating system to treat PFAS before that expansion could move forward. PFAS are often called “forever chemicals” because they break down very slowly.
Before the vote, a representative walked the Planning Board and city residents through what the proposed expansion would look like and how it would be effective.
Residents raise concerns
The decision to move forward drew concerns from a few local residents about landfill runoff.
“We’re concerned because the technologies they’re proposing, though they haven’t put in the full proposal, to remove, separate the PFAS is foam fractionation, which is not the best method. It cannot get rid of the dominant PFAS, which is short-chain PFAS. And as we know, PFAS causes cancer, teratogenic effects, effects on livers and kidneys,” environmentalist Grace Nichols said.
Hampden Director of Planning and Economic Development Amy Ryder gave an idea of what next steps would look like for the plan.
“There’s approval with conditions,” she said. “Of course, we want approval from Bangor Wastewater to make sure that they can carry this and are on board, as well as make sure they get the appropriate DEP permits. Once those are accomplished, then they will be approved to do the expansion.”
Leachate transfer
With the growth of the leachate storage tank, the amount of leachate being carried will increase as it is transferred through the Hermon sewer system to Bangor Waste Systems.

title: Mount Desert discusses recording all committee meetings
text:
MOUNT DESERT — In a special meeting Monday night, the Selectboard and members of the Warrant Committee discussed whether all committee meetings should be recorded and posted online.
The meeting was scheduled because of a request for all Warrant Committee meetings to be recorded.
Town Manager Alex Kimball opened the discussion by explaining this was not a legal conversation, and the town is in accordance with Maine law.
Harbor Committee, Planning Board and Selectboard meetings are recorded and uploaded to the town’s YouTube channel. Kimball said that the other town committees and boards are recorded “as best as we can.”
“We try to record them, we try to get them broadcast, but it quite frankly doesn’t always work.”
Kimball cited technical challenges and the need for a member of town staff to run the Zoom meeting as reasons some don’t get recorded. However, minutes are provided for all meetings.
The town’s Warrant and Sustainability committees do not currently record their meetings, but do provide minutes and allow members of the public to attend virtually.
The Warrant Committee is an advisory group, meaning they don’t vote to make final decisions. Its job is to review articles that will appear on the town meeting warrant and give a recommendation.
Selectboard Chair John Macauley opened the discussion, sharing his support for more accessibility. “My personal opinion is that anything we can do to inform the public about what the issues are is a positive for me,” said Macauley.
Member of the Selectboard David MacDonald brought up the concern of seasonal residents who may want to attend remotely. “I’m mindful that although they’re not voting residents of the town, we have a big summer community that pays a lot of taxes and is not here,” said MacDonald. “So having them able to understand what’s going on week to week, just in the name of open lines of communication, I support that.
“But I do want to hear from people who serve on these committees to understand if making a change would affect the quality of the discussion, the quality of the decisions, your participation, I’m all ears on that.”
“I feel like ‘as best we can’ does cover a lot,” responded Selectboard member Wendy Littlefield. “We do the best we can with the technology we have.”
Kimball noted that meeting recordings uploaded to the town’s YouTube channel receive positive engagement. “Slowly but surely more and more people watch the rebroadcasting,” said Kimball.
Kimball read a statement from resident Gail Marshall, who pushed back against virtual attendance replacing participating in person meetings.
Marshall serves on the MDES board, Planning Board, Comprehensive Plan Committee, Board of Assessment Review and is chair of the LUZO Advisory Group.
“In our very small town, we rely on people who volunteer to become informed about how we get things done for one another and at times take on personal responsibility to help our town succeed,” read a portion of the statement. “There is no virtual substitute to being present. As citizens, we owe one another more than just dialing in.”
Jerry Miller, a member of the Warrant Committee, shared his support for recording their meetings. He said he was glad to hear that people watch recorded meetings once they are uploaded. “And if people are seeing it that way, they’re at least seeing it.”
Warrant Committee Chair Phil Lichtenstein also attended the meeting and shared reservations about recording their meetings.
“We are an advisory committee. We also are the scrutinizers of all five of you and your decisions, and I think that’s where I sort of have my own personal concerns,” said Lichtenstein. “I’ve let my feelings be known that I don’t want to inhibit any member of the Warrant Committee to not speak up and speak their mind.”
He added that he will take what the Selectboard decides to the group and take it under advisement.
Another member of the Warrant Committee spoke and didn’t think recording their meetings would make a difference, although he stated other committee members have voiced their discomfort with being recorded.
Resident Lincoln Millstein brought up the initial request that the Warrant Committee record and upload every meeting. Millstein attended the meeting on Monday and emphasized his stance that the Warrant Committee should record its meetings.
The Warrant Committee does provide minutes for each meeting, and Millstein raised the concern that minutes are sometimes posted months after the meetings took place.
The most recently posted minutes for the Warrant Committee are from its March 10 meeting. They have had two meetings since then that do not yet have published minutes.
According to Section 1.1.2.2 of the town charter, the Warrant Committee “Shall choose its own officers and rules of procedure.” The Selectboard can recommend that the Warrant Committee record its meetings, but the committee can decide how they want to proceed.
At the end of the discussion, Macauley recommended the Warrant Committee record its meetings and suggested they discuss the issue at their next meeting, Jan. 5, 2027.

title: Would Biden have sought a second term if he’d known he had cancer? Here’s what he says
text:
(AP) - ATLANTA (AP) — Joe Biden says he did not know he had cancer while he was president and would not have sought a second term if he already had been diagnosed.
The former Democratic president’s comments came in an interview with People magazine before the release of his White House memoir on Tuesday.
“If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer,” said Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, “I would’ve not gone forward” with a 2024 reelection bid that ended after a disastrous debate performance against Republican Donald Trump.
Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025.
“I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running” for president, Biden said in the interview.
Still, he argued that the June 2024 debate, less than five months before Election Day, was not a seismic event even if it accelerated Democrats’ concerns about his age — he was 81 at the time — and his ability to defeat Trump.
“First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t,” Biden said. “But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”
Within weeks, Biden announced he was ending his campaign and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, who secured the nomination and lost to Trump in the general election.
Biden insisted he was able to perform his duties while he was in office. He said age itself was not disqualifying and meant he had experience and deep personal relationships with world leaders.
“I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job,” he said.
His son Hunter told the BBC in August that the cancer had spread and was causing his father pain. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects,” he said.
Since Joe Biden left office, his son has become a higher profile public presence, sparring with Republicans on social media, posting lengthy thoughts on the nation’s direction and launching his own cryptocurrency.
Joe Biden defended his son’s public persona and his decision to pardon Hunter Biden after the younger Biden’s 2024 conviction on federal felony gun charges and his guilty plea to federal tax charges. Hunter Biden also had faced years of scrutiny and withering Republican attacks over his international business dealings.
Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father’s legacy, but the former president said Trump’s penchant for vengeance made it necessary.
“He goes after people without any basis, whether they’re viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do,” Joe Biden said. “If I hadn’t pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who’s dealt with me — he would go back and try to do harm to them.”
Biden called his son “one of the brightest men I know,” adding, “I’m really proud of him.”

title: Guard reprimands group with Hegseth at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier after laughter was heard
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.
Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that “all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s top spokesman, said that “while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”
“The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” he added.
The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from World War I, World War II and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army’s 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as “The Old Guard,” since 1948.
Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that also was attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.
The effort was led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth’s critics were not successful in Tuesday’s vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach the defense secretary. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.
A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes.
“On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime,” Hegseth said Tuesday.
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth argued. “This is sabotage.”
Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.
Rep. Gwen Moore, D-Wis., said Hegseth demonstrated “his utter lack of fitness for his office.”
“One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier,” she wrote in a social media post.
It was not the first time members of Trump’s team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.
During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honor U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.
Trump, who had been invited by troops’ families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the “disaster” of the Afghanistan withdrawal.
U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

title: Flesh-eating New World screwworm making a comeback in states surrounding Oklahoma
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
New World screwworm surges in states surrounding Oklahoma, threatening livestock again
A parasite once eradicated from the U.S. is now making a comeback.
The New World screwworm has been detected in more than 120 animals since June, with November already seeing the highest number of cases yet. Those are numbers the U.S. hasn't seen in four decades, and the cases are in states surrounding Oklahoma. 
As of Tuesday, there are no confirmed cases of screwworm in Oklahoma. While the colder temperatures may keep the flies away, experts said the biggest concern is the parasite hitching a ride in.
"The last time we had case numbers anywhere near where we're at right now in the United States as a whole was in 1979," said Dr. Jonathan Cammack, the state extension specialist with Oklahoma State University.
The tiny fly is posing a big threat to America's livestock. New World screwworm cases are surging in states surrounding Oklahoma.
"Really, our concern is livestock," said Cammack.
The flesh-eating parasite lays its eggs in open wounds, where the larvae feed on an animal's living tissue. Cases have been reported in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona.
So, could it spread further?
Experts at Oklahoma State University told sister station KOCO 5 that cooler temperatures are working in Oklahoma's favor, but there's another way the parasite could cross state lines.
"These flies can generally only fly 6 to 10 miles in the course of their life, but we can put cows in a trailer and drive them 600 miles in a day," said Cammack.
Decades ago, the USDA fought back against the parasite by releasing sterile flies to stop reproduction and eventually pushing the parasite out of the U.S. and Central America.
But in 2022, experts said the screwworm reappeared. They still don't know exactly what went wrong.
"Something happened. We don't know if it was an illegal movement of livestock through or outside of that barrier zone, and then we've got cases 10 or 100 miles away from where we need to be looking," said Cammack.
According to the USDA, cattle and sheep make up the majority of animals infested. More information about screwworms can be found on Oklahoma State's website.

title: Jay begins solar rule review after voters approve 6-month moratorium
text:
JAY — The planning board will begin reviewing the town’s solar regulations next week following voter approval of a six-month moratorium.
The review comes as state environmental regulators outlined protections already required for large solar projects and identified issues left to municipalities.
The Select Board voted Nov. 9 to assign the planning board responsibility for reviewing the issues outlined in the moratorium petition, Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere confirmed in a follow-up email. The planning board will meet Nov. 17 at 6 p.m. at the Town Office to begin the process.
Any proposed ordinance changes could go before voters at the April town meeting.
Voters approved the 180-day moratorium Nov. 3 by a vote of 1,464-723, temporarily restricting new commercial ground-mounted solar development while the town reviews its regulations. The measure comes as Portland-based Walden Renewables pursues Alden Mill Solar, a proposed 150-megawatt project involving about 900 acres of solar panels at multiple locations in Jay.
Before discussing the moratorium, the Select Board held a workshop with Jessica Damon, director of the Maine Department of Environmental Protection’s land licensing division, to examine which protections already fall under state oversight and which might require additional municipal regulations.
Damon confirmed that Walden has not submitted a formal permit application to the DEP, although the agency has held a pre-application meeting with the developer.
“We don’t have a pending application,” Damon said. “They haven’t submitted an application to us.”
She explained that a project subject to Maine’s Site Location of Development Law can take up to 180 days to review after an application is accepted as complete.
Damon described DEP’s oversight of wetlands, wildlife habitats, water resources, stormwater runoff, scenic impacts and other environmental considerations. Large developments must also meet erosion-control requirements and use independent construction inspectors who submit weekly reports identifying potential problems.
However, some concerns raised during the workshop fall outside DEP’s jurisdiction.
“We do not look at traffic,” Damon said when questioned about construction vehicles and local roads.
The agency also does not establish specific residential property-line setbacks for solar installations, although it evaluates visual impacts and may require vegetative screening.
A resident questioned whether those protections would be adequate for neighborhoods near proposed solar sites, citing existing smaller solar developments and the possibility of panels being placed close to homes.
“We need actual firm rules about setbacks,” the resident said.
Damon explained that developers are often required to modify projects during environmental review to reduce impacts on neighboring properties and natural resources.
“Most things that come in don’t go out like they were proposed,” Damon said.
Another resident questioned how clearing wooded hillsides could affect stormwater runoff, wells and aquifers. He also challenged whether removing solar equipment decades from now could truly restore land where mature trees had been cut.
Damon said DEP engineers review stormwater plans and developers must address problems identified during construction. Maine’s solar decommissioning law requires solar arrays occupying 3 acres or more to have approved decommissioning plans and financial assurances covering removal and restoration costs.
Those financial assurances must be reassessed after 15 years and at least every five years thereafter. Damon also explained that freshwater wetland alterations of 15,000 square feet or more generally require compensation, such as wetland restoration, preservation or payments into an approved fund.
Following the presentation, LaFreniere outlined options for reviewing ordinances and developing additional standards. She suggested gathering the town’s shoreline zoning, subdivision and floodplain regulations, comprehensive plan and examples of solar ordinances adopted elsewhere before determining what changes might be necessary.
LaFreniere said proposed ordinance amendments intended for an April town vote would need to be prepared by about mid-February, leaving a relatively short period for research, drafting and review.
Select Board members considered whether to create a separate committee representing different perspectives on solar development or assign the work to the planning board, which already handles land-use matters and can seek assistance from outside experts.
The board voted to assign the review to the planning board.
The voter-approved petition identifies a broad range of issues for examination, including appropriate locations for solar facilities, setbacks from residences and roads, wildlife and forest habitat impacts, construction traffic, fire safety, emergency access, electrical infrastructure and financial protections for decommissioning.
It also calls for reviewing the disposal and recycling of solar equipment, restoration of sites after operations end and potential impacts on neighboring property owners.
The discussion clarified that any new solar ordinance would apply to qualifying developments throughout Jay according to the standards adopted, rather than exclusively to Walden’s proposal. New municipal regulations would require voter approval.
The decision prompted questions about public participation and whether the planning board could complete its work before April.
LaFreniere said planning board meetings are publicly noticed through the town’s website, Facebook page, email notifications, bulletin board and electronic sign at the Town Office. An agenda for the Nov. 17 meeting is expected Thursday, Nov. 12.
Damon also emphasized that residents will have opportunities to participate in DEP’s review once Walden submits an application. The state requires public notices, notification of nearby property owners and an informational meeting for projects subject to the full Site Location of Development Law. Residents may submit comments during the review and request a public hearing.
Walden has previously indicated that it expects to begin seeking state permits in early 2027. The proposed development encompasses six potential sites totaling up to about 1,600 acres, with solar panels occupying about 900 acres.

title: Jeffrey Cookson, 56, Of Burnham Dies After Bike Struck On Peltoma Avenue In Pittsfield
text:
Authorities Say A Waldo County Man Died In Pittsfield Tuesday After The Bike He Was Riding Was Hit By A Speeding Car
Authorities are investigating a fatal hit-and-run accident that involved a bicyclist and a speeding car in Somerset County Tuesday evening. They believe speed and alcohol were contributing factors.

According to the Pittsfield Police Department, dispatchers began receiving calls around 4:30 that afternoon that a car had struck a bicyclist on Peltoma Avenue in Pittsfield, and that the driver had sped away.
Officers headed in that direction and came upon the body of the cyclist. The road, right by the snowmobile club, was immediately shut down.

"Pittsfield Police Officers responded to the area just North of the snowmobile club on Peltoma Avenue, where the bicyclist was found deceased. The bicyclist has been identified as Jeffrey Cookson, 56, of Burnham. Officers spoke with several witnesses at the scene who reported seeing a dark-colored sedan traveling south at a very high rate of speed. They also described the sedan as a Volkswagen Jetta with a missing headlight and windshield damage."
Other local law enforcement agencies were asked to be on the lookout for the car that had sped off after being damaged in the collision.

Members of the Washington County Sheriff's Office, along with the Maine State Police, impounded the black 2003 Volkswagen Jetta with damage consistent with that description.
The overall number of crashes involving pedestrians/bicycles and cars/trucks made a huge jump last year, according to the Maine Department of Transportation, with Maine recording 244 collisions and 22 pedestrian fatalities as a result of those crashes. title: Mother and two young children killed in Missouri crash after semitruck struck their minivan
text:
Mother and two young children killed in Missouri crash after semitruck struck their minivan
Family members say a father is in mourning after a mother and two children were killed in a crash on 71 Highway in Kansas City, Missouri, on Monday.
Family members identified the victims as 35-year-old Olga Sorbalo and two children, 8-year-old Luis and 4-year-old Samir. Kansas City police also confirmed their identities Tuesday afternoon.
The family was in a Honda minivan that was struck by a white Volvo semi-truck that failed to slow down or stop for congested traffic.
"She always preferred to be on the positive side of things, and that's how she'll be remembered," said Sorbalo's brother, Eli Cosovan.
The driver of the van and another passenger were taken to an area hospital with critical injuries. Cosovan says the other passengers were Sorbalo's husband and his two sisters.
Two other drivers were also injured in the chain-reaction crash.
In a GoFundMe for the family, posted Monday, family members say they are raising money to transport Olga, Luis and Samir back to Vancouver, Washington, for funeral services.
The family is not from Kansas City; they were in town visiting the husband's sister from Washington.
Cosovan says Sorbalo was one of fourteen kids and that their father is a local pastor in Vancouver, Washington. He says their faith is what's giving them strength to get through this difficult time.
"We have our comfort in knowing that they are with Jesus and we know that it was for a reason," Cosovan said. "We don't know what reason or why, but at least we have that comfort and hope."
As of 11 a.m., that GoFundMe has raised nearly $70,000.
Kansas City police said the driver of the semi-truck was placed on an investigative hold. Charges were filed against him on Tuesday.

title: 4 tax perks military families often miss
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Every year, military families leave real money on the table simply because they don’t know which tax breaks apply to them. Service members earn benefits most civilians don’t get — but only if they claim them.
Here, Intuit TurboTax explores four of the most commonly missed tax breaks for service members and their families.
1. Travel expense for reservists
If you are in the National Guard or military reserve, you may be able to deduct your unreimbursed travel expenses. If you travel more than 100 miles from home and are away overnight, you can deduct your lodging, half of the cost of meals (up to per diem rate), mileage, tolls, and parking fees. For 2026, the mileage rate is 72.5 cents per mile through June 30 and 76 per mile from July 1 onward.
2. ROTC payments
If you are a student in the ROTC, you don’t have to pay tax on the allowance that you receive for your participation in advanced training. This rule doesn’t apply to any active duty pay that you receive.
3. Combat pay
The pay you receive for any month that you serve in a combat zone isn’t taxable. If you are a military officer, your tax-free pay may be subject to a cap. But even though your combat pay isn’t taxable, don’t overlook it. You can take that pay into account to qualify for the Earned Income Tax Credit.
4. Moving expenses
If you are on active duty and have moving expenses in connection with a permanent change of station, those moving expenses are deductible if they are not reimbursed to you.
Filing your tax return
If you are serving in a combat zone during tax filing season, you have at least 180 days beyond the traditional April 15 deadline to file your tax return. If you are hospitalized because of injuries you sustained in a combat zone, similar extensions of time to file apply.
If you are serving overseas in a non-combat zone, the April 15 deadline is automatically extended to June 15. If you are a civilian serving in a combat zone, the same rules apply, but you need to write the words “Combat Zone” and your deployment date in red across the top of your tax return.
Military members do not have to make this notation on their tax return. And if you are serving in the military and are not available to sign a joint return, your spouse can sign it under a power of attorney.
