title: How we reported Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
It’s no secret that many Maine households are struggling to keep up with the rising cost of living. Some families, especially in rural areas, have been in poverty for generations.
After years of covering food insecurity and homelessness in southern Maine, photographer Brianna Soukup and I knew there were stories left untold about how Mainers are getting by in other parts of the state.
We started by looking at new data released by the United Ways of Maine that measures the financial hardship people are experiencing in towns across the state. We anchored our reporting in three areas with unique challenges.
In western Maine, we focused on Oxford County’s River Valley, a place with a deep history of manufacturing, a tightknit community and multiple programs dedicated to helping. One reason we chose this community is because it has high numbers of people experiencing food insecurity.
In Midcoast Maine, we focused on Lincoln County, home to a large percentage of older Mainers, to highlight the challenges of aging in a rural state with limited access to public transportation and nearby healthcare. We spent most of our time on the Boothbay peninsula, where there are stark disparities between wealthy out-of-state property owners and year-round residents on fixed incomes.
We also traveled to Washington County, where many families have been trying to break out of the poverty cycle for generations. There, we focused primarily on the Machias area because of the programs working to help lift people out of poverty.
Through organizations offering assistance, we connected with people willing to share their experiences and talk about the choices they have to make when they don’t have enough money to cover their expenses.
Between us, Brianna and I made three reporting trips to Washington County, spending several days at a time meeting people at a food pantry and nonprofit programs. We took more than a dozen day trips to the River Valley and Boothbay peninsula to visit food pantries, soup kitchens, churches and community centers. We also visited people at home and at work, and went fishing and shared meals with families we were interviewing.
We logged more than 3,900 miles driving across the state.
Through our reporting, we learned that people who have been living with low incomes are struggling more than ever — and that even people who had not previously felt a financial strain are now having a harder time making ends meet.
We were struck by how often the people helping their neighbors had also experienced the same struggles, but gave back without hesitation.
We also put out a call for feedback from people across Maine about their own financial situations. More than 135 people have already responded to our survey, sharing details about how far their budgets fall short and how they decide what to pay for. Many said more needs to be done to help people who are struggling.
To help connect people, we created a guide for how to find help or offer help, a resource we will continue to update.
In the months ahead, we plan to host two events to share and discuss our work.
The first, on Dec. 16, is a forum at the Rumford Public Library that will feature a panel discussion with the reporting team, as well as Michelle Williams from Good Samaritan Missionary Services, Melissa McEntee from Rumford Group Homes and Rumford Town Manager George O’Keefe.
Beyond this project, in 2027 we will continue to prioritize reporting on affordability issues impacting so many Mainers.
This piece is part of the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham is a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.

title: ICE agent in deadly Biddeford shooting had history of anti-immigrant rhetoric, NYT reports
text:
ICE agent in deadly Biddeford shooting had history of anti-immigrant rhetoric, New York Times reports
The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent involved in the fatal shooting of a Colombian man that happened in Maine nearly four months ago expressed anti-immigrant sentiments in emails sent to his family members, according to a report from The New York Times.
David Brouillette had been identified by The Associated Press as the ICE officer who shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13. Both Brouillette's first ex-wife and his daughter told the AP that Brouillette told them he was the one who shot and killed Guerrero. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has declined to identify Brouillette as the ICE agent involved in the shooting.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that Brouillette's sister, Elizabeth Emen, shared a series of emails with The Times from 2021 in which Brouillette berated Emen and their relatives and criticized her for her longtime relationship with a Colombian man, with whom she had two children.
Emen later spoke about how she reacted to the news of the deadly shooting in an interview with ABC News.
"When I saw his actions on July 13, I just couldn't believe that it had been allowed to get to that point," Emen told ABC News. "I can't believe that he was onboarded into a federal agency and provided a weapon, and I'm really looking for answers around how that was allowed to happen."
The report from The Times also goes into detail about Brouillette's recruiting history, citing an anonymous source who said Brouillette was sped through the vetting process and that he was cleared to work for ICE in December 2025.
Maine's Total Coverage has contacted Homeland Security with a request for comment about the report from The New York Times, but has yet to receive a reply.
Ben Gideon, an attorney representing Guerrero's wife and his estate, has issued a statement in response to The Times' report on Brouillette.
"David Brouillette is the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training," Gideon said in his statement. "Johan Sebastian’s death was not an inevitable accident. It was a natural and predictable choice of the policies of our government and its political leadership."
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat who represents Maine's 1st Congressional District, said that she demanded answers from Homeland Security about training and background checks in the days following Guerrero's death, and that Wednesday's report from The New York Times makes a full, independent investigation even more urgent.
"DHS must release Brouillette's hiring, vetting, training, and deployment records and cooperate fully with independent investigators," Pingree said in a statement. "Responsibility reaches beyond the officer who pulled the trigger. It extends to the leadership that armed and deployed him, and to an administration that put its deportation agenda ahead of human life. Every official responsible must be held accountable. Johan Sebastián’s family deserves justice, and I will keep fighting until they get it."
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, the Maine Democrat who defeated five-term Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, told Maine's Total Coverage that he plans to push for hearings or an independent review of ICE's hiring practices.
"I have every faith in legitimate law enforcement. I've respected it and appreciated it. I think in this situation, you're dragging down legitimate law enforcement when you don't have proper vetting and you don't have people that have the training," Jackson said. "This is a stain, and I do think we have to have hearings about it and get this resolved, and weed out these type of people and have a legitimate process to hire immigration officers."
Pingree and U.S. Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, have said Guerrero was not the target of the ICE operation that ultimately resulted in his death. King and Pingree also said that Guerrero, the father of a 3-year-old girl, had no criminal history.
In September, another attorney representing Guerrero's family testified before members of Congress. The testimony was part of a public forum examining several deadly shootings involving federal immigration agents.

title: Veterans Day parade tradition continues in Portland
text:
Veterans Day parade tradition continues in Portland
This year was special, as the parade's Grand Marshal is passing the torch down after 25 years in the role.
Veterans Day parade tradition continues in Portland
This year was special, as the parade's Grand Marshal is passing the torch down after 25 years in the role.
Military service members marched down Congress Street on Wednesday, joined by local community groups looking to give thanks to veterans.
First responders, scout troops, Portland Sea Dogs, the Maine Celtics, and Deering High School's marching band were among those that marched in the procession.
The parade started at 10:30 a.m. at Longfellow Square. It followed Congress Street until stopping at Portland City Hall.
At city hall, a ceremony was held with remarks from Portland's mayor Mark Dion and historian Herb Andrews.
"Shake that veteran's hand. Look into their eyes. Hear their story," said Andrews.
Mike Verville is a U.S. Airforce veteran. He enlisted in 1977 and served for four years. He says he makes it out every year to see the ceremony in Portland.
"It's important to me to be able to come to these things," Verville said. "To pay homage to the service members that have served and provided us with the freedoms that we have today."
The parade's Grand Marshal introduced the wreath laying ceremony followed by ceremonial gunshots and Taps for those that made the ultimate sacrifice.
Some in the crowd were veterans, while others had veterans in their life. They were all there for the same reason.
"To remember the people that were willing to put their lives on the line for the rest of us. I mean, there's only 1% of the population that finds [its] way into the military. So that's a small percentage that benefits the masses," said Andrews.

title: ‘VisionQuest’ Post-Credits Scene Sets Up ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ and a Huge Character’s Return
text:
The ‘VisionQuest’ Post-Credits Scene Sets Up ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ – and a Major Marvel Return
The following post contains spoilers for the season finale of VisionQuest.
“Do you think that it’s possible with me, you and Billy still around, that...?
“We might ever see your mother again?”
That’s a question asked by Tommy and Vision at the end of the series finale of VisionQuest. Tommy’s mother, of course, is Wanda Maximoff (AKA the Scarlet Witch), who seemingly died at the end of Doctor Strange and the Multiverse of Madness.
But, of course, Vision died in Avengers: Infinity War. And then he sort of died again in WandaVision. (Sort of.) And Tommy and Billy seemed to be artificial creations of Wanda’s magic, and now they’re flesh and blood, and reunited with the restored Vision. So it’s a fair question.
In that scene, Paul Bettany’s Vision replies “We have said goodbye before. So, I suppose it stands to reason we might say hello again.”
That’s where Vision leaves it. But just a few minutes later, a post-credits scene at the very end of the VisionQuest finale, an additional scene gives a different answer.
READ MORE: Every Marvel Cinematic Universe Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
It shows Elizabeth Olsen’s Wanda in her final moments from Multiverse of Madness, when she sacrificed her own life to destroy Mount Wundagore as well as the corrupting influence of the evil Darkhold book. But then it shows none other than Doctor Doom lifting the rubble of Mount Wundagore off of Wanda, and declaring “Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine.” And then Elizabeth Olsen’s Wanda opens her eyes.
So yeah, expect to see Wanda somewhere in Avengers: Doomsday (or maybe its sequel, Avengers: Secret Wars). Or maybe both? And one would think this would also create a chance that we’ll see Vision, Tommy, and Billy all in one or both films as well.
The full season of VisionQuest is now streaming on Disney+. Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters in a little over a month, on December 18.

title: Women’s underwear labeled with sticky notes found in sex assault suspect’s home, police say
text:
TEMPE, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — Police in Arizona say a disturbing discovery was made in the home of a man accused of sexual assault on Halloween.
Newly released court documents detail how police say the assault happened and how the suspect was caught, including finding a collection of women’s underwear with some having sticky note labels.
A forensic psychologist who reviewed the allegations said the discovery raises concerns about the possibility of other victims.
Mach Kim, 46, was arrested Nov. 5 on charges of aggravated assault, kidnapping, sexual assault and sexual abuse in connection with an Oct. 31 attack on a woman in Tempe.
What police say happened
The alleged assault began in the afternoon in Tempe, where Kim allegedly forced a woman into his vehicle at gunpoint.
Court documents said the woman was walking home from a party when a driver stopped, pointed what she described as a black pistol at her and told her to get in or he would shoot her.
Kim reportedly made the woman put on an eye mask and drove her to another location, where he sexually assaulted her and forced her to give him her underwear.
Police said Kim then dropped the woman off, where she found someone nearby to help her call police.
The woman showed officers where she had been dropped off before she was taken for a sexual assault exam. Police found her phone and keys on the ground at the drop-off location.
Police said GPS data from her phone showed the route she was taken on, including where she was picked up and dropped off.
How police identified Kim
Police said they used the GPS information to help identify Kim as the sexual assault suspect.
Investigators reviewed camera footage along the route, matching it to the timeline from her phone’s GPS, which led them to a white Dodge Ram pickup registered to Kim.
Court documents said his driver’s license photo resembled a sketch the woman helped create.
Detectives then surveilled Kim on Nov. 5 and collected a DNA sample from a Wendy’s cup he threw away, according to court documents. Police said the DNA on the cup matched DNA collected in the woman’s sexual assault kit.
What police found
When police arrested Kim in Scottsdale, a search of his car uncovered a black CO2 gun shaped like a handgun, a black sleep mask, six pairs of women’s underwear, a pillow and a towel.
In his Chandler home, police say they found 13 pairs of women’s underwear and an eye mask. Seven of the pairs had sticky notes with dates and names.
Forensic psychologist John De La Torre said the labeled items could be connected to other victims and could have been kept as mementos. That was his assessment, not a confirmed finding about the items.
“The initial impulse in me is to think that all of these, because they’re labeled, all of these are meant as mementos,” he said.
De La Torre said keeping mementos is not limited to serial killers. He also said the allegations raise concerns about the possibility of escalation.
“All of these things, you know, raise a level of concern about the possibility of escalation,” he said.
After Kim was taken to jail, he invoked his rights and said he did not want to answer more questions about the charges without a lawyer.
Detectives believe there could be other victims who have not yet come forward. Potential victims or others with information are asked to call Tempe police at 480-350-8311.

title: ﻿Lessie Benningfield Randle, the last known Tulsa Race Massacre survivor, turns 112
text:
Lessie Benningfield Randle, the last known Tulsa Race Massacre survivor, turns 112
The last known living survivor of the Tulsa Race Massacre celebrated a big milestone this week.
Related video above: Remembering the Tulsa Race Massacre: 105 years since one of the darkest chapters in Oklahoma history
Lessie Benningfield Randle, who is affectionately known as "Mother Randle," turned 112 on Tuesday.
Randle, who has spoken out against censoring Black history in education, was born in 1914 and was a young girl when she survived the Tulsa Race Massacre in 1921. She likened the 18-hour period to a war.
"White men with guns came and destroyed my community," Randle said to members of Congress on Capitol Hill in 2021. "We couldn't understand why. What did we do to them?"
She is the last known survivor.
The thriving business district and residential area of the Greenwood neighborhood of Tulsa was referred to as “Black Wall Street.” But in 1921, more than 1,000 homes and businesses there were destroyed by white mobs.
Historians now believe as many as 300 people may have died, and the massacre is believed to be the single worst incident of racial violence in American history.
Two other survivors died in recent years. They were Hughes Van Ellis, who died in October 2023 at the age of 102, and Viola Fletcher, who died in November 2025 at the age of 111.
In 2021, the three spoke in front of Congress to describe the horrors of what happened a century before.
"I will never forget the violence of the white mob when we left our home," Fletcher said at the time. "I still see Black men being shot, Black bodies lying in the street."

title: Former NFL coach Rex Ryan turns himself in after alleged Nashville hit-and-run
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Former NFL coach Rex Ryan turned himself in Wednesday for allegedly hitting pedestrians with his car in Nashville and leaving the scene, police said.
Two pedestrians had the right of way crossing a main street in downtown Nashville’s popular tourist area last week when Ryan allegedly turned at a red light, running over the victims’ feet, Nashville police said Wednesday. They suffered minor injuries, police said.
Ryan, an ESPN analyst, was charged with two counts of leaving the scene of an accident, two counts of failure to give information or render aid and two counts of failure to obey a traffic control signal, according to court records, which did not identify an attorney for Ryan. All are misdemeanors. A judicial commissioner set Ryan’s bond at $6,000.
He was granted pretrial release Wednesday morning. Ryan is scheduled to appear in court next month.
Ryan is a former head coach of the Buffalo Bills and New York Jets, leading the Jets to the AFC Championship Game in consecutive years after the 2009 and 2010 seasons. His father, the late Buddy Ryan, was an NFL coaching legend who famously coordinated the 1985 Chicago Bears defense that was one of the best in history.
Since leaving coaching, Ryan is best known for his work at ESPN as one of the analysts on the network’s NFL pregame show.
“We are aware and are in touch with Rex,” ESPN said in a statement Wednesday. Ryan appeared Monday on “Get Up,” a morning ESPN show taped in New York.
A phone number believed to be Ryan’s had an automatic outgoing message, and a message could not be left.
___
Fingerhut reported from Des Moines, Iowa.

title: THE BEST VIEW: Scat and Track
text:
My paternal grandfather, an English Canadian from Ontario, was a lumberjack in the 1890s and early 1900s.
“Hay,” as my dad and his siblings called their father, was a 5’8″ 200 lb. man of solid muscle. In my child’s mind I imagined Superman dressed in woodsmen green wool pants, a wool plaid shirt, and a red and black mackinaw jacket, very much like the one my father wore to go deer hunting.
Hay loved and respected the forest. He taught my father that love, and my father taught me.
I was a city girl, born and raised in Waterville. The only way to teach me about the beauty of the forest was to take me out into the woods. On Saturdays, in good weather, my father, my mother and I went for rides in my father’s 1948 Studebaker.
Dad drove us up and down the dirt roads where he and his hunting friends went bird and deer hunting. When we got out of the car, we heard blue jays squawking alarm calls alerting other birds and animals of the human invasion into their private world.
One time we went into a treeless area with high grass and an old broken down wooden building. My father clapped his hands loudly, and a dozen partridges and pheasants flew noisily around us escaping into the sky above.
On these walking excursions I saw plenty of squirrels and chipmunks. Once we saw a rabbit. Dad told me that the racing rabbit would circle right back to us, and he did.
There were too many woodchucks to count. Driving slowly down these dirt roads, I spotted many of them on the roads’ edges watching our car to see us, the intruders.
I saw a small bear cub once on all fours running off the road into the bushes which hid him completely.
There were even animals in our backyards. We and other city residents drove to a pasture in Winslow in the evening where parked cars watched a proud cow moose with her twin calves out for a walk and supper.
Depending on the season, we found wild blueberries, strawberries, raspberries, black raspberries, grapes, and something called bunch berries that were red and tasteless.
My father explained to me about the animals that were hiding from us. He also warned that the berries we ate were favorites of the bears and moose that weren’t afraid of me but of whom I should be afraid.
“Always be aware of your surroundings,” he said. “See a bear or a moose, back off slowly and get out of there.”
I was reminded of these special memories the other day when I attended a lecture called “Scat & Track” presented by our local zoo.
They gave us papers with examples of area animals’ tracks and rubberized samples of those animals’ scat. These examples represented small animals like porcupines and skunks to large animals like bear, Burmese python, and the Florida panther.
I have seen opossums, raccoons, armadillos, and large land tortoises here in Florida. In fact, I have seen these animals near my home. The Ring videos on my neighbors’ doors have even recorded a coyote skulking around at night.
Continual building construction is eliminating the “jungle” homes of many creatures, so, as my father taught me, I am always aware.
I have not seen nor do I want to see an adult bear, a Burmese python or a panther although bear and panther tracks have been recorded in a reserve not too far from a friend’s house.
Dad would have enjoyed the zoo lecture just as I did. I think, though, that he would add an important third word to the title. I believe I would add that word, too.
“Scat, Track & (when necessary) VAMOOSE!”
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Woman loses more than $400K of retirement savings to gold courier scam
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WINNEBAGO COUNTY, Wis. (InvestigateTV) — It can start with a pop-up on the computer screen and sometimes ends with the innocent victim handing over their life savings to a scammer.
Criminals trick victims, often retirees, that their personal information has been compromised. The scammer then convinces them that in order to secure their assets, they need to convert cash into gold bars or coins.
Then the fraudsters send a fake courier to collect the gold in person.
“Forty years’ worth of savings, and it’s gone,” said the woman, who we will call Mary.
How it began
Mary said the scheme started when she clicked a pop-up on her computer while scheduling an appointment with her financial advisor. “With their logo on it,” she noted.
“They locked my computer to the point where I couldn’t even shut it off manually,” Mary said.
She then received a call from someone claiming to represent her investment company, who told her the account had been hacked and that she was a suspect in weapons dealing and money laundering.
“Someone just took out a high-interest loan in your name for $35,000,” Mary said, recounting what she was told.
“And they showed me eight places where my Social Security number was being used,” she said. “So now I’m terrified. I’m absolutely terrified.”
The callers told Mary her financial advisor was also a suspect and that she should not speak to anyone. They sent a non-disclosure agreement directly to her printer.
Impersonators and gold purchases
Calls continued from people impersonating the sheriff’s office, the FBI and the Federal Trade Commission, making her believe they were working to restore her account. “That’s the trick is to get your confidence.”
Mary said the callers told her she needed to purchase gold to protect her money.
Mary spent $131,208 on 24 gold coins.
Then came a twist: A call from the Better Business Bureau, telling her she’s been scammed.
“He said, ‘You’ve been working with the scammers. You need to stop right now. And I’m going to help you,’” Mary said.
But it was an imposter. The caller arranged for a courier to collect the gold coins from Mary in a fast food parking lot. Mary said she was given only a first name and a password to identify the courier — the courier had a description of her car and clothing, but she had no description of them.
Months of continued fraud
Mary said people at her bank and at the business where she purchased the gold questioned her about the large cash withdrawals.
“I had to keep making excuses why I wanted these large amounts of cash,” she said.
She continued because she believed her money was being recovered and could see it appearing to be restored in her account. She was also instructed to purchase Bitcoin and thousands of dollars in gift cards.
“I put 600 miles on my car just running all over town, buying gift cards,” Mary said. “But you see it put back into your account. It’s all there.”
The fraud continued for three months. It ended when Mary tried to call the person she believed was her BBB contact and found the number had been disconnected.
“I grabbed everything, and I went right down to the police station,” she said.
‘Unprecedented’ loss, officials warn
Mary also contacted the Wisconsin Better Business Bureau to report that imposters had stolen more than $400,000 in her name.
“The extent was unprecedented. I mean, this is probably the largest amount of money loss that we’ve had reported in one single scam,” said Lisa Schiller of the Wisconsin Better Business Bureau.
The Wisconsin Department of Financial Institutions said the scam is surging and frequently targets seniors, using gold as part of the ruse to convince victims they are protecting or recovering their money. Officials said the operations are often run by international crime networks that use couriers for pickups.
- Related link: Real government agents aren’t asking you to buy and deliver gold bars (FTC)
“Hang up your phone or shut down your computer, because once you engage with them, you go down the rabbit hole with them and it’s very hard to disengage at that point, psychologically,” said Robin Jacobs of the Wisconsin Department of Financial Institutions.
Investigation ongoing, no arrests
Local police investigating Mary’s case said in a statement: “We are looking at all aspects of this investigation to try and identify suspects; that would include trying to find video, if any is available. This investigation is still ongoing, and at this time we are not sure if it is connected with other crimes.”
No arrests have been made.
Mary said she does not know whether she will recover any of her savings.
“There’s no guarantee that any of it will come back,” she said. “The banks aren’t responsible, you’re responsible, because you did it.”
Mary is bravely sharing her story to prevent others from becoming victims.
“I don’t want this to happen to anybody else, because this is a nightmare,” Mary said. “I’m freaking out. Am I going to have to file bankruptcy? Am I going to lose my house? I mean, I’m terrified.”
Officials advise the public to never trust anyone who calls and instructs them to move money to protect it or to hand over gold.
They also warn against allowing people they do not know to access their computer or personal information. If you receive a call from an unknown number you’re advised to hang up, call someone you’re familiar with, or call the police.
Any suspected fraudulent activity to the FBI at ic3.gov

title: Missing South Carolina infant rescued after being buried alive in a dog crate for 24 hours
text:
When an 11-month-old infant was reported missing in South Carolina, dozens of first responders combed the countryside for the “bright boy with reddish blond hair” that the sheriff’s office said had disappeared while his grandmother ran errands.
After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil in the woods not far from the home of the boy’s grandfather. They began digging and soon unearthed little Koah Sharp, who was “clinging to life” after being buried alive in a dog crate wrapped in a towel, the sheriff said.
“Certainly, God is good,” Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said Tuesday at a news conference, not long after Koah was found. “He was screaming at the top of his lungs, which is a good thing in the baby world, I would guess.”
The child’s father, Michael Comer, 25, was arrested and was being held without bond on a burglary charge, Koon said. Investigators were working with prosecutors to confirm further charges, he said.
The towel probably created an air pocket that allowed the boy to breathe in the crate, the sheriff said. Cool temperatures also may have helped.
Koah, who disappeared Monday in the county just west of Columbia, was taken to a hospital. His condition was not immediately known Wednesday.
“We’re better now that we know that Koah is safe,” his great aunt, Amber Hammond, told The Associated Press in an interview. She was watching as he was freed from the crate.
Deputies who searched the grandfather’s home found the doors open and baby belongings inside, but they did not see Comer or the child, the sheriff said. Then the digging started.
“It was shallow,” Koon said. “I think once that crate hit the ground, it was probably about at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground.”
It was not immediately known if Comer had a lawyer. A phone number could not be found for him. The Associated Press sent emails seeking information to the public defender and prosecutors.
Nearly 100 first responders participated in the search.
Authorities said Koah had been in the care of Comer’s mother. She had to run an errand and left the boy in Comer’s care. Another caregiver was on the way, Koon said.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone, and Koah was gone with him,” Koon said.
Surveillance video from several businesses in the area showed Comer without the infant on Monday afternoon, Koon said. The father was found Monday night and was arrested.
Koah’s parents “have had some situations” regarding domestic violence charges, the sheriff said.
“Children,” he said, “sometimes get caught in the middle.”
Comer was sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence and aggravated breach-of-peace charges related to an arrest in July, Lexington County online court records show. Prosecutors dropped a gun charge as part of the plea deal.
___
Associated Press Writer Dave Collins contributed to this story.

title: New basketball courts to be unveiled on Brunswick Landing
text:
New basketball courts and sports lighting will be unveiled at the Midcoast Athletic and Recreation Complex next week, the latest amenities added in the multiyear MARC project.
The project envisions several sports courts and fields, playgrounds, an ice skating rink, pool and more in the 10-acre lot adjacent to the Brunswick Recreation Center on Brunswick Landing.
The Town Council at its meeting last week reallocated $180,000 of unused town funds for the design of the next phase of the MARC, which will include a splash pad, playground for 5- to 12-year-olds, a shade structure and a natural grass field.
The town is looking to raise $1.4 million for the next phase, which will have to come back before the council before breaking ground. Construction will likely begin on the next few elements in summer or fall 2027, Sally Costello, director of economic and community development, told the council last week.
Several facilities at the MARC are already in use, including eight pickleball courts, a skatepark, toddler-age playground, a shade structure and a walking trail.
The Navy transferred 10 acres that would become the MARC to the town in 2020, specifying that it be used for recreation. An advisory committee took on the job of planning the future complex the following year.
The Town Council approved $1.05 million in grants, recreation impact fees and donations for the basketball court and lighting phase of the project in the spring.
Brunswick Parks and Recreation will unveil the two new basketball courts and accompanied sports lighting — which will allow the facilities to be used for extended hours — at a Nov. 18 ribbon cutting at 4:45 p.m. After, the community is invited to play under the new lights, the parks and recreation department said in a press release Tuesday.

title: Couple who disliked sex offenders arrested in man’s killing, police say
text:
BULLHEAD CITY, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) — An Arizona couple who “expressed distaste” for sex offenders was arrested after a man they knew was found dead in the desert over the weekend, police said.
Jacob Dylan Middlebrook, 35, and Layne Justine McIntosh, 36, were arrested Saturday in the death of 29-year-old Arron Christopher Warren, according to the Bullhead City Police Department.
Body found along Silver Creek Road
Police said Warren, a registered Level 2 sex offender experiencing homelessness, was found stabbed to death in a desert area along Silver Creek Road, about a mile east of Bullhead Parkway.
Middlebrook and McIntosh, who were also experiencing homelessness, had known Warren for the past few months and disliked sex offenders, according to police.
The couple reportedly chose the desert location ahead of time and planned to leave Warren’s body there. Police said the couple also measured furniture along the side of the road that could be large enough to cover his body.
Arrests in Nevada
Hours after the body was discovered Saturday, Las Vegas Metropolitan Police officers found Warren’s stolen vehicle at a casino in Laughlin, just across the state line into Nevada.
Officers arrested Middlebrook and McIntosh. They were booked into the Clark County Detention Center in Las Vegas and are awaiting extradition to Mohave County.
Once they return to Arizona, they will likely face first-degree murder charges.
Police chief addresses sex offender notifications
Bullhead City Police Chief Paul George said in a written statement that the department shares information about Level 2 and Level 3 sex offenders as a public service when they move into the area or change addresses.
Required notifications are mailed to residents within about 1,000 feet of an offender’s registered address. The department also shares them on social media to reach a broader audience.
“Our goal is to provide information, not create fear or alarm. We believe an informed community is a safer community,” George said. “However, we want to be clear that we will not tolerate anyone using this information as a reason to threaten, intimidate, harass or harm another person.”
Police can decide when to release the addresses of Level 1 offenders, who are in the lowest risk classification. State law requires notifications about Level 2 and Level 3 offenders, who are classified as more likely to reoffend than Level 1 offenders.
George also said the department’s Bureau of Criminal Investigations conducts monthly address verification checks to make sure sex offenders are following registration requirements.

title: Donald Trump’s private message to Joe Biden emerges in new White House memoir
text:
A note to ‘46’: Donald Trump’s private message to Joe Biden emerges in new White House memoir
President Donald Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result having been stolen from him by Democratic forces, privately lauded incoming President Joe Biden as someone he believed "will be true to yourself and the American people."
That sentiment, along with others, was part of the letter Trump left for Biden upon leaving office in January 2021. Biden showed the note to some members of his staff after his inauguration in 2021 but didn't let anyone read it, describing it later that day as "very generous" but otherwise saying he considered it to be private.
Inclusion of the letter in Biden's "Promise Me, America," his White House memoir slated for release Nov. 17, was first reported Tuesday by The New York Times. The Associated Press has reviewed a photocopy of the two-page letter, handwritten in Trump's trademark black Sharpie on White House stationery and addressed "To '46,'" denoting Biden's place as the 46th U.S. president.
"Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats," Trump wrote. "Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people."
At the time of transition, Biden was said to have been surprised by how gracious he thought the letter was, given the animosity between the political rivals. Trump had opted out of other presidential traditions, like attending Biden's inauguration, or hosting the incoming president and first lady for tea at the White House.
Trump has said he thought it was up to Biden to share the letter, calling it "a nice note" during a September 2023 interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," adding, "I took a lot of time in thinking about it."
Elsewhere in the memoir, the first excerpt of which was published Monday by the Atlantic, Biden wrote of the deep damage Trump has inflicted, with an administration determined to "tear down institutions and inflame hatreds."
Lamenting Trump's Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, Biden wrote of Trump's "dismissive and destructive nature," describing his predecessor and successor as someone "who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else's accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down."
But Biden's harshest characterization so far was focused on Trump's role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, as Congress met to certify the 2020 election, which Biden had won. Writing that Trump "led an insurrection," Biden said Trump's "goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office."
"What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten," Biden wrote. "It should follow him to his grave."
Asked for comment on both the letter and Biden's memoir, White House communications director Steven Cheung called the former president "a disgrace" who "should have heeded the President's wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies."

title: ‘Huge inspiration’: 88-year-old Vermont woman keeps moving with Pilates
text:
BARRE, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Nearly every day, Sue Talmage walks on the land in Barre that she owns with Bruce, her husband of more than 40 years. Twice a week, she drives to Montpelier for something else entirely.
At 88, Talmage is sure she is the oldest student at Essential Physical Therapy and Pilates — and she has been taking classes there for close to two decades.
“It’s an important part of my life,” Talmage said.
What is Pilates?
Pilates is a combination of repetitive exercises focused on building balance, flexibility and core strength.
Studies show older adults are prone to losing muscle mass, which can lead to falls and other complications.
Instructor Willow Wonder leads Talmage’s class, which runs 45 minutes with no breaks.
‘Huge inspiration’
Wonder said Talmage’s physical ability stands out.
“If you think old people have balance issues, this is not the case,” Wonder said. “I think she’s very unique to have such ability, strength, balance, flexibility — all of the things at that age. I just have not seen much of.”
Wonder also said Talmage serves as an inspiration for others who come to the studio.
“Absolutely — huge inspiration to everyone that comes here,” Wonder said.
Talmage said she does not see herself that way. For her, staying fit is a personal goal.
“Eighty-eight is a long time,” she said.
After class, Talmage said she feels no soreness and returns home to her daily walk.
“I feel great and I can still do just about everything I want to,” she said.

title: Black University of Mississippi students wrestle with forgiveness in wake of racist gestures
text:
Three Black University of Mississippi students who shared a now-viral Ring camera video of two white students making monkeylike sounds and gestures outside their front door say they received an apology from one woman.
But the other only amplified her behavior, they said, divulging details of the rest of the encounter that weren’t captured on camera.
“She continued to make the gestures after the girl was apologizing. It was like a slap in the face,” Victoria Johnson told “CBS Mornings” in an interview that aired Wednesday.
Johnson was joined by her roommates, Jakiyra Metcalf and Kaiyden Caldwell, to talk about the incident that has ignited a firestorm on the Ole Miss campus and across social media. The animalistic gestures and sounds are seen as racist because they were reminiscent of ugly, old stereotypes comparing Black people to simians.
For it to happen at a college community in the Deep South with a long history of racism has added to the raw emotions.
Metcalf saw the video Friday and she and Johnson went outside to talk to the two women, who had another friend with them. She was only seen glancing at the door in the video.
They said one woman, Alaina Kunes, apologized but said they had been making animallike noises and gestures in front of other doors in the apartment complex. But the second woman, who lives in the complex, purportedly kept the antics going off camera.
Metcalf’s TikTok post has been viewed over 13 million times in four days. On Monday, the university posted a statement condemning the actions in the video as “offensive, hurtful, and unacceptable behaviors that conflict with our university values.” School officials also said the incident is being investigated and they are dedicated to “maintaining a safe and welcoming environment.”
Kunes, 18, issued a public apology Tuesday through a law firm.
“Before the incident on Nov. 6, I never met the women involved and was unaware of their race, however I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate and deeply harmful,” Kunes said. “I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color. I have apologized to the women and I pray they will forgive me.”
She has since withdrawn from school. She also said she would fully cooperate with any investigation.
The statement was originally posted on the firm’s website, but it had to be taken down because of ongoing harassment, said Kate Gardiner, a spokesperson for the firm.
Kunes will not be speaking beyond the statement, Gardiner added.
Outrage at taunting prompts opposition to social media shaming
The outrage against Kunes and the second woman, who has not publicly identified herself, has also stirred up opposition against using social media to malign them.
Tom Hennessey, an influencer tied to online fundraisers for people criticized for making xenophobic remarks, is credited with starting a fundraiser for the other woman on Christian fundraising platform GiveSendGo. It has raised over $30,000 as of Wednesday afternoon. The fundraising page states the “online mob (is) treating a juvenile stunt as a hate crime because the residents were Black.”
The fundraiser also says it could possibly be canceled if the woman “disavows our support and bends the knee” and apologizes.
When contacted via X, or Twitter, DM, Hennessey said there is a double-standard and less attention is given to Black-on-white crime. He declined to say whether he had been in touch with the student about the fundraiser.
This is not the first time the university has been the backdrop for a Black student dealing with taunting animallike mimicking. In a May 2024 campus demonstration over the Israel-Hamas war, a counterprotester made monkey sounds and gestures at a Black, female student. The interaction was filmed by a student journalist. The video got the attention of outgoing Georgia Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, who appeared to praise the behavior in a tweet.
University has ties to nation’s desegregation movement
Ole Miss also has a long history with racism, civil rights and segregation. In 1962, activist James Meredith was the first Black person to be admitted to the school after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in his favor.
Then-Gov. Ross Barnett tried to block his admission but could not disobey federal law, according to the National Museum of African American History & Culture. Still, white objectors instigated a riot on campus. Two bystanders died and over 200 arrests were made.
Metcalf, Caldwell and Johnson hedged when asked if they forgive Kunes.
“I still have very mixed feelings about it,” Metcalf said.
Caldwell said she appreciated the apology but said it doesn’t change what happened.
“It’s still hurtful, and it’s still devastating that someone would go to our camera and do that,” Caldwell said.

title: Stacy Keach, star of stage and ‘Mike Hammer’ series, dies at 85
text:
(AP) - Stacy Keach, one of America’s finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.
Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, “after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure,” his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.
Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.
Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating “World’s Most Amazing Videos” on TV. He played a deranged colonel in “The Ninth Configuration” (also known as “Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane”), led the TV show “Titus,” had a role in Alexander Payne’s Oscar-nominated drama “Nebraska,” and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama “Blue Bloods.” Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney’s bitter father in “Jay Kelly.”
“My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career,” he told New York magazine in 2012. “My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I’ve gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything.”
Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach’s son in the 2008 TV movie “Lone Rider,” said in a post on X that Keach was a “consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him.”
From TV to stage
He played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries “Mistral’s Daughter,” a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz’s novel “Princess Daisy,” Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli’s “Jesus of Nazareth” and Maj. Jonas Steele in “The Blue and the Gray.” He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds (16 kilograms).
Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play “Indians,” played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in “King Lear” on Broadway and had other onstage roles there in “The Kentucky Cycle” in 1993, “The Country Wife” in 1965 and “Other Desert Cities” in 2011.
He also headed the national touring company cast of “Frost/Nixon,” portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with “Sleuth” with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of “King Lear” at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for “Pamplona,” a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run’s cancellation.
A pivotal arrest
While he was still doing “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer” (later titled “The New Mike Hammer”), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London’s Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.
“As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats,” he wrote in his 2013 book, “All in All: An Actor’s Life On and Off the Stage.” He added: “It was the lowest moment of my life.”
He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book “The Blue and the Gray.”
The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.
In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, “The Long Riders.” He said the experience was “very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity.”
After prison, he narrated the TV documentary “High on the Job,” and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. “There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one’s existence,” he testified.
Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centers. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the “Hammer” series. He said he treasured her photos and letters behind bars.
Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.
Keach’s life after prison
His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, “Intimate Strangers” with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, “The Return of Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” also played well, and then the “Mike Hammer” series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS’ 1986-87 schedule.
Many years later, in the TV series “Prison Break” that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.
Born in Savannah, Georgia, Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.
In the summer of 1963, he worked with the Oregon Shakespeare Festival and played Henry V, Mercutio and Lord Berowne. He attended the Yale School of Drama and, in the summer of 1964, played several roles at New York’s Public Theater in “Hamlet” with Julie Harris. He went to study at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art as a Fulbright scholar and returned to New York to do various stage roles.
Keach made his film debut in 1968 in “The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter” and played stoner cop Sergeant Stedenko from the Cheech and Chong movies. He worked for director John Huston twice, in “Fat City” and “The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean” and had roles in “American History X” with Edward Norton and “The Bourne Legacy.” He played a tough trucker in “Roadgames,” was electrocuted in “Children of the Corn” and a robot removed his heart in “Class of 1999.”
His biggest break, though, came with the role of Hammer, whom he played as a modern-day knight, a champion of the underdog.
“Keach makes a dashing, dapper Hammer. He looks almost jaunty in his tilted gray fedora,” said Fred Rothenberg, a TV writer for The Associated Press, in 1983. “He knows how to speak lust with his eyes, and talk dirty with his fists.”
___
AP Entertainment Writer Andrew Dalton contributed reporting from Los Angeles.

title: Tales from the booth: Hear from some of Maine’s high school football announcers
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Chris Cifelli watches the offense, while his wife, Michelle, watches the defense.
She reports the jersey numbers, he finds the names and then keys the microphone. It’s his voice that spectators hear echoing through the speakers at Leavitt High’s Libby Field, but it’s her direction that helps keep things on track.
“We do have a little bit of a timing and cadence to what we do,” said Michelle. “There have been times along the way, here and there, where someone else has filled in for Chris or someone has filled in for me, and the timing is always off. … We have built up a bit of a cadence to what we do so that I know when to deliver information and when not to.”
Public address announcers like the Cifellis add to the atmosphere at high school football games across the state. Their voices boom over the loudspeakers, keeping fans informed and shining a spotlight on the players on the field. Each brings a unique style to the booth. All play a role in the operation of high school football games across Maine.
“There’s so many different styles of how people do (announcing),” Chris said. “Sometimes it’s a ‘Whoever’s willing to take the mic’ and there’s other people that hang around for 20 plus years.”
‘AN EASY DATE NIGHT’
The Cifellis are the husband-wife duo responsible for the public address announcements during Leavitt football games.
He’s the announcer, she’s his spotter. Up in the booth, they work together to provide information to fans, like which player caught the ball, which player made the tackle, what yard-line the ball is on or how many yards to go until a first down.
“We joke that it’s kind of an easy date night for us,” Chris said. “At least four times a season, we get to do something on a Friday or Saturday evening together, and you get out, you see people that you maybe haven’t seen, or go to homecoming and there are kids that played years ago or even were just students and it’s kind of neat to see that.”
Chris, who teaches psychology at Leavitt, thinks he’s been calling games since 1999. Michelle joined him in 2009.
“Chris has former students whose kids are now on the field … they’ll see us sort of walking out after a game or they will come up and say hello at halftime or something like that because they know that it’s him and they remember him in high school and now their kid is the one on the field,” Michelle said.
PROVIDE THE INFORMATION
Some announcers and spotters, like the Cifellis, have held their positions for years, becoming staples at their respective high schools.
Don Atkinson, for example, who also serves as the Maine Principals’ Association’s tennis tournament director, has been Deering’s announcer since 2001.
The thorough manner with which he recaps each play after it’s whistled dead has become synonymous with Rams football over the last two and a half decades.
“I’m privileged that it’s kind of passed down that the kids that play, a lot of them call me ‘the voice,’” Atkinson said. “They probably don’t have a clue what my name is, which is fine, but they’ll go, ‘Hey, it’s the voice.’ And that’s cool, because I do football, basketball and baseball at Deering, so there’s a lot of kids that hear me three seasons.”
Even though he’s the one announcing games at Memorial Stadium, Atkinson said a spotter is paramount to success. His spotter, Michael Atkins, coaches the Deering girls basketball team.
“(Atkins has) got the number, the information,” Atkinson said. “I could announce the game from home based on what he’s feeding me for information.”
NEWCOMERS ON THE SCENE
Other announcers are newer to the gig. Jeremy Bullock started calling games at Gardiner full time this season. He replaced longtime announcer Sam Shaw.
“(Announcing) was something I was just sort of interested in, and I think I called a couple games for our youth program, which I’ve been the president of that for a few years at this point,” Bullock said. “And it just seemed like it was something that would be fun and I kind of just did my best Sam Shaw impression.
“And then word kind of got around that, ‘Oh, Jeremy does an all right job.’ And then when Sam was talking about retiring, I got asked if I wanted to try it out full time.”
Bullock played for the Tigers and graduated from Gardiner in 2001. His oldest son, Evan, is a senior and played for the Tigers this fall.
“It’s definitely a thrill when Evan makes a big play on defense … when he makes a big tackle or a sack or something like that; always proud to announce his name over the intercom.”
Sam Stolkner started calling middle school football games in 2023. He saw an advertisement for an announcer opening at Lisbon on Facebook, and originally pitched the gig to his friends as a joke.
“I asked my friends like, ‘Oh, should I do this as a joke? This would be funny, right?’” Stolkner said. “… I was like, ‘Yeah, I doubt they’ll pick me, but I’ll do it.’”
What started as a joke three years ago has blossomed into a second career of sorts for the banking analyst.
Stolkner, who now has his own announcer social media page featuring video clips from the games he’s called, calls a variety of high school and college sports all over the state. He has been the PA announcer for Lisbon varsity football games since 2024 and had the opportunity to work a Division III football game between Colby and Amherst on Oct. 17.
“It’s just snowballed out of control where I’m reaching out to teams, but at this point, teams I’ve never (contacted) … I didn’t think I was good enough to do Colby, and they reached out to me, which was crazy,” Stolkner said.

title: Tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee sentenced
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee was sentenced in San Francisco on Tuesday to 16 years to life to prison.
A jury in December 2024 found Nima Momeni guilty of second-degree murder, rejecting the defendant’s claim that he had acted in self-defense. He has remained in custody since his arrest nine days after the April 4, 2023, killing.
Before imposing the sentence, San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon rejected Momeni’s request for a new trial. His attorneys have said they plan to appeal.
Members of Lee’s family addressed the court on Tuesday, including his 18-year-old daughter, Scout Lee, who spoke directly to Momeni.
“You did not just end his life, you ended an entire future built around a man,” she told Momeni, according to media reports.
Momeni, wearing an orange jail jumpsuit, maintained that he acted in self-defense. He told Lee’s family that he understood their loss.
“Unfortunately, we have completely different understandings of what transpired,” Momeni said.
Lee, a renowned tech mogul, was found staggering on a deserted downtown street, dripping a trail of blood and calling for help. Lee, 43, later died at a hospital.
Prosecutors said Momeni planned the attack on Lee, driving him to an isolated spot under the Bay Bridge and stabbing him three times, including once to the heart, with a knife he took from his sister’s kitchen. They said Momeni was angry with Lee for introducing his younger sister to a drug dealer she says gave her GHB and other drugs and then sexually assaulted her.
But Momeni testified on the stand that Lee was the one who attacked him with a knife, angry after the tech consultant chided him about spending more time with his family instead of searching for a strip club that night. Momeni, who studies martial arts, said he didn’t realize he had fatally wounded Lee or that Lee was even hurt.
Lee had created mobile payment service Cash App and was the chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin when he died. He had recently moved to Miami from the San Francisco Bay Area, where his ex-wife Krista Lee lives with their two children, and had returned to California for a visit.
Jurors in the end rejected a charge of murder in the first degree, which required prosecutors prove that Momeni acted deliberately, willfully and with premeditation. Murder in the second degree does not require premeditation.

title: World War I veteran finally laid to rest 45 years after death
text:
RANDOLPH CENTER, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - On a typical day at the Vermont Veterans Memorial Cemetery, the only sound on these hallowed grounds is an American flag flapping in the gentle breeze and birds chirping from a distance.
“It is definitely interesting,” said Collin Johnson, who makes sure the Randolph Center cemetery’s grounds stay pristine for the over 6,000 veterans and their spouses who are buried there.
Ducharme bought Clifford’s Funeral Home last year. Everything came with the business, including a basement with rows of cremated remains.
“The family didn’t pick up, or there was no one to take care of the matter,” Ducharme said.
One caught Ducharme’s attention -- Mr. Irwin. Very little was known about the man other than he was born in New Jersey in 1897 and served during World War I. Why he came to Vermont or if he had any living relatives to collect his ashes remains a mystery.
He died in a nursing home in Rutland. Irwin was just days away from turning 84.
For over a year, Ducharme became a desktop detective, dealing with different government agencies.
“They did come up with his right Social Security number, his right VA file number, the right date of birth, but the name was wrong,” Ducharme said. “It was frustrating, it was very frustrating for sure.”
It took over a year before everything matched up.
“We could not find any family members left; we couldn’t even find any close friends,” Ducharme said.
The word, though, got out about Private Irwin’s saga. Elaine Manghi-Buck heard the news at her church. “I’m here to honor this veteran,” said the Brookfield woman. “It seems to be important to be here.”
The Combat Veterans Motorcycle Association also roared in for the service after hearing the news at their American Legion.
“Yes, yes, it’s remarkable, we’re honored to be here,” said the association’s Ed Barton.
Total strangers treated Private Irwin like family. What was going to be a simple service at the grave site moved into the chapel.
“He has been on a bit of a journey for a long time. He’s a World War I veteran, and it’s our great pleasure to find him a final resting place,” said Robert Burke with Vermont Veterans Affairs.
“This is what we do, we show up for each other,” said Chris Noble, the deacon of Our Lady of the Valley Church. “Most of you, maybe all of us, didn’t even know him. But we know what he stood for, and we know what he did. And we honor that service.”
“We don’t know a lot about him, but as the deacon said, he was a human being,” said United Church of Bethel Rev. Tom Harty. “We ask you to grant him everlasting peace.”
“Thank you for your service, and sorry that it took so long to get you where you needed to be,” Ducharme said.

title: Tremont Select Board approves new pickup truck for fire department
text:
TREMONT — In an effort to replace aging equipment, the Select Board unanimously approved the purchase of a new pickup truck for the Tremont Volunteer Fire Department.
The department requested approval to purchase a 2027 Ford F-350 Super Duty for $67,744. The truck will replace an older truck and comes equipped with updated safety features, including a backup camera and larger display, along with running boards.

title: Portland gallery exhibit teems with Monhegan Island’s artistic magic
text:
If you’ve never visited Monhegan Island, about a dozen nautical miles off the coast of Maine, you are missing one of the most quintessentially “Maine” experiences there is. In its four-and-a-half square miles, it packs in an abundance of features we associate with the state: a working fishing village, vertigo-inducing cliffs that plunge beneath crashing waves 160 feet below, Cathedral Woods where hikers improvise “fairy houses” using materials foraged from the forest, the arching flight paths of gulls.
And, of course, art. Monhegan has been a thriving artist colony since the mid-1800s. Its dramatic landscapes, golden light and abundance of natural and human subject matter has attracted, among others, James Fitzgerald, George Bellows, Rockwell Kent, Edward Hopper, Jamie Wyeth, Lynne Mapp Drexler and countless others. During the summer season, the lighthouse and outbuildings presiding at its highest point, now the Monhegan Island Museum of Art and History, presents exhibits of all these artists and many others.
But one reason to rejoice in “The Monhegan Show” at Pearl Gallery in Portland (through Dec. 18) is because exhibitions devoted to contemporary art of Monhegan are rare. The Monhegan Museum’s policy is to only exhibit non-living artists. Yet painters have not stopped coming here. Singling out living artists for exhibition is, of course, a political hot potato within a small island community, so the “no living artists” policy skirts the controversy.
That leaves most of us piecing together the current vibrancy of the island’s art community through individual and disparate exhibitions where a painting or two of Monhegan by an artist or two who visited there might occasionally appear. If you’ve had no experience of it, then Monhegan’s significance — and its magical quality — are lost on you.
The Pearl Gallery exhibition does an admirable job of trying to rectify this situation. Owners Gary Perlmutter, M.D., and Rhonda Pearle have summered on Monhegan for over 20 years. Perlmutter, an orthopedic surgeon, is also a painter, as is his wife, Pearle. In the early days, they used to paint with Don Stone, a modern impressionist painter who died in 2015 (and is represented here by a few paintings, most resplendently the golden-hued “First Light Manana” of the island across the channel from Monhegan). The couple has assembled 27 artists — all but six still actively working — to give us a snapshot of what is happening there today.
The show grounds us with work by deceased painters from past generations of Monhegan artists. There is a wonderful watercolor “Mariners” by James Fitzgerald (1899-1971), the oldest work in the show. It exhibits all the qualities we’ve come to admire from this painter: the simplified forms, large areas of white space, the chalky palette. Yolanda Fusco’s (1920-2009) “Gull Rock” depicts this marine landmark as a mound of multicolored blocky forms. It’s an abstraction that would have paired beautifully with living artist Bruce Kornbluth’s “Gull Pond,” which essentially composes his watercolor in the same way, except that he outlines the forms in black ink, giving his picture the stained-glass quality of a Georges Rouault painting.
But Fusco’s oil-on-canvas is downstairs in the coffee shop, while the Kornbluth resides on the second floor. Bruce Kornbluth, of course, is the son of Frances Kornbluth (1920-2014), who is represented nearby with two abstract landscapes in her late 1980s-early 1990s style (my guess since there are no dates on works, unfortunately). She spent 57 summers in Monhegan, studying under Reuben Tam, William Kienbusch and Robert Richenburg (none of whom are in the show). By the date of this painting, she had developed a style that subtly segmented the surface into bands or, like Richard Diebenkorn, fractured it into prisms. It is interesting to juxtapose her linearity with her son’s more rounded, organic forms.
There are other family connections here. The actor Zero Mostel (1915-1977), who used to joke that he acted so he could afford to paint, is represented by “Aspects of the Moon,” a very atypical work that looks almost like a pastel-colored Paul Klee. Mostel’s palette was usually as bold and brash as his personality. One wonders whether he was experiencing a rare moment of peace and serenity when he painted “Aspects.” His son Josh Mostel, also an actor, offers two ink-and-colored-pencil works on paper of fleshy pink nudes, which are cropped to focus on torsos and limbs of the women’s bodies. They are lighthearted and not at all influenced — at least not apparently — by his father’s work.
Tobias Mostel, however, is one of the show’s revelations. He presents two watercolors (my favorite is “Monhegan Forest Afternoon”). They are almost completely abstract, save for vaguely discernible forms of trees. I say vague because they are easy to miss amidst the restless cacophony of brush strokes. Hundreds of quick jots in prismatic colors make the work feel electrically charged. Though Zero also flirted with this dance between abstraction and representation, he was too fond of the figure to go this far. These made me want to see more of this Mostel’s work.
Another Zero connection is Perlmutter’s oil-on-linen, “Zero’s Trinkets.” He and Pearle have often rented out the house where Zero lived (now home to Josh). Perlmutter assembles still-life paintings from groupings of objects he finds on the shelves. This one, like much of Perlmutter’s work, is charming. But it is also executed with considerable skill, which keeps the essentially kitsch character of the objects in check.
Pearle is known to folks who pass by the H.H. Hay Building on Congress Street as a painter of expressionistic barn fowl and huge poppies with fairy-like beings hanging from their petals, which she hangs in the windows of the building. Judging by the two paintings in this show, she would do well to refocus her attention on landscape. Her “View from Mostel House” is a truly lovely painting that gets the spirit of that landscape exactly right. But “Wind Through the Trees” in the coffee shop reminded me of the landscapes of Carl Sprinchorn. Vividly colored with energetic brushwork, it makes the phenomenon of wind coming off the water and blowing the trees into a leftward sweep come alive.
Other highlights are two paintings that reenact the rituals of the island — one of which is bidding farewell to visitors at the ferry dock (often your host brings wildflowers picked from the island for you to throw overboard as the boat pulls away, which supposedly assures you will return). Alison Hill’s version of this is one of the most resonant paintings in the exhibition. We feel the heat of the sun on the bodies of the young people gathered there. It is perfectly composed, with the boat out of sight, but the slightly sad feeling of farewell lingering in the golden light.
Stan Moeller’s appreciation of the everyday life of the island is apparent in two wonderful paintings: “Novelty/Evening Light,” which shows a woman in an apron behind the counter of the popular store, and “Table for Four,” which captures a busy night at the restaurant of the Island Inn, which Moeller fills with that very particular low, slanting glow that makes one feel that everything in the world is perfect. Both are evocatively painted and feel at once unremarkable as subjects, yet entirely essential to this special place.
There is, of course, much more. Those who have spent a fair amount of time on the island will feel longing for the woozy, magical spell Monhegan invariably casts, especially in high season. But what the show asserts — aside from its sense of summer’s warmth and abundance mixed with the melancholy that descends as it passes into fall — is that these scenes are not preserved in amber. The island is a constancy and a locus. Yes, Edward Hopper and George Bellows came here years ago. But the painters never stopped coming, never got tired of taking a new stab at the view of Fish Beach or Manana across the water. It is still very much a living, breathing inspiration. These paintings will make you want to visit.
Jorge S. Arango has written about art, design and architecture for over 35 years. He lives in Portland and can be reached at [email protected]. This column is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.
“The Monhegan Show” Pearl Gallery, 594 Congress St., Portland. Through Dec. 18. Thurs.-Sat., 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. or by appointment. For more, 207-712-9499 or pearlgallerymaine.com

title: These key races remain too early to call one week after Election Day
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The size of Democrats’ majorities in the House and Senate remained undetermined one week after Election Day as more than a dozen races were still too early to call Tuesday.
Democrats are on track to hold 54 Senate seats in January, but could pick up one or two more from Republicans as votes are counted in Alaska and Mississippi. With 255 seats in the House, Democrats will have their largest majority elected to the chamber since 2008, with the potential to pick up several more seats as the remaining races are called.
Here’s a look at where things stand in some of the uncalled races:
Mississippi’s Senate seat remains too early to call
Late in the afternoon Tuesday, Democrat Scott Colom was about 2,600 votes ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for Senate in Mississippi.
There are two key deadlines in the vote-counting process in Mississippi this week: Mail-in absentee ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday.
It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count.
Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, Associated Press journalists and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.
The state will certify its results on Dec. 3.
On Monday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said about 14,200 provisional ballots had been processed, of which about 80% were accepted, and about 2,700 mail-in absentee ballots had not yet been returned.
Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is eligible for a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
The vote count is ongoing in Alaska’s Senate race
Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 votes in Alaska’s Senate race on Tuesday afternoon, with an estimated 76% of the vote counted. The results of some absentee ballots are expected to be released late Tuesday, though the final absentee ballots mailed back from outside the U.S. are accepted as late as Nov. 18, 15 days after Election Day.
Ranked choice voting could also affect the timeline. Peltola is just over 1 percentage point short of the majority needed to win outright. If neither candidate wins a majority, the race will proceed to ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18. The state’s “target date” for certifying the election results is Nov. 25.
Recounts in Alaska are automatic only in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request a recount within five days of the state’s certification.
More than a dozen House races are still up in the air
In most of the House races that have not been called, the margin between the leading candidates was less than 1 percentage point among votes counted as of late Tuesday afternoon.
In North Carolina, four races remain undecided, the most of any state, and Republican incumbents were being challenged in all. There are no automatic recounts in North Carolina, but candidates may request a recount if the margin between candidates is 1% or less of the total votes. The state must receive the recount request by noon Eastern time Nov. 17, two business days after the county canvass in the state. The state is scheduled to certify its results Nov. 24.
In California, only one of the remaining House races, in the 23rd District, will affect the chamber’s balance of power. The other uncalled race is between two Democrats. Mail ballots must be received by Tuesday and counties must certify their results Dec. 3. The state will certify its results Dec. 11.
In South Carolina’s 2nd District, a recount is ongoing in the race between Republican incumbent Joe Wilson and Democrat Zyon Khalia. Wilson led Khalia by only about 3,000 votes in the original tally by late Tuesday afternoon, when 99% of the votes had been counted.
In Minnesota’s 1st District, the race was still undecided late in the afternoon Tuesday, with about 300 votes separating the top two candidates and an estimated 99% of votes counted. Recounts are not automatic in Minnesota, but a candidate can request a publicly-funded recount if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is less than 0.25% of the vote.
In Tennessee’s 4th District, about 300 votes lay between Democrat Victoria Broderick and Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais as of late afternoon Tuesday. In that state, recounts are held only as part of a legal challenge in the courts. There are no automatic recounts, and losing candidates may not request recounts.
Two governorships remain undecided
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher led state Republican Senate President Ty Masterson in the race for governor of Kansas by less than 1 percentage point late Tuesday afternoon. On Nov. 4, the state announced that a close-race audit of election results requiring a hand count of selected ballots had been triggered in six close Kansas races, including the gubernatorial race. The audit must be completed before Nov. 16, the day by which counties must certify their results.
In the race for governor of Alaska, only about 76% of votes were estimated to had been counted late Tuesday afternoon, and the Democratic candidate, Jonathan S. Kreiss‑Tomkins, was leading Bernadette M. Wilson by about 45,000 votes, 49.6% to 28.9%. The race will advance to ranked choice tabulation if no candidate receives more than 50% of votes.
