title: Obituary: John S. Marr
text:
FALMOUTH – John Marr, 95, of Falmouth, passed away peacefully at his home on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026.
Born in Portland on November 7, 1931, John was the son of the late Sherman and Anna (Meskill) Marr..
John grew up in South Portland where he was a member of the state championship finals basketball team and continued his playing career at Bowdoin College where he majored in Biology. In 1955 he began a long career in technology with a position at IBM, an assignment as a Naval officer during the Korean War, and later as Founder and President of Process Inc. which later became MUNIS.
John and his beautiful wife, Josephine, moved back to Maine in 1962 and settled on Falmouth Foreside which became the centerpiece for generations of family gatherings; card games, birthday parties by the pool, and lively conversations by the fire. Later in life, after Josephine was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s Disease, John became a philanthropist and advocate for Alzheimer’s research, as well as countless people and causes in need.
John was predeceased by his beloved wife, Josephine Patricia (Morris) Marr; his parents, Sherman and Anna Marr; his sisters, Mary McGarry and Joanne Marr; and his grandson, Patrick John Marr.
He is survived by his five children, Elizabeth Savasuk and her husband, Michael; John S. Marr Jr. and his wife, Rebecca; Timothy C. Marr and his wife, Jamie; William M. Marr and his wife, Lisa; and Abigail Psyhogeos and her husband, George. He is also survived by his grandchildren, Michael, Kathryn, John, Stephanie, Andrea, Jennifer, Molly, Charlie, Matthew, Meghan, Anna, Olivia, Mary, and Peter; and 14 great-grandchildren.
Visiting hours will be held on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, from 4-7 p.m., at the new Conroy-Tully Walker Cremation, Funeral and Gathering Center, 300 Allen Avenue, Portland. A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, at 11 a.m., at Holy Martyrs Church, 266 Foreside Road, Falmouth. Burial will follow at Pine Grove Cemetery in Falmouth.
The family would like to express its heartfelt gratitude to Patti Bruce whose kindness, patience, and friendship has meant so much to Papa and our entire family.
Arrangements are under the direction of Conroy Tully-Walker Cremation, Funeral and Gathering Center, 300 Allen Avenue Portland. To view John S. Marr’s Memorial Page or to share an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.
In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to support the Josephine and John Marr Alzheimer’s Research Fund at Mass General Brigham. Contributions may be made online at fundraise.massgeneralbrigham.org/JohnMarrSr or by mailing a check to Mass General Brigham Development Office, Attn: Gift Administration, 399 Revolution Drive, Suite 1330, Somerville, MA 02145. For donations through a donor-advised fund or other giving methods, please email [email protected].

title: Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed says he would vote for ‘Trumpcare’ for all
text:
(Gray News) - Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, said Tuesday that he supports “cradle-to-grave” healthcare and would vote for “Trumpcare” for all.
El-Sayed made the comments in an interview with CNN anchor and chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins.
“Donald, if you’re watching, we can put your name on it. I know you like to put your name on stuff. You can finally meet the unmet promise in America to guarantee everybody healthcare, so it’s on the table if you want to do it,” he said.
El-Sayed said he wants everyone to have healthcare in America and what it is called is a secondary issue.
“If we’re able to guarantee everybody cradle-to-grave coverage without a co-pay, a premium, or deductible ... I think that would be a win. So if he wants to call it Trumpcare for all, like, I’m game,” he said.

title: Former Bangor mayor’s historic downtown home available for $1.1M
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A historic Bangor home, once considered “among the finest” in the city, is for sale for the first time in half a century.
Located at 50 Broadway near the intersection of State Street and Broadway, the stately Colonial Revival-style home offers more than 4,200 square feet of living space.
The home holds more than a dozen rooms, including five bedrooms and four bathrooms, according to Jan Currier of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Northeast Real Estate, the listing agent for the property.
With an asking price of $1.1 million, the property has already garnered interest from prospective buyers after hitting the market early last month, Currier said.
Designed by renowned architect Wilfred Mansur, the home was built around 1911 on the site of another property owned by a local pastor. That home was destroyed in Bangor’s Great Fire of 1911, Currier said.
Arthur Chapin, a relative of John Adams, the second president of the United States, commissioned the home. Chapin was known locally for opening a successful grocery store, Arthur Chapin & Co., on Broad Street. Born in 1855, Chapin also served as Bangor’s mayor from 1899 to 1901, according to the Bangor Historical Society.
Bangor Daily News records from 1911 describe the Chapin House as “among the finest residences of its kind in Bangor.”
The home was most recently owned by Dr. Moshe Myerowitz, who both lived in and operated his chiropractic practice there. The floor-to-ceiling cabinets in the butler’s pantry still hold labels from the spices and various homeopathic remedies he used to treat patients, Currier said.
This prior use makes it well-equipped to serve as a home office or private practice again, or be transformed into a studio space. The property’s size also lends itself to becoming a multigenerational family home or a rental property, Currier said.
Other interested parties have reimagined it as a small assisted living facility, as the home is already set up to hold live-in caretakers, Currier said. There are accessible entrances, and the grand central staircase has a chairlift installed by the previous owner.
“There are a lot of possibilities because of its location, and it has a ton of parking, which is unusual,” Currier said.
The home sits in the city’s Broadway Historic District, which dictates how the home can be maintained and updated over time to ensure it maintains its historic appearance and integrity.
The home is filled with built-in shelving and storage, along with several century-old features, including a dumbwaiter and working call buttons that once alerted staff when residents needed help.
Other charming features, believed to be original to the house, include light fixtures, solid wood doors and crystal doorknobs, according to Currier.
Aside from the home’s soaring ceilings and many original features, Currier said she’s most captivated by the natural beauty and quality of the home.
“You don’t hear much squeaking, but in some of the older houses you’ll hear a lot of squeaking,” Currier said. “It’s very solid, with the quality of those beautiful built-ins.”
The grand home holds two staircases, numerous pocket doors, four fireplaces, at least three entrances and an enclosed sun porch. There are also some modern touches, including updated windows and heat pumps, Currier said.
The building’s sprawling attic and walk-out basement, which once acted as a root cellar and laundry area, offer additional storage space, Currier said.
Outside, there’s a small parking lot and spacious deck on the south side of the house. A driveway on the home’s north side leads to a detached carriage house that offers additional storage for a vehicle or other equipment. That outbuilding was recently rebuilt following a fire in January, Currier said.
It’s also rumored Theodore Roosevelt gave a speech on the home’s front parapet overlooking Broadway, though there’s no known record of such an event, she said.

title: South Portland schools vote down AI moratorium
text:
The South Portland School Board voted down a temporary moratorium of generative AI use for kindergarten through eighth grade students on Monday.
Many school board members said that artificial intelligence is a pressing matter for educators and policy makers to reckon with, but they said they trust the administration’s plan to develop sensible policy recommendations.
The AI steering committee will present its findings to the board in January, including guidelines, ethics language, examples of expected and prohibited use, and charts delineating different options for different age groups, according to Andy Wallace, the technology director.
“Things have to change,” Wallace said. “This is a huge moment in education.”
Claire Holman, who brought forth the motion, was the only board member who voted in support of a moratorium, calling the issue “an emergency.” Member Daniel Feller was absent.
Superintendent Angela Atkinson Duina said she feels confident in educators’ judgment and has faith in the steering committee’s work. She said board members should feel empowered to provide guidance to the committee.
School Board Member Tyler Smith said it would be an overstep for the board to disregard the advice it’s hearing from specialists like Wallace and educators who are working with the technology on a daily basis.
“We don’t know enough about what’s going on in these classrooms to make a decision,” he said.
A few teachers and school librarians shared how the temporary moratorium would have directly interfered with their planned curriculum.
Cidney Mayes, a librarian at the middle school, said that the last four weeks of her course is dedicated to AI. She walks students through how it works, the pros and cons and the environmental impacts.
“My job is not to tell kids what to think about it,” she said. “My job is to give them the critical thinking skills to make the decisions for themselves about what they think about AI.”
By requiring administrative approval for each use, the moratorium would have directly impacted her curriculum, she said.
Sarah Gay, the president of the teacher’s union, said that her bargaining unit did not have enough information or time to prepare a unified statement.
Under the proposed moratorium, all staff members would be required to receive two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training by the end of the school year. Afterward, teachers would only be able to use tools sanctioned by the school district on school-issued devices. No teacher would be required to use student-facing AI.
Some educators who spoke at the board meething said that the district should bring back the technology integration specialist, a position that was cut in the budget a couple of years ago.
Mike McCann, who used to hold that position, said that hands-on support can help teachers decide what appropriate use looks like.

title: Obituary: Daniel J. Crowley Jr.
text:
WESTBROOK – Daniel J. Crowley Jr., 74, affectionately known as “Danny,” unexpectedly passed away on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, at Northern Light Mercy Hospital in Portland.
Born at Bethesda Naval Hospital in Maryland on Dec. 26, 1951, to Daniel J. Crowley Sr. (USMC), and Kathryn T. (McLoon) Crowley, he grew up as a U.S. Marine Corps dependent.
Danny attended many schools in various states, including Castner School in Damariscotta, where he had the same first-grade teacher as his mom, and Lincoln Academy in Newcastle. When he was a sophomore at Lincoln, he worked at Fairfield’s Diner in Damariscotta busing tables and washing dishes, enjoying the paycheck but especially enjoying the best breakfasts as a reward for his work.
Whether attending schools at Camp LeJeune (N.C.), Romulus (N.Y.), or Maine, Danny was active in and excelled at several sports, including football, baseball, basketball, and soccer. Although small in size with the nickname of “Peanut,” he earned several athletic awards and recognitions. Dan graduated high school in 1971 from Romulus Central School in New York and obtained a degree in drafting/design from SUNY Morrisville.
After retiring from the Marine Corps, Kathryn and Dan came home to Damariscotta, then settled in Westbrook, and Danny joined them. He thoroughly enjoyed summer vacations out at Pemaquid Lake in Damariscotta with his family and friends. Danny truly looked forward to those times when he would play cards and more recently tussle with Teagan the cat over who would get the best chair first at camp.
Danny was employed at Nichols Portland, Inc. Technologies in Portland as a mechanical designer for many years before retiring. While there, his colleagues became friends and continued to keep in touch by playing golf, gathering for breakfast, and participating in football pools. Danny’s ability to analyze team stats and his knowledge of sports usually placed him at the top of the winnings. He was a fan of the Boston Red Sox, Boston Bruins, Boston Celtics, and the … Indianapolis Colts -What!!?? He was also a huge history buff, especially of the civil war, and had researched his great-grandfather’s role in the Union army.
Danny was predeceased by his parents; uncles, James, Charles “Shike” (Irma), Joseph Charles, George (Dana), Joseph Bernard, and Arthur “Doug” McLoon, and aunts, Florence McLoon, Clara Horie (Everett) and Ruth House (Calvin).
He is survived by his uncle and aunt, John and Martha Cannon of Rochester, N.H.; brother Timothy W. Crowley, of Westbrook; sister and brother-in-law, Sheila and Michael Clements, of Augusta; their son Matthew Clements and his children, Julian, Landon, and Taylor; aunt Mary Jane McLoon; and several much-beloved cousins.
Relatives and friends are invited to join the family on Saturday, November 21, for a time of visitation from 12:30-1 p.m., with a service to follow at 1 p.m., at Strong-Hancock Funeral Home in Damariscotta.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main Street, Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences, and messages for his family, may be expressed by visiting: http://www.StrongHancock.com.
Should friends and family desire, please consider donating to the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland, PO Box 336, Westbrook, ME 04098 (www.arlgp.org/memorial); or to the Marine Corps Reserve Toys for Tots at (https://www.toysfortots.org).

title: Police arrest son of actors Antonio Sabàto Jr., Virginia Madsen in fatal hit-and-run
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - Police in Alaska arrested a 32-year-old Anchorage man in connection with a deadly hit-and-run crash on Monday morning.
Crash details
Charging documents state that 32-year-old Jack Sabàto was driving a white Chevrolet Tahoe when he hit a pedestrian near the intersection of Airport Heights Drive and DeBarr Road at 5:35 a.m. Monday.
The pedestrian was identified as Carl Simmonds, according to charging documents.
Simmonds was the ninth pedestrian hit and killed by a vehicle in Anchorage this year.
Suspect’s family
Sabàto is the son of Antonio Sabàto Jr., a “General Hospital” actor, and Virginia Madsen, an actress known for her roles in movies like “Candyman,” “Sideways” and “A Prairie Home Companion.”
Madsen’s brother Michael Madsen was also an actor whose film credits included “Reservoir Dogs” and “Kill Bill: Volume 2.”
How police identified the vehicle
Police responded to the scene of Monday’s hit-and-run around 5:48 a.m.
Police recovered video of the collision from the Blood Bank of Alaska and were able to identify the car. They traced the vehicle registration to Sabàto’s home address, where a neighbor confirmed his place of work.
At 12:45 p.m., police located a Tahoe parked at the workplace that had “fresh damage to the right front corner that was consistent with a pedestrian strike,” according to the charging document. After obtaining a warrant, police seized the car.
Statement to police
At 2:46 p.m., Sabàto called police saying he hit an animal with his Tahoe and wanted to talk to officers, according to the charging documents. He told officers that he was on his way home after “doing late night Door Dashing” when he turned onto the road by the hospital. He said that “’something’ suddenly appeared in the road” and his headlights went out.
The charging documents state that Sabàto knew he hit “something” but didn’t want to check because he was scared that he did not have insurance. He also allegedly told police he called them because he “knew the worst.”
Charges and court
Sabàto was arrested and sent to the Anchorage Correctional Complex on charges of leaving the scene of an accident without assisting the injured and leaving the scene of an accident that resulted in injury or death.
Sabàto was arraigned in court Tuesday afternoon at the Anchorage Jail Courtroom.

title: More than 200 turkeys to be given away in Wells
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 200 turkeys to be given away in Wells
More than 200 turkeys to be given away in Wells
Hot Radio Maine, Channel 8 WMTW and other local partners are coming together to give away more than 200 turkeys to Maine families ahead of Thanksgiving.
Beginning at 11 a.m. on Nov. 24, the Tuesday before Thanksgiving, families can pick up a free turkey at the IGA in Wells, no questions asked.
The program has been running for 14 years and is headed by program director and Hot Radio Maine morning show host Ryan Deelon.
"We wanted to do something to give back to the community, and we know it can be expensive around the holidays. So we decided to do a free turkey drive and hand out free turkeys to those in need."
Deelon said families are limited to one turkey, but this year, more donations have come in, so folks can also walk away with traditional Thanksgiving sides.
Deelon added that oftentimes they will see those who are picking up for others who might not be able to make it the day of the giveaway.
"We had a couple lunch ladies last year that I think had some parents at the school where they work for that needed some help. And we made sure we delivered them turkeys," recalled Deelon.
According to Deelon, the turkeys go fast. He expects the first 100 turkeys to go in the span of the first 30 minutes.

title: A roadmap for Democrats who want peace in Gaza
text:
Daniel Kagan of Freeport is a retired trial attorney with 37 years of practice.
The midterm elections are over. It is time to govern.
In your campaigns, many of you prioritized ending Gazan suffering. Here is how you can get there.
Start by stating publicly that the time for incendiary campaign rhetoric is over. It has been painful and divisive and will get in the way of finding solutions. Admit both of these truths: that Hamas committed horrific atrocities against Israeli civilians on Oct. 7, 2023, and that Gaza’s civilian population has suffered greatly with Israel’s military response. And stop describing these truths with accusatory and divisive language that hardens each side’s resistance to progress toward peace. Then you get to the hard part.
Lasting security in the Middle East requires physical security, political stability and economic success for its people. Gaza, at present, has none of these. Peace requires that the Gazan people have a meaningful opportunity to build for themselves a viable economy, political stability and a thriving middle class with a personal stake in peace. It also requires that Gaza present no military or terrorist threat to Israel.
We know this can be accomplished. Egyptian/Israeli hostilities ended 47 years ago and that peace has held. To achieve that peace, Israel agreed to turn over all of the Sinai to Egypt. If it worked in Egypt, it can work in Gaza.
We know Israel will agree to it; it already did, once. Twenty-one years ago, in September 2005, consistent with an explicit objective of American foreign policy, Israel withdrew from Gaza. Israel removed all its settlements in Gaza and withdrew its military forces. It did so because it expected that the international community would help Gaza dedicate itself to its own economic development and self-sufficiency for its people.
The United States helped make Israel’s withdrawal happen. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice embraced the initiative and called for international support to “revitalize the Palestinian economy.” In November, after helping negotiate the Agreement on Movement and Access, she explained its purpose: “This agreement is intended to give Palestinian people the freedom to move, to trade, to live ordinary lives.” An international initiative led by former World Bank president James Wolfensohn envisioned for Gaza agricultural development, expanded trade, improved transportation and access to foreign markets.
It was an extraordinary opportunity, and it could have worked. But Hamas thwarted it. The chronology is revealing.
September 2005: Israel completed its withdrawal of settlers and permanent military forces from Gaza.
November 2005: Israel and the Palestinian Authority reached concrete agreements on commerce, transportation and development (the Agreement on Movement and Access).
January-April 2006: Hamas wins Palestinian legislative elections. It formed a government that refused to honor its agreements with Israel, and refused to either recognize Israel or renounce using violence against it. In response, the United States and its partners in the peace initiative backed off on its commitment of financial support since it would go to the Hamas-led government. The fragile framework toward peace disintegrated, and armed conflict flared once again.
June 2007: Hamas’ brutal battle with Fatah, its rival for Palestinian leadership, resulted in Hamas taking exclusive control of Gaza. Gazans became further isolated as both Egypt and Israel tightened their borders with Gaza.
That is how Israel’s 2005 withdrawal from Gaza and movements toward peace with Palestinians failed. So why try again? Because there are lessons to be learned from 2005 about what each party needs for an agreement to endure, and what the United States and its peace partners can do to assure it.
What the United States can do:
Security: Identify and support Gazan leaders committed to ending armed confrontation and prioritize economic development for its people. Work toward Israeli withdrawal by rebuilding trust that America will honor its commitments to Israel as well as Gaza. It worked in Israel’s peace with Egypt and it can work again here.
Economic independence: Establish and provide sustained oversight of an internationally supervised, independently audited development authority, to manage building of infrastructure, private investment, entrepreneurship and employment. Do what America can do best — help Gazans build businesses and avoid long-term reliance on social services in perpetuity.
Commercial opportunity: Create and secure reliable market access for Gazan businesses. Let Gaza compete in the global market on a level playing field. Help it build an airport and a commercial port.
Political accountability: Help Gazans create a legal system with independent courts with the power to check excesses of its legislative bodies. Pursue and support judicially enforced property rights, credible elections, and freedom from intimidation.
These, I suggest, are signposts on the road to peace. Follow them, as they lead away from the hateful and divisive words and slogans that dominated the midterm campaign season. Lasting peace for Gazans can only emerge when serious people holding positions of responsibility focus on pragmatic solutions that Israelis and Gazans can live with.
The campaign is over, and it’s time to do the hard work of crafting solutions.

Veterans Day dates back to Nov. 11, 1918, when the truce between U.S. allies and Germany to end World War I was signed on the 11th day of the 11th month at the 11th hour.
President Woodrow Wilson originally proclaimed it Armistice Day, but in 1954, President Dwight Eisenhower officially renamed it Veterans Day.

title: Historic ocean liner is sunk to make largest artificial reef off Florida’s Panhandle
text:
GULF OF MEXICO (AP) — The historic SS United States, once the fastest ship on the seas, made a slow final journey beneath the waters Wednesday.
The famous ocean liner — which is longer than the Titanic and crossed the Atlantic more than 800 times — was deliberately sunk Wednesday to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico, where the once-luxurious behemoth was set to begin a new chapter as the world’s largest artificial reef.
It was a long goodbye. Hours after the sinking began on a cloudy afternoon, much of the hulking ship could still be seen in the dark waters off the coast of the Florida Panhandle by nightfall. Organizers had predicted the sinking could finish in as quickly as an hour.
Finally, around 9 p.m., the vessel leaned on one side and then quickly submerged.
“She is an amazing lady who will not lay down without a fight,” Coleen O’Malley, president of Coleen Marine, the company sinking the ship, said before the vessel disappeared beneath the water. “Much like the amazing nation she was named after.”
The event — described by officials as a controlled sinking — was a long-planned $13.5 million project aimed at attracting more divers and fishing enthusiasts while creating a home for tuna, marlin and swordfish.
The slower-than-expected descent was partly due to crews filling 128 fuel and lubricant tanks aboard the ship with water so that it would rest evenly on the ocean floor, said Nick Tomecek, a spokesperson for Okaloosa County, which helped organize the sinking. He said the process “took longer than we thought.”
“She’s a big ship,” Tomecek said.
A massive vessel with a long history
The project will keep what had been a technological marvel when it made its maiden voyage in 1952 from becoming scrap metal.
Famous passengers included Hollywood stars like Grace Kelly and Elizabeth Taylor. Other passengers have included Presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy and Britain’s former King Edward VIII. In 1968, a young Bill Clinton took it when he went to Oxford University, decades before he was elected president.
Once aboard, passengers were treated to dinners that included caviar, roast duckling, smoked ox tongue and Calf’s Head en Tortue.
In preparation for the sinking, organizers removed the 65-foot (20-meter) smokestacks and plan to have them anchor a new museum that celebrates the ship.
Explosives were not allowed to be used
Federal environmental and explosives rules prevent Okaloosa County, Florida, and its contractor from using explosives to scuttle the ship, Tomecek said. Concerns about inclement weather prompted officials to move up the sinking by a day.
The SS United States has pipes that pulled seawater into tanks as part of the system that cooled its boilers, he said, and those tanks have been removed so that once the valves are opened, water will flood the hull. Workers also have cut 10-foot by 10-foot (3-meter by 3-meter) holes in the decks, and more than 400 portholes have been removed.
The ship is to sink in about 180 feet (55 meters) of water, with its top deck about 60 feet (18 meters) below the surface — shallow enough that inexperienced divers can visit. It will settle on the floor of the waters about 25 miles (40 kilometers) southwest of Destin, between Panama City and Pensacola.
Larger than the Titanic, the ship set a speed record on its first voyage
More than 3,000 workers helped build the SS United States in 1950 and 1951 in Virginia. An Associated Press reporter and Truman’s daughter, Margaret, were among 1,700 passengers for the first voyage.
The ship’s average speed for that trip was almost 41 mph (66 kph), besting a record set by Britain’s RMS Queen Mary in 1938 by 4.5 mph (7.2 kph), according to the AP’s dispatch.
The SS United States set the record even though its journey ended in the face of a full gale that reached 69 mph (111 kph) — “so strong it blew a ping pong table off the deck,” AP reported.
At 990 feet (302 meters), the ship is 108 feet (33 meters) longer than the ill-fated Titanic, which hit an iceberg and sank on its first voyage across the Atlantic.
“She really embodies and expresses this country’s best,” said Susan Gibbs, the granddaughter of the ship’s designer. “She represents pride and resilience and strength and beauty.”
The ship’s resting place has many artificial reefs
More than 500 artificial reefs are located in the waters near where the SS United States will rest.
Previously, the largest artificial reef came from the 2006 scuttling of an aircraft carrier, the USS Oriskany in the Gulf off Pensacola — near enough to the SS United States site that an experienced diver could visit both in the same day, Tomecek said. The Oriskany, launched in 1950, was 911 feet (278 meters) in length.
“We’re trying to be the best diving destination in the world,” Tomecek said.
The ship was decommissioned in 1969. Attempts by a hotel magnate and Norwegian Cruise Lines to use the ship never floated, and from 1996 until recently, it sat along a dock in Philadelphia.
Tim Mullane, a Navy veteran and chief operating officer of Coleen Marine, called the huge funnels — the smokestacks that have been removed to anchor the new museum — “works of art.”
“I’m just so happy that we are able to save parts of her,” Gibbs said.
___

title: “Return the Favor” campaign encourages consumers to recognize businesses with a positive review
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As the holiday shopping season approaches, Better Business Bureau (BBB) is encouraging consumers to recognize the businesses that have made a difference in their lives. This November, BBB’s Thank a Business Month campaign invites everyone to “Return the Favor” by leaving one honest review for a business they appreciate at BBB.org/thanks. A few minutes of recognition can help a business stand out and give other consumers the confidence to choose it.
Every day, consumers turn to online reviews when searching for a reliable contractor, a neighborhood restaurant or a trusted service provider. Yet, after a great experience, many satisfied customers move on without sharing their feedback. According to BrightLocal’s 2026 research, 74 percent of consumers focus on reviews from the past three months. Although 69 percent wrote a review in the past year, most posted only four to six reviews. The same research found that 83 percent leave a review when asked, showing how a simple reminder can make a difference.
The “Return the Favor” message is simple: think about the reviews that helped you find a good business, then share your own experience so someone else can benefit. The review written this November may be exactly what another customer needs to make a decision in the months ahead. Recent, authentic feedback helps businesses demonstrate the service they provide today, build credibility and reach new customers.
Reviews can also have a meaningful impact on purchasing decisions. Research from the Spiegel Research Center found that products with five reviews were 270 percent more likely to be purchased than products with none. As more consumers use digital and AI-powered tools to discover businesses, current customer feedback can help keep a business’s reputation visible and relevant.
Beyond leaving a review, BBB encourages consumers to keep supporting businesses they trust, recommend them to friends and family, share positive feedback online and shop locally when possible. Businesses can join the effort by inviting satisfied customers to share honest reviews after a positive experience. From local shops to service providers, these businesses help strengthen communities through jobs, services and support for local causes.
This November, take a few minutes to thank a business that earned your trust. Someone else may be counting on your review, just as you have counted on theirs. Return the Favor at BBB.org/thanks.

title: Analysis: UMass series epitomizes UMaine men’s hockey’s close, low-scoring season
text:
This past weekend’s series against the University of Massachusetts at Alfond Arena is a microcosm of what was expected from the University of Maine men’s hockey team this season.
UMass won the opener, 2-1, and UMaine took the second game, 2-0.
The expectation entering the year was that UMaine would be in a lot of close, low-scoring games. The weekend series against UMass marked the fourth and fifth times this season that the Black Bears have been involved in games in which the two teams combined for three goals or less.
UMaine outshot UMass 47-22 the first night and 44-16 the second night.
It should have been a Black Bear sweep, but goals aren’t going to come easy for UMaine.
Remember, UMaine has only three players who have scored more than seven goals in a college season in left wingers Owen Fowler and Tanner Klimpke and center Max Scott.
But you also have to give credit where credit is due and UMass freshman goalie Ethan Eskit was absolutely superb and was deservedly named the Hockey East Rookie of the Week.
It was certainly an encouraging weekend for UMaine when considering how the Black Bears dominated puck possession and offensive zone time.
They consistently swarmed the puck, finished their checks and won the vast majority of the puck battles.
UMass did a good job limiting their high-percentage chances the first night which was one of the keys to its win, but UMaine was able to generate a lot more of them the second night.
“We got outcompeted quite significantly [on Saturday night],” said UMass head coach Greg Carvel. “We didn’t have the puck very much and give Maine all the credit for that.”
That’s how UMaine will have to play in order to win.
UMaine is currently averaging 2.5 goals per game, which is tied for 42nd among 62 Division I schools. It has outshot its opponents in nine of its 10 games by an average of 13.4 shots per game.
Last year’s UMaine team averaged 3.3 goals per game.
But UMaine has been much stingier this season, allowing just 2.1 goals per game compared to last year’s 2.7. It is currently ranked 12th in goals-against average. UMaine has held teams to two goals or fewer six times and has three shutouts.
One way UMaine can amp up its scoring is on the power play and that has been in a funk of late with just one goal in its last 15 opportunities.
UMaine can also benefit from more production from its veterans.
UMaine has five forwards who are in either their third or fourth years playing at UMaine in Owen Fowler, Sully Scholle, Charlie Russell, Thomas Pichette and Oskar Komarov and they have combined for only three goals so far.
Fowler has two of them. Scholle has the other.
Fowler showed his value as a leader by scoring just 19 seconds into Saturday’s win and he has been a constant presence in every game. He sets the tireless work standard and the grit that the team follows.
He may not be a natural goal scorer but he will produce goals through his work ethic, net-front drive and toughness.
He is averaging 19 minutes and 38 seconds of playing time per game which is a high among the forwards and second only to sophomore defenseman Lukas Peterson’s 21:11. Peterson is currently sidelined with an injury.
The newcomers have had an immediate impact, with Robert Morris transfer Tanner Klimpke and UMass Lowell transfer Lee Parks sharing the team scoring lead with second-year Black Bear and Brown University transfer Max Scott. All have eight points. Klimpke and Parks each have registered five goals and three assists. Scott has tallied two goals and six assists.
Klimpke and Parks share the team lead in game-winning goals with two each. Bemidji State transfer Isa Parekh leads the defensemen in points with six on two goals and four assists. Albin Boija has looked like the Albin Boija of two years ago when he was second team All-American. He struggled mightily a year ago.
Boija is minimizing his movement, playing his angles well, tracking the puck and doing a better job hanging onto pucks and not spilling rebounds.
The Black Bears will receive a stern test this weekend when they travel to take on the Hockey East-leading Vermont Catamounts, who are a surprise this year after finishing last in the conference ago. UMaine is 5-5 overall and 1-3 in Hockey East, while UVM is 5-3-1 and 4-1-1. The Catamounts are coming off a sweep of New Hampshire, followed by a win and a tie at Boston College last weekend.
UMaine must continue to outwork its opponents and get to the net front to screen the goalie and score those greasy goals in and around the crease.

title: Long-standing Allagash land dispute will go to 2027 federal trial
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Maine U.S. District Court jury will settle a long-standing property and boundary dispute next June for an Allagash family that has had “adverse possession” of 80 acres of Irving land since 1936.
Joseph P. Kelly, his wife, Manda Kelly, and sister, Cara Merrill, allege in a lawsuit against Allagash Timberlands and other family members that they, as the heirs of John Kelly Sr., have openly worked and possessed the land for 90 years, despite not being the original owners, according to court documents.
It’s not the first land dispute lawsuit filed in this northern Maine town of 237 residents in recent years.
In 2024, 11 community members sued the town following a land swap deal officials made with two residents who had used a small piece of town land near the fire station since 1978. After two lawsuits and a local crusade, the disputed piece of Allagash town land that was lost in the controversial land swap deal was returned to the community last year.
To own land through hostile, adverse possession in Maine, the Kellys must show that they have openly worked the land as if it was their own, knowing it belonged to Irving, for at least 20 years.
The case was originally filed in Aroostook County Superior Court in Caribou, but was transferred to the federal court in April. In late October, Magistrate Judge Karen Frink Wolf ruled that the defendant must disclose experts for the case by Dec. 18, with discovery complete by March 26, 2027, and all parties must be ready for trial on June 3, 2027.
In the current controversy, Allagash Timberlands contends they own the 80 acres in question and have filed a countersuit against all parties. Additionally, other members of the Kelly family — Regina Kelly, Lance Kelly and Taylor Jo Kelly — claim they have the right to possess the parcel.
According to the Joseph P. Kelly heirs’ lawsuit, the family has owned the land through a continuous chain of warranty deeds. Additionally, the disputed boundary has been marked by visible, long-standing monuments and visibly marked lines since at least 1936, including an old red blazed possession line, blazed trees, and other markers that have been visible and maintained by the family for nearly a century.
As Maine law requires, they must demonstrate that they have openly owned and used the land as their property without Irving giving them permission to do so.
The lawsuit cites seven public actions that meet this aspect of the law: They have posted “No Trespassing” signs and applied purple paint on boundary trees; they have blocked access roads annually; blocked access during deer season; constructed a pond on the property; cut wood/timber; hunted on the land; and farmed, worked and maintained it.
In their suit they asked for a jury trial and a court ruling to resolve the controversy, remove the cloud on the title, and confirm their ownership, the federal lawsuit states.
The family asks the court to rule that Joseph P. Kelly owns the disputed property by adverse possession, and that the land and boundary is theirs free and clear of any claim by Irving Pulp & Paper Ltd. or the other Kelly family members noted in the lawsuit.
They have also asked the court to award costs and attorney fees to Kelly.

title: 3 dead after car crashes into people outside Los Angeles metro station during rush hour
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The driver of a minivan that crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station, killing three women and critically injuring two more, was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence and three counts of murder, police said Wednesday.
Authorities said the driver was able to talk but appeared to be in shock after Tuesday’s crash, which hit pedestrians and food vendors at a busy intersection in the North Hollywood neighborhood during the height of the evening commute.
Police identified the driver as Ihor Demianenko, 61, who lives in the Valley Village neighborhood. Demianenko was booked early Wednesday and his bail was set at a little over $6 million, records show. He was treated for minor injuries at a hospital, police said.
It wasn’t immediately clear if Demianenko had a lawyer who might speak on his behalf. In California, drivers under the influence of drugs or alcohol can be charged with murder under certain circumstances.
The case had not been presented to the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office as of Wednesday afternoon, spokesperson Venusse Dunn said in an email.
The white Toyota Sienna was traveling at an “unsafe speed” at around 6 p.m. when it veered to the right, ran off the road and collided with a light, Los Angeles police said in a news release Wednesday. It came to rest under a food vendor’s tent.
The force of the collision threw victims in different directions, according to the news release. The driver was trapped in the vehicle until rescuers arrived.
Luis Luna-Guzman was working at a nearby burger stand when he heard a loud boom and saw people on the ground along with food and cups. People started running toward the crash.
Luna-Guzman said he found an injured woman lying near some bike racks, her face, arms and legs bloody. Her eyes were closed as she moaned in pain.
“I told her, ‘Don’t move, help is coming,’” Luna-Guzman said, adding that he saw a woman’s body nearby, while another woman was lying unmoving on the stairs leading to the station.
The three women who died were between the ages of 40 and 60, according to the police news release. Authorities haven’t released their names. The two injured women are in their 50s.
The minivan was still on the sidewalk Tuesday night under the food vendor’s tent, its driver’s-side door open and an air bag deployed. Fire engines and emergency crews worked nearby as a helicopter flew overhead.
Investigators will go through video of the crash frame by frame, Police Chief Jim McDonnell said.
“It will be probably a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here,” he said.
The California Supreme Court ruled in 1981 that drivers who kill someone with a vehicle can be charged with second-degree murder if they are found to have acted with “wantonness and a conscious disregard for life” that could support a finding of implied malice. The court upheld a prosecutor’s decision to file murder charges against a driver who was determined to be legally intoxicated at the time of a fatal crash and drove at high speeds, ran a red light and had a near miss right before.
___
Thanawala reported from Atlanta.

title: Caribou ceremony honors veterans and teaches children
text:
CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) - Veterans and civilians of all ages stood side by side at the veteran cemetery in Caribou on Veterans Day to honor those who serve. Veterans there said the ceremony was just as important to them as seeing the children who attended.
Chase Cochran, a Boy Scout, was one of many children at the ceremony. As the ceremony ended, the boyscouts ran towards an area where veterans had conducted the 21-rifle salute just moments ago.
“So when they shot the guns, shells came out, and some of the kids wanted to get some,” Cochran said.
Before his friends ran to get shell casings, they stood in the cold and listened as local veterans were honored.
“The younger ones come out, and they get to see, and they look at it as kind of like a role model for the future,” said Paul Watson, District 1 commander of the VFW.
The ceremony was also about teaching the younger generation about what it takes to be a veteran, said Roger Felix, commander of the VFW in Caribou.
“They took the oath, and they continued to march forward because they knew they weren’t doing it for them. They were doing it for the people back home, and if the fire, that drive, dissipates over years, then what do we have?” Felix said.

title: How to speak up for yourself or a loved one during a medical crisis
text:
(Aging Untold) — When you or someone you love is facing a medical crisis, it can be hard to think clearly, let alone know what questions to ask.
The Aging Untold experts share ways to speak up, understand the care plan and help make sure your loved one’s needs and wishes are heard.
Speak up when something doesn’t seem right
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose described advocating for her husband when he was expected to leave the hospital and return later for surgery.
She didn’t think he was ready to go home, so she raised her concerns with a nurse and contacted a social worker. By the time she returned to the hospital, a plan was in place for him to stay.
A couple of days later, she noticed that he seemed to be getting worse rather than better. She brought that concern to a nurse, who began making calls.
Ambrose said the team discovered that her husband was missing a medication and that he improved after receiving it.
“That’s what we mean by advocacy, is paying attention and asking questions and being vocal,” Ambrose said.
If something feels different from your loved one’s usual condition, tell a member of the care team what you’ve noticed and when the change began.
Ask questions until the plan makes sense
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said you don’t have to have medical training to support your family member. It is important to ask questions and support your loved one, she said.
“A story is being told and you should be able to connect the dots to that story,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “And if you can’t, you have to keep asking until you fill in the missing pieces.”
Build a team and know your loved one’s wishes
Advocacy doesn’t mean doing everything alone.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said knowing what you don’t know and where to go to find it is a skill as a medical advocate. You also need to know hospital systems or who can explain them because you’re helping coordinate a discharge plan, she added.
“And know your person, know what you’re advocating for. If you don’t know their values and their priorities, it’s hard to advocate for them,” O’Rourke said.
Keep good records, write things down and keep track so you can share relevant details with the care team when needed, O’Rourke added.
“You’re really just trying to get an understanding too. Yes, we want what’s best, but we also just want to understand. We’re just trying to make sure that things are going the best that they can,” Ambrose said.

title: What to keep out of AI chatbots to protect your personal information
text:
(InvestigateTV) — What you type into an AI chatbot can be stored by the company behind it. Depending on the service and your settings, that information may also be used to train AI.
R.J. Cross, a data privacy advocate with U.S. PIRG, said there are other privacy concerns as well.
Cross pointed to recent cases in which information shared with a chatbot appeared elsewhere online.
“Another risk is that it’s possible information you give a chatbot could be surfaced in other people’s google searches,” Cross said.
That has happened with some shared chatbot conversations. It does not mean private chats automatically become public.
Cross said chatbots sometimes tell users when they sign up that their data will be used for training, but not that it will also be stored.
“Sometimes the chatbots will say when you’re signing up for account, hey, we’re going to use your data for training. But it’s not saying this also means we’re going to store your data on our servers and that could be surfaced in other people’s chats or it could be exposed to hack,” Cross said.
Cross recommends keeping sensitive information out of chatbots, including Social Security numbers, medical information and personal documents.
“You don’t want to give it the highly sensitive stuff that you wouldn’t want ending up in the hands of someone else because using those chatbots come with those risks,” Cross said.
Cross also recommends reviewing a chatbot’s privacy settings and limiting the personal details shared about friends and family.

title: 4 tax perks military families often miss
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Every year, military families leave real money on the table simply because they don’t know which tax breaks apply to them. Service members earn benefits most civilians don’t get — but only if they claim them.
Here, Intuit TurboTax explores four of the most commonly missed tax breaks for service members and their families.
1. Travel expense for reservists
If you are in the National Guard or military reserve, you may be able to deduct your unreimbursed travel expenses. If you travel more than 100 miles from home and are away overnight, you can deduct your lodging, half of the cost of meals (up to per diem rate), mileage, tolls, and parking fees. For 2026, the mileage rate is 72.5 cents per mile through June 30 and 76 per mile from July 1 onward.
2. ROTC payments
If you are a student in the ROTC, you don’t have to pay tax on the allowance that you receive for your participation in advanced training. This rule doesn’t apply to any active duty pay that you receive.
3. Combat pay
The pay you receive for any month that you serve in a combat zone isn’t taxable. If you are a military officer, your tax-free pay may be subject to a cap. But even though your combat pay isn’t taxable, don’t overlook it. You can take that pay into account to qualify for the Earned Income Tax Credit.
4. Moving expenses
If you are on active duty and have moving expenses in connection with a permanent change of station, those moving expenses are deductible if they are not reimbursed to you.
Filing your tax return
If you are serving in a combat zone during tax filing season, you have at least 180 days beyond the traditional April 15 deadline to file your tax return. If you are hospitalized because of injuries you sustained in a combat zone, similar extensions of time to file apply.
If you are serving overseas in a non-combat zone, the April 15 deadline is automatically extended to June 15. If you are a civilian serving in a combat zone, the same rules apply, but you need to write the words “Combat Zone” and your deployment date in red across the top of your tax return.
Military members do not have to make this notation on their tax return. And if you are serving in the military and are not available to sign a joint return, your spouse can sign it under a power of attorney.

title: Son stabs his mom at Target, claims the Illuminati told him to kill her, affidavit says
text:
WACO, Texas (KWTX/Gray News) - A 21-year-old Texas man remains behind bars after stabbing his mother at Target and claiming the Illuminati told him to kill her, according to an arrest warrant affidavit.
Galveston Elijah Vriseno, 21, is accused of stabbing his mother in the neck at Target and claiming the Illuminati told him to do it, an arrest warrant affidavit obtained by KWTX states. He is charged with aggravated assault of a family member causing serious bodily injury.
The Illuminati was a secret society founded in 1776 that is now the subject of conspiracy theories claiming a hidden group controls world events.
Victim found lying next to ‘a pool of blood’
Waco police officers were dispatched to a possible domestic disturbance involving a stabbing at Target around 2:22 p.m. Sunday.
Upon arrival, officers found the victim, Ashley Norwood, lying on the floor next to “a pool of blood.” The affidavit describes a stab wound to the left side of Norwood’s neck.
Bystanders helped the victim sit up when officers arrived. She could not speak at the time, so witnesses provided a description of what Vriseno was wearing at the time of the assault, the affidavit states.
Officers reviewed camera footage of the assault in which they saw Norwood and Vriseno walking around the store’s optical area. The affidavit describes Vriseno stabbing his mother with a knife and running out of the store right after.
Around 4 p.m., officers were informed Vriseno had called police. He was found at a Jack in the Box across the street from Target, wearing the same clothing that witnesses previously described, including a blanket.
When officers found Vriseno, it appeared he was trying to get rid of the blanket and other items witnesses described by throwing them in the trash and washing the blood off his hands, the affidavit states.
After Vriseno was advised of his Miranda rights, the arresting officer asked if the knife in his front left cargo pocket was the weapon he used to stab his mom, and Vriseno admitted it was, according to the affidavit.
Suspect claimed Illuminati told him to kill mother, sister says
Vriseno’s sister called police while they were looking for him and said Vriseno made comments two days earlier that the Illuminati told him to kill his mother and sister.
Norwood was taken to the hospital, where she underwent surgery and is in stable condition, according to her daughter.
Vriseno was being held on a $100,000 bond.
Earlier this year, Vriseno was arrested for allegedly assaulting his pregnant girlfriend after they argued over a car part, according to an arrest warrant. He was charged with assault of a pregnant woman, a third-degree felony.

title: Golden should have endorsed Dunlap
text:
I voted for Rep. Jared Golden in every election in which I was eligible to vote before 2026. I did so despite substantial disagreements with many of his positions, because I believed he was the better choice to represent Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
I know I wasn’t alone. Golden built his political career with the support of voters who didn’t always agree with him but were willing to put those differences aside. That’s why I found his refusal to endorse Matt Dunlap so disappointing.
Nobody was asking Golden to abandon his beliefs or spend his final year in Congress campaigning for Dunlap. A simple endorsement, encouraging the people who trusted his judgment to support the Democratic nominee, would have been enough. Instead, Golden publicly congratulated Paul LePage on his victory without even acknowledging Dunlap.
I reached out to Golden’s political operation asking why he declined to endorse Dunlap. I received no response.
I can’t know what motivated Golden’s decision. But if personal resentment over Dunlap’s primary challenge played a role, I think voters deserve to know that. For years, Golden benefited from people like me putting aside our disagreements to support him. When the opportunity came for him to do the same, he declined.
I don’t expect politicians to agree with me on everything. I do expect them to demonstrate the same willingness to compromise that they ask of their constituents.
Greg Siekman
Auburn

title: Accountability is not revenge
text:
Is it truly “retribution” to seek accountability?
I am increasingly frustrated by calls to “move on,” “fix the economy” or “let it go” to avoid appearing vengeful. We can — and must — address past abuses of power while simultaneously working to prevent future misconduct. Why is “moving on” always the refrain? Can we not advance key priorities while addressing the destruction of the past two years?
There is a distinct difference between seeking revenge for personal grievances and holding individuals accountable for violating the law. Sweeping violations under the rug on the assumption that someone has “learned their lesson” directly undermines our justice system.
Holding individuals and agencies accountable for their actions is essential to protecting our institutions and preventing future abuse.
Jan Strout
Gray

“Sometimes the chatbots will say when you’re signing up for account, hey, we’re going to use your data for training. But it’s not saying this also means we’re going to store your data on our servers and that could be surfaced in other people’s chats or it could be exposed to hack,” Cross said.
Cross recommends keeping sensitive information out of chatbots, including Social Security numbers, medical information and personal documents.
“You don’t want to give it the highly sensitive stuff that you wouldn’t want ending up in the hands of someone else because using those chatbots come with those risks,” Cross said.
Cross also recommends reviewing a chatbot’s privacy settings and limiting the personal details shared about friends and family.

title: ‘The help they deserve’: Buckfield veteran tells story of trauma in an effort to aid those who can’t
text:
There is a particular song that can take Jamison McAlister to a safe place, and it might surprise some to hear that it’s “Highway to Hell,” from the 1980 AC/DC album “Back in Black.”
When you hear the 23-year Army combat veteran of two Middle East wars talk about it, though, it all makes sense.
His recall is of a Black Hawk helicopter in the Middle East, where he heard “Highway to Hell” and other rock ‘n’ roll songs played repeatedly. Another is “You Shook Me All Night Long,” from the same album.
“Every day, you’d have to go up in a helicopter,” he said, “and they’d play rock and roll music.”
One day he asked the pilot, a Vietnam veteran, why tunes were always blasting. The answer?
“He said, ‘because it calms the infantry guys down,’” McAlister said. “He said, ‘they were so nervous … they would hear something, or something would trigger them. They’d click their safety off, and next thing you know, we’d hit a bump or air pocket and they’d start shooting holes in the floor. Or the top.’”
That pilot continued the practice through his years of service, and by the time McAlister found himself in Iraq in 1990, the two AC/DC songs had become mainstays.
“That’s how long it took us to get to the battlefield,” he said. “By the end of the second song, we’d be on the ground. Two songs and we’re on the ground and moving.
“To this day, if I hear these songs, which I do a lot, my mindset clicks. I’m no longer scared. You could put me in the worst scenario and I’m fine. I’m as cool as a cucumber.”
McAlister, who is 56, carried that coolness for years, all through his 23-year career and into his post-service years.
He never gave serious thought to post traumatic stress disorder. He did not believe in it, even as friends would later talk about the effects it had on them.
That concept was drilled into him and fellow recruits 35 years ago by platoon commanders with years of experience, and possibly the knowledge that repression can be the strongest survival skill they might teach.
“These guys were the A Shau Valley guys. Mekong Delta. Hamburger Hill. To privates, recruits — they’d say PTSD was a bunch of bull—-. And no one had the right to claim PTSD. They hadn’t earned it,” McAlister described.
‘I WASN’T HERE’
One of McAlister’s buddies, who finished his military service at the same time he did, started having problems. He told him he was having flashbacks, but McAlister brushed it off.
His friend was put on a prescription regimen, which included medical marijuana.
“The thing was, if you claim you have it (PTSD), you’re weak,” he said. “So, I’d listen to him, but you know, I just thought it was bull.”
Whatever care the man was receiving, it didn’t help. He became over medicated and would get so stoned he would take even more.
“He’d say, ‘hey Mac, what’s the day?’ On Monday he wouldn’t remember taking his pills and then he’d call the next day and say ‘what day is this’ and wouldn’t remember taking them the day before, even if I told him he had.
“He just kept taking them,” McAlister said. “And then he finally overdosed and died.”
Despite what McAlister had been trained to think, it was learning that his friend was gone that triggered his own PTSD incident, the first of many.
One minute he was in his bedroom, sitting on a waterbed. The next thing he knew was he was no longer there.
“I’m not sitting on my bed,” he said. “I’m sitting on a helicopter that’s full of body bags. … I was there. I wasn’t here.”
Other suppressed memories began popping up. By that time he had returned to live on the family farm in Buckfield and care for his 90-year-old father.
For years after retiring from the military he had lived a nomadic lifestyle, following jobs offered by friends who continued to work in the field.
Once he found himself in the familiar environment he had once limited to brief visits, though, McAlister’s PTSD finally caught up with him.
He planned his return to be a visit. He would help his father, get the farm’s affairs in order and then go. But this time he was not able to leave. His family needed him to stay.
“It had been my coping mechanism, to cycle through short 30-day stays before redeploying,” he said. “That cycle prevented me from confronting my trauma.”
‘WE STICK TOGETHER’
Now, McAlister was the one in need of help — help he had never used because he did not believe he needed it and had never been told was available.
It did not occur to him when he got a toothache that he could have a $3,500 dental treatment taken care of by Veterans Affairs … until his civilian dentist told him.
“I was out 12 years before I ever went to the VA,” he said. “And the people there, they’re great.”
The experience of seeing combat veterans wait for services behind others who never saw battle became a new trigger for him.
“We were told we didn’t earn the right,” he repeated. He did not know he deserved it.
Finally, McAlister sought counseling for his PTSD. It was at a session that his sister accompanied him to when he had a breakthrough.
“The therapist asked me, why hadn’t I come home before,” he said. “At first I said it was because my dad didn’t need me until now. But she pushed it and I just said it — ‘I haven’t earned the right to.’”
Pressed to consider why he felt he had not earned the right, he had another realization. “I didn’t feel I had the right because we didn’t win the war,” he said.
Using cognitive recall, McAlister’s counselor helped him draw out and face old traumas. He shared a few of his past experiences while being interviewed. “Stuff that I didn’t think was still there,” he said. “Combat veterans have a switch in them.”
One other key part of coming to terms with his condition was a return to school and writing it out. It has helped to validate and give form to his voice.
Recognizing his own PTSD and finally taking care of himself through VA medical and behavioral health services, McAlister noticed something else about veterans. Something he feels is not right.
“I was at the VA clinic,” he said, “either Lewiston or Rumford. I’m waiting and this woman comes in, and her husband comes in. He is shaking. I could see his tattoos were military unit symbols, and he was old enough he had to be a Vietnam vet. I concluded he was probably in a PTSD moment.”
McAlister approached the older man and asked if he was OK. He said he was, but his shaking and demeanor told a different story. He wanted to know who McAlister was and why did he care?
“I told him I was infantry. That we stick together,” he said. “And all of a sudden he calmed down and was able to have a normal conversation. He said he needed to talk to someone right then.”
McAlister checked to see what the man’s wait would be.
“There were four veterans sitting there. I asked if any served in combat, had served in Vietnam, or anything. Nope. One did four years, one did 15, one did 11, and whatever. I asked if they minded if this guy went ahead of us,” McAlister said.
“One guy looked me in the eye and said, ‘I’ve waited two and a half months to get this appointment and I’m not about to miss it, so no.”
Before McAlister had a chance to bristle at the other veteran’s callousness, a counselor intervened, took the Vietnam veteran into an office and left the five men standing there. He told the four veterans what he thought of their responses.
After the words were said, the wife accompanying her husband made a point to call out McAlister, too.
“She told me I was the first person who he could talk calmly with in more than a week. ‘I didn’t know how to get to him,’ she said.
“For me, it goes back (to my counseling). Deserve or earn. Most of us combat veterans that went outside the wire, we still don’t believe we’ve earned the right for these benefits,” McAlister said. “While one who served for 30 seconds knows they deserve every one.”
McAlister knows that civilians and even noncombat veterans might not understand his frustration, since he is entitled to the same benefits and it is a choice to exercise them or not.
He went through years of denial and hell before getting to where he found his voice. He reached out to tell his story because he knows there are others like him, in the shadows, hiding the depth of their struggles. He wants them to ask for what they deserve.
“They should go first. They should not have to wait,” he said. “A disabled combat veteran, someone who got their arms blown off. They should go first.
“The reason I’m telling my story, is because of our deserve/earn mentality. You can tell by looking them in the eye if a veteran is combat.
“For that one person out there in the same boat — I want them to get help. I had a toothache and I saw that people out there really do care. And still so many have never ever gone for the help they deserve.”

title: Bessent moves to a military base over safety concerns, sources says
text:
Bessent moves to a military base over safety concerns, sources says
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was recently forced to relocate to a military base over concerns for his safety.
The move comes as Bessent has spent the last several months executing a massive economic campaign against Iran aimed at severing all of Tehran's remaining financial ties around the world.
A person familiar with the matter, who spoke to The Associated Press on Wednesday on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details, said the relocation was partly due to media reports that helped identify Bessent's home address. The relocation was earlier reported by The New York Times.
Recent U.S. intelligence showed that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel in the Middle East and elsewhere, which contributed to the State Department last month reducing staffing at four U.S. embassies in the region.
President Donald Trump said this week that the more than 8-month-old Iran war "militarily is effectively over," but his administration has kept up the financial warfare in a bid to get Iran to capitulate to U.S. demands over Tehran's nuclear program.
The Treasury Department in August pledged an "economic D-Day" against Tehran, and it has become a massive sanctions and influence campaign.
U.S. officials have spent the past few months traveling from Europe to the Middle East and meeting behind closed doors on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly to make the case to some of Tehran's closest and most vital trading partners: Sever those financial ties or face retaliation from the United States.
And it appears some have followed suit. The United Arab Emirates and Turkey — key trading partners and regional neighbors — halted Iran's top commercial bank from issuing transactions in their countries, while some of the country's top airlines were cut off from critical regional routes from Istanbul to Muscat, Oman.
Other top Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, also live on military bases.

title: Ocean liner being sunk to make largest artificial reef off Florida Panhandle coast
text:
GULF OF MEXICO (AP) — The historic SS United States, once the fastest ship on the seas, made a slow final journey beneath the waters Wednesday.
The famous ocean liner — which is longer than the Titanic and crossed the Atlantic more than 800 times — was deliberately sunk Wednesday to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico, where the once-luxurious behemoth was set to begin a new chapter as the world’s largest artificial reef.
It was a long goodbye. Hours after the sinking began on a cloudy afternoon, much of the hulking ship could still be seen in the dark waters off the coast of the Florida Panhandle by nightfall. Organizers had predicted the sinking could finish in as quickly as an hour.
Finally, around 9 p.m., the vessel leaned on one side and then quickly submerged.
“She is an amazing lady who will not lay down without a fight,” Coleen O’Malley, president of Coleen Marine, the company sinking the ship, said before the vessel disappeared beneath the water. “Much like the amazing nation she was named after.”
The event — described by officials as a controlled sinking — was a long-planned $13.5 million project aimed at attracting more divers and fishing enthusiasts while creating a home for tuna, marlin and swordfish.
The slower-than-expected descent was partly due to crews filling 128 fuel and lubricant tanks aboard the ship with water so that it would rest evenly on the ocean floor, said Nick Tomecek, a spokesperson for Okaloosa County, which helped organize the sinking. He said the process “took longer than we thought.”
“She’s a big ship,” Tomecek said.
A massive vessel with a long history
The project will keep what had been a technological marvel when it made its maiden voyage in 1952 from becoming scrap metal.
Famous passengers included Hollywood stars like Grace Kelly and Elizabeth Taylor. Other passengers have included Presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy and Britain’s former King Edward VIII. In 1968, a young Bill Clinton took it when he went to Oxford University, decades before he was elected president.
Once aboard, passengers were treated to dinners that included caviar, roast duckling, smoked ox tongue and Calf’s Head en Tortue.
In preparation for the sinking, organizers removed the 65-foot (20-meter) smokestacks and plan to have them anchor a new museum that celebrates the ship.
Explosives were not allowed to be used
Federal environmental and explosives rules prevent Okaloosa County, Florida, and its contractor from using explosives to scuttle the ship, Tomecek said. Concerns about inclement weather prompted officials to move up the sinking by a day.
The SS United States has pipes that pulled seawater into tanks as part of the system that cooled its boilers, he said, and those tanks have been removed so that once the valves are opened, water will flood the hull. Workers also have cut 10-foot by 10-foot (3-meter by 3-meter) holes in the decks, and more than 400 portholes have been removed.
The ship is to sink in about 180 feet (55 meters) of water, with its top deck about 60 feet (18 meters) below the surface — shallow enough that inexperienced divers can visit. It will settle on the floor of the waters about 25 miles (40 kilometers) southwest of Destin, between Panama City and Pensacola.
Larger than the Titanic, the ship set a speed record on its first voyage
More than 3,000 workers helped build the SS United States in 1950 and 1951 in Virginia. An Associated Press reporter and Truman’s daughter, Margaret, were among 1,700 passengers for the first voyage.
The ship’s average speed for that trip was almost 41 mph (66 kph), besting a record set by Britain’s RMS Queen Mary in 1938 by 4.5 mph (7.2 kph), according to the AP’s dispatch.
The SS United States set the record even though its journey ended in the face of a full gale that reached 69 mph (111 kph) — “so strong it blew a ping pong table off the deck,” AP reported.
At 990 feet (302 meters), the ship is 108 feet (33 meters) longer than the ill-fated Titanic, which hit an iceberg and sank on its first voyage across the Atlantic.
“She really embodies and expresses this country’s best,” said Susan Gibbs, the granddaughter of the ship’s designer. “She represents pride and resilience and strength and beauty.”
The ship’s resting place has many artificial reefs
More than 500 artificial reefs are located in the waters near where the SS United States will rest.
Previously, the largest artificial reef came from the 2006 scuttling of an aircraft carrier, the USS Oriskany in the Gulf off Pensacola — near enough to the SS United States site that an experienced diver could visit both in the same day, Tomecek said. The Oriskany, launched in 1950, was 911 feet (278 meters) in length.
“We’re trying to be the best diving destination in the world,” Tomecek said.
The ship was decommissioned in 1969. Attempts by a hotel magnate and Norwegian Cruise Lines to use the ship never floated, and from 1996 until recently, it sat along a dock in Philadelphia.
Tim Mullane, a Navy veteran and chief operating officer of Coleen Marine, called the huge funnels — the smokestacks that have been removed to anchor the new museum — “works of art.”
“I’m just so happy that we are able to save parts of her,” Gibbs said.
___
This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Eisenhower.
___
Hanna reported from Topeka, Kansas.

title: Women’s underwear labeled with sticky notes found in sex assault suspect’s home, police say
text:
TEMPE, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — Police in Arizona say a disturbing discovery was made in the home of a man accused of sexual assault on Halloween.
Newly released court documents detail how police say the assault happened and how the suspect was caught, including finding a collection of women’s underwear with some having sticky note labels.
A forensic psychologist who reviewed the allegations said the discovery raises concerns about the possibility of other victims.
Mach Kim, 46, was arrested Nov. 5 on charges of aggravated assault, kidnapping, sexual assault and sexual abuse in connection with an Oct. 31 attack on a woman in Tempe.
What police say happened
The alleged assault began in the afternoon in Tempe, where Kim allegedly forced a woman into his vehicle at gunpoint.
Court documents said the woman was walking home from a party when a driver stopped, pointed what she described as a black pistol at her and told her to get in or he would shoot her.
Kim reportedly made the woman put on an eye mask and drove her to another location, where he sexually assaulted her and forced her to give him her underwear.
Police said Kim then dropped the woman off, where she found someone nearby to help her call police.
The woman showed officers where she had been dropped off before she was taken for a sexual assault exam. Police found her phone and keys on the ground at the drop-off location.
Police said GPS data from her phone showed the route she was taken on, including where she was picked up and dropped off.
How police identified Kim
Police said they used the GPS information to help identify Kim as the sexual assault suspect.
Investigators reviewed camera footage along the route, matching it to the timeline from her phone’s GPS, which led them to a white Dodge Ram pickup registered to Kim.
Court documents said his driver’s license photo resembled a sketch the woman helped create.
Detectives then surveilled Kim on Nov. 5 and collected a DNA sample from a Wendy’s cup he threw away, according to court documents. Police said the DNA on the cup matched DNA collected in the woman’s sexual assault kit.
What police found
When police arrested Kim in Scottsdale, a search of his car uncovered a black CO2 gun shaped like a handgun, a black sleep mask, six pairs of women’s underwear, a pillow and a towel.
In his Chandler home, police say they found 13 pairs of women’s underwear and an eye mask. Seven of the pairs had sticky notes with dates and names.
Forensic psychologist John De La Torre said the labeled items could be connected to other victims and could have been kept as mementos. That was his assessment, not a confirmed finding about the items.
“The initial impulse in me is to think that all of these, because they’re labeled, all of these are meant as mementos,” he said.
De La Torre said keeping mementos is not limited to serial killers. He also said the allegations raise concerns about the possibility of escalation.
“All of these things, you know, raise a level of concern about the possibility of escalation,” he said.
After Kim was taken to jail, he invoked his rights and said he did not want to answer more questions about the charges without a lawyer.
Detectives believe there could be other victims who have not yet come forward. Potential victims or others with information are asked to call Tempe police at 480-350-8311.
