title: The Best New Movies to Watch at Home This Weekend
text:
The Best New Movies You Can Watch at Home This Weekend
New movies are coming to streaming this week and every week, at a faster pace than ever before. As always, ScreenCrush has your back, with a weekly guide to the latest releases on streaming (and digital rental or purchse) that deserve your attention. Sit back, relax, and check out what’s coming to a TV or computer (or, sigh, a phone) near you.
Then you’ve got all weekend to watch up with these titles. The theater is still the best, of course, but some weekends you just can’t muster the energy to get off the couch and haul yourself to the multiplex.
New Movies Streaming This Week and Weekend
This week you can watch Chris Rock’s latest Hollywood satire, Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor face off with dinosaurs, and two different opportunities to watch Jessica Chastain: Either as a crusading country singer searching for her missing niece or as Other Mommy. (Maybe Other Mommy took the country singer’s niece? I’m just saying I don’t trust Other Mommy.)
If these titles don’t do it for you, you can also check out some other recent streaming releases here. Or just keep scrolling, and see the new movies you can stream or rent on digital at home this weekend.
Misty Green
Chris Rock’s fourth film as a director — and his first since 2014’s Top Five — follows the plight of a struggling actress (played by Rosalind Eleazar) who once won an Emmy, but now finds herself out of work, on bad terms with most casting directors in Hollywood, and desperate to find a new gig before she gets kicked out of her apartment. Rock wrote and directed the film and appears in a cast that also includes Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick, and Topher Grace.
Where to watch Misty Green: Netflix.
The End of Oak Street
I’m not sure why this satisfying thriller got such middling response from audiences and even some critics. It’s a hoot. Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor play a married couple whose whole suburban neighborhood gets transported back to the age of dinosaurs. The inhabitants ain’t interested in any of that Jurassic Park awe and wonder garbage; they just want to eat people, and that’s bad news for Anne and Ewan. The film is sharply directed by David Robert Mitchell, the guy behind It Follows and Under the Silver Lake.
Where to watch The End of Oak Street: Premieres on November 13 on HBO Max.
Avedon
Famed photographer Richard Avedon is the subject of this new Netflix documentary, which da ’Flix claims received “unprecedented access to his personal archives — never-before-seen stills, intimate behind-the-lens footage, and new interviews with his closest collaborators.” It’s directed by Ron Howard, who is best known as a fiction filmmaker (A Beautiful Mind, Apollo 13) but whose recent documentaries include works on the Beatles, Luciano Pavarotti, and Jim Henson.
Where to watch Avedon: Netflix.
Heartland
In Heartland, directed by Shana Feste, Jessica Chastain plays a former country music star who goes searching for her missing niece, who is also a country musician. Netflix is not only hyping the movie but also its soundtrack which they boast includes music from the cast “including Academy Award winner Jessica Chastain, three-time Grammy winner Jennifer Nettles, Ross Lynch and CMA nominee Carter Faith, alongside Margo Price, Carly Pearce, Eddy Dunlap, Channing Wilson and Dave "Fergie" Ferguson.”
Where to watch Heartland: Premieres on November 13 on Netflix.
Other Mommy
Or if Chastain in a country hat ain’t your cup of tea, you could go instead with Other Mommy. Admittedly, the reviews for this horror film about Chastain as both the mom to a sweet little girl and a terrifying monster that wants to steal her child, were not fantastic. (It currently holds a 19 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes.) But man, that first trailer for the movie was terrifying; easily one of the best trailers of the year. Aren’t you a little curious about Other Mommy? I know I am. What’s going on with that ball pit??
Where to watch Other Mommy: Prime Video, Apple TV, Fandango.

title: Maine cites fire, rescue departments after deadly Searsmont sawmill explosion
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Department of Labor has cited six fire departments for lacking an effective system to track firefighters at the scene of the deadly May fire and explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont.
The department also cited four of those fire departments, Searsmont, Morrill, Montville, and Belmont, as well as Searsmont Rescue over personal protective equipment protocols. Morrill was cited for 11 items in all.
The findings follow workplace safety investigations involving the Searsmont, Morrill, Montville, Belmont, Appleton and Lincolnville fire departments, as well as Searsmont Rescue.
Firefighter tracking and protective equipment
Firefighters from across the region responded to a silo fire and subsequent explosion at Robbins Lumber on May 15. Morrill volunteer firefighter Andrew Cross, 27, was killed, and more than a dozen other people were injured.
Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury, 76, died in June from injuries he sustained while responding to the incident. Mill co-owner Alden Robbins died from his injuries in July.
A federal report released in August found officials did not realize Cross was missing until two hours after the incident.
The state cited all six fire departments over the lack of an effective accountability system for tracking firefighters’ locations at the scene. Searsmont Rescue was cited for actions including the setup of a firefighter rehabilitation area within 50 feet of the silo fire.
Kate Burkhart, director of the Bureau of Labor Standards, said every department and town worked with the state on plans to correct the issues.
“It’s not enough just to point out when there is a workplace safety or health violation. It’s really important to support the employer as they fix the problem and move forward,” Burkhart said.
“They are all invested in improving the safety for their employees and their volunteers. That’s really important here, is a lot of these fire departments rely on volunteers.”
Penalties and training
The labor department is suspending nearly all of the $108,000 in penalties it issued. Montville must pay $1,000 because of a record of one repeat fit-testing violation.
“We believe that it is more important for these towns and departments to allocate their resources toward the improvement efforts than it is to pay a civil penalty,” Burkhart said.
Those efforts include implementing or improving accountability systems. Most of the departments are moving toward the same system.
“If we have a standardized procedure and a standardized system, then it makes it that much easier for everybody,” Ron Harford said.
“We know what we got to do better next time,” Harford said.
The Maine Department of Labor is coordinating with the Maine Fire Chiefs’ Association and the Maine Fire Service Institute to provide training for the departments’ chiefs and officers. It will be held in Belmont in February.

title: Kennedy family members ask a judge to block Trump’s Arlington memorial arch
text:
(AP) - Nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty asked a judge Tuesday to block President Donald Trump’s plan to build a towering memorial arch, saying the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would cast a shadow over their relatives’ gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery.
The shadow would “fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites,” the relatives argued. They filed a motion to intervene in two existing lawsuits seeking to block construction of the arch.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan last week prohibited the Trump administration from breaking ground on the structure for 14 days.
The nine Kennedy family members who filed suit are children and grandchildren of Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, brothers of the slain U.S. president John F. Kennedy, both of whom served in the U.S. Senate. They are buried close to the eternal flame that marks JFK’s gravesite, a trio of memorials that are a major draw for the millions of people who visit the Arlington cemetery each year.
Building the arch would be a “permanent denigration” of the gravesites, and the Kennedy offspring “would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended,” lawyers for the relatives wrote. They are represented by veteran Washington lawyer Norm Eisen and Democracy Defenders Fund.
“It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery,” said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle. “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation.”
Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s health and human services secretary who has a fractured relationship with many of his relatives, did not join the lawsuit.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections.
The White House last week unveiled a glitzy new website to showcase the arch, which is slated to rise in a mass of gold ornamentation and stately gray granite between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

title: Maine's Highest-Earning Cities Have Been Revealed
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
THE LIST: The Richest Cities in Maine Might Surprise You
If you have spent time living in more than just a couple of towns/cities, you have probably realized that the average salary varies a lot from town to town.
Clearly, this is really noticeable when you move between different parts of the country. For example, as a kid from Aroostook County my mind was blown at what fast-food employees were making in New York City.
That being said, there are massive differences in pay between different towns here in Maine. For example, Portland has a higher minimum wage than the statewide minimum wage. On top of that, there is an enormous difference between what a skilled worker in Southern Maine makes compared to what the same person would make in Caribou.
So, in which Maine towns and cities are you likely to earn the most?
The Highest-Earning Cities and Towns in Maine
Thanks to the team at Stacker, we have a pretty good idea about the highest-earning cities and towns in Maine. These are the municipalities where the majority of top earners live.

title: Son stabs his mom at Target, claims the Illuminati told him to kill her, affidavit says
text:
WACO, Texas (KWTX/Gray News) - A 21-year-old Texas man remains behind bars after stabbing his mother at Target and claiming the Illuminati told him to kill her, according to an arrest warrant affidavit.
Galveston Elijah Vriseno, 21, is accused of stabbing his mother in the neck at Target and claiming the Illuminati told him to do it, an arrest warrant affidavit obtained by KWTX states. He is charged with aggravated assault of a family member causing serious bodily injury.
The Illuminati was a secret society founded in 1776 that is now the subject of conspiracy theories claiming a hidden group controls world events.
Victim found lying next to ‘a pool of blood’
Waco police officers were dispatched to a possible domestic disturbance involving a stabbing at Target around 2:22 p.m. Sunday.
Upon arrival, officers found the victim, Ashley Norwood, lying on the floor next to “a pool of blood.” The affidavit describes a stab wound to the left side of Norwood’s neck.
Bystanders helped the victim sit up when officers arrived. She could not speak at the time, so witnesses provided a description of what Vriseno was wearing at the time of the assault, the affidavit states.
Officers reviewed camera footage of the assault in which they saw Norwood and Vriseno walking around the store’s optical area. The affidavit describes Vriseno stabbing his mother with a knife and running out of the store right after.
Around 4 p.m., officers were informed Vriseno had called police. He was found at a Jack in the Box across the street from Target, wearing the same clothing that witnesses previously described, including a blanket.
When officers found Vriseno, it appeared he was trying to get rid of the blanket and other items witnesses described by throwing them in the trash and washing the blood off his hands, the affidavit states.
After Vriseno was advised of his Miranda rights, the arresting officer asked if the knife in his front left cargo pocket was the weapon he used to stab his mom, and Vriseno admitted it was, according to the affidavit.
Suspect claimed Illuminati told him to kill mother, sister says
Vriseno’s sister called police while they were looking for him and said Vriseno made comments two days earlier that the Illuminati told him to kill his mother and sister.
Norwood was taken to the hospital, where she underwent surgery and is in stable condition, according to her daughter.
Vriseno was being held on a $100,000 bond.
Earlier this year, Vriseno was arrested for allegedly assaulting his pregnant girlfriend after they argued over a car part, according to an arrest warrant. He was charged with assault of a pregnant woman, a third-degree felony.

title: Low-cost home fixes and age tech can help older adults stay safe at home
text:
(Aging Untold) — Small changes around the house can make the difference between staying home safely and a fall that changes everything.
Tara Ballman, executive director of the National Aging in Place Council, joined Aging Untold to talk through low-cost fixes, signs that long-distance caregivers should watch for and technology that can help.
Evaluate your home for trip hazards
Ballman said two low-cost areas have a high impact.
The first is trip hazards.
“You probably don’t remember where your throw rugs are, how long they’ve been there, and it might be coming up on the sides,” Ballman said.
She said the hazards go beyond rugs. Electrical cords that run to a lamp, shoes piled by the front door and clutter from pets or robot vacuums can also be trip hazards.
“I would love for everyone to go take a fresh look at their homes from new eyes, and see where those trip hazards are,” Ballman said. “That’s free for you to evaluate your own home.”
Check the lighting
Lighting is the second area.
“As you age, your eyes are affected by the light,” she said. “So you might need more light in some areas. Or if the light is too bright and creating a glare, that can be dangerous as well.”
What long-distance caregivers can look for
Ballman said some signs that a home is no longer working for a parent or loved one are small and easy to miss until you visit in person.
She suggested asking:
- Is your loved one sleeping in the bed, or on a sofa or chair in the living room?
- Are they able to use their shower, or are they using a sink to sponge bathe?
Age tech: a safety net without surveillance
Ballman described “age tech” as technology that helps people stay in their homes longer and more safely. She said the options are not expensive.
Examples she gave include:
- A sensor on a door that shows whether it opened three or four times for someone who lets dogs in and out each day.
- A countertop system that brings you your medicine every day, so you don’t have to wonder whether you took it.
- Smart toilet seats that, based on how a person sits and stands, can measure blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen levels.
- Pressure-sensitive grab bars that can sense extra weight.
- Pressure-sensitive floor mats that alert a loved one if someone falls in the bathroom.
“There’s a way that you can make sure they’re safe without putting cameras in their homes,” Ballman said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said the goal is to preserve dignity and longevity at home while keeping safety nets in place.
Automatic lighting for nighttime and entryways
Ballman said automatic lights matter most on the path from the bed to the bathroom at night. She also recommended automatic sensors outside, at the door and on multiple levels, including ceiling fixtures, floor lamps and lights that come up from below.
“The automatic sensors for lights are something that every home should have, whether you have an older adult in it or not,” Ballman said.
Start the conversation now
Ballman encouraged families to begin conversations before a crisis.
“Get comfortable with being uncomfortable, because knowledge is power,” she said. “The more that you know and the more research you can do ahead of time, it’s just going to give you more options when you’re not in a crisis situation than when it’s a crisis, and there’s this many options and you don’t know how to pay for it.”
Six easy things you can do
- Look for trip hazards. Check rugs, electrical cords, shoes by the door and clutter from pets or robot vacuums.
- Review the lighting. Older eyes may need more light in some areas, and glare from light that is too bright can also be dangerous. Upgrade and balance lighting if necessary.
- Watch for changes in routine. Where a loved one sleeps and how they bathe can show the home is no longer working for them.
- Consider age tech. Door sensors, medication systems, pressure-sensitive grab bars and floor mats can help without cameras in the home.
- Add automatic lights. Ballman said sensors from the bed to the bathroom, and at entrances, are something every home should have.
- Talk early. Researching options before a crisis gives families more choices.

title: Thornton Academy football junior has grabbed his opportunities
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SACO — How’s this for a statistic: Logan LeBlanc has touched the football 39 times this season for Thornton Academy and scored 16 touchdowns. Plus, one of his non-TD catches made ESPN’s Top 10 plays of the day.
That’s explosive, game-changing ability from a wide receiver who last year was a kind-of-skinny kid spending most of his playing time in junior varsity games.
“I was a small kid last year,” said LeBlanc who is 6-foot-3 and 185 pounds. “I can’t be a small kid trying to do what I do. Just using my athleticism to the full max that I can. I feel like I can outjump anyone. And I know I can beat kids with my speed.”
Teaming with deadly accurate senior quarterback Noah Fullerton, LeBlanc has re-invigorated the pass game for Thornton, the No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine football poll.
LeBlanc, a Saco native, will surely be a key focus of attention this Saturday (1 p.m.) when Thornton (10-0) hosts Bonny Eagle (9-1) in the Class A South championship at Hill Stadium.
The Scots saw LeBlanc score four touchdowns in Thornton’s 49-14 Week 8 romp in Saco. LeBlanc put the Golden Trojans on the board with a 90-yard kickoff return touchdown. His leaping, one-handed, toe-tapping ESPN catch along the sideline set up the offense’s first touchdown. LeBlanc added touchdown catches of 26, 44 and 28 yards, and finished with six catches for 129 yards.
“He’d been our leading receiver before that game, but obviously that was a big stage and he had a phenomenal game that day, and obviously ending up on ESPN doesn’t hurt either,” said Thornton coach Kevin Kezal. “He’s had a great year for us since the first game of the year.”
LeBlanc has 27 catches for 665 yards (24.6 yards per catch) and 13 touchdowns. He’s added two kick return touchdowns and one punt return touchdown. Overall he has 1,026 all-purpose yards with a per-touch average of 26.3 yards.
As a sophomore, LeBlanc did start the first two games at varsity because of another player’s injury but his main action came in JV games and practice. He said getting to “touch my toes into the water,” at the varsity level, combined with a season of development, made him better prepared for this season.
Fullerton has also made major strides in his second season as Thornton’s starting quarterback. He’s not throwing a lot because Thornton still has a potent rushing attack, but Fullerton has been on target all season. Against Bonny Eagle, Fullerton was 7 of 8 for 134 yards and the three TDs to LeBlanc. Overall, the 6-foot-4, 210-pound senior has completed 58 of 81 passes for 1,044 yards and 21 touchdowns against three interceptions.
“We’ve got a great trigger guy this year who is throwing the heck out of the ball,” Kezal said.
Thornton’s passing game might be even better if senior slot receiver Quinn Cook hadn’t suffered a season-ending injury at Westbrook in Week 4.
“Logan realized that his brother was down, and I think that’s a big story with this team,” Fullerton said. “When someone goes down, someone else steps up. And I think Logan has put that on his back and helped this team a lot.”
Here’s a quick note about LeBlanc’s ESPN highlight: LeBlanc said he made a better catch as an eighth-grader, also against Bonny Eagle. He said that immediately after his four-TD day and he was sticking with that opinion Tuesday.
“It was back corner of the end zone. I had to go up above (the defender) and get my feet down in the corner,” LeBlanc said. “I definitely thought that was a better catch.”

title: Obituary: Francis S. Driscoll Jr.
text:
WESTBROOK – Francis S. Driscoll Jr., 68, passed away unexpectedly Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at his home in Westbrook.
He was born on July 26, 1958, the son of the late Francis S. Driscoll Sr. and Marian “Mary” Driscoll. Born in Michigan, Francis moved to Bangor as a teenager where he graduated from Bangor High School, class of 1976. Francis then went on to attend the University of Maine at Orono, class of 1980.
After college, Francis began a long career first as a commercial truck driver then working for R.J. Grondin and Sons for over 30 years.
In addition to his parents, he is predeceased by his wife, Ellen (Murphy) Driscoll, with whom he was married to for 19 years. He is survived by his sister and his two daughters, Taylor Driscoll of Braintree, Mass., and Jenna Driscoll of Waltham, Mass.
Relatives and friends are invited to attend a memorial visitation on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, from 11 a.m. – 1 p.m., at Dolby, Blais & Segee Funeral Home, 35 Church St., Westbrook. A memorial service will follow at 1 p.m., at the funeral home.

title: US charges 3 men with plotting terror attacks, including planned assault on UK air base
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A man jailed on terrorism charges in New York was able to pass secret messages to Iranian operatives planning an attack on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force, according to an indictment unsealed Tuesday.
The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode shrouded in mystery since Sept. 27, when a group of men were detained on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward a British air base where U.S. bombers were stationed.
The new charges accuse Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national jailed at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, of a role in plotting to attack the Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, in western England, even though he’d been arrested last spring.
According to prosecutors, al-Saadi used coded language in phone and video calls to his mother and sister in Iraq to pass messages encouraging associates to carry out the air base bombing.
Two other men have been charged in the case, which accuses Iran-backed operatives of plotting nearly 20 terror strikes on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S.
Neither of those men, Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national, and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, are in U.S. custody.
US attorney says men sought to unleash a ‘campaign of terror’
“These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche said: “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American service members will be prosecuted by the United States government.”
Seven men arrested in the United Kingdom in connection with the incident at the RAF base in Fairford were all released on bail. One of those men was subsequently rearrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service and charged, along with another man, under the National Security Act, British authorities said.
British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to the United States.
RAF Fairford, 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
Man accused of fueling plots from jail with coded messages
U.S. prosecutors said in the indictment that while speaking to his family from the Brooklyn jail, al-Saadi told them he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass messages to him about “work,” a term al-Saadi used to describe terrorist activity.
“What are they doing about all our old work?” al-Saadi asked his sister on a July 30 call, according to the indictment. It said he asked her whether it had been canceled or just put on pause, to which she responded that “it isn’t canceled.”
On a Sept. 24 call, al-Saadi asked about al-Hassani, whom he was told had been transferred to the “International Section,” and instructed his family to “give him money so we can do it,” it said.
Since his May arrest, al-Saadi had been held in solitary confinement. The Justice Department said he was dangerous because of his desire to attack U.S. and Israeli interests.
New charges come amid court battle over al-Saadi’s phone access
Al-Saadi was permitted phone and video calls with his family, but each call was monitored and recorded by the FBI, according to court filings.
In September, al-Saadi’s lawyer complained that some of his calls were repeatedly interrupted and cut off without explanation. Citing concerns that he was using coded language, including “work” and “a job,” the government later said it was limiting him just to a single hourlong call each month.
Still, from June through September, al-Saadi participated in nine phone or video teleconference calls from jail, according to a court filing by prosecutors. In one, al-Saadi’s mother told him to stop talking about a topic because “they may end the call,” according to a court filing that said the FBI then terminated the call.
The indictment alleged the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terror attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.
In one instance in mid-April, the indictment said, al-Saadi, al-Hassani and Mohajeri directed an individual to carry out an arson attack on a Jewish charity organization in London in real time as they watched it on video that was projected from a laptop computer onto a large screen. The next day, they directed another attack on a synagogue in London, with al-Hassani directing the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree,” the indictment said.
In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a “prisoner of war.” He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday.
Both Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hizballah commander.
___
This story was first published Nov. 10, 2026. It was updated Nov. 11, 2026, to correct that only one of the two individuals charged under the National Security Act was previously arrested in Britain in connection with the suspected plot.
___
Tucker reported from Washington. Associated Press Writer Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington also contributed.

title: Maine Mountain Quilters honor five local veterans with Quilts of Valor
In debut novel, Portland writer weaves together ‘big stories’ with a coming of age tale
text:
“Black Dog” — Portland writer Erica Kent’s debut novel — begins with the titular dog’s jaws on the narrator’s throat, small bones popping as she fights for breath. It turns out to be a dream, or more accurately a nightmare, but the strangled urgency remains in the frenetic first-person narration, a testament to Kent’s skill at her craft.
Surface level, it’s an account of tween-becomes-teen in the early 1980s, that at times reads like an ode to that era — hard rock and riding your bike around the neighborhood until dark — but is always waiting around to knock the wind out of you with a sucker punch, should you slip into nostalgia. The result is a heartfelt tangle of teen angst, drinking, drug abuse and a quickly deteriorating home life that leaps from the page and pulls you in by the neck, ready or not.
Kent spoke with the Press Herald about growing up in outer Boston in the 1980s, the all-too-common intertwining of adolescence and addiction, her writing process and the interplay of the “big story” with the “small story.”
The book begins with the narrator waking up from a nightmare to learn that John Lennon has been killed. It’s hard not to see this as a loss-of-innocence event for the character. How significant was Lennon’s death to you, and what significance is it meant to hold to the narrator?
When Lennon died, I think there was a collective sense of shock melding into disillusionment that a figure of counterculture, someone outside of politics, could suddenly be gone. But given that I was 11 at the time, any real perspective on it came later. It was more like one minute me and my friends were playing spin-the-bottle, sneaking booze and cigarettes, and listening to “Hey Jude,” and the next minute Lennon was murdered.
For Jessica Ryder, Lennon’s death is an accelerant to what she’s already primed for. When her dad hands over his beer that night, it provides the relief she’s seeking, and with that relief, a heady desire for more. Converging a “big story” with a “little story” felt like a cool way to get things going — although it was only later I understood my intentions. If I had sat down and planned out the business about Lennon, the whole thing would’ve been forced. In general, when I write, I want to be open to surprise, without an agenda.
Throughout the book, the reader is tethered to the 1980s timeline by sections beginning with the year and major national or global events that happened. How did you land on this idea?
For me, characters always come first. The structure of “Black Dog” emerged later, after a lot of fumbling around, when I was trying to figure out how to clarify the passage of time. The sections provide a larger context, the “big story,” in which Jessica’s story, the “small story,” takes place, as well as a pause in a fairly heavy-duty progression of addiction. Within each short list are contrasts, seismic historical events put next to pop culture references, reflected within the contradictory emotional life of the “small story.” Also included is the title of a book published that year as a kind of homage to reading, something very important to me growing up.
One of the joys of this book is the narrator’s voice. It walks a very fine line between biting and beautiful; is this the narrative voice you always write in or is it specific to this character?
I’ve had Jessica’s voice in me for a long time, although her voice is not my voice, and it is not the main narrative voice I write in. It’s probably a voice born out of three attempts at a coming-of-age novel with male protagonists. When I switched to a female point of view, Jessica’s voice came alive for me. The emotional core of the story stems from my experience, but much of the plot and characters of the novel are fictional. Books always inspire me. In “Black Dog,” there are a number of writers and books mentioned, but two important novels that do not appear are Denis Johnson’s “Jesus’ Son,”and “The Virgin Suicides” by Jeffrey Eugenides.
How much of the neighborhood was pulled from your life experience? Is there an autobiographical element to Ryder growing up in Brookline?
Absolutely. Brookline and Boston in the 1980s were the setting of my adolescence. Originally, my family lived in Andover, a suburb north of the city. After my parents divorced, my mom moved to Brookline and got an apartment not far from Fenway Park. While I was working on the book, that landscape and time was pretty easy to conjure. Although Brookline is sprawling and more suburban in places, the full-on suburban landscape of Jessica’s neighborhood is mainly stolen from Andover.
The eponymous Black Dog looms over the narrator’s psyche through the novel. I’m curious where the idea for ‘Black Dog’ came from, what it represents to you and to the protagonist.
The term “black dog” is an allusion to Winston Churchill’s idea of the “black dog of depression” following him around, although he didn’t coin the phrase. When I began to work on the first black dog story something clicked with thinking of the term as the embodiment of addiction, something that tracks you, that you can’t get rid of. It’s also a nod to that original story, where a girl — who became Jessica — is waiting in line at a liquor store and the Led Zeppelin song “Black Dog” is playing on the radio.
Without giving anything away, I think it’s fair to say that drinking and drug use feature heavily in the novel. Is this a particularly meaningful topic for you? What made you want to combine these themes with a coming-of-age style narrative?
For me, coming of age and addiction go hand in hand. The first time I got sober I was 20, and so drinking and drugs were part of my childhood; a mixture of innocent joy, a bit of bad news experimentation mixed in with clueless fun, all set in the context of a pretty turbulent family life. That said, Jessica’s story is much more complex and dramatic than mine. Combining those two themes felt like a potent mixture and provided an opportunity for not just one crossing over from innocence to experience, but numerous crossings over and back, again and again.
It was important to me not to write a traditional narrative arc of addiction, as in everything got terrible, and then everything became amazing. I think this kind of black-and-white thinking misrepresents an issue full of gray areas, full of nuance. There can be beauty, euphoria, in active addiction; there can be heartbreak in recovery. But, overall, getting and staying sober is liberating. You’re free of a major shackle.
There is a lot of sadness and loss in this book. But also humor, love and hope. In your mind, is it a sad story?
No, I don’t see it that way. For me, the story examines something difficult, which means including darker parts to tell the whole thing. People have often said my work is on the darker side, but I don’t worry about it too much. I just try to write as honestly as I can.
Ezra Koch is a writer and Realtor who lives in South Portland with his wife and children. His writing has appeared in several publications on the East and West coasts, and online. He is currently working on a novel.

title: Video captures heroic police officer helping pull driver out of burning car following crash
text:
DAVIS, Calif. (KXTV) — Davis police Cpl. Pheng Ly broke the driver’s window of a burning car and pulled the man inside to safety in the early morning hours of Nov. 1, according to the Davis Police Department.
Ly arrived at the scene of a car fire and was met with people screaming. His body-worn camera video shows him breaking the window to reach the driver.
Corporal describes the rescue
The incident happened after Halloween night. Ly was in the Davis area when the call came out.
The crash technically fell under California Highway Patrol jurisdiction, but Ly said he was nearby and wanted to help.
“I tried to pull the door to open the door to get him out, but the door was locked,” Ly said. “So I took out my pocket knife, which has a window punch on it, and I was able to smash out the driver’s window, reach inside, unlock the door, open the door and yank the driver out of the vehicle after undoing his seatbelt.”
Ly said he was the first to arrive at the scene and the fire was spreading toward where the driver was seated.
“I remember when I reached in to undo his seat belt and grab him out, the wall of fire was right there in front of him through that clear windshield, so I’m glad I got there when I did,” Ly said.
Driver arrested after treatment
Davis police said CHP investigated the collision. The driver was arrested on suspicion of DUI after being treated for his injuries.
The department commended Ly for actions it said may have saved the driver’s life.
Similar rescue about six years ago
Davis police also recalled a separate incident about six years ago, when Ly rescued a woman in Solano County.
“A woman had driven her car off the roadway, and the vehicle had overturned and caught fire,” Ly said. “Once again, I was nearby. I heard it on the police radio. I got there first and I was able to pull her out of the vehicle.”
Ly: ‘I just move’
Ly said he was doing his job. He is a father of four, and said the driver he rescued was a few years older than his oldest son.
“I see a situation where someone’s life is in danger. Of course I’m scared. I’m very scared, but I’m not scared for me. I’m scared for the person that’s trapped in the car,” Ly said. “I’m afraid that I might fail him or let him down, and so I just move and let my experience take over, and you know, everything worked out right.”
Ly has been with the Davis Police Department for 25 years. He plans to retire in a year and a half.

title: Maine to face Hockey East leader No. 20 Vermont on the road this weekend
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Maine is coming off a home split last weekend against UMass.
The Black Bears scored three goals in the series on 91 shots.
“When you’re playing well and the puck doesn’t go in, it’s easy to start smashing your stick. We’ve seen a little bit of that the weekend prior. So for us, it’s just culturally just keep going,” said Ben Barr, head coach.
“I think (it’s about) grinding through those times where (goals are) coming hard for us right now. But, if we just keep producing those numbers for shots, I think obviously they’ll definitely start falling. (It’s) just committing to going to the net fronts and banging home a rebound goal or something like that,” said Owen Fowler, graduate forward.
“It’s important to focus on the process. Results are outcome based. I’m just trying to focus on playing the right way, doing whatever it takes to do the little things, and then the results will show,” said Sully Scholle, senior forward.
Maine’s going to Vermont this weekend. The Catamounts are currently atop the Hockey East standings.
“They’ve come back in games like down late in the game. Last weekend, I think they scored two with an empty net against BC on the road. In order to do those things, it takes a lot of belief. That’s years and years of sticking with it, going through the ups and the downs, and so obviously they’ve done a great job of that,” said Barr.
The Black Bears explained how Gutterson Fieldhouse is a unique, tough place to play like Alfond Arena.
“It’s just kind of a different game, similar to BU’s ice and BC’s ice: a little longer, a little wider, but (it’s) not too much (different). You’ve got to take care of the pucks in certain areas, try and get the puck out of the corners, and get to the net,” said Fowler.

title: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Sets Streaming Premiere
text:
‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Sets Streaming Premiere Date
As the ending of VisionQuest made abundantly clear, right now Marvel is laser-focused on just one thing: Hyping Avengers: Doomsday. To that end, a few weeks ago they released a slightly new cut of Avengers: Endgame to theaters. Dubbed Avengers Endgame: Encore, it included several new post-credits scenes designed to bridge the gap between the two movies — and to get audiences hyped to come out for Doomsday at the end of the year.
With Endgame: Encore’s theatrical run concluded, Marvel is now putting the new cut of the film on Disney+. This version will surprisingly debut on streaming by the end of the week.
They also hyped the film’s streaming arrival with a new teaser encouraging Marvel fans to brush up on their Marvel Cinematic Universe viewing on the service prior to Doomsday’s theatrical debut.
READ MORE: How Endgame: Encore Sets Up Avengers: Doomsday
Beyond the additional post-credits material — three added scenes plus a little sound effect calling back to the very first Iron Man — Avengers Endgame: Encore remains the same as the original theatrical release, with the surviving members of the Avengers struggling to reverse the effects of Thanos’ “snap” that erased half of the entire universe during Avengers: Infinity War.
The new material in Encore teased the undoing of Steve Rogers’ happy ending from Avengers: Endgame in order to allow his return in Avengers: Doomsday, showed Bruce Banner get confronted by Doctor Doom, and a final sequence (which was only shown at certain screenings) where the TVA from Marvel’s Loki television series observe numerous universal “incursions” which indicate that the destruction of the multiverse is imminent.
Avengers Endgame: Encore debuts on Disney+ on Friday, November 13. And, yes, Avengers: Doomsday follows in a little over a month, on December 18.

title: Remember When Maine Had 13 Friendly’s? Here’s What They Look Like Now
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Used to Have 13 Friendly’s Restaurants. What Happened to Them?
Maine has only one Friendly's restaurant as of today, but that wasn't always the case.
Travel back in time to, say, the year 2000, and you'd find there were a bunch more locations in the state serving up classic burgers and a variety of ice creams. (Always had to save room for the Mint Cookie Crunch!)
Ever wonder what happened to them all? You might have even driven past a former Friendly's and not even realized it. I was able to find 13 of them from back in the day and what's in their spots now.
Friendly’s Started in Massachusetts and Once Had Over 850 Restaurants in the US
Friendly first opened in Massachusetts in 1935 (I didn't know it didn't get its apostrophe until 1989), over 90 years ago, according to its website. By 1951, there were 10 locations total in Massachusetts and Connecticut.
The Washington Times reported that by the mid-'90s, Friendly's had reached its peak number of restaurants across the country at about 850.
The First Friendly's in the Portland Area Opened in 1970
I couldn't confirm the first Friendly's location in Maine, but through the Portland Public Library Special Collections & Archives, I was able to find a photo of the grand opening of the first one in the Portland area.
That would be in South Portland at 581 Main Street in 1970, which is now the site of a Dunkin'. Classic.
Another photo from the Portland Public Library Digital Commons indicated that another South Portland location opened in 1974, and that was right inside the Maine Mall. I always remembered just the one at 210 Maine Mall Road, but that clearly was a new spot to replace the Maine Mall one. Still, it must have been wild to do a little shopping in the mall and just walk on over for some Friendly's.
All of that said, it got me thinking about how the popular restaurant felt like it was everywhere back in the day, and so I took to the Wayback Machine, an internet archive of websites, to check out where and when 13 Friendly's locations existed and what they've become today.
Let's take a trip to the past!
Then and Now: 13 Places in Maine Where Friendly's Restaurants Used to Be
Gallery Credit: Sean McKenna
READ MORE: There's a New Year-Round Ice Cream Shop That Just Opened in Maine
It's interesting to see the variety of transformations. You've got a few Five Guys spots, a dentist, a bank, and various other restaurants.
And when you see the side-by-side of some of these places, it's wild to view the transformation from the past to the present. Some spots still have that unmistakable Friendly's building design, too.
While the Washington Times revealed that there are only about 80 or so Friendly's locations left in the U.S. in 2026, Maine still has one Friendly's left.
That would be the Maine Mall Road location in South Portland, and it's still going strong.
Hopefully, it stands the test of time, and remains that iconic New England spot well into the future. Makes me want to go get some ice cream...

title: Stacy Keach, star of stage and ‘Mike Hammer’ series, dies at 85
text:
(AP) - Stacy Keach, one of America’s finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.
Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, “after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure,” his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.
Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.
Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating “World’s Most Amazing Videos” on TV. He played a deranged colonel in “The Ninth Configuration” (also known as “Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane”), led the TV show “Titus,” had a role in Alexander Payne’s Oscar-nominated drama “Nebraska,” and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama “Blue Bloods.” Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney’s bitter father in “Jay Kelly.”
“My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career,” he told New York magazine in 2012. “My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I’ve gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything.”
Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach’s son in the 2008 TV movie “Lone Rider,” said in a post on X that Keach was a “consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him.”
From TV to stage
He played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries “Mistral’s Daughter,” a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz’s novel “Princess Daisy,” Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli’s “Jesus of Nazareth” and Maj. Jonas Steele in “The Blue and the Gray.” He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds (16 kilograms).
Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play “Indians,” played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in “King Lear” on Broadway and had other onstage roles there in “The Kentucky Cycle” in 1993, “The Country Wife” in 1965 and “Other Desert Cities” in 2011.
He also headed the national touring company cast of “Frost/Nixon,” portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with “Sleuth” with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of “King Lear” at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for “Pamplona,” a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run’s cancellation.
A pivotal arrest
While he was still doing “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer” (later titled “The New Mike Hammer”), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London’s Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.
“As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats,” he wrote in his 2013 book, “All in All: An Actor’s Life On and Off the Stage.” He added: “It was the lowest moment of my life.”
He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book “The Blue and the Gray.”
The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.
In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, “The Long Riders.” He said the experience was “very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity.”
After prison, he narrated the TV documentary “High on the Job,” and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. “There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one’s existence,” he testified.
Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centers. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the “Hammer” series. He said he treasured her photos and letters behind bars.
Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.
Keach’s life after prison
His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, “Intimate Strangers” with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, “The Return of Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” also played well, and then the “Mike Hammer” series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS’ 1986-87 schedule.
Many years later, in the TV series “Prison Break” that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.
Born in Savannah, Georgia, Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.
In the summer of 1963, he worked with the Oregon Shakespeare Festival and played Henry V, Mercutio and Lord Berowne. He attended the Yale School of Drama and, in the summer of 1964, played several roles at New York’s Public Theater in “Hamlet” with Julie Harris. He went to study at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art as a Fulbright scholar and returned to New York to do various stage roles.
Keach made his film debut in 1968 in “The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter” and played stoner cop Sergeant Stedenko from the Cheech and Chong movies. He worked for director John Huston twice, in “Fat City” and “The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean” and had roles in “American History X” with Edward Norton and “The Bourne Legacy.” He played a tough trucker in “Roadgames,” was electrocuted in “Children of the Corn” and a robot removed his heart in “Class of 1999.”
His biggest break, though, came with the role of Hammer, whom he played as a modern-day knight, a champion of the underdog.
“Keach makes a dashing, dapper Hammer. He looks almost jaunty in his tilted gray fedora,” said Fred Rothenberg, a TV writer for The Associated Press, in 1983. “He knows how to speak lust with his eyes, and talk dirty with his fists.”
___
AP Entertainment Writer Andrew Dalton contributed reporting from Los Angeles.

title: Candidate leading supervisor race two months after his death
text:
CALAVERAS COUNTY (KCRA) - Bruce Giudici, who died in August while campaigning for Calaveras County supervisor, is leading Clyde Clapp in the race for the District 5 seat as ballots continue to be counted.
Giudici died after falling on a steep driveway while campaigning. His name remained on the ballot, and his campaign continued.
“Our campaign team kept door knocking. We texted people,” said Carrie Biggs-Adams, a campaign volunteer.
Biggs-Adams said the decision to continue was complicated and emotional.
“We felt very strongly that Bruce had wanted to do this, and that was his mission. And our goal was to finish his mission,” she said.
What happens next
The campaign is confident Giudici will win, Biggs-Adams said, although more ballots remain to be counted.
“There are a few hundred ballots left to process, but it is unlikely that the outcome of the race will change,” she said.
Biggs-Adams said the governor’s office would appoint a replacement from people who volunteer to run. She thanked voters for their support and said the campaign would help ensure someone is selected.
District 5 includes Milton, Jenny Lind, Rancho Calaveras and Salt Spring Valley.

title: Bessent moves to a military base over safety concerns, an AP source says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was recently forced to relocate to a military base over concerns for his safety.
The move comes as Bessent has spent the last several months executing a massive economic campaign against Iran aimed at severing all of Tehran’s remaining financial ties around the world.
A person familiar with the matter, who spoke to The Associated Press on Wednesday on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details, said the relocation was partly due to media reports that helped identify Bessent’s home address. The relocation was earlier reported by The New York Times.
Recent U.S. intelligence showed that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel in the Middle East and elsewhere, which contributed to the State Department last month reducing staffing at four U.S. embassies in the region.
President Donald Trump said this week that the more than 8-month-old Iran war “militarily is effectively over,” but his administration has kept up the financial warfare in a bid to get Iran to capitulate to U.S. demands over Tehran’s nuclear program.
The Treasury Department in August pledged an “economic D-Day” against Tehran, and it has become a massive sanctions and influence campaign.
U.S. officials have spent the past few months traveling from Europe to the Middle East and meeting behind closed doors on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly to make the case to some of Tehran’s closest and most vital trading partners: Sever those financial ties or face retaliation from the United States.
And it appears some have followed suit. The United Arab Emirates and Turkey — key trading partners and regional neighbors — halted Iran’s top commercial bank from issuing transactions in their countries, while some of the country’s top airlines were cut off from critical regional routes from Istanbul to Muscat, Oman.
Other top Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, also live on military bases.

title: A roadmap for Democrats who want peace in Gaza
text:
Daniel Kagan of Freeport is a retired trial attorney with 37 years of practice.
The midterm elections are over. It is time to govern.
In your campaigns, many of you prioritized ending Gazan suffering. Here is how you can get there.
Start by stating publicly that the time for incendiary campaign rhetoric is over. It has been painful and divisive and will get in the way of finding solutions. Admit both of these truths: that Hamas committed horrific atrocities against Israeli civilians on Oct. 7, 2023, and that Gaza’s civilian population has suffered greatly with Israel’s military response. And stop describing these truths with accusatory and divisive language that hardens each side’s resistance to progress toward peace. Then you get to the hard part.
Lasting security in the Middle East requires physical security, political stability and economic success for its people. Gaza, at present, has none of these. Peace requires that the Gazan people have a meaningful opportunity to build for themselves a viable economy, political stability and a thriving middle class with a personal stake in peace. It also requires that Gaza present no military or terrorist threat to Israel.
We know this can be accomplished. Egyptian/Israeli hostilities ended 47 years ago and that peace has held. To achieve that peace, Israel agreed to turn over all of the Sinai to Egypt. If it worked in Egypt, it can work in Gaza.
We know Israel will agree to it; it already did, once. Twenty-one years ago, in September 2005, consistent with an explicit objective of American foreign policy, Israel withdrew from Gaza. Israel removed all its settlements in Gaza and withdrew its military forces. It did so because it expected that the international community would help Gaza dedicate itself to its own economic development and self-sufficiency for its people.
The United States helped make Israel’s withdrawal happen. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice embraced the initiative and called for international support to “revitalize the Palestinian economy.” In November, after helping negotiate the Agreement on Movement and Access, she explained its purpose: “This agreement is intended to give Palestinian people the freedom to move, to trade, to live ordinary lives.” An international initiative led by former World Bank president James Wolfensohn envisioned for Gaza agricultural development, expanded trade, improved transportation and access to foreign markets.
It was an extraordinary opportunity, and it could have worked. But Hamas thwarted it. The chronology is revealing.
September 2005: Israel completed its withdrawal of settlers and permanent military forces from Gaza.
November 2005: Israel and the Palestinian Authority reached concrete agreements on commerce, transportation and development (the Agreement on Movement and Access).
January-April 2006: Hamas wins Palestinian legislative elections. It formed a government that refused to honor its agreements with Israel, and refused to either recognize Israel or renounce using violence against it. In response, the United States and its partners in the peace initiative backed off on its commitment of financial support since it would go to the Hamas-led government. The fragile framework toward peace disintegrated, and armed conflict flared once again.
June 2007: Hamas’ brutal battle with Fatah, its rival for Palestinian leadership, resulted in Hamas taking exclusive control of Gaza. Gazans became further isolated as both Egypt and Israel tightened their borders with Gaza.
That is how Israel’s 2005 withdrawal from Gaza and movements toward peace with Palestinians failed. So why try again? Because there are lessons to be learned from 2005 about what each party needs for an agreement to endure, and what the United States and its peace partners can do to assure it.
What the United States can do:
Security: Identify and support Gazan leaders committed to ending armed confrontation and prioritize economic development for its people. Work toward Israeli withdrawal by rebuilding trust that America will honor its commitments to Israel as well as Gaza. It worked in Israel’s peace with Egypt and it can work again here.
Economic independence: Establish and provide sustained oversight of an internationally supervised, independently audited development authority, to manage building of infrastructure, private investment, entrepreneurship and employment. Do what America can do best — help Gazans build businesses and avoid long-term reliance on social services in perpetuity.
Commercial opportunity: Create and secure reliable market access for Gazan businesses. Let Gaza compete in the global market on a level playing field. Help it build an airport and a commercial port.
Political accountability: Help Gazans create a legal system with independent courts with the power to check excesses of its legislative bodies. Pursue and support judicially enforced property rights, credible elections, and freedom from intimidation.
These, I suggest, are signposts on the road to peace. Follow them, as they lead away from the hateful and divisive words and slogans that dominated the midterm campaign season. Lasting peace for Gazans can only emerge when serious people holding positions of responsibility focus on pragmatic solutions that Israelis and Gazans can live with.
The campaign is over, and it’s time to do the hard work of crafting solutions.

title: 11-month-old boy chokes to death on balloon while celebrating Halloween
text:
KENOSHA, Wis. (WISN) - An 11-month-old Wisconsin boy died after swallowing and choking on a balloon on the way home from a Halloween event. Now, his mother is sharing an important warning for parents.
Kisha Avitia-Wilson took her 11-month-old son, Don’vyaire Avitia-Mays, to an Oct. 24 trunk-or-treat event in Racine. On their drive home, she heard a loud sound coming from the back seat.
“Two of the balloons had just popped, and one of them had came undone,” Avitia-Wilson said.
Within seconds, Don’vyaire swallowed a piece of the balloon. His mother immediately pulled over, called police and then desperately tried to save him.
“I looked at him. He was blue. I tried to dig my fingers down his throat. I tried to do CPR. I tried to do everything that I could,” Avitia-Wilson said.
Kenosha Police say officers responded to the scene in minutes. Emergency crews tried to save Don’vyaire, but it was too late.
“I lost my baby boy in a matter of five seconds. There was nothing that I could have done to save his life,” said Avitia-Wilson through tears.
Avitia-Wilson, who was 31 weeks pregnant at the time, says the stress caused her to go into labor early.
“It was just very heavy on me, and I contracted that whole day, just trying to fight through it because I wanted to make it to my baby boy’s funeral,” she said.
She brought one son into the world on a Wednesday then buried a son on Friday.
Don’vyaire never made it to his first birthday. His mother wants to share her story as a warning for all parents.
“I just want all mothers to know balloons are dangerous. This can happen to anyone’s child, and I just want my son to make it the last child,” Avitia-Wilson said.
A GoFundMe has been set up to help support the family.

title: Boy who helped first responders better comfort children with autism named TIME’s Kid of the Year
text:
HENRICO, Va. (WWBT/Gray News) - A Virginia boy has been named TIME’s Kid of the Year thanks to his role in helping first responders better comfort children with autism.
Nine-year-old Ledger is getting honored for his work, which has included working alongside Henrico County firefighters, paramedics and police officers.
First responders in Henrico have been deploying a new set of specialized tools designed to comfort and improve communication with patients on the autism spectrum during emergency calls with the help of Ledger.
Known as “LGM Bags,” the clear backpacks are filled with sensory-friendly items, communication boards and therapeutic tools.
The program began with a crisis in Prince George County, where Ledger’s father, Sergeant J.T. Mann, a 28-year veteran of county emergency services, was dispatched to search for a missing child with autism.
After several hours of searching, the child was found safely, hiding under a grill cover behind a residence.
Knowing that individuals on the spectrum are often drawn to water or wooded areas to escape loud noises and strangers, Mann said he asked his son Ledger, who was diagnosed with autism at age 2, what would make him feel safe if he were ever lost and found by a first responder.
Ledger immediately began brainstorming comfort items, including stuffed animals, noise-canceling headphones and fidget spinners.
The 9-year-old also insisted that the backpack holding the items must be completely clear so that non-verbal children could easily see inside and point to what they need.
Ledger then emptied $100 from his piggy bank to fund the very first prototypes.
“He said, ‘Dad, I want to do this myself initially,’” Mann recalled. “He took a hundred dollars out of his piggy bank and made the first bags himself and didn’t want the money back or anything. And those were the first bags we distributed, actually out of his own money.”
To date, the “LGM” program, named after Ledger’s initials, has distributed over 432 bags across Virginia, West Virginia, North Carolina and Florida.
The initiative has garnered national and international attention, including being featured in TIME and People and even billboard recognition as far away as Australia.
The program’s expansion into Henrico County was championed by Lakeside Station 5 Firefighter Courtney Koppelman.
Koppelman, who recently joined the Henrico Division of Fire after serving in Hanover County, grew up with a brother who had spina bifida and a learning disability.
“It’s really close to my heart with having a brother who was special needs growing up, and the world not always meeting him where he was at,” Koppelman said. “So it’s great to meet people where they are and make them feel safe and heard and helped.”
Koppelman had previously created her own personal sensory bags to carry on calls.
She knew from experience that emergency scenes can be terrifyingly loud and visually overwhelming, especially inside an ambulance.
“Ambulances are very overwhelming, with the engine revving, monitors beeping and other loud sounds,” Koppelman said. “The noise-canceling headphones alone provide a much more comfortable ride for our patients.”
Koppelman saw that sensory tools were valuable not just for children on the spectrum, but also for elderly patients experiencing dementia and adults suffering from severe anxiety or trauma.
She requested that Henrico County leadership explore a department-wide program.
Henrico leaders quickly embraced the idea.
Dr. Anjali Ferguson, who spent nearly a decade as deputy medical director before taking the OMD role full-time two years ago, noted that these bags fill a critical void in pre-hospital care.
“When I’m in the hospital, we have child life specialists that come in with these toys and distracting agents or even iPads,” Ferguson said. “But we don’t have that in the field. So this sort of bridges that gap between what we have available to us in the field and what we have in the hospital.”
According to Ferguson, the bags do more than just soothe anxious minds; they directly enable first responders to provide safer and more efficient medical treatment.
“Everyone in Henrico County is passionate about providing the most elite service for citizens,” Koppelman said. “And I feel like this is just a small component to upping that service provided on a daily basis. It makes my heart happy. I’m glad we’re able to provide that service for people.”
The donated bags have since been placed on all frontline Henrico ambulances, EMS captain vehicles, and with police crisis intervention officers.

title: MTV's '16 and Pregnant' star faces up to 44 years for Georgia man’s fatal overdose
text:
MTV's '16 and Pregnant' star faces up to 44 years for Georgia man’s fatal overdose
Whitney Purvis, who appeared on MTV’s “16 and Pregnant,” has entered an Alford guilty plea to charges stemming from a Georgia man’s fatal overdose, according to Floyd County court records.
On Friday, Purvis entered the plea to involuntary manslaughter, sale of fentanyl and illegal use of a communication facility, WSB-TV reported. She could face up to 44 years in prison under the plea agreement.
An Alford plea allows a defendant to maintain their innocence while acknowledging that prosecutors have enough evidence to likely secure a conviction.
The overdose case
The charges stem from the death of John Mark Harris, who was found dead at a home in Rome on Feb. 16, 2025. Police found possible drug paraphernalia at the scene, according to reporting by The Associated Press.
An arrest warrant accused Purvis of giving Harris a substance presented as “Tranq,” which authorities described as a mixture of fentanyl and xylazine. The warrant alleged that the substance contributed to his death from a toxic overdose.
Purvis was arrested in July 2025 by Drug Enforcement Administration agents and local officers. She was initially charged with involuntary manslaughter and two drug-related offenses.
Her time on MTV
Purvis appeared on “16 and Pregnant” in 2009, which followed her and then-boyfriend Weston Lewis Gosa as they prepared to become teenage parents.
Their son, Weston Owen Gosa Jr., died in June 2025 at age 16. Purvis shared the news on social media, calling his death her “worst nightmare come true.”

title: Maine volunteers pack care packages for troops spending holidays away from home
text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - Volunteers gathered at Box of Maine on Veterans Day with a common mission: send a little comfort from home to Maine service members spending the holidays far away.
The group packed 500 care packages filled with Maine-made products as part of the Maine Soldier Box program. 35 area businesses sponsored the effort, while students at 15 schools in the region contributed hundreds of thank-you cards.
For returning volunteers and newcomers alike, the event was a way to honor those who have served while supporting those serving today.
“It feels good to bring people together as a community and I do think that there’s something special about Maine when it comes to that,” said Daniel Finnemore, owner of Box of Maine.
A community effort
Box of Maine has put together care packages for Maine service members for about a decade. The business invited the community to help pack boxes three years ago, and the effort has grown each year.
Veterans, families, neighbors and children joined this year’s packout. The goal is to ship the care packages by November 30.
“Just happy to be here and supporting the folks overseas,” volunteer Gerry said.
Bangor Savings Bank sponsored the packing event. Moe’s Original BBQ provided catering, and Tim Hortons supplied coffee and donuts.
A special thank-you for veterans
Among the volunteers was 10-year-old Evan Hunter, who also gives back through his own initiative, Evan’s Veterans Project. WABI introduced viewers to Evan last year.
Evan hands out cards and creates gifts to thank local veterans for their service. After the packout, he planned to deliver more cards.
“It makes them feel like they’re heard and makes them feel like they’re loved,” Evan said.
Box of Maine is still seeking the community’s support of reaching their 1,000 goal.

title: Elementary students honor veterans in Corinth

“One of my best friends got me to join. He talked about it and come down. I attended drill with him, and it ended up being a 24-year excursion after that. It’s something I thought I should do,” said Towel, “Not everybody is willing to do that.”

title: QUINN QUESTIONS: The world’s greatest athlete?
text:
At lunch, several of us guys got to talking about who is the best athlete, human or animal.
Surprisingly, the world’s greatest may be the spittle bug, who’s jumpier than a pickpocket at a police station.
The adult spittle measures only one-fourth inch long. But this guy possesses remarkable leg strength, and if you loaned him a toothpick he could probably pole vault.
This powerful dude can leap two feet. No, not jump over my shoes, but actually bound 24 inches, or 96 TIMES its size!
That’s like a six-foot man clearing a 48-story building. I never saw anybody do this, but one time my friend Tom jumped to the wrong conclusion, and his girlfriend told him to take a flying leap.
Actually, the animal kingdom is filled with great athletes. A cheetah can run nearly 70 mph. A millepede can walk on 1,000 legs without stepping on anyone’s toes.
And the ant can lift 50 times its weight, much more than its insect counterpart, the uncle.
When it comes to endurance, few can top those amazing birds, the arctic terns. In the course of a year, some migrate up to 22,000 miles.
But one flock member misjudged his altitude, collided with a dizzy eagle, and landed on a sheep.
That’s how he became the first “ill eagle ewe tern.”
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: World War I veteran finally laid to rest 45 years after death
text:
RANDOLPH CENTER, Vt. (InvestigateTV) - On a typical day at the Vermont Veterans Memorial Cemetery, the only sound on these hallowed grounds is an American flag flapping in the gentle breeze and birds chirping from a distance.
“It is definitely interesting,” said Collin Johnson, who makes sure the Randolph Center cemetery’s grounds stay pristine for the over 6,000 veterans and their spouses who are buried there.
Three men were laid to rest recently. Private Edward James Irwin was one of them. His final goodbye comes almost 45 years after his death. He served in the Army during World War I from 1917 to 1918.
You may wonder why a World War I vet who died in November 1981 is finally going to be laid to rest. Well, it goes back to Walter Ducharme’s funeral business in Rutland.
Ducharme bought Clifford’s Funeral Home last year. Everything came with the business, including a basement with rows of cremated remains.
“The family didn’t pick up, or there was no one to take care of the matter,” Ducharme said.
One caught Ducharme’s attention -- Mr. Irwin. Very little was known about the man other than he was born in New Jersey in 1897 and served during World War I. Why he came to Vermont or if he had any living relatives to collect his ashes remains a mystery.
He died in a nursing home in Rutland. Irwin was just days away from turning 84.
For over a year, Ducharme became a desktop detective, dealing with different government agencies.
“They did come up with his right Social Security number, his right VA file number, the right date of birth, but the name was wrong,” Ducharme said. “It was frustrating, it was very frustrating for sure.”
It took over a year before everything matched up.
“We could not find any family members left; we couldn’t even find any close friends,” Ducharme said.
The word, though, got out about Private Irwin’s saga. Elaine Manghi-Buck heard the news at her church. “I’m here to honor this veteran,” said the Brookfield woman. “It seems to be important to be here.”
The Combat Veterans Motorcycle Association also roared in for the service after hearing the news at their American Legion.
“Yes, yes, it’s remarkable, we’re honored to be here,” said the association’s Ed Barton.
Total strangers treated Private Irwin like family. What was going to be a simple service at the grave site moved into the chapel.
“He has been on a bit of a journey for a long time. He’s a World War I veteran, and it’s our great pleasure to find him a final resting place,” said Robert Burke with Vermont Veterans Affairs.
“This is what we do, we show up for each other,” said Chris Noble, the deacon of Our Lady of the Valley Church. “Most of you, maybe all of us, didn’t even know him. But we know what he stood for, and we know what he did. And we honor that service.”
“We don’t know a lot about him, but as the deacon said, he was a human being,” said United Church of Bethel Rev. Tom Harty. “We ask you to grant him everlasting peace.”
“Thank you for your service, and sorry that it took so long to get you where you needed to be,” Ducharme said.
