title: Michael Joseph retains Winslow District 1 council seat after a recount
text:
WINSLOW — After the town’s first recount in recent memory, District 1 Town Councilor Michael Joseph retained his seat by just nine votes.
Retired career firefighter Scott Holst called for the recount Nov. 4 after unofficial results showed he lost by 12 votes. The recount took just over three hours Wednesday morning in the Parks and Recreation Department.
Joseph lost two votes, finishing at 249. Both Holst and Erin McCullough — who originally came in third, six votes behind Holst — gained a vote. Holst finished with 240 votes and McCullough finished with 234.
Holst said he was nervous before hearing the results, but he was “glad the system did its job … with that many votes, you have to look back at it.”
Joseph, who said he was not nervous about the count but declined to comment further, was first elected in 2023, when he ran on a platform of cutting “unnecessary spending” in the town budget.
Joseph and Holst both attended the recount, along with Police Chief Vicente Morris and Councilor Doris Labranche. Town Clerk Audra Fleury led the recount.
Volunteers spent about an hour separating District 1 ballots from the rest before six volunteers counted ballots in batches of 50. Counters worked in pairs, with one calling out the vote and one making a tally, although both made sure to look at the ballot.
Joseph and Holst each suggested two volunteers as ballot counters, and Fleury called two other election day volunteers to complete the group of counters.
Holst said he’d be “absolutely happy” if Joseph won, but there was no question that he would call for a recount with such a close race, noting that candidates have called recounts in races with much wider margins.
Holst said he plans to run for the councilor at-large seat next year.
Although no one ran for Winslow’s District 5 school committee seat, Andrew Giroux received three write-in votes, Fleury said, winning that election.

title: How to speak up for yourself or a loved one during a medical crisis
text:
(Aging Untold) — When you or someone you love is facing a medical crisis, it can be hard to think clearly, let alone know what questions to ask.
The Aging Untold experts share ways to speak up, understand the care plan and help make sure your loved one’s needs and wishes are heard.
Speak up when something doesn’t seem right
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose described advocating for her husband when he was expected to leave the hospital and return later for surgery.
She didn’t think he was ready to go home, so she raised her concerns with a nurse and contacted a social worker. By the time she returned to the hospital, a plan was in place for him to stay.
A couple of days later, she noticed that he seemed to be getting worse rather than better. She brought that concern to a nurse, who began making calls.
Ambrose said the team discovered that her husband was missing a medication and that he improved after receiving it.
“That’s what we mean by advocacy, is paying attention and asking questions and being vocal,” Ambrose said.
If something feels different from your loved one’s usual condition, tell a member of the care team what you’ve noticed and when the change began.
Ask questions until the plan makes sense
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said you don’t have to have medical training to support your family member. It is important to ask questions and support your loved one, she said.
“A story is being told and you should be able to connect the dots to that story,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. “And if you can’t, you have to keep asking until you fill in the missing pieces.”
Build a team and know your loved one’s wishes
Advocacy doesn’t mean doing everything alone.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said knowing what you don’t know and where to go to find it is a skill as a medical advocate. You also need to know hospital systems or who can explain them because you’re helping coordinate a discharge plan, she added.
“And know your person, know what you’re advocating for. If you don’t know their values and their priorities, it’s hard to advocate for them,” O’Rourke said.
Keep good records, write things down and keep track so you can share relevant details with the care team when needed, O’Rourke added.
“You’re really just trying to get an understanding too. Yes, we want what’s best, but we also just want to understand. We’re just trying to make sure that things are going the best that they can,” Ambrose said.

title: Biddeford organizations will not be asked to leave community center
text:
Biddeford organizations can now breathe easier knowing they won’t have to vacate the J. Richard Martin Community Center, four months after a proposal that would have ended some groups’ permanent spaces there.
The City Council voted Oct. 20 to postpone a request for organizations to leave their leased spaces within the community center to make room for other groups. Instead, the St. Louis Alumni room, which will soon be empty, will become available for use by community groups.
The St. Louis Alumni Association — which represents graduates and supporters of the former St. Louis High School, shuttered in 1960 — recently announced that it would disband due to an aging alumni population.
Lisa Thompson, director of the recreation department, said the alumni association’s current space will be available to use or rent, by the hour, to any group or organizations that need meeting or program space.
After six months, the City Council will evaluate whether more space is still needed at the community center.
Unless there is further council action at a future date, there is no requirement for groups with leases to vacate their space, city spokesperson Danica Lamontagne said.
Those groups include AgeMaine (formerly the Southern Maine Agency on Aging), which operates Meals on Wheels; as well as La Kermesse, the Biddeford Cultural and Heritage Center, the Biddeford Fifty Plus Club and Biddeford Adult Education.
Some of the other organizations that have shown an interest in using the space are local homeowners associations, Alcoholics Anonymous, youth sports groups, the Maine Peoples Alliance, Project Home Maine, and other city departments and commissions, Thompson said.
GROUPS FEARED UPHEAVAL
Since proposed changes to space usage at the community center were made in July, the organizations currently using space at the center have been vocal about the need to remain in their rooms.
Ashley Perrone, director of AgeMaine, said Meals on Wheels serves hundreds of people each month out of the Biddeford community center.
“If Meals on Wheels had to relocate, the consequences would be significant,” Perrone said. “It would be extremely difficult to find an affordable, accessible location with enough space for meal storage, volunteer packing and our Community Café.”
Diane Cyr, president of the Biddeford Cultural and Heritage Center, said groups like hers provide free services that benefit residents. Asking groups to leave the community center, she added, would go against the purpose of the building.
“These groups provide real public value,” Cyr said.
Former Biddeford Mayor Alan Casavant, the vice president of the Cultural and Heritage center, said the council’s decision puts the group “between a rock and a hard place.”
The community center isn’t the perfect place for storing archives, Casavant said: The heating and cooling systems aren’t reliable, the Wi-Fi is spotty, and the building isn’t open on the weekends. But finding another place to rent is close to impossible.
“It’s problematic in a lot of ways, but at this time, it’s the best we have,” he said. “Our vision is that we want to move, but finances are critical in doing that.”
COUNCIL IN SUPPORT
City councilors last month spoke in support of helping organizations stay at the community center but acknowledged a space problem that needs to be addressed.
At-large Councilor Marc Lessard described the space issue as “trying to fit 8 pounds in a 5-pound bag.”
“I don’t have any intention of taking archives and just throwing them in a trashcan or putting them in a big pile and lighting them on fire,” he said. “In fact, if there are archives that are worth something, we should be putting them on display instead of in a closet.”
It was also Lessard who suggested turning the former St. Louis Alumni room into flex space, with Ward 1 Councilor Patricia Boston making a motion to do so. That motion passed 6-2, with Ward 7 Councilor Brad Cote and Ward 6 Councilor Jake Pierson opposed.
But there is the possibility that, when councilors revisit the issue next year, they could decide to move forward with the original plan.
“I don’t think there’s a perfect fit for everyone there, but I think what has to be done is to look at the merits of the organizations that are there,” Casavant said. “It’s a complicated situation.”

title: I sat in someone else’s tree stand — and got more than I bargained for
text:
Editor’s note: This was originally published Jan. 6.
Deer hunting alone in the North Maine Woods, I parked the truck at the entrance to an old, partially grown logging road that snaked through open hardwoods. It looked inviting.
It was a typical November morning in the big woods, cold and frosty, with the promise of a freshening wind as the sun worked its way above the salmon-colored horizon. After a 10-minute stalk on this tote road, an unusual sight caught my attention.
Off to the right, not far from the road, was a spanking-new plywood deer blind built up on a two-by-four support structure. It would be best described as a “shooter’s shack.” In the conventional sense, it wasn’t a portable stand. Freshly painted, it was strategically situated adjacent to what looked like a funnel for deer on the move.
Curious, I walked closer. The wind was picking up, increasing the chill factor. I pulled my orange stocking cap snug around my head and neck. For a moment, I stood at the bottom rung of the stout ladder leading up to the structure.
“This construction is excellent,” I thought to myself. Hmm.
There was no padlock on the door, just a latch with a twig holding it shut. “I’ll just have a look-see inside.” Swinging open the door, I beheld an inviting, clean cubicle complete with a chair and a seat pillow, and a shooting window that dropped open on a pulley rig.
The inside beckoned me like a seductress with arched eyebrows and ruby lips. A gust of wind caught the open door, and I stepped up another rung to find a purchase so I could hold the door against the wind.
“Just for a minute,” I assured myself, and stepped in and sat down out of the wind in the plastic chair. “Oooo, this is some comfy,” I said out loud. For about 30 minutes, I luxuriated in someone else’s well-crafted domain. Then I began to have second thoughts about being there at all and decided to get out and back into the woods.
Backing my way cautiously down the shack ladder, as any old man would, I caught an out-of-place smell — a noxious whiff of cigarette smoke — and at the same moment heard a gruff voice shout from behind me.
“What the #$%! are you doing in my stand?”
He was a middle-aged guy with a weather-beaten face and a cigarette dangling from his lips, attired in an orange sweatshirt and unlaced boots. He continued to utter profanities and berate me.
I have not been chewed out with such intense vitriol since my weeks at Navy boot camp. I tried to apologize, but he was not to be placated or calmed down. The verbal beating continued as I strapped on my day pack. As I made my exit, his stream of condemnation toward me included a snarky comment about me “writing about this in the Northwoods Sporting Journal.”
As I headed back to my truck, the angry man, who was carrying a rifle, which I assumed was loaded, walked ahead of me and continued his stream of invective. Normally, when braced like this, there is a limit to just how much verbal abuse I will take. I tend to stand up for myself and talk back — but not when both parties are armed with high-powered rifles. I bit my tongue, for I was in the wrong.
I got what I deserved, right? Is it an ethical or legal issue? Or is it both?
If I find a hunter in my tree stand, I don’t get all torqued up and curse him out. I tell him it’s my stand and “my turn, Bud.” In all my years in the deer woods, there has never been a confrontation of any kind over tree stands.
A game warden tells me that if you come upon a tree stand, no matter how inviting, it is a form of trespass to use it if the stand is legally labeled with the owner’s name, address and phone number.
Big buck hunter Hal Blood, who never sits in tree stands, believes that another guy’s tree stand is sacred, not only because it is his property, but because he went to some work to find a good strategic location. Using another guy’s stand “is cheating,” Blood says.
Views on this issue differ, even among seasoned guides and woodsmen. However, there does seem to be consensus in one area: If a hunter does come upon a tree stand that is obviously abandoned or not legally labeled with the owner’s name and address, using it should not get you in any trouble.
As for my shooter-shack transgression, I have not disclosed the whole story. There is an amusing conclusion, the revealing of which could possibly invite recrimination or an act of revenge.
I have learned a new lesson for the deer woods. Even in my advanced years, it is one I will not soon forget.

title: Jay data center could create up to 1,000 construction jobs, 150 permanent positions, developer says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — A data center proposed for the former Androscoggin Mill, which appears to have new life after the developer pulled out in June, could create as many as 1,000 construction jobs and 150 permanent positions, a partner in the project said Tuesday.
In addition, a redesigned cooling system would limit water usage — often a concern in data center projects — to a one-time fill rather than the substantial daily replacement water previously anticipated, said Tony McDonald, a partner in JGT2 Redevelopment LLC.
McDonald confirmed that Sentinel Data Centers remains involved in the project and that the company is moving forward with an amendment to its state environmental permit.
“We never walked away from this project or this town,” McDonald said in written responses provided through Dan Cashman, public relations director at Sutherland Weston Marketing Communications.
The proposal earlier this year drew the attention of Gov. Janet Mills, who vetoed a bill that would have temporarily banned data centers in Maine because it did not include an exemption for the Jay project.
Still, the project stalled after Sentinel announced in June it was stepping away.
The news that Sentinel’s project was back on reached Augusta as well, with Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree saying Jay should not be a “testing ground” for data centers and that Maine needs “strong regulations in place.”
Residents in a number of communities, including Lewiston, have come out fiercely against data center construction, raising concerns about environmental impact and energy usage. On Nov. 3, eight Maine municipalities passed permanent or temporary bans on data centers.
“We have seen the damage in Virginia and Texas: higher electric bills, strained grids, pollution, and communities not getting promised benefits,” Pingree said in a statement.
“Jay deserves good jobs and investment at the mill site, but not at the cost of ratepayers, neighbors or the environment.”
PROJECT UPDATE
The updated plans offer a clearer picture of the proposed redevelopment. McDonald said the project would reuse about 1 million square feet of former mill buildings and the property’s existing electrical connection, with no grid upgrades anticipated.
The most significant change involves water consumption.
During a March 23 presentation to the Jay Select Board, McDonald described a closed-loop cooling system requiring about 300,000 gallons of water daily to replace evaporation losses. The latest concept calls for a one-time permanent fill with no discharge into the Androscoggin River, he said.
“Our water system concept has changed since the spring; we are looking at a closed-loop, one-time permanent fill with no discharge to the river,” McDonald said.
He estimated the initial fill would require less than 1% of the 35 million to 45 million gallons of water the paper mill previously used each day. The estimated total fill is 260,000 gallons, with no additional water required during operation, he said.
The developer also revised its employment projections, anticipating 800 to 1,000 construction jobs and 125 to 150 permanent positions across three shifts. Earlier estimates called for about 800 construction jobs and more than 100 permanent positions.
The proposed development was previously valued at $550 million. McDonald did not provide an updated investment estimate or anticipated construction start date.
The project’s electrical demand drew statewide attention earlier this year when lawmakers considered legislation temporarily restricting permits for large data centers. McDonald previously estimated the facility would initially require about 82 megawatts of electricity.
In his latest responses, McDonald said the project would use the mill’s existing electrical contract and grid connection, eliminating the need for upgrades. He also maintained that the development would not negatively affect local electricity bills, although no independent assessment of potential ratepayer impacts was provided.
McDonald said discussions with Sentinel continued despite the company’s decision in June not to proceed at that time.
“Our discussions never stopped,” he said. “Yes, Sentinel is involved in the project.”
Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere told the Select Board on Monday that the companies were moving forward again but had not reached a final agreement.
McDonald emphasized that the latest permitting activity involves the original development rather than a replacement proposal.
“This isn’t a new project or a new application,” he said. “It’s the same project, the same owner, the same site, moving forward through the state’s public review with DEP.”
AMENDMENTS AND OPEN HOUSE
According to a public notice, JGT2 is seeking a minor amendment under Maine’s Site Location of Development Act and a new minor source air emission license. The proposal includes reusing existing buildings for computing equipment and converting former parking and rail yard areas to accommodate heating, ventilation and air conditioning equipment.
The permitting schedule remains uncertain, and McDonald said the company is prioritizing regulatory review and assembling the appropriate construction team over committing to a specific timeline.
The redevelopment could also increase municipal tax revenue, although updated estimates of the property’s anticipated taxable value have not been provided.
JGT2 plans next month to hold a public open house at the former mill, where residents can ask questions about the proposal, including its electricity and water requirements. LaFreniere said Dec. 10 is under consideration, but the date has not been confirmed.
McDonald said the company will announce the date and time at www.TheJayMill.com, where residents can also submit questions as plans develop.

title: Searsmont EMS Chief to be released from hospital 6 months after deadly mill fire

After more than six months of recovery, one of the last surviving victims of the devastating fire at the Robbins Lumber mill in Searsmont is preparing to come home.
Searsmont EMS Chief Sarah Tompkins to be released from hospital 6 months after deadly mill fire
After more than six months of recovery, one of the last surviving victims of the devastating fire at the Robbins Lumber mill in Searsmont is preparing to come home.

title: Accountability is not revenge
text:
Is it truly “retribution” to seek accountability?
I am increasingly frustrated by calls to “move on,” “fix the economy” or “let it go” to avoid appearing vengeful. We can — and must — address past abuses of power while simultaneously working to prevent future misconduct. Why is “moving on” always the refrain? Can we not advance key priorities while addressing the destruction of the past two years?
There is a distinct difference between seeking revenge for personal grievances and holding individuals accountable for violating the law. Sweeping violations under the rug on the assumption that someone has “learned their lesson” directly undermines our justice system.
Holding individuals and agencies accountable for their actions is essential to protecting our institutions and preventing future abuse.
Jan Strout
Gray

title: Republicans pick party leadership after midterm election losses
text:
Republicans pick party leadership after midterm election losses
Democrats are having similar leadership debates as the party prepares to take control of Congress in January.
Republicans pick party leadership after midterm election losses
Democrats are having similar leadership debates as the party prepares to take control of Congress in January.
Republicans reflected on what went wrong and started to chart the path forward on Tuesday, one week after enduring sweeping losses in the midterm elections.
During closed-door meetings, Republicans chose leadership teams who will steer GOP minorities in the House and Senate moving forward.
These picks have implications for the future of the party and the American people. Party leaders set the tone on Capitol Hill and shape the policy playbook.
Senate Republicans re-elected South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader on Tuesday. Thune ran unopposed, but some GOP Senators called for delaying the vote to allow for more discussion about midterm defeats.
"There was a lot of interest in delaying this. I'm not sure, again, necessarily what that achieves," Thune said. "I think what I want to see us do is come out of this knowing full well that we took a big electoral defeat, but come out swinging."
Rep. Jim Jordan elected House Minority Leader
In the House, Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio beat out Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana for the top Republican leadership spot on a 106-73 vote. House Speaker Mike Johnson previously announced that he would step down from his leadership role, teeing up the showdown.
Jordan made the case that his experience chairing the House Judiciary Committee has prepared him to fight back against the slew of investigations that Democrats are promising against the Trump administration. Jordan also co-founded the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus.
Jordan didn't take questions after the vote but made brief remarks about his mission.
"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. When Democrats offer more government, we will offer more freedom, and we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor, and on the stump every single day," Jordan said.
Who will lead Democrats?
Democrats are having similar leadership debates as the party prepares to take control of Congress in January.
Current Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York expressed confidence on Tuesday that he will be re-elected as majority leader, adding there is "great unity" in the party.
But earlier Tuesday, Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan sent a very different message. Sanders said he doesn't plan to support Schumer, and Slotkin called for a more rigorous election process.
"I think whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they're going to govern differently, what they're going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people's pockets, and then, in particular, how they're going to communicate differently," Slotkin said. "I am not actively seeking this job. I am seeking change."
Several newly elected senators have echoed that sentiment.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has emerged as a potential challenger, but he has not formalized his bid for majority leader.
In the lower chamber, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries appears poised to become House Speaker when that election is held in January, but he too has faced criticism from some fellow Democrats.

Veterans Day: Here's a list of deals and what's open and closed
Veterans Day is a federal holiday that honors those who have served in the U.S. military. It is observed annually on Nov. 11.
Video above: Artist lends talents to new Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial in Washington, D.C.
President Woodrow Wilson established the holiday in 1919 to recognize the end of World War I. Congress officially recognized Veterans Day as a federal holiday in 1926.

title: China select board deals with complicated issues
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
China select board members had several complicated issues on their Nov. 2 agenda, not all ripe for decision. They decided three:
— Board members unanimously approved a new, less comprehensive proposal from Raegan LaRochelle to assist with developing China’s revised Tax Increment Financing (TIF) plan (see the Oct. 22 issue of The Town Line, p. 3). LaRochelle will receive $3,200 for about three weeks spent educating the select board and the public and working with them and Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood to identify town projects eligible for TIF funding. Her fee will come from the TIF account.
— After discussion of the town’s partly-outdated Telecommunications Ordinance, board members unanimously accepted Harmoni Towers’ bond in the amount of $68,637.75. The bond is intended to cover the cost of removal when the tower the company has approval to build on Parmenter Hill becomes obsolete (see the Oct. 29 issue of The Town Line, p. 2).
The bond amount did not have the professional engineer’s endorsement that the ordinance requires. Codes Officer Nicholas French said confirming removal cost estimates is “not what professional engineers do.”
— By yet another unanimous vote, board members changed China’s HRA (Health Reimbursement Account) from the current administrator to Consumer Health Solutions, saving $470 and, Hapgood hopes, getting as good or better service.
The HRA is related to the town employees’ health insurance plan, topic of a quarter-hour discussion and no decision. The Maine Municipal Employees Health Trust currently offers five plans; China is enrolled in the middle one, in terms of employee costs and benefits. The town would save money by switching to a less generous plan.
Hapgood said with the HRA covering employees’ costs, like deductibles and co-pays, last year was the first year the town didn’t “make employees whole.”
She invited select board members to send her questions to be answered at the Nov. 16 board meeting. With open enrollment starting Nov. 15, she expects a decision on Nov. 16.
Another issue involving money and potential complications is dispatching emergency services. Currently, China uses the Kennebec Sheriff’s Office (KSO), which in turn uses the state system. This system, Select Board Chairman Brent Chesley said he learned at a meeting the previous week, is outdated, and the state won’t spend money to update it.
Therefore, KSO intends to switch to the City of Augusta’s dispatching service, at a higher cost.
Chesley was indignant about several aspects of the planned new system. Each town’s charge is based on a 1987 formula, 75 percent on population and 25 percent on call volume, which he said is contrary to state statute.
The formula also hurts China and Chelsea, two Kennebec County towns that contract for KSO patrols, Chesley said. Every time a KSO deputy calls in to check a license plate, China gets billed for a call.
Chesley was more indignant because he had learned that towns with their own dispatching service don’t pay the county anything. He said he asked at the meeting if there is a county service China doesn’t use, can the town be exempted from paying for it?
A final insult, he said, was when county officials proposed starting the new service – and billing for it – on April 1, instead of waiting for the towns’ new fiscal years to begin July 1.
The dispatch bill will be separate from the annual county tax bill, he said.
Also needing decision soon is whether to renew the contract for disposal of bulky waste and construction debris or to seek a new company. The current contract with Waste Management ends Dec. 31. Hapgood said Transfer Station Manager Thomas Maraggio is seeking prices from several services.
Board members heard of, but did not discuss, one more potential expense increase, for Delta Ambulance. The towns of Fairfield and Benton have notified Delta that they intend to stop using its service in February 2027. Delta officials will have to find some way to continue to pay bills without those two towns.
As the meeting ended, Hapgood reminded those present that all town departments will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 11, for the Veterans’ Day holiday; and Thursday and Friday, Nov. 26 and 27, for the Thanksgiving holiday.
The Nov. 16 select board meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. in the town office meeting room.

title: Maine's Highest-Earning Cities Have Been Revealed
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
THE LIST: The Richest Cities in Maine Might Surprise You
If you have spent time living in more than just a couple of towns/cities, you have probably realized that the average salary varies a lot from town to town.
Clearly, this is really noticeable when you move between different parts of the country. For example, as a kid from Aroostook County my mind was blown at what fast-food employees were making in New York City.
That being said, there are massive differences in pay between different towns here in Maine. For example, Portland has a higher minimum wage than the statewide minimum wage. On top of that, there is an enormous difference between what a skilled worker in Southern Maine makes compared to what the same person would make in Caribou.
So, in which Maine towns and cities are you likely to earn the most?
The Highest-Earning Cities and Towns in Maine
Thanks to the team at Stacker, we have a pretty good idea about the highest-earning cities and towns in Maine. These are the municipalities where the majority of top earners live.
In some cases, these towns make perfect sense. Portland, for example. However, some of these were a complete surprise to us. In fact, we were really surprised by the town that took the top spot on the list.
Check out the list and let us know your thoughts.
The 19 Highest Earning Cities In Maine
Do any of the towns or cities on this list surprise you? Let us know your thoughts. Let us know by sending us a message using our app.

title: Hannaford evacuated for propane check
text:
At 9:46 a.m. on Nov. 11, Boothbay Harbor Fire Department responded to a call from Lincoln County Communications (LCC) about a possible propane incident at Hannaford. After two hours of on-site testing, BHFD and Dead River had not found propane issues at the store, Fire Chief Glenn Tilton said.
Tilton had been headed to the store for some things when the call came in. "When I went in, the manager came out and told me that it was strictly coincidence that there was still an issue,” he said. “When I got there initially, there was a faint, faint smell.”
The first of two Boothbay Harbor fire trucks arrived on the scene within minutes and reported back to the chief the situation required response for a fire alarm. “We shut everything down, called Dead River, and sent our crew into the building and on the roof,” said Tilton adding, “There’d been zero (propane) readings right from the get-go. But Dead River still had to do their thing with leak tests and all."
A second Boothbay Harbor fire truck with a gas detector arrived about an hour after the first. There were four firefighters and two Boothbay Harbor Police Department units on site to help the fire department evacuate everyone from the building and to block the parking lot entrances.
The incident wrapped up at 11:46 a.m. with only Dead River still on site finishing up testing, Tilton said.

title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction
text:
Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction
Democratic nominee Scott Colom has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, and it will echo through the country as well. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.
The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43 year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state's large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term.
"They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.
"It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better, and we don't come up with excuses as to why we can't do it," he said.
A race Washington once viewed as a longshot
The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, drawing attention from Democrats who belatedly infused cash into Colom's candidacy. The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized.
Colom attracted particular notice for some of the year's most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith, 67, seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they'd "pick another senator instead."
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.
Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: "Is this not the best president in our lifetime?"
Then she stepped away.
"I love that," Trump replied when he continued his 80-plus minutes at the microphone. "Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes."
The appearance tracked Colom's tactic of criticizing Trump's policies — especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a non-entity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state that has been accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.
There is some irony to Hyde-Smith finding herself flat-footed against Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi's senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom's confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president's choices for federal judicial positions in their home state.
Colom said his Senate bid was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
Colom called on Mississippi's history
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family.
"In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection," Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction.
"He was killed for helping Mississippians vote," Colom said. "On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right."
Black Democrats, including Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, highlighted Colom's bid early. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.
Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks.
Despite Republicans' domination, the path was always there
With the largest share of Black voters of any state, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Then-Gov. Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story.
"My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values," he said, "and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I've done that they shouldn't get a chance."

title: Missing-in-action WWII soldier will be buried in Bangor year after his remains were identified
text:
The remains of Willard Orr, who went missing in action in World War II, have been identified and will be buried in Bangor this week.
Orr, a 1939 Bangor High School graduate, enlisted in the United States Army Air Corps in December 1940. He was a head cook at Hickam Field in Hawaii, and was presumed killed in the Pearl Harbor attacks.
The Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency, which recovers and identifies missing U.S. service members, identified his remains in November 2025.
His remains will be buried Saturday at Maple Grove Cemetery in a service coordinated by Brookings-Smith Funeral Home in Bangor.
When Japanese military forces attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941, nearby military installations including Hickam Field were also targeted. During a 4-hour attack, 91 soldiers died at Hickam Field, and their bodies were buried in the Schofield Barracks Cemetery. In 1947, all but 12 of their identities were confirmed. The unidentified remains were buried at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific.
The Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency exhumed the unidentified remains in 2019. In November 2025, a laboratory analysis and circumstantial evidence confirmed the identity of one of the unknowns as Orr.
Orr is the namesake of the Willard C. Orr Pedestrian Bridge in Bangor, originally constructed around 1980 and rededicated in 2021. The bridge spans the Kenduskeag Stream between Pickering Square and Exchange Street.
He was posthumously awarded the Purple Heart and is memorialized on the Tablets of the Missing at Honolulu Memorial, Honolulu, Hawaii.

title: Big storm chances fade, but snow in Maine still possible
text:
Big storm chances fade, but snow in Maine still possible
Tracking a chance for snow Friday morning, but our weekend is trending drier
Big storm chances fade, but snow in Maine still possible
Tracking a chance for snow Friday morning, but our weekend is trending drier
Colder air is settling across the region over the next several days, bringing a brief touch of early winter. All eyes have been on a developing storm off the New England coast, but consistent model guidance over the last 72 hours continues to keep the storm from making a major impact on Maine. While some coastal effects will still linger, a direct hit remains unlikely at this time.
Rain chances begin late Thursday afternoon in southern Maine and New Hampshire, then spread inland through the evening and overnight. Showers could change to snow, especially over higher terrain. Snow is likely across many parts of the state by the Friday morning commute. While overall accumulation will be light, wet snowflakes could coat grassy surfaces and vehicles, creating some slick travel conditions for the morning drive.
Precipitation will taper off quickly on Friday as the storm tracks further south, leaving only isolated rain or snow showers through Saturday. High temperatures will remain in the low to mid-40s with easterly breezes gusting up to 25 mph. However, conditions break warmer by Sunday afternoon, kicking off a sunny, warmer-than-average stretch next week.

title: Proposed Portland Hearts of Pine stadium draws excitement and concern along working waterfront
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Proposed Portland Hearts of Pine stadium draws excitement and concern along working waterfront
The roughly 10,000-seat stadium is slated for land at Cassidy Point, but some worry it will take away a valuable piece of Maine's maritime economy.
Proposed Portland Hearts of Pine stadium draws excitement and concern along working waterfront
The roughly 10,000-seat stadium is slated for land at Cassidy Point, but some worry it will take away a valuable piece of Maine's maritime economy.
The proposed Portland Hearts of Pine stadium at Cassidy Point is making its way through the city's planning process. Included in that is the city rezoning an area of Cassidy Point. The site has long been used to store coal and is currently closed to the public.
The club said the project would remove the coal storage operation, create new public waterfront and recreational areas, and preserve marine industrial activity at the property's 600-foot pier. The pier is not included in the proposed stadium footprint and would remain zoned for marine uses. But it is the part that would be rezoned that is causing some concern.
"Yeah, we love soccer and would love to have a stadium there, but it does not have to be on the water," said Jack Humeniuk, an opponent of the project.
Humeniuk has worked as a longshoreman for decades, and said Maine needs all the working waterfront space it can get. He also cites state funding that has been invested into Cassidy Point, and believes the site should be kept to expand cargo storage or potentially bring in new business.
"Once you take away a maritime use, you can never get it back," said Nick Mavodones, another opponent of the project.
The team said the project will significantly boost Portland's economy, and cites the infectious energy from fans across Maine for a stadium in the team's namesake.
"We want to build this front porch to Portland; we want to have this civic asset as you come across the bridge. And 365 days a year, it is a place you can walk your dog, get a beer or a burger in addition to the games we put on there," said Kevin Schohl, President of Portland Hearts of Pine.
Schohl said the team is working in collaboration with businesses along the working waterfront, and that fans want a stadium that is easy to access via car, public transit, or on foot. He also said it does not make sense to build a stadium in other cities, as fans want it in Portland. Schohl also said the site is appropriate for a stadium, and would be a hard sell for other types of development.
"The fact that is in a flight path with planes overhead means it is not suitable for housing or other things, actually," said Schohl.
There is a planning board hearing set for December. Portland City Council will have the final vote on the project's approval.

title: Frontier Airlines opens first-class bookings, plans more legroom and in-seat power
text:
(Gray News) – A major airline is announcing plans to offer more legroom in seats.
Frontier Airlines opened reservations Tuesday for new first-class seats and shared plans to bring in-seat power to select passengers.
First-class and extra-legroom seats
First-class seats with up to 37 inches of pitch will be configured in the first two rows of the aircraft. Additional extra-legroom seats will also be in rows three through eight with up to 34 inches of pitch, the company described.
The in-seat power connections will be limited to the first eight rows.
Booking and travel dates
The first-class seats can be booked now, but will not be available for travel until March 5, 2027.
Other onboard changes
The changes are part of Frontier’s push to improve the experience onboard planes; other enhancements include Starlink Wi-Fi.
“We’re transforming what customers can expect when they fly Frontier,” chief marketing officer Bobby Schroeter said. “First Class seating, more room to stretch out, in-seat power and fast, reliable Starlink Wi-Fi will bring a new level of comfort and convenience to flying with us.”

title: Kyle Busch posthumously wins NASCAR Cup Series most popular driver award in Miami
text:
Samantha Busch accepts Kyle Busch's posthumous NASCAR fan award after his death at 41
The late Kyle Busch was recognized as the Cup Series’ most popular driver Tuesday at NASCAR’s season-ending awards banquet.
Busch’s widow, Samantha, was on hand to accept the posthumous trophy at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts. It was the first time Busch was honored with the award in a 25-year NASCAR career that spanned all three national series.
Related previous coverage in the video player above: ‘Legacy of life’: North Carolina family shares how Kyle Busch’s Bundle of Joy Fund helped them overcome infertility
He died at age 41 in May after severe pneumonia progressed into sepsis, resulting in rapid and overwhelming complications. His death stunned the NASCAR community, which responded with weekly tributes to the two-time series champion (2015, 2019).
Chase Elliott of Hendrick Motorsports had won the previous eight most popular driver awards in the Cup Series, but he asked the National Motorsports Press Association to remove him from consideration in 2026.
Busch became the first driver not named Earnhardt or Elliott to win the fan vote since Darrell Waltrip in 1990.
Bill Elliott won every year between 1991 and 2000. Dale Earnhardt was posthumously awarded the title following his on-track death in 2001.
Elliott picked up the trophy again in 2002, then Dale Earnhardt Jr. started a 15-year run that ended with his retirement from full-time racing in 2017. Chase Elliott took it from there.
Busch won 234 times across NASCAR’s top three national series — the most of any driver in history — and he is considered a first-ballot Hall of Famer.

title: With Democrats in power, will Congress stop ICE raids in Maine?
text:
Democrats dominated local and federal races in Maine and across the country by galvanizing anger with President Donald Trump and his administration. Immigration was one of the top issues that fueled their gains.
The topic came to the forefront of Maine’s race for U.S. Senate several times over the last year: First in January when Immigration and Customs Enforcement sent a surge of agents to the state for what was dubbed “Operation Catch of the Day,” and again in July when ICE agents shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian man, outside his home in Biddeford.
Now that Democrats are set to control both houses of Congress, it’s likely that they will look to exert more control over ICE, which has acted with near-impunity for months by investigating itself, stymieing local inquiries and rejecting oversight from Democratic legislators in the wake of fatal shootings and detainee deaths.
Maine immigrant advocacy groups are cautiously optimistic in light of last week’s election results. But how much power Congress can or will exert over an agency housed under the executive branch remains an open question.
“Just because there’s this majority in Congress doesn’t mean raids are going to stop. It doesn’t mean arrests are going to stop,” said Ruben Torres, policy director at the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition. “This tension will still be there and we need to be prepared for that.”
Immigration was the third most important issue to Maine voters, according to a September poll conducted by The New York Times, the Portland Press Herald and the Siena Research Institute — trailing only inflation and the economy.
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson has described ICE as a “rogue agency” and said the country needs immigration reform, “not masked raids and fear.” Abolishing ICE was a position central to his campaign.
“It’s time that ICE is disbanded and we go back to putting that money into Customs and Border Patrol,” Jackson said during an October debate. “They have training, they’re law enforcement, people respect them — we don’t respect ICE.”
Jackson isn’t the only Democratic senator-elect who campaigned on abolishing ICE. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota have both called to dismantle the agency. Many other Democrats elected this year campaigned on the more moderate position of reforming it.
Jackson’s transition team did not respond to questions about whether he still seeks to abolish ICE or how feasible that goal ultimately is.
It’s unlikely there’s enough political appetite to abolish ICE, according to Marcela Escobari, a senior fellow at the nonpartisan Brookings Institution and a former immigration adviser on the National Security Council. What’s more probable is for Congress to investigate ICE’s alleged abuses and reform some of its recently employed enforcement tactics, she said.
“Congress is likely to shed light on how ICE and CBP operate,” Escobari said. “Who are they stopping? How are agents being trained? Are they following the law?”
Though only the president and ICE’s directors have authority over its operations, which have grown increasingly aggressive during Trump’s second term, Congress can attempt to control how much money the agency receives and how it is allocated.
“It’s likely they bring transparency to how the money is spent and how enforcement is being delivered,” Escobari said.
To do so would involve clawing back some of the $70 billion in funding for immigration enforcement that Congress passed in June.
Some federal officials have signaled a willingness to shift their hardline stances on immigration in the wake of the midterms. Vice President JD Vance said in a lengthy post-election X post that “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance.”
Even Trump said his immigration policies “might be too tough” in a “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday. He also expressed willingness to compromise with Democrats in Congress moving forward.
But Trump also signaled that more of the same is coming in his second term when he elevated Stephen Miller, a staunchly anti-immigration figure in his administration, to the post of chief of staff last week.
Maine immigrant rights organizations are hoping for the best while bracing for the worst.
“I take (Trump’s comments) with a grain of salt and a shot of whiskey,” said Torres, with the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition.
Torres and other Maine immigrant advocates expressed a desire for Jackson and the new congressional majority to focus not just on reversing the changes to ICE’s tactics in recent years, but to reform America’s broader immigration system and widen pathways to citizenship.
Lisa Parisio, policy director of the Maine Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project, said the election results in Maine and around the country signal a “clear and powerful rejection” of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda.
“The new Congress must reflect the short- and long-term will of the people through robust oversight and investigation and an uncompromised legislative agenda that takes strategic steps to protect people now while building towards citizenship for all who call the United States home,” Parisio said.
But while Congress can scrutinize budget priorities and line items, Parisio noted the huge amount of new funding that ICE has been apportioned through 2029. And much of that spending is at ICE and Trump’s discretion.

title: Mississippi fined $250K after fans threw trash on field during loss to Georgia
text:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (AP) — The University of Mississippi has been fined $250,000 by the Southeastern Conference after fans threw trash on the field and delayed the game during the first half of a blowout home loss to Georgia over the weekend.
In announcing the fine, the SEC said the objects thrown on the field during the second quarter interrupted competitive play and endangered participants. The penalty was assessed under the conference’s sportsmanship, game management and alcohol availability policies.
“The actions taken by the Conference are consistent with SEC bylaws and commissioner’s regulations related to the availability of alcoholic beverages at athletics events which state, ‘If cans or plastic bottles are used as projectiles or otherwise cause game management issues, the institution is subject to an immediate fine and suspension of the alcohol sales privilege,’” the statement said.
Ole Miss is not having alcohol sales banned for home games at this point, though the SEC reserves the right to do so in the future.
The Rebels, at the time ranked 12th, lost 42-7 on Saturday to the then-second-ranked Bulldogs. Georgia is now atop the AP Top 25, while Ole Miss fell to No. 19.

title: Golden should have endorsed Dunlap
text:
I voted for Rep. Jared Golden in every election in which I was eligible to vote before 2026. I did so despite substantial disagreements with many of his positions, because I believed he was the better choice to represent Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
I know I wasn’t alone. Golden built his political career with the support of voters who didn’t always agree with him but were willing to put those differences aside. That’s why I found his refusal to endorse Matt Dunlap so disappointing.
Nobody was asking Golden to abandon his beliefs or spend his final year in Congress campaigning for Dunlap. A simple endorsement, encouraging the people who trusted his judgment to support the Democratic nominee, would have been enough. Instead, Golden publicly congratulated Paul LePage on his victory without even acknowledging Dunlap.
I reached out to Golden’s political operation asking why he declined to endorse Dunlap. I received no response.
I can’t know what motivated Golden’s decision. But if personal resentment over Dunlap’s primary challenge played a role, I think voters deserve to know that. For years, Golden benefited from people like me putting aside our disagreements to support him. When the opportunity came for him to do the same, he declined.
I don’t expect politicians to agree with me on everything. I do expect them to demonstrate the same willingness to compromise that they ask of their constituents.
Greg Siekman
Auburn

title: Vassalboro planners quickly approve lone applicant
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Vassalboro planning board members quickly approved the only application on their Nov. 3 agenda, and spent another half hour discussing other things they need to, or could, do.
The application was to amend the permit approved at the board’s Sept. 1 meeting for Ahmed Al Abbass to open a car dealership at 29 Mudget Hill Road.
Codes Officer Eric Currie explained that the originally-planned parking lot turned out to be difficult to build, so it needs to be relocated. Board members approved unanimously. Chairman Virginia Brackett asked for a new map showing the change.
Board member Paul Mitnik recommended ordinance changes that would eliminate the need to permit farm stands.
Currie is working on amendments to the town’s subdivision ordinance, required by changes in state law. He plans to have a draft for discussion at the next board meeting.
Board member Paul Mitnik recommended ordinance changes that would eliminate the need to permit farmstands, by reclassifying them as home occupations. Other board members, without disagreeing, proposed perhaps limiting the size of the structure and having a time limit and a requirement to provide off-road parking.
Brackett said the building permit ordinance also needs updating.
Brackett and Currie mentioned several junkyards that are being cleaned up. Currie is checking three such properties monthly and getting cooperation, he said.
The codes officer is also in touch with the Amish group that has settled on the former Peter Bragdon farm, making sure their development conforms to town ordinances. Their plans include building houses and a pole barn and applying for their own school, Currie said.
Mitnik is pleased that the area will stay farmland.
The next regular Vassalboro Planning Board meeting is scheduled for 5:30 p.m., Tuesday, Dec. 1, in the town office meeting room.

title: Leaders demand action to slow global warming and help world adapt at global summit US is absent from
text:
'At war with a crisis we did not create': Island nations demand climate action at global summit US is absent from
World leaders called for urgent and decisive action on global warming Wednesday as formal talks began at the United Nations climate conference in Turkey, saying the crisis is disproportionately harming some of the world’s most vulnerable countries.
“You might as well bomb us. That might have been easier than watching climate change tear apart our homes piece by piece,” said Surangel Whipps Jr., president of the island nation of Palau. “We are at war with a crisis we did not create. A war no peace treaty can end, only urgent action can.”
The annual summit follows a year of deadly floods, heat waves and other disasters. Leaders said geopolitical conflicts had diverted attention from climate change.
Earlier this year, the United Nations said it is inevitable that the world will warm beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels.
Limiting warming to that threshold was a goal of the 2015 Paris Agreement and remains a focus of international negotiations. The U.N. wants the world to limit how long and how much temperatures shoot past that mark and somehow get back down below it by the end of the century. That's called overshoot.
“The evidence is now in. We did not try hard enough,” said Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley, who said five years ago that the 1.5-degree threshold was necessary for survival.
“Overshoot is not a new target, it’s a debt," she added. "A debt of heat borrowed against our children’s future and it must be repaid.”
She said every five years of delay increases projected peak warming by a tenth of a degree, "and a tenth of a degree, my friends, is a coral reef. It’s a harvest, it’s a village, and lives and livelihoods will be affected. Ask Nepal, where more than 1,400 people died in the floods in August, and thousands are still missing.”
'Every fraction of a degree counts'
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres outlined a framework for climate negotiations, saying they must prioritize ending fossil fuel reliance, adapting to a warmer world, increasing financial support for poorer countries bearing the brunt of climate change, and promoting cooperation over conflict.
“We know the truth. Now we must act on it because climate action is more than a fight over a number or a thermometer,” Guterres said in his opening speech. “We are in the fight for our lives and our children’s future."
“We do not need countries to agree on everything. But we do need them to cooperate on the things no country can solve alone,” he said.
Addressing climate change has been overshadowed by wars, inflation and geopolitical conflicts, Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said. He pledged to protect the Amazon, the world’s largest rainforest, and urged world leaders to work together for a just, sustainable future. “Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet,” said Lula, who recently won reelection.
Micronesian President Wesley Simina said his country is already suffering irreversible losses of coral reefs that “protect our shores, sustain our fisheries, feed our families and carry the stories and traditions of our communities.”
He called climate change the “single greatest threat to the security, livelihoods, and well-being of Pacific peoples, but perhaps worse than what we’ve already experienced is what has yet to come” as temperatures continue to rise.
Both Simina and Mottley called for these climate talks to come to an agreement to slash methane — a short-lived and extra powerful heat-trapping gas — which Mottley said could “buy time to supercharge” technology to help cut longer-lived carbon dioxide. She said cutting methane by about half by 2030 could help avoid almost 0.3 degrees of warming by the 2040s "and save 250,000 lives every year.”
Amy Pope, director general of the International Organization for Migration, called for more funding to help communities adapt to climate change and build resilience.
Climate change displaced almost 30 million people in 2025, while hundreds of millions more live in places unprepared to withstand future risks, Pope told The Associated Press.
Leaders of some major polluting nations absent
More than 70 world leaders and senior government officials are speaking at the summit. But the top leaders of the world’s three biggest polluting nations — China, the United States and India, which together account for more than half of global carbon dioxide emissions — skipped the summit at COP31.
“It really is a disgrace that just one of the seven G7 heads of state and only a handful of G20 leaders are attending this summit,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate and energy think tank. “The world’s biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others.”
The United States, the world’s second-largest polluter after China, is absent from the talks for the second consecutive year. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax, has targeted offshore wind projects and removed rules limiting power plant emissions.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attended, but many leaders of European countries stayed away.
“If Europe wants to help steer the global transition, it needs to show up and be part of it," Climate Action Network Europe Director Chiara Martinelli told the AP.
Conference colored by fears over speed of climate action
The gap between nations’ climate plans and actions is widening, according to an annual climate change performance index published Wednesday by Germanwatch and the New Climate Institute.
Turkey, which is hosting COP31, and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, ranked among the worst performers in curbing emissions.
The talks come as the war in Iran has driven up global prices for oil, gasoline and products such as fertilizers and pesticides, prompting governments to rethink energy policies and investment in renewable sources such as wind and solar.

title: Cheverus softball star Addison DeRoche signs with Florida State
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
PORTLAND — Addison DeRoche signed the paper on the table, stood in front of a room full of supporters — family, friends and coaches, many clad in garnet and gold — and raised both fists.
“Go ‘Noles!” she said.
DeRoche, the standout pitcher for the Cheverus softball team, officially made Maine history by signing with Florida State on Wednesday, becoming the state’s first player to join an NCAA Division I power conference school.
DeRoche committed to Florida State in the fall, but said her future of playing big-time softball “got way more real” with the signing, which she and her family celebrated with a gathering at Bruno’s Restaurant and Tavern.
“I really have dreamed of this moment forever, ever since I was a little girl,” the Cheverus senior and Westbrook resident said. “Just sitting at home watching TV, determined to be there one day. … I’m overwhelmingly grateful.”
The room was decorated with Florida State colors, and one wall had jerseys from the four teams DeRoche has played for: New England Elite, Rhode Island Thunder, Mojo and finally Cheverus, where she’s played three years, won three Gatorade and Varsity Maine Player of the Year awards, and become the nation’s No. 5 ranked recruit in the Class of 2027 while compiling 647 strikeouts in 272 innings with a 0.26 ERA.
John Eisenhart, who coached DeRoche at Cheverus all three years before stepping down after taking a new job, was on hand for the celebration.
“It’s so great to see all of her hard work come to fruition and pay off,” he said. “She’s so talented and driven. We all knew this day would come. … I’m so excited to see what she’s going to do in the future.”
DeRoche, the 2025-26 Varsity Maine Female Athlete of the Year, has been on the fast track for the upper reaches of Division I since her freshman year at Cheverus, when she led the Stags to the Class A title while playing a busy national schedule of showcases and tournaments with her Mojo team.
Those busy days haven’t eased up: She played in Illinois, California and Georgia earlier this fall, and is turning around Thursday to play in Clearwater, Florida, before heading to El Salvador for the Pan-American Games.
During one of the few opportunities DeRoche has had to sit still, all the focus was still on where she’ll be going — a place where she’s wanted to play well before making her plans official.
“I think I always pictured myself in the garnet and gold,” she said. “When I was growing up (the Seminoles) were like a dynasty, they were there every year. (I’m excited) to be there and compete at the highest level.”
And a level no Maine player has reached.
“This is my opportunity and I get to share it with everybody else,” she said. “They can follow my lead as well. It’s pretty awesome.”
NEW LEADER ON BOARD
DeRoche’s signing capped a busy few days for the defending state champion Stags. Cheverus also announced the hiring of Grace McGouldrick, who will take over for Eisenhart as the head softball coach.
McGouldrick, 26, was the Miss Maine Softball winner at Gorham in 2018 before going on to play at the University of Maine. But even during her playing days, she knew coaching would eventually be her calling.
“I just really enjoyed doing all those Little League clinics with our high school team, so I kind of figured out at that point that I was really into coaching and helping out the younger kids,” she said. “To help them find the love for it that I still have is No. 1. … I love seeing an individual or an entire team have a light bulb (go off) and really go and execute something.”
McGouldrick, who has coached travel teams from 10U to 18U at the Edge Academy for the past 2 1/2 years, said the Stags, who have reached the regional final each of the past three seasons and won two state championships, are a match for her approach to the sport.
“They take it really seriously, which I really appreciate. I’m a very naturally competitive person, so I appreciate when the teams that I coach align with me in that way,” she said. “At the end of the day it’s a game. It’s fun. … But I want to go win, and I know the girls want to go win.”
McGouldrick will inherit a team that brings back emerging standouts in Cameron Gagnon, Abby Kelly, Maddie Brow and Temperance Lovejoy, but the key piece is DeRoche, who alone will make the Stags favorites again.
“It’s been so fun to listen to all the younger girls go and talk about how awesome it is to have someone show that just because you’re from Maine, it doesn’t mean you can’t go to high places,” McGouldrick said. “She’s brought so much more light to the game of softball in the state of Maine.”
DeRoche said she was “heartbroken” to hear about Eisenhart’s departure, but said she’s eager to play for McGouldrick, whom she’s come to know during practice sessions at the Edge Academy.
“She’s a role model,” DeRoche said. “She’s going to be really fun to play for. … I’m really excited to take the field.”

title: Opinion: Serving those who served: A Maine veteran's perspective
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Brad Bean, who is retired from the U.S Navy, is a local veteran employment representative with the Maine Department of Labor.
It has been over 30 years since I wore my U.S. Navy uniform for 20 years. All these years later, it seems that Veterans Day means a little more each year. For the first few years after my military service, I shied away from letting people know I had served. Part of that was not wanting to be singled out, and part was that I really didn’t think it was a big deal, especially while I was still “transitioning” from a military lifestyle to a civilian lifestyle, a transition that took a lot longer than I expected or wanted to admit.
As time went by, I began to experience Veterans Day from the other side: The public’s appreciation for the men and women willing to sacrifice for the freedom we enjoy every day. While you are serving, you don’t fully understand the gratitude of those back home. But when you can see it from the thankful citizen’s side, it begins to mean more to you.
Here we are, 30 years later, and now I have the awesome privilege of working with veterans and transitioning service members and influencing their transition. A few years ago, I saw a veterans representative position posted with the Maine Department of Labor CareerCenter and thought, “what a cool job!” I learned that the job was about meeting the veteran exactly where they were and helping them find out what is available to them and how to overcome any barriers that may be in their way. What a privilege!
Veterans come into the CareerCenter for help finding a job and leave with so much more. Before we talk about jobs and resumes, we talk about where they are and what their needs are. Have they filed for a service-connected disability? Are they aware of the educational benefits they have earned? Are they connected to the VA? These questions help us understand the full picture and how we can best help.
And to make this easier, we live in Maine, a state with a strong reputation for being veteran friendly and leaders committed to keeping it that way. I am proud not only to say that I am a veteran, but that I am a veteran from Maine. We know how to serve those who served. I know veterans who moved to Maine because of our reputation for caring for veterans.
Over the last few years, I have seen veterans’ lives changed because they were made aware of a program designed for their situation, whether it was an educational or training program, a veteran service officer who helped them get a service-connected disability rating, or learning about the Veterans Emergency Financial Assistance Program, which helped them in a time of great need.
Another cool thing I get to do is serve as co-chair of the Maine Hire-A-Vet Campaign. We have a big kickoff event in Augusta and then go to other areas of the state, bringing employers and veteran resource providers together to talk with veterans and all job seekers. Our final Hire-A-Vet event of 2026 will be Nov. 12 from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. at the Norway Armory. I hope to see you there. Since 2015, the Maine Hire-A-Vet Campaign has connected more than 2,200 veterans with jobs.
If I could say one thing to all the veterans living in Maine, it would be this: Make sure you are receiving all the benefits you earned when you wore that uniform. There is so much available, and you may not know about all of it. There is more than a free lunch on Veterans Day. There could be life-changing opportunities waiting for you.
If you aren’t sure where to start, contact your local CareerCenter and ask to speak with a veterans representative.
Happy Veterans Day!

title: How we reported Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
It’s no secret that many Maine households are struggling to keep up with the rising cost of living. Some families, especially in rural areas, have been in poverty for generations.
After years of covering food insecurity and homelessness in southern Maine, photographer Brianna Soukup and I knew there were stories left untold about how Mainers are getting by in other parts of the state.
We started by looking at new data released by the United Ways of Maine that measures the financial hardship people are experiencing in towns across the state. We anchored our reporting in three areas with unique challenges.
In western Maine, we focused on Oxford County’s River Valley, a place with a deep history of manufacturing, a tightknit community and multiple programs dedicated to helping. One reason we chose this community is because it has high numbers of people experiencing food insecurity.
In Midcoast Maine, we focused on Lincoln County, home to a large percentage of older Mainers, to highlight the challenges of aging in a rural state with limited access to public transportation and nearby healthcare. We spent most of our time on the Boothbay peninsula, where there are stark disparities between wealthy out-of-state property owners and year-round residents on fixed incomes.
We also traveled to Washington County, where many families have been trying to break out of the poverty cycle for generations. There, we focused primarily on the Machias area because of the programs working to help lift people out of poverty.
Through organizations offering assistance, we connected with people willing to share their experiences and talk about the choices they have to make when they don’t have enough money to cover their expenses.
Between us, Brianna and I made three reporting trips to Washington County, spending several days at a time meeting people at a food pantry and nonprofit programs. We took more than a dozen day trips to the River Valley and Boothbay peninsula to visit food pantries, soup kitchens, churches and community centers. We also visited people at home and at work, and went fishing and shared meals with families we were interviewing.
We logged more than 3,900 miles driving across the state.
Through our reporting, we learned that people who have been living with low incomes are struggling more than ever — and that even people who had not previously felt a financial strain are now having a harder time making ends meet.
We were struck by how often the people helping their neighbors had also experienced the same struggles, but gave back without hesitation.
We also put out a call for feedback from people across Maine about their own financial situations. More than 135 people have already responded to our survey, sharing details about how far their budgets fall short and how they decide what to pay for. Many said more needs to be done to help people who are struggling.
To help connect people, we created a guide for how to find help or offer help, a resource we will continue to update.
In the months ahead, we plan to host two events to share and discuss our work.
The first, on Dec. 16, is a forum at the Rumford Public Library that will feature a panel discussion with the reporting team, as well as Michelle Williams from Good Samaritan Missionary Services, Melissa McEntee from Rumford Group Homes and Rumford Town Manager George O’Keefe.
Beyond this project, in 2027 we will continue to prioritize reporting on affordability issues impacting so many Mainers.
This piece is part of the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham is a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.
