title: Bell rings out as WWII soldier and other veterans parade through Bangor
text:
Of the dozens of service members who participated in the Bangor-Brewer Veterans Day parade, 102-year-old Don Gallupe was the only World War II veteran.
The Bangor native was a gunner for Army Air Corps, the precursor to the U.S. Air Force, and has appeared in the parade since it began. Gallupe was part of Bangor High School’s JROTC program before he was drafted.
Gallupe is among the roughly 30,600 WWII veterans still alive across the United States, according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. That’s a small fraction of the more than 16 million who served. In 2022, six surviving WWII veterans participated in the Bangor-Brewer Veterans Day parade.
“We had some pretty big outfits years ago in the parade,” Gallupe said. “There aren’t as many now as there used to be, but I’m still trying to do it.”
Gallupe followed the Cole Land Transportation Museum’s Freedom Bell, a giant bell that rang throughout the parade in remembrance of all the service members who died in World War II.
The bell, which has appeared in Bangor’s Veterans, Memorial Day and Independence Day parades for more than 70 years, is reminiscent of the bells that rang across the country when World War II ended in 1945.
Hundreds gathered along the parade route amid brisk weather on Wednesday morning to cheer for and thank veterans for their service.
Dozens of veterans from the Korean War, Vietnam War and the Global War on Terrorism marched behind Gallupe. Some stopped to hug their children, grandchildren and other loved ones along the route.
The parade, sponsored by the Bangor High School Army JROTC, stretched from Wilson Street in Brewer, across the Joshua Chamberlain Bridge and snaked through downtown Bangor until it ended on Exchange Street.
All branches of the military were represented in the parade alongside Junior ROTC programs for multiple high schools, including Bangor, Brewer, Hermon and Nokomis.
Governor-elect Hannah Pingree also marched in the parade. She issued a statement on Wednesday thanking Maine veterans and their families for their service and vowed to “never forget what you have done for us.”
“Your courage and commitment to something larger than yourselves have protected our freedoms and strengthened our communities, and that service doesn’t end when the uniform comes off,” Pingree wrote.

title: Firefighters dig through rubble after NYC building collapse kills 2, traps people
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-story building in Brooklyn after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site Wednesday afternoon, killing at least two people and trapping others beneath the wreckage.
Scores of firefighters and police officers wielding pickaxes and power saws clambered over the rubble pile for hours, punching holes through the ruins to pull dust-covered people from beneath piles of twisted wood and brick.
At least 17 people were hospitalized with injuries, including four in critical condition, officials during a news conference. New York City Fire Department officials said their search and rescue operations would continue into the night. It was unclear whether people might still be trapped.
“This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. “This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for.”
The cause of the collapse was under investigation, but New York City’s buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, noted that when the building fell, construction workers were excavating an empty lot next door for a new building.
Much of the rubble from the collapsed building — a mixed-use structure with apartments sitting atop ground-floor commercial space — wound up in a huge pile inside the construction pit. Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.
About 250 firefighters were working the scene, Mamdani said.
At around 6:30 p.m., firefighters pulled a woman — still alive and moving — out of a hole they had dug into the rubble pile, hoisting her up on a stretcher and rushing to a waiting ambulance.
Additional people were pulled from beneath the pile as the night went on. Seven of the casualties were children, authorities said, without specifying whether any were among the dead.
A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked.
FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the rescue teams were performing “dangerous and perilous” work. “Every move is choreographed,” she said.
One firefighter sustained minor injuries, fire officials said.
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.
One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, told the New York Post he was at work when his wife called and said she and their two kids, ages 7 and 2, were trapped in the wreckage.
“She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her. She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off,” he said.
Velez said he later learned that his family had been pulled from the rubble alive.

title: Trump says the towering arch he wants to be build might be dedicated to military veterans
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump observed Veterans Day by suggesting that the towering arch he wants to build in his own honor would also be dedicated to the U.S. military and those who served in its ranks.
That’s despite three veterans having sued to stop the project — which a federal court has since temporarily blocked. Some military groups have cheered the arch, but many others have opposed it or joined efforts to stop construction.
Trump has said for months that the 250-foot (76-meter) arch set for construction near Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial would be inspired by the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, and might even be called the “Arc de Trump.”
He’s also insisted that Washington has wanted a similar structure for centuries — even though that’s not true. In comments during an annual ceremony at Arlington Cemetery on Wednesday, however, Trump suggested it was actually veterans who had longed for an arch in the capital.
“And soon we’re going to dedicate a magnificent triumphal arc to our veterans,” he said. “And that’s in honor of our great veterans and our great militaries.” He added: “They’ve been waiting for it for 200 years.”
Veterans’ legal efforts to stop the arch are ongoing
Though the arch received approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, the three veterans are among several groups suing to block the arch’s construction. Last week, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order, prohibiting work for 14 days.
With Democrats soon taking control of Congress after big wins all over the country in last week’s midterm elections, Trump’s renovation projects will encounter far more scrutiny and roadblocks — from his effort to put his own name on the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and building his massive White House ballroom and the arch.
Despite the midterm defeats by his party and the potential legal and legislative hurdles, the White House has continued to promote the arch project.
That includes a slick website unveiled last week which proclaimed that it’d be known as the United States Military Triumphal Arch and was “long overdue, and has been sought for many years, especially by the Military.”
The website prominently displays a picture of and quote from Trump. It also features the word “Triumph” in gold cursive script recalling the typeface used at the president’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida and similar flourishes that have been affixed to the White House as part of his overhaul of the Oval Office and West Wing.
The arch’s plans call for its columns to store munitions and areas on the pedestal and observation deck to be set aside for a sniper’s nest. Its base would be designed to launch drones, and the site says that the overall monument “will be Highly Secretive but, at the same time, a Top Level and Lethal structure, the likes of which has not been seen in this Country before.”
The website does not say how much the project will cost or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100 million.

title: Frankie Muniz taken to hospital but ‘awake and alert’ after crash ahead of Daytona Veterans Day race
text:
'Malcolm in the Middle' star Frankie Muniz released from hospital after crash
Frankie Muniz, an actor and professional racing driver, has been released from a hospital following a practice-lap crash.
Muniz was practicing for a special Veterans Day race on Wednesday at Daytona International Speedway.
Muniz, known for his role as Malcolm in TV's "Malcolm in the Middle," was set to be part of Ford Racing's 12-driver lineup in Wednesday's "Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic," a benefit race at Daytona Speedway's road course, according to an October press release from NASCAR.
“I am disappointed I won’t be able to take part in Ford’s Proud to Honor event tonight," Muniz said in a statement. “I was looking forward to honoring the service of our veterans and racing against these other amazing drivers.”
Muniz said he was a “little sore," but the Mustang he was driving did its job to protect him.
“I want to thank everyone at Ford Racing, Daytona International Speedway and the staff here at the hospital,” Muniz said. "I especially want to thank everyone who has reached out and for all the prayers.”
ET said it had a TV crew at the speedway at the time and said they had been set to interview Muniz when the crash occurred. ET also reported that the track was not yet open to the public at the time of the crash.
Muniz, alongside driver Austin Cindric, had been planning to represent Team Air Force in the exhibition race, which kicked off at 8 p.m. ET. The event benefits six different nonprofits that support military and veteran communities through the Proud to Honor Fund, according to NASCAR. Half of ticket proceeds benefit Blue Star Families, NASCAR said.
A dozen Ford Racing drivers were split into six teams to race head-to-head in Mustang Dark Horse cars in honor of a branch of the U.S. military.
Other drivers/teams in the race are:
- U.S. Army: Brad Keselowski and Joey Hand
- U.S. Marine Corps: Robert Noaker and Ben Hobson
- U.S. Navy: Ryan Preece and Logan Sargeant
- U.S. Space Force: Noah Gragson and Layne Riggs
- U.S. Coast Guard: Joey Logano and Ty Majeski
Musical performances by the Zac Brown Band, Russell Dickerson, Jo Dee Messina, Brittney Spencer, and Warren Zeiders were also part of the event.  According to the Ford Veterans Day Classic website, actor Bryan Cranston, who played Muniz on-screen dad in "Malcolm in the Middle," was scheduled to be a special guest at the event.
Muniz was nominated for an Emmy and two Golden Glove Awards for his work in “Malcolm in the Middle” and was one of the best-known child actors of his time. He has also appeared in films such as “Big Fat Liar,” “Deuces Wild," "Agent Cody Banks" and “Racing Stripes.”
According to his website, Muniz took a hiatus from the entertainment world in 2006 to pursue professional racecar driving.
He began competing in the Formula BMW USA Championship and later went on to race in the Champ Car Atlantic Championship from 2007-09. Muniz was fourth in the 2009 championship standings with two races to go before a season-ending injury resulted in multiple surgeries, the website said.
In 2024, Muniz ran 38 races each on the NASCAR O'Reilly Auto Parts and trucks series.
He's participated in 117 trucks series races over the last three years, with one top-10 finish at Daytona in 2025.
_____
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Russia and Ukraine agree to large exchange of prisoners of war, officials in Abu Dhabi say
text:
Russia and Ukraine agree to large exchange of prisoners of war, officials in Abu Dhabi say
Officials at U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine said Wednesday that the sides have agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war.
“One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow,” Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said after the two days of talks in Abu Dhabi ended.
Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv’s delegation in Abu Dhabi, confirmed the planned exchange.
Hopes were low for any major breakthrough in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped prisoners during their nearly five-year war.
U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.
Kushner says he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The context of the negotiations has changed since the last meeting in February in Geneva. The Trump administration has to reckon with Democrats, who could demand more support for Ukraine, taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections.
Also, Russia’s wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.
Umerov said Kyiv’s delegation is expected to meet Wednesday with European officials.
Moscow doesn’t want European countries, which are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. However, representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi and were consulting with the Ukrainian delegation, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday’s session was “constructive and quite substantive.”
The talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including possible prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country, he said.
Security guarantees also were discussed, he said. However, Russia and Ukraine have shown no sign of a willingness to compromise on their demands.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the meeting “very productive,” while cautioning that a breakthrough on stopping the war will take time.
The Abu Dhabi talks are being held against the backdrop of continued fighting on the front line, where little territory has changed hands this year.
Meanwhile, both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones.
Overnight, Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to the regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko.
He said that the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of the main facilities for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers.

title: Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
text:
Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
Gadi Eisenkot, the politician tasked with forming a new Israeli government, pledged on Tuesday to reverse many of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies as the new parliament was sworn in.
The pledge sets the stage for a consequential month of legislative action and coalition negotiations. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Netanyahu's opponents now control a solid majority in parliament.
Related video above: Israel's Prime Minister Netanyahu suffers a setback in Tuesday's election
Eisenkot's bloc introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Netanyahu and his policies. They include launching an official government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. It was not immediately clear how quickly or far those bills would advance in the weeks ahead.
Competing calls for unity
The former general, who campaigned as a no-nonsense straight shooter, reiterated on Tuesday that his goal was a government that all Israelis could trust, not one that represents only certain factions.
“We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment,” Eisenkot said ahead of the Knesset swearing-in ceremony.
Netanyahu has sought to undermine the certified election results after his bloc fell short of a majority. He has repeated unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties “stole” the elections.
In a speech following Tuesday’s ceremony, Netanyahu reiterated his claim that Arab politicians, who represent a minority comprising 20% of Israel’s population, cannot be trusted. He attacked Jewish opposition leaders who have signaled a willingness to partner with Arab parties to form a government. Eisenkot has left that possibility open if the parties meet several conditions, including accepting Israel’s identity as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist group.
“I ask you: Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?” said Netanyahu.
Eisenkot said Netanyahu's speech was “divisive” and “hate-filled,” adding: “I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute.” He later said he had canceled a meeting with Netanyahu's Likud party planned for Wednesday because of the speech.
Netanyahu's opponents already have a legislative agenda
Eisenkot's bloc also triggered a process on Tuesday to install a new parliamentary speaker as they kicked off work on their legislative agenda.
A majority of members submitted signatures calling for the ousting of the current Netanyahu-backed speaker, Amir Ohana, the first step toward a vote on his replacement. The vote can take place even before a coalition government is in place.
The Knesset speaker is a powerful position. The speaker determines what bills the Knesset will take up, meaning one picked from among the Eisenkot-led opposition parties could propel their legislative agenda forward.
The opposition nominated Matan Kahana, a senior member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, for the job. A vote to appoint him speaker could come as early as this week.
Netanyahu as caretaker
The swearing-in of the new Knesset ushered in an unusual transitional period in Israeli politics — Netanyahu and his Cabinet remain in power, while the new lawmakers can introduce legislation.
Meanwhile, Eisenkot will meet with party leaders as he works to build a coalition that would likely make him prime minister. If he fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to give Netanyahu the next opportunity to form a government.
As caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu faces court-imposed limits on his powers. But he can still pursue appointments and could try to block new legislation. He retains full authority over national security, including the military.
Netanyahu has argued that Jewish-led parties should form a unity government to counter the threat of an Iranian attack. He renewed that call Tuesday, urging them to “set aside all other considerations,” and said Israel should work to topple the Iranian government.
A governing coalition without Netanyahu could leave him politically vulnerable as he faces an ongoing corruption trial and possible findings of security failures in the lead-up to the Oct. 7 attacks.

title: ICE increases security at Scarborough facility amid vandalism, armed protests
text:
SCARBOROUGH, Maine (WMTW) - Vandalism and the presence of near-daily protesters, some of them armed, have led to increased security at the Scarborough ICE facility, according to a spokesperson for the agency.
There has been a small group of protesters outside the Scarborough facility ever since ICE agent David Brouillette shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian father, when he was leaving for work in Biddeford last July.
According to the lawyer for Guerrero’s widow and members of Maine’s congressional delegation, Guerrero was not the intended target of the ICE operation and was in the U.S. under a valid federal work authorization.
Nearly four months after his death, ICE observers still have a presence outside the agency’s facility on Manson Libby Road in Scarborough. Some are monitoring the movements of agents in and out of the facility and sharing that information on social media. Others are calling for the prosecution of Brouillette and “abolishing” ICE entirely, arguing that the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown is unlawful and is spreading fear within immigrant communities in Maine.
Those fears were cited by the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition on Monday, when the organization notified community members that recent sightings of “several new vehicles” arriving at the Scarborough facility were assigned to building security, not immigration enforcement.
“We understand that any increase in immigration enforcement presence can cause fear and uncertainty,” wrote Ruben Torres, the director of advocacy and policy at the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition. “We are sharing this update to provide context and help community members distinguish this change in Scarborough ICE building security from broader enforcement activity.”
Democratic congresswoman Chellie Pingree took to Facebook to share a similar message, writing that security had increased specifically because of armed protesters.
“Mainers deserve to know what’s happening in their communities and I’m continuing to monitor the situation closely,” wrote Rep. Pingree. “Maine has endured too much chaos and violence at the hands of this rogue, unaccountable agency already.”
On Tuesday, at least one protester could be seen outside the Scarborough facility with a firearm. Open carry is legal in Maine, assuming the firearm holder is legally allowed to possess one.
A spokesperson for ICE told WMTW Tuesday that the agency’s officers are “under constant threat from violent agitators.” The spokesperson claimed that there have been six different occasions of vandalism at the Scarborough facility in the past three months.
ICE would not disclose whether the agency had plans for increased enforcement operations in Maine, citing “operational security purposes.”

title: EVENTS: Back of the Napkin Challenge returns for fourth year
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Challenging students to think big, innovate boldly, and create meaningful change in their communities.
Dirigo Labs, a program of the Central Maine Growth Council, in collaboration with Thomas College, Kennebec Valley Community College, and Colby College, is excited to announce the 4th Annual Back of the Napkin Challenge, a student entrepreneurship competition that encourages creative thinkers to transform innovative ideas into solutions for real-world challenges.
The challenge invites students from participating institutions to record and pitch an idea, encouraging them to develop it into a solution that can make a meaningful difference in their communities. Whether inspired by a local challenge, a new opportunity, or a passion project, participants will explore entrepreneurship and innovation while developing concepts that have the potential to create lasting impact in their own backyard.
The competition will culminate during Dirigo Labs’ Incubator Demo Day on November 17, 2026, where Back of the Napkin finalists will pitch their ideas before a panel of judges and a live audience. The event will also feature startup demonstrations, networking opportunities, and a celebration of innovation taking place throughout Maine.
Monetary awards will be presented to standout pitches based on their viability, community impact, and entrepreneurial potential.
“Every company starts as an idea someone was willing to say out loud,” said Jeff Frank, Program Manager at Dirigo Labs. “The Back of the Napkin Challenge gives students a real stage to test their ideas and see that the problems they notice in their own communities are worth solving.”
Representatives from each participating institution emphasized the importance of providing experiential learning opportunities that allow students to apply their creativity outside the classroom.
Entrepreneurship is about recognizing opportunities and taking action,” said Kim Kennedy, Business Administration Faculty at Kennebec Valley Community College. “This challenge encourages students to think beyond what exists today and develop solutions that can make a difference for our local communities, region, and beyond.”
At the Halloran Lab, we view entrepreneurship as a way of thinking that empowers students to identify meaningful challenges and develop solutions that create real impact,” said Jonathan Godbout, Deputy Director of the Halloran Lab for Entrepreneurship at Colby College. “The Back of the Napkin Challenge gives students the opportunity to explore ideas, test assumptions, and build the confidence to turn a simple concept into something that can positively influence their communities.”
“At Thomas College, we believe in preparing students to become innovators, problem-solvers, and leaders,” said Nate Pelsma, Executive Director of Business Innovation and Corporate Campus at Thomas College. “The Back of the Napkin Challenge gives students a unique opportunity to test ideas, gain confidence, and experience what it takes to bring a concept to life.”
The event is open to the public and welcomes students, entrepreneurs, educators, business leaders, community members, and anyone curious about innovation, entrepreneurship, and the future of Maine. Join us on Tuesday, November 17, at 5 p.m., at Kennebec Valley Community College, in Fairfield, to celebrate bold ideas, connect with emerging innovators, and support the next generation of entrepreneurs.
For more information about the Back of the Napkin Challenge, student participation opportunities, or attending Dirigo Labs Incubator Demo Day, visit https://www.dirigolabs.org/back-of-the-napkin-challenge/.
Funded in part through a Cooperative Agreement with the U.S. Small Business Administration’s (SBA) Federal and State Technology (FAST) Partnership Program. Additional support is provided by the Maine Technology Institute (MTI) and the Northern Border Regional Commission (NBRC). Together, these partners help drive innovation, entrepreneurship, and economic opportunity across Maine.

title: Quiet evening, colder night ahead
text:
Quiet evening, colder night ahead
Late-week storm trending drier for Maine
Quiet evening, colder night ahead
Late-week storm trending drier for Maine
Temperatures are running right at average for this point in November, with highs mainly in the 40s and low 50s Wednesday afternoon. A quiet evening is expected before temperatures fall into the 20s to mid-30s overnight.
That will make for a colder start on Thursday, which will be a dry day in many spots, except in far southwest Maine where a few scattered showers are possible during the afternoon and evening.
The late-week storm threat continues to wind down, though parts of Maine likely get clipped with a little rain and snow. Thursday night's forecast is the hardest to pin down, with big questions as to how far north and east rain and snow will push. The highest chances will again be in southwest Maine.
A coating to 2 inches of snow is possible, mainly on grassy surfaces outside of the mountains and foothills. Higher elevations in the White Mountains could pick up 3 to 6 inches. Mountain snow favors New Hampshire, with very little moisture to work with across Northern Maine.
Gusty winds are possible, especially along and near the coast from Thursday through Sunday, with wind gusts up to 20 to 35 mph. The forecast is trending nicer for the weekend, though chilly and breezy, with only an isolated rain or snow shower left over on Saturday. Looking ahead to next week, a warm-up is expected with no storms in sight.

title: Family remembers Bangor woman known as ‘Ma’ after fatal house fire
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Loved ones of 80-year-old Kathleen Mackie are remembering her generosity and working to keep her legacy alive after a fire at her Bangor home on Oct. 14.
The Medical Examiner’s Office has not yet officially identified Mackie, but her loved ones say she died in the fire at the home on the corner of Cedar and Second streets. Known to many as Kathy, she was called “Ma” by people she helped care for and raise.
“She was truly an angel walking among the rest of us,” a loved one said. “The world knew her as Kathy, but to those of us she helped care for and helped raise she will forever be called ‘Ma.’”
Remembering ‘Ma’
Family members say Mackie opened her home and heart to people who needed support.
“She was one of the most caring souls I’ve ever met,” said her daughter, Jessica Martin. “Never met a person that she wasn’t willing to take in, especially if they didn’t have family.”
Rachelle, who became part of the family and built a sisterhood with Jessica, recalled being welcomed into Mackie’s home.
“She brought me back to her house, and Ma said that I could stay,” Rachelle said.
Benefit supper planned
The family is hosting a benefit supper and silent auction on Friday, Nov. 13, from 6 to 8 p.m. at the Hilton Garden Inn in Bangor. Rachelle says all proceeds will go to family members directly affected by the fire. Two couples were living with Mackie at the time of the fire, she said.
The family is also awaiting Mackie’s remains and says a backlog at the Medical Examiner’s Office has delayed funeral planning.
As loved ones mourn, they hope to carry Mackie’s love for the community forward.
“Nothing is promised, so just if I had one word of advice for everyone out there, live your life like it’s going to be your last, live it to the fullest extent that you can,” Krishauna Boucher said.

title: Obituary: Judi Ann LeBel
text:
BURNHAM – Judi Ann LeBel, formerly Judi Jannaccio, 66, passed away on Nov. 9, 2026. Born on Nov. 1, 1960, in Waterbury, Conn., Judi later made her home in Burnham, Maine.
Beloved wife of Edward LeBel, leaves behind her daughters, Erica Hyer and Melissa Cummings, and stepdaughter, Michelle LeBel. She was a proud grammy to Aaron, Elyza, and Charlotte LeBel.
Judi was a very dear niece to Susan and Walter Cole of Waterbury, Conn.
She shared a special lifelong friendship with Sonia DiDonato of Manchester, NH. Their friendship was a treasured part of Judi’s life.
Judi found happiness in life’s simple pleasures, like enjoying a good cup of coffee, tending to her plants, and Josh Groban’s music.
One of Judi’s greatest companions was her beloved dog, Sofi. Their bond was incredibly special.
Judi will be remembered for the little things that made her happy, the relationships she cherished, and the memories she created with those she loved.
Her absence will leave an emptiness in the hearts of her family and friends, but the love she shared will live on forever.

title: Tales from the booth: Hear from some of Maine’s high school football announcers
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Chris Cifelli watches the offense, while his wife, Michelle, watches the defense.
She reports the jersey numbers, he finds the names and then keys the microphone. It’s his voice that spectators hear echoing through the speakers at Leavitt High’s Libby Field, but it’s her direction that helps keep things on track.
“We do have a little bit of a timing and cadence to what we do,” said Michelle. “There have been times along the way, here and there, where someone else has filled in for Chris or someone has filled in for me, and the timing is always off. … We have built up a bit of a cadence to what we do so that I know when to deliver information and when not to.”
Public address announcers like the Cifellis add to the atmosphere at high school football games across the state. Their voices boom over the loudspeakers, keeping fans informed and shining a spotlight on the players on the field. Each brings a unique style to the booth. All play a role in the operation of high school football games across Maine.
“There’s so many different styles of how people do (announcing),” Chris said. “Sometimes it’s a ‘Whoever’s willing to take the mic’ and there’s other people that hang around for 20 plus years.”
‘AN EASY DATE NIGHT’
The Cifellis are the husband-wife duo responsible for the public address announcements during Leavitt football games.
He’s the announcer, she’s his spotter. Up in the booth, they work together to provide information to fans, like which player caught the ball, which player made the tackle, what yard-line the ball is on or how many yards to go until a first down.
“We joke that it’s kind of an easy date night for us,” Chris said. “At least four times a season, we get to do something on a Friday or Saturday evening together, and you get out, you see people that you maybe haven’t seen, or go to homecoming and there are kids that played years ago or even were just students and it’s kind of neat to see that.”
Chris, who teaches psychology at Leavitt, thinks he’s been calling games since 1999. Michelle joined him in 2009.
“Chris has former students whose kids are now on the field … they’ll see us sort of walking out after a game or they will come up and say hello at halftime or something like that because they know that it’s him and they remember him in high school and now their kid is the one on the field,” Michelle said.
PROVIDE THE INFORMATION
Some announcers and spotters, like the Cifellis, have held their positions for years, becoming staples at their respective high schools.
Don Atkinson, for example, who also serves as the Maine Principals’ Association’s tennis tournament director, has been Deering’s announcer since 2001.
The thorough manner with which he recaps each play after it’s whistled dead has become synonymous with Rams football over the last two and a half decades.
“I’m privileged that it’s kind of passed down that the kids that play, a lot of them call me ‘the voice,’” Atkinson said. “They probably don’t have a clue what my name is, which is fine, but they’ll go, ‘Hey, it’s the voice.’ And that’s cool, because I do football, basketball and baseball at Deering, so there’s a lot of kids that hear me three seasons.”
Even though he’s the one announcing games at Memorial Stadium, Atkinson said a spotter is paramount to success. His spotter, Michael Atkins, coaches the Deering girls basketball team.
“(Atkins has) got the number, the information,” Atkinson said. “I could announce the game from home based on what he’s feeding me for information.”
NEWCOMERS ON THE SCENE
Other announcers are newer to the gig. Jeremy Bullock started calling games at Gardiner full time this season. He replaced longtime announcer Sam Shaw.
“(Announcing) was something I was just sort of interested in, and I think I called a couple games for our youth program, which I’ve been the president of that for a few years at this point,” Bullock said. “And it just seemed like it was something that would be fun and I kind of just did my best Sam Shaw impression.
“And then word kind of got around that, ‘Oh, Jeremy does an all right job.’ And then when Sam was talking about retiring, I got asked if I wanted to try it out full time.”
Bullock played for the Tigers and graduated from Gardiner in 2001. His oldest son, Evan, is a senior and played for the Tigers this fall.
“It’s definitely a thrill when Evan makes a big play on defense … when he makes a big tackle or a sack or something like that; always proud to announce his name over the intercom.”
Sam Stolkner started calling middle school football games in 2023. He saw an advertisement for an announcer opening at Lisbon on Facebook, and originally pitched the gig to his friends as a joke.
“I asked my friends like, ‘Oh, should I do this as a joke? This would be funny, right?’” Stolkner said. “… I was like, ‘Yeah, I doubt they’ll pick me, but I’ll do it.’”
What started as a joke three years ago has blossomed into a second career of sorts for the banking analyst.
Stolkner, who now has his own announcer social media page featuring video clips from the games he’s called, calls a variety of high school and college sports all over the state. He has been the PA announcer for Lisbon varsity football games since 2024 and had the opportunity to work a Division III football game between Colby and Amherst on Oct. 17.
“It’s just snowballed out of control where I’m reaching out to teams, but at this point, teams I’ve never (contacted) … I didn’t think I was good enough to do Colby, and they reached out to me, which was crazy,” Stolkner said.

title: OBITUARIES for Thursday, November 12, 2026
text:
VICKI L. SAINT AMAND
WATERVILLE – Vicki Lou Saint Amand peacefully passed away on Friday, September 25, 2026. Born in Bangor, she began living in Dover-Foxcroft with her parents and two sisters. Later the family moved to Fairfield.
Enjoying her family and friends, she played cello and sang in the chorus, as well as excelling in school subjects through the years. She graduated in 1965 as valedictorian of Lawrence High School, in Fairfield.
She started working right out of high school, starting at The A & W, Montgomery Ward, Laverdiere’s and KVRHA, gaining work experience along the way. She started to further her education by applying herself to become a teacher, attending Adult Education, then the University of Maine-Farmington, and others, raising both of her daughters and working. She received diplomas to educate others.
She started her teaching career as a substitute teacher in the Gardiner school system. She did dabble for a bit and then became a case worker for The State of Maine, in Augusta. She had found her niche. She helped many different people, working hard for many years, and made great friendships along the way. She then retired.
Vicki had two daughters and then years later had two supercalifragilisticexpialidocious granddaughters, in which she thought the world was in a better place, because we were in it!
She had much interest in the arts, visiting bodies of water, friendships, her pets, Common Ground Country Fair, her family, being up in the air, gardening, reading, being vegan, holiday parties, music, wishing rocks, no-go roads, relationships, watching nature, giraffes, seeing beautiful things and traveling to new places. Her favorite time of the year was autumn which, of course, includes Halloween.
Vicki had a special relationship with Michael King for many years, as she was raising her daughters, working and attending school. She went to car shows and traveled in the 1957 Chevy to Classic Chevy conventions, going to concerts, watching TV, traveling and having many family gatherings.
She was predeceased by her father and mother, Rodney and Arlene Michaud; two sisters, Judith Brown and Wendi Tibbetts; nephew, Stephen Phillis.
She is survived by two daughters, Lisa Jamison and TerryAnn Towers Saint Amand; two granddaughters, Samantha Jamison and Tessa Saint-Towers; three nieces, Lynn McNeff, Tawni Lively and Tara True and their families; two life partners, Michael King and Algene (Ike) Raven, and their families.
A celebration of life will be determined at a later date.
In lieu of flowers, please make this place that we call earth a better and healthier place for the present and future generation to live in.
PETER A. LaBONTE
WATERVILLE – Peter A. LaBonte, 71, of Waterville, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, following a long battle with cancer.
Born on August 28, 1955, to Roland and Grace (Grady) LaBonte, Peter grew up in Waterville and attended local schools. In 1974, he enlisted in the United States Navy and proudly served aboard the USS Sylvania as an electrical repairman until his honorable discharge in 1978.
After returning home, Peter worked at Kimberly-Clark (Scott Paper Company), in Winslow, for 12 years, until the mill closed. He later continued his career as an electrician with the local IBEW until his retirement.
Peter was a quiet man who found happiness in the simple things in life. Over the years, he could often be found on the sidelines, proudly watching his children play soccer. He enjoyed reading and doing the daily crossword puzzle, rarely letting one in the newspaper go unfinished, and he had a genuine love of history. Each Christmas, his kids kept up a special tradition of giving him a daily calendar filled with jokes, Jeopardy questions, or bits of history, a gift he always looked forward to and enjoyed throughout the year.
In the summer months, he loved watching his grandson Lincoln learn to swim and proudly showing off his tricks from the diving board. It was especially meaningful because it happened in the same pool where he had once watched his own kids grow up and spend their summers.
Peter will be deeply missed by his daughters, Nicole and Melissa, his sons, Jacob and Joshua; and his grandson, Lincoln. He also leaves behind his brothers, Paul and Thomas, his sisters, Catherine and Rachel; as well as his extended family.
He was predeceased by his parents, Roland and Grace LaBonte.
A private burial will be held at a later date.
BRENDA H. DUDLEY
FAIRFIELD – Brenda Howard Dudley, 59, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at MaineGeneral Medical Center, in Augusta. Brenda was born on Thanksgiving day, November 26, 1966, the only daughter to Gerald and Judy Howard Sr.
She had a lot of different jobs throughout her life.
Brenda is survived by her parents, Gerald and Judy Howard Sr.; two sons, Travis Coro and Nathan Dudley; her grandson, Mason Coro; her brothers Jerry Howard Jr., and Bryan Howard; several aunts and uncles.
She was buried in Maplewood Cemetery, in Fairfield.
BEVERLEY J. ANDREWS
OAKLAND – Beverley Jane Andrews, 85, of Oakland, passed away peacefully on the afternoon of Tuesday, October 20, 2026, just shy of her 86th birthday. Beverley (“Bev”) was born on November 10, 1940, at Friendship Hospital, in Bangor, to Natalie and Everett Stimpson.
Bev spent her early childhood in the Old Town area and loved to tell stories about her time at her grandparents’ Cunningham family farm. There she learned the value of hard work and formed a special bond with her grandfather. It was also there that her love of animals began, and it grew throughout her life. From the pony she had as a child, to the many cats and dogs that followed, each held a special place in her heart. Her lifelong love of gardening began on the farm as well. Planting beautiful flowers brought her great joy, and everything she planted seemed to thrive under her care.
Beverley, spelled with “ley,” as she would often remind everyone, attended elementary and high school in Old Town. Her treasured keepsakes reflect her dedicated involvement in many booster clubs and school spirit activities.
Bev met her future husband, Wayne Gary Andrews, on a blind date at a friend’s house near the Stillwater Bridge. After a brief courtship and engagement, they were married in Old Town in 1961. In 1970 they moved to Oakland, where they made their home for the rest of their nearly 64 years of marriage.
Bev worked in retail in the Old Town–Bangor area and embraced opportunities to model clothing. She later worked with special needs adults in the Waterville area, as well as at several local nursing homes and a hotel, before settling into long-term employment at Hannaford Supermarket in Waterville.
Bev was always fun to be around, always willing to help when help was needed, always considerate and appreciative of others, and always showed how deeply she cared. She worked hard to reach her own goals and to help her children achieve theirs. She was a selfless and devoted mother, grandmother, and friend. She loved to shop and bake, and she sent gifts to family and friends all year long, always going above and beyond. Every card and package was decorated with elaborate stickers and stamps, and prepared with the utmost care.
Known to many as “Nana,” Bev raised her two children and helped raise two grandchildren into happy, healthy, and successful adults. She supported her family in a strong, no-nonsense, yet gentle way. She often offered “pocket money,” and when someone tried to refuse, she would warn, “Never refuse an offer of money, as it may not happen again…” or simply insist, “I want you to take it!” She sure loved to talk about her family, and was so proud to share their adventures and accomplishments. Those who knew her were lucky to have her as an inspiration and role model.
Bev had a gift for conversation, and we were always amazed by the stories of the people she met. She would come home from medical appointments and share the family histories of her providers, recalling every detail with a memory as sharp as a tack. She truly loved socializing, and many of the people she met over the years became her friends.
Bev faced health challenges in later years that limited her ability to drive, travel, and experience new places. Through it all, she remained resilient, kept a great sense of humor, and stayed optimistic.
Bev was predeceased by her parents, Natalie and Everett Stimpson; her son, Wayne Gary Andrews II, in 2021; her husband, Wayne Gary Andrews, in 2025; her sisters, Ruth Boucher and Rosemary Stone; and many beloved pets.
She is survived by her daughter, Deborah Luce and Deborah’s husband Brian; her grandchildren, Neil and Katie Luce, all of Sidney; and her sister-in-law, Shireen Burse; and niece, Lisa Burse, both of Eastport.
Interment services will be held on Sunday, November 15, 2026, at 11:30 a.m., at Lewis Cemetery, on Cottle Road, in Oakland. A memorial gathering will follow at Governor’s Restaurant in Waterville.
Services are under the care of Wheeler Funeral Home, in Oakland. Please visit wheelerfh.com to sign an online guestbook or share a memory.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Humane Society Waterville Area, 100 Webb Rd., Waterville, ME 04901.
CHERYL A. MARTIN-HUNT
FAIRFIELD – Cheryl Ann Clark Martin-Hunt, 75, passed away on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, following an arduous and fierce battle with appendiceal cancer. Cheryl was born April 21, 1951, in Augusta, the daughter of Gerald “Jack” and Irma O. (Fowles) Clark.
Cheryl did not come into this world alone – she was accompanied by her twin, Carol, and they remained close for Carol’s entire life.
Cheryl attended Readfield Elementary School and graduated from Kents Hill School in 1969. She attended the University of Maine at Orono for a time, and after college, Cheryl returned home to pursue various lines of work. These included waitressing and retail, owning her own business, Martin’s Sandwich Shop, on Water Street, in Augusta, and working in real estate and insurance in New Jersey. She was employed by the state of Maine for 24 years and retired from the Department of Transportation as Executive Assistant to the Commissioner of the DOT. She thoroughly enjoyed her work there and made many friends.
Cheryl was a beloved wife, adored mother, and revered friend to many people, some since her sub-primary years. She was always there when needed and gave generously of her time and attention to both people and causes, such as the homeless program in Bangor and the Veterans of Foreign Wars. Cheryl was a consummate homemaker and enjoyed cooking, reading, travel (unless a plane or cruise ship was involved!), gardening, the Ogunquit Playhouse, and going to the movies. She hosted amazing New Year’s Eve parties for many years and never forgot a birthday.
Cheryl dearly loved her twin sister, Carol, and they had many grand adventures together. Their bond was unbreakable, and Cheryl was shattered by Carol’s passing in 2020. Cheryl was also predeceased by her parents; her sister, Joan Shailer, her brother, Gerald “Jerry” Clark and wife, Francine; nephew Gene Clark, and niece Grace Shailer.
She is survived by her husband of 32 years, Eric Hunt Sr., of Fairfield; daughter April Cameron and husband, Travis, and son Ryan Martin; former spouse Clyde Martin; brother Earnest “Gene” Clark; grandsons Austin Cameron and companion, Amber, Logan Cameron and fiancée, Clarrissa Lettre; great-granddaughters Aubree, Hadlee, and Gabriella Cameron; brother-in-law, Bruce McLeod; aunt Jane White; nieces Debra Sue, Stephanie, and Heather, nephews Robert and Jon Shailer; and Michael Clark and wife, Jennifer, and their sons Nathan and Alex; and her bonus children Michelle Kew; Michael Hunt-Dubois and husband, Matt Dubois, and their son Jensen; Tiffany Stewart and husband, Jonathan, and their children, Emma Berkoski and husband Jake, Eli, Lauren, and Tewolde, and Eric Hunt, Jr., and his children Katelyn, Alyssa, and Cole; and many dear cousins.
There will be a celebration of Cheryl’s life at the MacCrillis-Rousseau VFW Post #8835, hall, in Winslow, on Saturday, November 21, 2026, from 1 to 3 p.m. All are welcome to attend.
Interment will be in the Niche Wall at the Augusta Veterans Memorial Cemetery, at a later date.
GREGORY FORTIN SR.
VASSALBORO – Gregory Fortin Sr., 79, passed away peacefully on Thursday, November 5, 2026. He was born in Waterville, on March 28, 1947, to the late Bernard H. and Phyllis I. (Dyer) Fortin.
Greg was married to Rose-Marie Fortin, of Vassalboro, for 59 years. Together they raised three sons and enjoyed traveling, fishing, gardening, and especially spending time with their grandchildren.
Greg attended Lawrence High School, in Fairfield, and earned an associate’s degree from the University of Maine, Orono. He served his country honorably in the U.S. Army National Guard and the Air National Guard. He was a self-employed plumber and worked at Bath Iron Works as a pipefitter for 25 years.
Gregory was a life-time resident of Vassalboro and served on the Vassalboro Volunteer Fire Department for a number of years, was the Plumbing Inspector for Vassalboro for several years, and served as Scoutmaster of Troop #410 for about eight years, seeing all three of his sons earn their Eagle Scout rank. Greg enjoyed fishing Moosehead Lake, hunting, bowling, tying streamer flies, spending countless hours on his zero-turn mower, and putting up with the shenanigans of his three sons and grandchildren. He was also an avid reader and cribbage player.
Gregory was predeceased by his parents, Bernard and Phyllis (Dyer) Fortin, grandparents, and numerous aunts and uncles.
Gregory E. Fortin, Sr. is survived by his wife of 59 years, Rose-Marie (Lemieux) Fortin; his three sons, Gregory E. Fortin Jr. and his wife Jennifer (Cole), of Vassalboro, Robert C. Fortin and his wife Michelle (Gavin), of Surry, and Bernard P. Fortin and his wife Jennifer (McGreevy), of Vassalboro; grandchildren, Emma, Morgan, Cole, and Brandon Fortin, and Zackery and Jacob Lewis; and Breanna McGreevy; and his great-grandchild, Ashton McGreevy; cousin, Timothy and Corrine Dyer, of Yucca Valley, California.
Catholic Mass will be celebrated at Notre Dame Catholic Church, 116 Silver St., Waterville, on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at 9 a.m. A graveside service for family and friends will follow directly at the North Vassalboro Village Cemetery, on Cemetery Street, in Vassalboro, with a reception to follow at the Notre Dame hall.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to Vassalboro Fuel Fund, P.O. Box 203, North Vassalboro, ME 04962, or to Harold Alfond Center for Cancer Care, 361 Old Belgrade Rd., Augusta, ME 04330.
DENNIS A. ROLLINS
WINSLOW – Dennis A. Rollins, 89, passed away at his home, in Winslow, on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, from complications due to lymphoma.
He was born in 1937 at Pleasant Ridge as the only son of Avery L. and Ruth H. (Beane) Rollins, and grew up as a hard-working and well-respected member of the community.
As a young man, he attended Bingham area schools, graduating as class valedictorian from Bingham High School in 1956. While in high school, he enlisted in the U.S. Army National Guard, eventually serving for nine years and becoming both a tank commander and a .45 caliber marksman. He was on heightened alert status during the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
Also while in high school, Dennis met his future wife, Charlene Washburn, of Solon. He quickly became infatuated with her, with his first date at the age of 15, taking her to the Skowhegan Fair. Dennis would follow her into movies at the Colby Theater, in Bingham. She would show up at his high school baseball games, once skipping classes to watch a game in Bingham – she was caught by Solon school officials, who “punished” her by making her attend additional games and writing a report on what she saw. The pair fell in love and were married in Pleasant Ridge in 1957, the start of a 57-year marriage.
After a year at the University of Maine, Dennis moved to the Maine coast to become a machinist apprentice at Bath Iron Works beginning in 1958. After his apprenticeship was completed, Dennis and Charlene moved to Winslow, and he worked for a time as a machinist and then foreman for the Keyes Fibre Company machine shop. In 1974, he went to work for former co-worker Doug Sukeforth as chief estimator at Mid-State Machine, in Winslow. He worked there until his retirement in 1999.
Dennis and Charlene loved to travel, visiting Europe, Hawaii, Mexico, the Caribbean, and various locations throughout the United States and Canada. They also enjoyed their time spent at the camp they built together on Embden Pond, where they, their children, and their grandchildren spent many happy days together.
As a young man, Dennis loved to hunt and fish; as he got older, he would go snowmobiling regularly. Dennis also spent time building furniture, designing bureaus, desks, and cabinets for his house, and the houses of his daughters, as well as designing custom furniture for a period of time for disabled children at the Pine Tree Camp, in central Maine.
After Charlene passed away in 2015, Dennis met Cynthia Morency Lambert, of Winslow. They fell in love and spent ten happy years together, enjoying times dancing, gardening, and visiting with members of both his and her families. Cynthia was a tremendous comfort to him as he dealt with his diagnosis and was with him as he passed.
Dennis was predeceased by his parents, Avery and Ruth Rollins, by his step-father Millard Flanders, and by his wife Charlene Washburn Rollins.
He was survived by his sister Phyllis (Rollins) Pratt, who passed away three weeks after Dennis did, she being the last member of Avery and Ruth’s family.
He is survived by his two daughters, Valerie and Sheri, and their husbands Ed and Matt, respectively; his son Rick, and Rick’s wife Dai; his grandchildren Alex, Omen, Kenny, Greg, and Christina; and several nieces and nephews; his partner Cynthia Lambert, her children John, Renee, Rachel, and Michael; a great-grandchild of Cynthia, Archie’s.
At Dennis’s request, his body was cremated, and there was no funeral. A private graveside service was held October 21, 2026, at St. Francis Cemetery, in Waterville, to inter Dennis and Charlene’s ashes.

Maine woman wanted on drug charges after previous arrest tied to infant overdose

The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office said Brittany Wood, 36, is wanted after a traffic stop Sunday led to the seizure of illegal drugs
A woman previously arrested in connection with an infant overdose in Eddington is now wanted on new drug-related charges, according to the Penobscot County Sheriff's Office.
Brittany Wood, 36, of Eddington, is wanted on an active arrest warrant following a traffic stop on Sunday, Nov. 8.
During the stop, authorities seized suspected illegal drugs and prevented Wood from destroying potential evidence, according to the sheriff's office.
Authorities said testing conducted over the following two days confirmed the substances were illegal drugs.
The sheriff's office said deputies made several unsuccessful attempts to have Wood voluntarily surrender before obtaining an arrest warrant.
Wood is now wanted on charges of unlawful possession of scheduled drugs, falsifying physical evidence and violation of conditions of release.
Wood was previously arrested in July in connection with a May 31 incident in Eddington involving an infant who reportedly overdosed on drugs.
She was charged with domestic violence aggravated assault and endangering the welfare of a child in that case and was later released on bail.
Wood was also identified in previous reporting as a member of the RSU 63 School Board, representing Eddington.
The sheriff's office said Wood remains wanted.
Anyone with information about her whereabouts is asked to contact the Penobscot County Sheriff's Office at 207-947-4585.

title: Would Biden have sought a second term if he’d known he had cancer? Here’s what he says
text:
(AP) - ATLANTA (AP) — Joe Biden says he did not know he had cancer while he was president and would not have sought a second term if he already had been diagnosed.
The former Democratic president’s comments came in an interview with People magazine before the release of his White House memoir on Tuesday.
“If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer,” said Biden, who turns 84 on Nov. 20, “I would’ve not gone forward” with a 2024 reelection bid that ended after a disastrous debate performance against Republican Donald Trump.
Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office in 2025.
“I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running” for president, Biden said in the interview.
Still, he argued that the June 2024 debate, less than five months before Election Day, was not a seismic event even if it accelerated Democrats’ concerns about his age — he was 81 at the time — and his ability to defeat Trump.
“First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t,” Biden said. “But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”
Within weeks, Biden announced he was ending his campaign and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, who secured the nomination and lost to Trump in the general election.
Biden insisted he was able to perform his duties while he was in office. He said age itself was not disqualifying and meant he had experience and deep personal relationships with world leaders.
“I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job,” he said.
His son Hunter told the BBC in August that the cancer had spread and was causing his father pain. “It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects,” he said.
Since Joe Biden left office, his son has become a higher profile public presence, sparring with Republicans on social media, posting lengthy thoughts on the nation’s direction and launching his own cryptocurrency.
Joe Biden defended his son’s public persona and his decision to pardon Hunter Biden after the younger Biden’s 2024 conviction on federal felony gun charges and his guilty plea to federal tax charges. Hunter Biden also had faced years of scrutiny and withering Republican attacks over his international business dealings.
Hunter Biden has said the pardon damaged his father’s legacy, but the former president said Trump’s penchant for vengeance made it necessary.
“He goes after people without any basis, whether they’re viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do,” Joe Biden said. “If I hadn’t pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who’s dealt with me — he would go back and try to do harm to them.”
Biden called his son “one of the brightest men I know,” adding, “I’m really proud of him.”

title: Topsham considers restrictions on where sex offenders can live
text:
Topsham’s Select Board members were recently surprised to learn that it is up to them to regulate where sex offenders can live. In Maine, there is no statewide restriction.
Andrea Imrie, a Topsham resident who runs an in-home daycare program, brought the issue to the Select Board on Nov. 5. The Select Board passed a motion instructing town employees to draft an ordinance that would keep sex offenders from living near schools and parks.
Since 2009, state statute has allowed towns to restrict where sex offenders can live if they have been convicted of Class A, B, or C sexual crimes involving victims age 14 or younger. Town ordinances can prevent these individuals from living within 750 feet of parks, schools and other spaces owned by the state or a town that are primarily used by children.
“I believe additional protective measures are necessary and wanted to help safeguard these locations and provide families with a greater peace of mind,” said Imrie.
This ordinance would not apply to sex offenders who already live in town. Topsham currently has 14 — two are registered for 10 years, four for 25 years and eight for life. Topsham Police Chief Mark Hagan said that three new sex offenders were registered in the past year — two moved to town and one resident was added to the registry.
Hagan said that in his six years in Topsham, the issue of sex offenders living near schools and parks has not come up. He said even without a town ordinance, many sex offenders already have residency restrictions because of the crime they committed. If these individuals are on probation, their probation officers are responsible for telling them where they can and can’t live.
Town Manager Mark Waltz said enforcement of this ordinance would happen through civil courts. Violators could be fined and prosecuted by the town’s attorney. The ordinance could also stipulate that if prosecution is necessary, the sex offender would need to reimburse the town’s legal fees.
Waltz said the ordinance would likely prevent sex offenders from moving near schools and parks in the first place. If a sex offender tried to move to a restricted area, the town could notify the landlord.
“I think most of it can be dealt with up front, as opposed to having to be chasing people after the fact,” Waltz said.
At the Select Board meeting, Imrie said she believes this issue should be tackled as soon as possible. “This is about being proactive rather than reactive. We should not wait for something to happen before taking a serious look at the protections available to our community.”
Some information about sex offenders is public, including places of employment and towns of primary residence. Exact addresses are not available, but if law enforcement officers think a sex offender is a risk to nearby residents, they will let the neighbors know.
Hagan said when a resident registers as a sex offender or an existing sex offender moves to town, the police department conducts a risk assessment. This is based on the crime the sex offender committed and the features of the neighborhood they want to move to, namely its size and whether it includes a school. If police officers decide the individual poses a risk, they will knock on doors and hand out flyers to ensure nearby residents are aware.
Waltz said the police department is reviewing similar ordinances from other Maine towns to use as a basis for Topsham’s version.
Once the ordinance is drafted, the town will hold a public hearing to decide if it should be on the town meeting warrant in May.

title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any U.S. state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.
“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”
The Associated Press called the race in Colom’s favor after local officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch.
Hyde-Smith, 67, called Colom late Wednesday afternoon to concede and released a concession speech online shortly afterward.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society, and he repeated that pledge after his victory.
“My commitment to you, each and every one of you, is that first I’m going to treat your children like I want my children to be treated,” Colom said. “I’m going to treat your parents the way I want my parents to be treated. I’m gonna treat your future the way I want my future to be” and “work to make every Mississippian’s life better.”
National Democrats, activists and Mississippians celebrate
Party leaders hailed the senator-elect’s triumph, with nods to the South’s emerging status as a political battleground after other victories from North Carolina and South Carolina to Georgia and Texas.
“Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online.
Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won “because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back.”
Vera Finley was among those supporters.
“I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields,” Finley said ahead of Colom’s victory speech. “Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great-grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history.”
Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state’s voters, most notably Black voters, “made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out” in a state that has seen “some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights.”
A race Washington once viewed as a long shot
The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, finally drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia’s Raphael Warnock and Maryland’s Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see it as winnable.
The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom produced one of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October to rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited to enter. He introduced himself and asked about their concerns.
Later, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said only nine words in six seconds before stepping away: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”
Colom’s appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war that drove up gas prices and tariffs that caused headaches for Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state accustomed to long-serving, powerful senators.
There is some irony in Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
Colom called on Mississippi’s history
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist.
Colom told the story of Evers’ military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction. “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”
At the lectern Wednesday night, Colom said it was appropriate that the race be called on Veterans Day, as he again paid tribute to Evers.
“He served his country, came home to Mississippi, and they wouldn’t let him vote,” Colom said. “But he had faith that Mississippi could make progress.”
Despite Republicans’ domination, the path was always there
Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican discontent and an uptick in Democrats’ usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who’d also been Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of his candidacy but said he cares more about what it means for others.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”
__
Barrow reported from Atlanta and Washington.

title: Police accuse midcoast man of being drug dealer bodyguard
text:
A Woolwich man who police say is a bodyguard for out-of-state drug dealers was arrested and charged with firearm offenses.
Aaron W. Morse, 45, was arrested Nov. 8 by the Knox County Sheriff’s Office and charged with possession of a firearm by a prohibited person and possessing a loaded firearm in a motor vehicle.
Justice Sean Ociepka set bail at $5,000 cash. Assistant District Attorney Mari Wells had sought bail of $7,500 while defense attorney for the day James Gioia asked for bail to be set at $1,000.
An affidavit filed in the state court in Knox County by the Sheriff’s Office stated that a deputy was on patrol when he spotted a van going by him on Route 1 in Warren with the plate light out.
The deputy followed the vehicle and pulled it over.
The female driver had a suspended driver’s license, according to the affidavit. Morse was the passenger in the vehicle. Morse, also known as Viking, is known as a body guard for out-of-state drug dealers and a middle man, the affidavit stated.
In the back seat, under items, was a pump action shotgun with its barrel sawed down. There were five shells in the weapon, according to the police report.
Both Morse and the woman driver denied knowledge of the gun. The driver said that the last person to use the vehicle other than her was Morse.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Obituary: Geraldine (Martin) Greco
text:
CUMBERLAND FORESIDE – Geraldine (Martin) Greco, 94, passed away on Nov. 5, 2026, in New Hampshire. She was born in Madawaska, on March 24, 1932, the daughter of Lenard and Laura (Guerrette) Martin.
Known affectionately as Gerry, she graduated from Madawaska High School and married Arthur Greco in 1953. Together, they raised two children. Gerry devoted herself to being a wife and mother. She was poised, gracious, and loving, with a warm disposition and a genuine love of entertaining and hosting gatherings. She was a wonderful cook and possessed many other talents. As a younger woman, she enjoyed skiing, tennis, golf, and playing bridge with friends.
Gerry was a member of the Women’s Golf Association at the Portland Country Club, where she served on several committees. She was also a past member of the Women of Rotary Club of Portland.
She was a communicant of Holy Martyrs Church, where her strong faith and spirituality brought her comfort throughout her life.
She was predeceased by her beloved husband of 67 years, Arthur, and her brother, Gerald.
She is survived by her daughter, Lee, and her husband, Tom Farrell; her son, Martin, and his wife, Amanda; and her grandchildren, Nicole, Marie, Andrew, and Christina. She was also blessed with four great-grandchildren.
A Mass of Christian Burial will be celebrated at 10 a.m., on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, at Holy Martyrs Church, 266 Foreside Road, Falmouth, followed by graveside services at Pine Grove Cemetery, Falmouth.
Arrangements are under the direction of the Conroy-Tully Walker, Cremation, Funeral, and Gathering Center, 300 Allen Ave. Portland. To view Gerry’s memorial page, or to leave an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.
In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Parish of the Holy Eucharist.

title: Maine Shrine Lobster Bowl Classic raises record-breaking $250K
text:
Maine Shrine Lobster Bowl Classic raises record-breaking $250K for Shriners Children's hospitals
This year's Maine Shrine Lobster Bowl Classic raised a total of $250,000 for the Shriners Children's hospitals in New England, doubling the previous all-time record for Maine's premier high school football all-star game, which has been held for 36 years.
Each year, players, cheerleaders and coaches who participate in the Lobster Bowl raise money for the Shriners hospitals in Boston and Springfield, Massachusetts.
The Lobster Bowl's board of directors also said that Logan Vigue of Medomak Valley High School set a new all-time individual fundraising record of $27,000. Dawson Sukeforth of Bucksport High School and Lily Alley of Ellsworth High School also raised more than $10,000 each.
Joe Hersom, president of the Maine Shrine Lobster Bowl Classic, said several news events and increased promotion by the players on social media helped this year's game shatter the previous fundraising record of $125,000 and set a new bar.
"As we look across the other football games that support Shriners Children's, we've been fortunate enough to be in the top three or the top five year after year," Hersom said. "This is going to make a big difference towards pushing us to number one."
The money raised from this year's Lobster Bowl was split evenly between Shriners Children's Boston and Shriners Children's New England in Springfield, with each hospital receiving a $125,000 donation.
Planning for next year's game is already underway. More information about sponsorship opportunities and how to donate is available on the Maine Shrine Lobster Bowl website.

title: American Legion Post 93 hosts Veterans Day celebration in Bucksport
text:
BUCKSPORT, Maine (WABI) - Members of the community came together at the Bucksport Area Veterans Memorial for a Veterans Day ceremony honoring those who have served.
The ceremony, put on by American Legion Post 93, included a dedication, a prayer for veterans and a rendition of ‘America the Beautiful.’
The commander of the local legion who says this day is an opportunity to recognize all veterans.
“I think we have a duty to the community, I think we have a duty to our veterans. And I think that’s why you see so many active veterans organizations. We have a duty to each other, we have a responsibility to our nation, and we have a responsibility to our community. And I think that’s what we did today just shows that,” said Post 93 Commander Vince Christinziano.
Post 93 also supports high school activities, senior projects and veterans projects.
