title: Ocean liner SS United States heads to final destination near Destin, Florida
text:
WATCH: Historic SS United States is sunk off Florida's coast, after a long goodbye
The historic SS United States, once the fastest ship on the seas, made a slow final journey beneath the waters Wednesday.
The famous ocean liner — which is longer than the Titanic and crossed the Atlantic more than 800 times — was deliberately sunk Wednesday to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico, where the once-luxurious behemoth was set to begin a new chapter as the world's largest artificial reef.
Related video above: National Aquarium's Read to Reef Book Club Returns
It was a long goodbye. Hours after the sinking began on a cloudy afternoon, much of the hulking ship could still be seen in the dark waters off the coast of the Florida Panhandle by nightfall. Organizers had predicted the sinking could finish in as quickly as an hour.
Finally, around 9 p.m., the vessel leaned on one side and then quickly submerged.
“She is an amazing lady who will not lay down without a fight,” Coleen O’Malley, president of Coleen Marine, the company sinking the ship, said before the vessel disappeared beneath the water. “Much like the amazing nation she was named after.”
The event — described by officials as a controlled sinking — was a long-planned $13.5 million project aimed at attracting more divers and fishing enthusiasts while creating a home for tuna, marlin and swordfish.
The slower-than expected descent was partly due to crews filling 128 fuel and lubricant tanks aboard the ship with water so that it would rest evenly on the ocean floor, said Nick Tomecek, a spokesperson for Okaloosa County, which helped organize the sinking. He said the process “took longer than we thought.”
“She’s a big ship,” Tomecek said.
A massive vessel with a long history
The project will keep what had been a technological marvel when it made its maiden voyage in 1952 from becoming scrap metal.
Famous passengers included Hollywood stars like Grace Kelly and Elizabeth Taylor. Other passengers have included Presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy and Britain’s former King Edward VIII. In 1968, a young Bill Clinton took it when he went to Oxford University, decades before he was elected president.
Once aboard, passengers were treated to dinners that included caviar, roast duckling, smoked ox tongue and Calf's Head en Tortue.
In preparation for the sinking, organizers removed the 65-foot (20-meter) smokestacks and plan to have them anchor a new museum that celebrates the ship.
Explosives were not allowed to be used
Federal environmental and explosives rules prevent Okaloosa County, Florida, and its contractor from using explosives to scuttle the ship, Tomecek said. Concerns about inclement weather prompted officials to move up the sinking by a day.
The SS United States has pipes that pulled seawater into tanks as part of the system that cooled its boilers, he said, and those tanks have been removed so that once the valves are opened, water will flood the hull. Workers also have cut 10-foot by 10-foot (3-meter by 3-meter) holes in the decks, and more than 400 portholes have been removed.
The ship is to sink in about 180 feet (55 meters) of water, with its top deck about 60 feet (18 meters) below the surface — shallow enough that inexperienced divers can visit. It will settle on the floor of the waters about 25 miles (40 kilometers) southwest of Destin, between Panama City and Pensacola.
Larger than the Titanic, the ship set a speed record on its first voyage
More than 3,000 workers helped build the SS United States in 1950 and 1951 in Virginia. An Associated Press reporter and Truman's daughter, Margaret, were among 1,700 passengers for the first voyage.
The ship's average speed for that trip was almost 41 mph (66 kph), besting a record set by Britain's RMS Queen Mary in 1938 by 4.5 mph (7.2 kph), according to the AP's dispatch.
The SS United States set the record even though its journey ended in the face of a full gale that reached 69 mph (111 kph) — “so strong it blew a ping pong table off the deck,” AP reported.
At 990 feet (302 meters), the ship is 108 feet (33 meters) longer than the ill-fated Titanic, which hit an iceberg and sank on its first voyage across the Atlantic.
“She really embodies and expresses this country’s best,” said Susan Gibbs, the granddaughter of the ship's designer. “She represents pride and resilience and strength and beauty.”
The ship's resting place has many artificial reefs
More than 500 artificial reefs are located in the waters near where the SS United States will rest.
Previously, the largest artificial reef came from the 2006 scuttling of an aircraft carrier, the USS Oriskany in the Gulf off Pensacola — near enough to the SS United States site that an experienced diver could visit both in the same day, Tomecek said. The Oriskany, launched in 1950, was 911 feet (278 meters) in length.
“We're trying to be the best diving destination in the world,” Tomecek said.
The ship was decommissioned in 1969. Attempts by a hotel magnate and Norwegian Cruise Lines to use the ship never floated, and from 1996 until recently, it sat along a dock in Philadelphia.
Mullane called the huge funnels — the smokestacks that have been removed to anchor the new museum — “works of art.”
“I’m just so happy that we are able to save parts of her,” Gibbs said.

title: Maine deregulated electricity 26 years ago. Time for a rigorous review.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bill Webster of Georgetown is a former superintendent of schools in Lewiston. He was also controller for Hannaford Bros. and owned and operated Haven’s Candies. He is now an active SCORE mentor, providing free mentoring to existing and aspiring entrepreneurs.
Would most Maine residential customers pay 20 cents per kilowatt hour if they knew that a 12-cent option was available? Probably not. Do most Mainers know who supplies their electricity and what their rate is per kilowatt hour?
Most Mainers know who delivers it to them: Central Maine Power or Versant Power, depending upon where you live. These distributors also send you the bill, maintain the power lines and restore service after storms. But the company that actually supplies your electricity is an entirely different business.
I suspect many Mainers couldn’t identify their electricity supplier without searching through their monthly bill. Until recently, I thought I knew mine.
In 1997, Maine enacted legislation restructuring the state’s electricity industry. Beginning in March 2000, consumers could choose among competing electricity suppliers, while utilities such as CMP continued to deliver the electricity. The premise was straightforward: Competition would provide more choices and encourage lower prices.
For customers who didn’t choose a supplier, the state established the Standard Offer, with rates determined through competitive bidding overseen by the Maine Public Utilities Commission.
More than a quarter-century later, it’s worth asking whether that experiment has delivered the promised benefits. Consider my recent experience.
Earlier this summer, I contacted CMP and confirmed that I was receiving electricity through the Standard Offer. My June bill clearly identifies it as my supplier. Imagine my surprise when I discovered that my supplier had subsequently changed to SmartEnergy, at a rate of 20.4 cents per kilowatt-hour, approximately 60% higher than the Standard Offer rate of 12.721 cents. The price difference certainly helps fund the rebates that SmartEnergy offers.
When I contacted SmartEnergy, I was told that my wife had authorized the change during a telephone conversation in May. She recalls responding to a solicitation concerning a rebate but says she never knowingly agreed to change our electricity supplier.
The solicitation itself was intriguing. Prominently displayed were the words, “Please choose a payout option for your rebate.” It also identified us as CMP customers. Was this an offer from our electricity provider, a refund we were entitled to receive, or a marketing promotion designed to attract new customers?
Apparently, we didn’t understand what was being offered.
Whether the record of the phone call establishes that proper authorization was obtained remains to be determined. But the experience illustrates how difficult it can be for consumers to understand the choices they are making.
And there’s more. Like many Mainers, I also participate in a community solar program. That arrangement involves credits against my CMP bill and a separate monthly statement from another company. Between the delivery company, the electricity supplier and the solar program, understanding my household’s electricity costs has become surprisingly complicated.
Does all this competition actually save us money?
According to a January 2026 report presented by Maine’s Office of the Public Advocate, Maine residential customers purchasing electricity from competitive suppliers paid an estimated $156 million more between 2016 and 2024 than they would have paid under the Standard Offer.
The report also found that low-income customers were disproportionately affected. These results were also similar to a study done in Massachusetts. That is a disturbing finding for a system intended to benefit consumers through competition.
Competition can be valuable. Some suppliers offer renewable energy options or fixed-rate contracts that may appeal to certain customers. But competition only works well when consumers understand what they are purchasing and can compare prices and terms.
At a minimum, every electricity supplier should be required to disclose prominently its rate alongside the current Standard Offer, the length of the contract, what happens when it expires and exactly what a consumer is authorizing. Solicitation materials should make unmistakably clear that accepting an incentive may involve changing electricity suppliers.
Perhaps Maine should go further and reconsider whether its current system of residential
electricity competition is delivering sufficient benefits to justify its complexity. I hope this becomes a priority of the next Legislature.
Electricity is an essential service, not a discretionary purchase. Mainers deserve reasonable prices, understandable bills and informed choices. After 26 years of deregulation, shouldn’t we be asking whether the system is working for the people who pay for it?

title: Acclaimed jazz trumpeter Adam O’Farrill brings brash, lyrical sounds to Portland
text:
Trumpeter and bandleader Adam O’Farrill has earned a solid reputation on the contemporary jazz scene as a member of a prestigious musical family with roots in Cuba and beyond.
National Public Radio has called him “one of the most important jazz musicians of the 21st century,” and he has been hailed by the New York Times as “among the leading trumpeters in jazz” and “perhaps the music’s next major improviser.”
On Nov. 21, O’Farrill will bring his latest ensemble, the Elephant quartet, to Space in Portland, comprising O’Farrill, Walter Stinson on bass, Russell Holzman on drums, and Maine native Yvonne Rogers on piano. O’Farrill and Rogers may also add some electronic sounds to the mix.
The group’s eponymous first album has been lauded for its “smart, engaging music” featuring the leader’s “capacities for brashness and lyricism.” I would add adjectives like hypnotic and ethereal to describe some fascinating passages from the disc. It is an album that will likely make multiple top 10 jazz lists for 2026.
O’Farrill notes that his bandmates “carry perception and playfulness in equal measure.” They “like to push each other’s buttons a little,” he said, while also following his preference that “the improvised moments … feel earned and justified” within the compositions.
O’Farrill shows his respect for both traditional and newer approaches to music, counting many legendary trumpeters, both past and present, from Louis Armstrong to Ambrose Akinmusire, among his favorites.
The appearance at Space is a return engagement, and he calls the venue “very hand-crafted” and “singular.”
O’Farrill has praise for pianist Rogers, who grew up in the town of Penobscot. He finds her “creative and probing, constantly adding and finding new wrinkles” in the music.
Long-time Maine Jazz Camp supporter Paul Lichter remembers Rogers dabbling in saxophone while attending the camp as a teenager. But the piano was always her first instrument while growing up. “I liked that the piano was so versatile,” she notes.
After completing her formal education at the Eastman School of Music and the University of Rochester, Rogers moved to New York where she connected with O’Farrill. She instantly found him to be both an amazing and challenging bandleader whose music is “so rich and unique.”
Rogers admits to a certain nostalgia for life in Maine. “I spent my whole childhood outdoors,” she remembers. She still longs for “the nature, stillness, quiet, slow pace, seasons,” of her home state as she continues to make her mark on the international jazz scene.
Steve Feeney is a freelance writer who lives in Portland.
Adam O’Farrill’s Elephant, Nov. 21 at 8 p.m. at Space, 538 Congress St. Doors open at 7:30 p.m. Tickets $20 advance, $25 day of show, $2 off for Space members. Tickets available on eventbrite or at the box office (cash only). For more, call 207-828-5600 or space538.org

title: The Latest: Efforts to impeach Pete Hegseth are blocked by House Republicans
text:
The House has turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his conduct in office and handling of the war against Iran, which some Republicans blame for sweeping midterm losses.
More than a dozen House and Senate races remain undetermined one week after Election Day. Democrats could have 56 Senate seats when the counting is done in Alaska and Mississippi. Democrats already have 255 seats in the House, their widest majority in decades.
And Sen. Bernie Sanders said he won’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer as majority leader. He said there needs to be a new generation of leadership and a vigorous debate about the Democratic Party’s party’s direction.
Here’s the Latest:
A note to ‘46’: Trump’s private message to Biden emerges in new White House memoir
Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result as having been stolen from him by Democratic forces, privately lauded incoming President Joe Biden as someone he believed would “be true to yourself and the American people.”
That sentiment, along with others, was part of the letter Trump left for Biden upon leaving office in January 2021. Biden showed the note to some members of his staff after his inauguration in 2021 but didn’t let anyone read it, describing it later that day as “very generous” but otherwise saying he considered it to be private.
Inclusion of the letter in Biden’s “Promise Me, America,” his White House memoir slated for release Nov. 17, was first reported Tuesday by The New York Times. The Associated Press has reviewed a photocopy of the two-page letter, handwritten in Trump’s trademark black Sharpie on White House stationery and addressed “To ‘46,’” denoting Biden’s place as the 46th U.S. president.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio elected to lead House Republicans in the minority
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio has won a party contest to serve as House Republican leader as the party prepares for its new role in the minority and a flurry of Democratic investigations aimed at its standard-bearer in the White House.
Jordan, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, defeated Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana in a secret-ballot election of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress. Tuesday’s vote was 106-73.
Jordan, 62, co-founded the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus. His candidacy appealed to those looking for new leadership in the wake of last week’s election debacle and to those who like his hard-hitting political style.
Jordan will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power for Trump’s final two years in office. Leading the party back to a House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories.
Bernie Sanders won’t support Schumer for Senate Democratic leader, saying it’s time for change
Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he would not be supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as the Democratic majority leader in the new Congress, setting up a seismic confrontation after the party’s sweep to power in the midterm elections.
Sanders was joined by Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan at a news conference at the Capitol, and together called for a new generation of leadership and a vigorous debate about the party’s direction. A number of incoming Democratic senators have echoed the call, signaling that they would support another candidate over Schumer.
“The time is now for change,” said Sanders, the independent from Vermont and essentially the father of modern progressivism in the U.S. “And I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”
Slotkin, who said she is not actively seeking the job herself, explained that she wants potential Senate leaders to present a full plan about the new majority’s priorities.
“I’m a no until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said.
Pete Hegseth impeachment effort blocked by House Republicans
The House has turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for his conduct in office and handling of the war against Iran.
The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary Tuesday, blocking the effort in a near party-line vote.
The effort was led by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. The vote Tuesday may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take charge in January, stood firmly behind the push, saying Hegseth has “abused his power” and “undermined America’s national security.”

title: Celtics storm back to beat Raptors for 5th straight win
text:
TORONTO — Jayson Tatum made the tying and go-ahead free throws with 25.2 seconds remaining and the Boston Celtics overcame a 22-point deficit to beat the Toronto Raptors 98-93 on Wednesday night, extending their winning streak to five.
Tatum scored 24 points, Derrick White had 19 and Payton Pritchard added 14. Neemias Queta had 11 points and 13 rebounds as the Celtics improved to 4-0 against Atlantic Division opponents.
Boston’s Paul George sat out because of an illness a night after he scored 36 points in a winning return to Philadelphia.
Tatum shot 6 for 21 and finished 2 for 11 from 3-point range. He was 10 for 12 at the free throw line.
Toronto’s Ja’Kobe Walter scored 17 points and rookie Allen Graves added a career-high 13, but the Raptors fell below .500 for the first time at 5-6.
Raptors forward Kawhi Leonard (left knee) missed his ninth straight game but is “progressing well” with individual conditioning, coach Darko Rajakovic said before the game. On Tuesday, the Raptors said they’d update Leonard’s status in a week.
Scottie Barnes (left groin) missed his third straight game but Immanuel Quickley returned after missing the past two because of a sore right hamstring. Collin Murray-Boyles started for the fourth time after sitting out a loss to Memphis on Monday because of illness.
Walter scored all 12 of his points from long-range as the Raptors tied a franchise record for 3-pointers in a quarter by shooting 10 for 18 from distance in the first.
Toronto shot 6 for 25 from distance the rest of the way.
The Raptors led 59-37 after Jamal Shead’s free throw with 5:24 remaining in the second, but the Celtics answered with 16 straight points. Tatum scored the first 10 by himself as Boston cut the deficit to 61-54 at halftime.
Up next
Celtics: Host Dallas on Sunday.
Raptors: At Philadelphia on Thursday.

title: Missing baby in South Carolina found buried alive a day after authorities say his father took him
text:
Father of boy who survived being buried alive charged with attempted murder in South Carolina
A baby in South Carolina, who authorities say was taken by his father, was found alive Tuesday, buried in a dog crate in the woods after apparently spending about 24 hours underground, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Office.
Koah Sharpe, an 11-month-old boy, was taken by his father, Michael Comer, on Monday afternoon, according to investigators.
Comer, 25, has been charged with attempted murder. He has been in custody since Monday, when Koah disappeared.
Investigators searched for Koah near Comer’s father’s house, and they found pine straw and “freshly disturbed dirt,” Sheriff Jay Koon said during a news conference on Tuesday.
Once they started digging, they heard Koah crying. “It was the most joyful sound you ever heard of a crying baby,” he added.
They said they believed the child could have been buried for about 24 hours in a dog crate that had been wrapped in a towel.
Koah was taken to a hospital after the rescue.
Comer was arrested on charges of burglary and resisting arrest, Koon said. Investigators are working with prosecutors on additional charges Comer could face, the sheriff said.
Timeline of the case
Koah had been in the care of his paternal grandmother Monday when Comer came over, Koon said. The grandmother went to run an errand and left Koah with Comer while another caregiver was on the way. When that caregiver arrived, Comer and the baby were gone.
Deputies were called around lunchtime Monday and after some investigation went to a home where Comer’s father lives, Koon said. They found the doors open and the baby’s belongings inside – but no sign of the child or his father.
Investigators obtained video showing Comer at several locations without the baby as authorities searched for the pair Monday, according to Koon.
“Certainly we got worried, hoping and praying that he dropped the baby with another person,” the sheriff said. “As the day went on and nobody came forward, it was certainly more and more concerning.”
Comer was found later that night in an outbuilding at a property in Batesburg and arrested, Koon said. But Koah was not with him.
The urgent search for the baby continued into Tuesday, involving nearly 100 law enforcement officers and other public safety personnel.
Eventually a search team noticed freshly disturbed dirt in pine straw about 50 yards into the woods near the home of Comer’s father, Koon said.
As investigators began searching the site and digging, they heard the baby crying.
“As you imagine, the race was on. Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out,” Koon said.
The baby was pulled from the buried crate and “screaming at the top of his lungs,” Koon said.
Koon estimated the child was underground for about 24 hours. He said the towel around the wire crate “probably created an air pocket.”

title: Ellsworth track project moving forward
text:

title: NYT: ICE agent who fatally shot Biddeford man had record of anti-immigrant hostility
text:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who fatally shot a Colombian man in Biddeford in July had a history of anger toward immigrants, especially Colombians, according to an investigation by the New York Times published Wednesday.
Four years before David Brouillette fatally shot 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero four times in his car on July 13, the Times said he sent an email to his sister lashing out at the Colombian man with whom she was in a longtime relationship.
Brouillette called the man entitled and ignorant, and said his “bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”
The target of Brouillette’s rage was a graduate student studying for a Ph.D. in education at the time and was in the U.S. legally, according to the Times.
Brouillette’s sister and others interviewed by the Times described the email as a snapshot of an attitude toward people born outside the U.S. that he didn’t hide.
The same year that Brouillette sent the email, he became a volunteer firefighter in Manchester, Maine. The fire chief at the time told the New York Times he quickly realized he’d made a mistake, calling Brouillette “a loose cannon.”
The new reporting adds to a record of documented claims of abuse and mental health struggles that family members say worsened after he returned from serving in Afghanistan in 2013, and a severe injury in which he was struck in the head by a steel beam while in a firefighter training program at Southern Maine Community College, according to the Times.
Brouillette, 38, joined ICE during a hiring spree earlier this year as the agency escalated its immigration enforcement efforts into a sprawling wave of chaotic and often violent arrests around the country, ending, in several cases, with fatal shootings of U.S. citizens and documented immigrants.
When he got the job, his ex-wife told the New York Times she recalled asking him how he kept getting jobs with guns, and that “he laughed.”
On the morning of July 13, Brouillette was part of a group of agents that ICE said was conducting targeted surveillance on someone with a final removal order.
According to ICE, Durán Guerrero “attempted to flee” during an attempted traffic stop, and “fearing for public safety” an officer shot him.
The agency has not named Brouillette as the one who pulled the trigger, but his ex-wife identified him, saying he called her shortly after the shooting and asked her to “lie for him” and to “cover for his character,” describing him as “unusually calm.”
A Hallowell official told the Portland Press Herald after the shooting in July that Brouillette had “too many red flags” to be hired by the town’s police department in 2024. His mother told the New York Times in a text message that Brouillette “is dangerous and should not have weapons,” and to “believe his victims, not him.”
In a statement on Wednesday, Mary Erin Casale, a lawyer for Durán Guerrero’s widow, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, and his estate, framed the New York Times report as the latest indictment on ICE’s loose hiring practices.
“David Brouillette is the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training,” Casale said.
The Department of Homeland Security’s Inspector General and Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey have independently said they are investigating the shooting. A lawyer for the Durán Guerrero family told the New York Times that investigators recently told him that Frey plans to announce any decision in the case before his term of office ends in December.
ICE has booked more than 350,000 people this year and has roughly 65,000 detained currently, according to its own published data. ProPublica found that the agency has detained more than 500 U.S. citizens, many for filming or observing agents.
The agency claimed to be targeting the “worst of the worst,” but of the nearly 200 people detained in Maine during a January surge, only 11 had criminal convictions.

title: Maine’s family caregivers deserve support
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Bridget Quinn is the AARP Maine associate state director for advocacy and outreach.
November is National Family Caregivers Month, a time to recognize the people who quietly do extraordinary things every day for someone they love.
Across Maine, family caregivers help aging parents, spouses, friends and other loved ones live safely and independently at home. They prepare meals, provide transportation, manage medications, and take on countless other responsibilities. They do this not because it is their job, but because someone they love needs them.
In Maine, nearly three in 10 adults are family caregivers or have provided care within the past year. Together, that represents more than 300,000 people helping loved ones remain in their homes and communities, where they want to be.
These caregivers deserve our gratitude. They also deserve our support.
Caregiving can be deeply rewarding, but it can also take a toll that can include a physical emotional and even financial effect. Consider, for example, that according to the latest AARP “Valuing the Invaluable” report, caregiving has become more demanding and complex as chronic illnesses rise and more care shifts into homes. In fact, family caregivers are spending more time providing care, averaging 27 hours each week. More than half, 57%, now provide high-intensity care meaning they spend more hours helping with daily tasks like bathing and dressing as well as complex medical and nursing tasks like wound care and administering injections.
In addition, many family caregivers are balancing caregiving with full- or part-time jobs. Some are raising children at the same time. Others suddenly find themselves navigating complicated health care systems and making difficult decisions they never expected to face.
No one should have to navigate those challenges alone.
At AARP Maine, we are committed to being in the corner of family caregivers, both by fighting for policies that make their lives easier and by connecting them with practical resources they can use today.
That commitment is one reason AARP Maine advocated for paid family and medical leave. No caregiver should have to worry about being able to care for a loved one or keeping their job.
Maine’s Paid Family and Medical Leave program gives eligible workers access to paid, job-protected leave for circumstances including caring for a loved one with a serious health condition. It represents an important step toward helping Maine people balance the responsibilities of work and family without having to choose between caring for someone they love and protecting their own financial security.
But policy is only part of what caregivers need. Sometimes what matters most is knowing where to turn for help right now.
AARP Maine offers a free Maine Family Caregiver Resource Guide to help. Whether you are stepping into a caregiving role for the first time or have been providing care for years, the guide can connect you with information about caregiver support, transportation, respite care, legal and financial resources and other programs across Maine.
We have also partnered with 2-1-1 Maine to make finding local help easier. Caregivers can contact 2-1-1 and connect with trained specialists who can help identify resources available in their own communities.
Caregiving will touch nearly every Maine family at some point. As our state grows older, supporting the people who make it possible for loved ones to remain at home will only become more important.
This National Family Caregivers Month, let’s thank Maine’s caregivers and fight for commonsense solutions that offer meaningful support. If you are caring for someone you love, you are not alone. Learn about paid family and medical leave, download the Maine Family Caregiver Resource Guide, explore caregiving tools and find local assistance through 2-1-1 Maine at aarp.org/mecares.
We are all in this together.

title: Hermon football prepares to take on defending state champion Greely in Class C state semis
text:
Hermon football will travel to take on two-time defending state champion Greely in the Class C state semifinals on Friday night.
With a wire-to-wire 34-6 win over Nokomis on Nov. 6, the Hawks are now just one win away from a second state championship berth in three years. Last season’s Class C state champs, the Greely Rangers, stand in their way.
“We talk a lot to our players about not making any moment bigger than it is,” said Hermon head football coach Kyle Gallant. “We talk about winning each play and just living in the now. Regardless of who’s on the other side, it’s just another high-school football game in their eyes.”
Hermon will likely rely on its balanced rushing attack once again in Friday’s clash.
In last week’s win over Nokomis, the Hawks collected a total of 259 yards on the ground. Junior Griffin Dunton paced Hermon with 134 rushing yards and a touchdown. Senior Sam Hopkins added 81 yards and two rushing scores.
Gallant understands the challenges, however, of moving the ball in any facet against a stout Greely defense. The Rangers, who won the 2024 8-Player Large Division state title and the 2025 Class C state title, are allowing just 11.9 points per game this season.
“We’re definitely a little run heavy compared to our passing game, but the main thing we have to do is control the time of possession,” Gallant said. “We have to keep being good at what we know we’re good at, keep the football moving, and stay on the field as long as possible to keep their offense off the field.”
Over the last five seasons, Gallant has overseen the most successful period of Hermon football since the program began in 2011. The Hawks reached the Class C state championship in 2024 and are set to appear in their fourth state semifinal since 2021.
A win Friday night against Greely would represent the program taking an even further step.
“The belief this team has in what it can do has grown exponentially since Week 1, even since Week 7 or 8,” Gallant said. “We’ve found our identity these past few weeks, and it’s led to us playing out best football of the season right now. And that’s what it’s going to take.”
Hermon will travel to Greely for the Class C football state semifinal on Friday, Nov. 13. The game is slated for a 7 p.m. kickoff.

title: Russian ambassador to the US dies 'suddenly' in Moscow
text:
Russian ambassador to US dies 'suddenly,' foreign ministry says
Russia’s ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, died in Moscow aged 66, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
Darchiev “passed away suddenly,” the ministry said in a statement, describing him as an “exceptional professional.” He had been struggling with a chronic illness, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova.
“Alexander Darchiev served in one of the most demanding areas of Russian foreign policy,” the ministry’s statement added. “We extend our deepest and most heartfelt condolences to Alexander Darchiev’s family and loved ones.”
The Russian ambassador had left the embassy in Washington, DC before returning to Moscow, where he was receiving treatment for a long-term illness, a source familiar with the matter told CNN.
Darchiev, a veteran diplomat known for his stinging condemnations of the West, had served as ambassador to Washington since March 2025. His time in office was marked by a thawing of US-Russia relations as President Donald Trump opened bilateral talks with Moscow and scaled back aid to Ukraine.
A U.S. State Department spokesperson told CNN they were aware of Darchiev’s death and offered condolences to his family and loved ones.
Darchiev previously headed the Russian Foreign Ministry’s North Atlantic Department in Washington, according to the Russian embassy in the U.S., as well as serving as Russia’s ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2021.
Nearly a decade ago, another Russian diplomat died suddenly aged 64. Vitaly Churkin, an ambassador to the UN, passed away following cardiac arrest in 2017, just one day before his 65th birthday.
The average life expectancy for a man in Russia is 68 years old, according to the World Bank.

title: High school football parent caught on camera pooping in rival school’s hallway, police say
text:
GROSSE POINTE FARMS, Mich. (WWJ) - Police in Michigan say the father of a high school student was caught on camera defecating in the hallway at a rival school during a district championship football game.
Officials with Grosse Pointe Public Schools say the father of a Bedford High School student entered Grosse Pointe South High School without permission Friday night during a football game between the two schools and took a bowel movement in the middle of a hallway.
“It seems very immature for a parent to act that way,” resident Christina Dzul said.
Officers with Grosse Pointe Farms Police are investigating the incident, which was caught on camera. They say the father got into the school through a door that had been left open for a scheduled band concert.
Police say the school’s security footage shows the man walk past multiple bathrooms before allegedly defecating on the hallway floor.
Police used the video to identify the father. During the investigation, he reportedly said he had experienced a medical emergency. However, police say they are still looking into the incident.
“This behavior is wholly unacceptable and is inconsistent with the standards of conduct and respect that the District expects of anyone entering its school facilities. The District has filed a police report regarding this incident and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate,” said Grosse Pointe Public Schools in a statement released Monday.
Bedford Public Schools Superintendent Carl Shultz also released a statement that said, “At Bedford Public Schools, we hold our students, staff, and community to high standards of safety, respect, and sportsmanship, both on and off the field. We are fully cooperating with the host district and local law enforcement.”
One resident named Andrew says he isn’t surprised by the incident, given the current state of youth sports.
“Honestly, these days with youth sports and parents and the way people get into their feelings, nothing surprises me,” he said. “People are animals.”
Grosse Pointe South beat Bedford 42-0 in Friday night’s football game.

title: Two heroes, two wars: Patten community center to honor local fallen servicemen
text:
PATTEN, Maine (WABI) - This Veterans Day, the town of Patten is celebrating an incoming addition dedicated to two hometown heroes.
A planned community center and library will bear the names of two Patten servicemen killed in action nearly four decades apart.
The Dickinson-Harris Community Center will honor Leslie “Dickie” Dickinson, who was 23 when he died in Vietnam in 1968, and Dustin Harris, who was 21 when he died in Iraq in 2006.
Patten’s previous community center and library closed in 2020, leaving residents without a gathering place and forcing the library to move into the kitchen of the Lumbermen’s Museum.
“The select board said ‘The town does not have the money to put in a new building, but if you feel you can do that, as we had seen some libraries in our region do, then feel free.’ So, that’s how our friends group started. We formed a non-profit,” said Rae Bates, chair of the Friends of the Veterans’ Memorial Library and Community Center.
Bates said the project is $220,000 shy of reaching its $5.7 million fundraising goal.
But before breaking ground in the spring, the group had to think of a name.
“We thought we would do best going through records of residents of Patten who have fought for their country and died for their country, that we would do well to recognize someone from the Vietnam War and somebody from the wars that have been taking place in the Middle East,” Bate explained. “That led us, obviously, to Dickie Dickinson and Dustin Harris.”
Lorna Harris, Dustin’s mother, described her late son as “your everyday kid,” who loved playing Army as a child and read every children’s book at the Veterans’ Memorial Library.
It was the 9/11 terrorist attacks that inspired Harris to enlist, which he did after attending community college a few years later.
“He loved it,” Harris said of her son’s service. “He loved to jump out of a perfectly good airplane. He was the lead gunner in the turret position for over 60 of the most dangerous missions.”
Frank Rogers, president of the Lumbermen’s Museum, grew up with Dickinson in Shin Pond. Dickinson left Colby College to enlist in the Marine Corps.
Known as a poet and a “smart as a whip” academic, Dickinson wanted to join the service to gain experience to supplement his writing, Rogers said, “à la Ernest Hemingway.”
“The entire town mourned,” Roger recalled of Dickinson’s death. “And I almost think half of Colby College was here for his memorial.”
As Bates explained, the dedication honors the ultimate sacrifice of two young men across generations.
“We look at the distance that we’ve come as a country from Vietnam, where service members were not recognized in the same fashion that they are today. Thankfully, that whole tenor of the country has changed,” Bates said.
For Harris and Rogers, it reflects the tight-knit community’s commitment to honoring veterans and keeping their memories alive.
“Since day one, this community has helped hold us up. And obviously the community will still continue to honor and remember both Dustin and Dickie,” described Harris. “It’s said you die twice, once when your heart stops beating, and a second time when your name is said for the very last time. So these men will be remembered.”
Bates credited a $3.9 million grant from Sen. Susan Collins’ office, as well as $606,000 from the Northern Border Regional Commission, for helping fund the project. The rest of the money has been raised through a combination of smaller grants and private donations.
To learn more or contribute, visit the Friends’ of the Veterans’ Memorial Library and Community Center’s website.

title: Clinton Fire Rescue mourns unexpected loss of firefighter-EMT
text:
CLINTON, Maine (WABI) - Clinton Fire Rescue and the Clinton Professional Firefighters Association are dealing with a devastating and unexpected loss Wednesday. Clinton Fire Rescue announced the death of one of its members Tuesday night. On Wednesday afternoon, they identified the firefighter-EMT as Becky Stuart.
Fire Chief Rick Barton asked the community to keep Stuart’s family, friends and fellow firefighters in their thoughts.
West Forks Volunteer Fire and Rescue confirmed on Facebook that Stuart was also a member of its department.
Barton’s statement included contact information for crisis support. It did not specify a cause of death.
Jason Mills, co-owner of Resilient Responder Wellness Center, works with first responders across Maine. He said caring for their mental health is an important part of the job.
“We try to normalize that mental health, it’s part of occupational readiness,” Mills said. “Like you would do training to stay proficient in your skills in EMS, or like you would train to stay physically fit, taking care of ourselves mentally is an occupational requirement.”
“We’re trying to really drive home that point of you’re one of the people that are worth taking care of, and you’re one of the people that people want to help,” he said.
Wally Fraser, co-founder of the Toned Out Project, said support is available for first responders, including options out of state.
“There are lots of treatment programs throughout the country that are designed specifically for first responders. And when you go to treatment, you are there with first responders, you’re not there with people that you just transported to the hospital or were working with in some capacity,” Fraser said.
Procession planned
Clinton Fire Rescue is organizing a procession Thursday from Veilleux Funeral Home in Waterville to the medical examiner’s office in Augusta.
The department said interested friends, family members, and fire and rescue units can line Route 201 between Winslow and Augusta to pay their respects. The procession begins at 9:45 a.m.
If you or a loved one needs support, call or text 988 to reach the Maine Crisis Line 24/7.

title: High-speed chase from Bowdoinham to Augusta ends with a drug bust
text:
An Auburn man was arrested early Monday with over three pounds of cocaine after fleeing police in a high-speed chase that spanned from Bowdoinham to Augusta on Interstate 295.
Lawz Lepenn, 44, was charged with aggravated trafficking of scheduled drugs and eluding a police officer after fleeing his vehicle on foot into the woods. He was apprehended near Augusta State Airport, according to a news release from the Sagadahoc County Sheriff’s Office.
Shortly after midnight, a police officer pulled Lepenn over for speeding after he was driving 90 mph on I-295 northbound in Bowdoinham near Exit 37. When the officer realized Lepenn was on probation for aggravated drug trafficking, he requested backup.
Lepenn sped off in his vehicle after officers asked him to step outside, resulting in a high-speed pursuit where speeds reached 120 mph.
Maine State Police troopers set up spike strips near Exit 109 in Augusta, which Lepenn drove over and continued to drive for a mile until the car was disabled.
After Lepenn fled his car, he discarded a sports bag containing 3 pounds of cocaine onto the highway, before running into the woods. Officers from the Maine State Police, Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office and the Augusta Police Department set up a perimeter and Maine State Police used a drone to locate Lepenn near the airport.
Lepenn was transported to Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset, where he is being held without bail on a probation violation. He is scheduled to be arraigned Thursday.

title: Susan Collins was not owed our votes
text:
Jody Telfair of Bristol has a Ph.D. in clinical counseling and has spent 45 years in private practice.
Sen. Susan Collins has served in the U.S. Senate for 30 years. When her constituents voted her out of office last week, one would expect her to give a gracious speech thanking Mainers for giving her the opportunity to serve them for 30 years. Instead, she gave an angry interview with the New York Times berating those constituents for being too angry.
So it’s all right for her to be angry at us, but we have no right to be angry at her?
Sen. Collins is showing her true colors in defeat. I witnessed a shocking level of control and entitlement back in the early 2000s when myself and three friends scheduled an appointment to meet with her. We were told by a staff person that we could only speak with her about two issues and asked to express no emotion.
Susan Collins does not engage with constituents except under very controlled circumstances. She has not held a town hall for at least 25 years. She seems to feel that she was entitled to reelection because she works hard and had brought money and various projects to Maine. But that is what she was elected to do.
Engaging with the people of Maine and listening to their concerns and issues, even when she disagrees, is also part of her job, and Collins failed at that aspect of serving the people of Maine.
Even though I am angry at Collins, I abhor attacks and threats on her or any other elected official. I voted for Troy Jackson, not because I am angry with Collins, but because his policies and values, such as universal healthcare, ending the war in Iran, standing up to Donald Trump and working to bring down prices for working people align with my own.
In her interview with the New York Times, Collins sounds like she feels betrayed. Well, many of us Mainers have felt betrayed by her for years — her vote for Brett Kavanaugh (and others) and taking no responsibility for the overturn of Roe v. Wade; the way she has fallen in line with Trump; voting to cut Medicaid and health subsidies in the so-called “big, beautiful bill” while giving huge tax benefits to the wealthy; voting for Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to lead the Department of Health and Human Services; Kristi Noem to head the Department of Homeland Security and Pam Bondi as attorney general.
And she has voted to support the war in Iran. In the debates with Jackson, Collins was unable to point out a single time she voted against Trump when her vote mattered. Finally, I was appalled at the elitist comment from one of her leading supporters, Bill Green, calling Jackson a “bumpkin.”
Sen. Collins seems to have forgotten in her 30-year run as a senator that she serves the
people of Maine at our pleasure. We owe her respect, but not our vote.

title: Houlton Honors Those Who Served
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WAGM) - Across the nation cities are honoring veterans and it’s no different here in Aroostook County. One ceremony took place in Houlton today at Monument Park.
Several veterans spoke during the Veterans Day ceremony in Houlton. Before the ceremony began, they shared why it’s important to celebrate Veteran’s Day and what the day means to them.
Joe Michaud, Commander of the American Legion Dept. of Maine said: “This is Veterans Day. This honors all veterans past and present. So, anybody that’s in the military right now is considered a veteran and we’re honoring them for their service. We put our lives on the line when we signed our name on the line. You basically sign a blank check that says up to and including death and a lot of us did not make it bac but today we’re celebrating the ones who did make it back.”
Some veterans shared their personal connections to the day. Charles Clark Sr., Post Commander of American Legion Chester L. Briggs Post#47 added: “Veterans Day is important to me because back in WWI it ended the first great war and serving alongside brothers and sisters this day is our day. Memorial Day is for the day that’s departed that can no longer be with us.”
Speakers said they’d like to remind locals that it’s important to check in on veterans during Veterans Day. Fred Anderson, District Commander of American Legion District#16 said: “For me as a veteran it brings up a lot of PTSD stuff. So, we lose 23 veterans a day from suicide. So, we kind of reach out to our fellow veterans. We have to remember what people sacrificed and what’s still going on today. I have a grandson that’s in the army. He’s getting ready to get deployed to Kuwait.”
Speakers also had a message to give to veterans. “To all of our veterans that have served and are serving in the United States and abroad. I hope everybody that’s serving knows exactly what this day means. I thank you for giving us the freedom that we have of choice, liberty, and justice,” continued Clark Sr.
For veterans in Houlton, today was a chance to remember the people they served alongside and remind them they’re not alone.

title: Patten to name new community center for two hometown heroes
text:
A new community center in the Penobscot County town of Patten will recognize two hometown members of the armed services who died in action.
The Friends of the Veterans’ Memorial Library and Community Center announced that the building’s entrance will bear the names of Second Lt. Leslie A. Dickinson Jr. and Army Specialist Dustin J. Harris.
Both men died in wars nearly four decades apart. Dickinson was 23 when he died of his wounds in Vietnam, while Harris was 21 when he was killed in Iraq.
“The freedoms we celebrate didn’t come without sacrifice, and there isn’t a community in this country that hasn’t known both the pride and the loss that come with sending its own to defend them. Patten is no exception,” said Rae Bates, chair of the board of the Friends of the Veterans’ Memorial Library and Community Center. “It feels right to welcome people into the region’s largest gathering space — a place for meetings, discussions and education — through doors that will carry their names.”
Funds for the project were raised through donors, organizations, foundations and others. The organization has raised 95% of the funds needed, but is still accepting donations.
Work on the 8,400-square-foot library and community center, designed by Bangor-based Haley Ward, is expected to start in spring 2027.
About the veterans
Dickinson, known to his family as Dickie, was a student at Colby College when he enlisted in the Marine Corps in June 1967. Six months later, he was in Vietnam, leading the 2nd Platoon, Company G, 2nd Battalion. He was critically wounded on Jan. 30, 1968, and died four days later, just after turning 23. He is remembered as a poet and academic. His parents, Leslie Sr. (Dick) and Dorothy (Dot), ran the Patten Drug Store for more than three decades and served the town through its church, schools and civic groups.
“Though I never had the chance to know my uncle, I grew up knowing his love of learning and his deep commitment to service and sacrifice,” said Maria Cabaniss, a niece of Dickinson’s. “It means so much to see his memory honored in Patten through a library and community center that serves the community and carries those values forward.”
Harris had a knack for fixing things and studied diesel mechanics at Eastern Maine Community College. He enlisted in the Army in 2004, training as a paratrooper at Fort Benning, Ga. He was deployed to Mosul, Iraq, in August 2005. On April 6, 2006, a month before turning 22, he was killed by an improvised explosive device while serving as lead gunner on a combat logistics patrol. He is survived by his parents, Scott and Lorna Harris, his brother, Dylan, and many family members and friends.
“His commitment to go a little further, endure a little longer, and look closer to see how to add effort were the basic building blocks of his noble service,” said Col. William Keyes, U.S. Army (Ret.).

title: Veterans Day in Wiscasset brings memories and honoring
text:
Dresden's Bill Pelkey recalled, after his service during the Vietnam War era, it was hard to follow the orders he and others were given to "behave ourselves" at the rude reception they got "at every airport we hit" on the way home.
"The coming home wasn't like it is today to welcome the troops. The protesters I see (these days), I grin, well you're the grandchildren of the idiots that welcomed us home." The Native American community, however, did welcome them home back then and at powwows still does welcome and honor the veterans, the Air Force veteran who went on to join the Army National Guard told Wiscasset Newspaper near the veterans wall in Wiscasset Nov. 11, Veterans Day.
American Legion Post 54's morning observance on the town lawn was full of welcoming by all, for all, among the Post and Auxiiliary members and other area residents.
Before and after the ceremony were lots of handshakes and thanking veterans for their service; some hugs, many smiles and the occasional peep of a horn from a passing vehicle on Route One. The ceremony had as always the pledge of allegiance, a gun salute, laying of wreaths and Woolwich's Tom Stoner's playing of "Taps." Less usual for an observance at the wall was the sun. The clouds overtook it by ceremony's end.
"I took my jacket off because it was warm (out). Now I'm gonna go put it back on," Auxiliary President Diane Munsey said.
Post Cmdr. William Cossette Jr. said he would have liked a bigger turnout. In the ceremony, he told attendees it is sad more employers don't close for Veterans Day.
After the ceremony, Burnt Orange Bagels co-owner Steve Smith was asking Legion members if he could treat them to bagels soon by delivering some to the Post hall.

title: Skowhegan man who set 2022 fire resentenced for attempted murder, arson
text:
SKOWHEGAN — A 67-year-old Skowhegan man is set to serve one fewer year behind bars per a new sentence handed down Tuesday, four years after he admitted to attempting to set his apartment on fire to kill himself, his wife and neighbors.
Neil T. MacLean’s new sentence for the convictions of attempted murder and arson amounts to 24 years in prison, with all but 14 years suspended, and four years of probation.
Chief Judge Brent A. Davis handed down the sentence during a hearing at the Skowhegan District Court.
Davis, who did not oversee MacLean’s 2024 trial that resulted in guilty verdicts, was tasked with conducting a new sentencing analysis, as the Maine Supreme Judicial Court had thrown out MacLean’s original sentence in August.
Former District Court Judge Andrew Benson had sentenced MacLean to 25 years, with all but 15 years suspended, and four years of probation, on the Class A attempted murder charge. Benson, who has since resigned from the bench to become Maine’s top federal prosecutor, also sentenced MacLean to 15 concurrent years in prison on each of two Class A arson counts.
The law court, which affirmed MacLean’s convictions, ruled that Benson should have merged all three counts for the purposes of sentencing. Prosecutors and MacLean’s appellate attorney agreed that was the proper legal conclusion.
The high court decision instructed Davis to conduct one sentencing analysis on all of the charges together, rather than an individual analysis on each count. Davis called the merging of counts a “tricky, complicated issue.”
At Tuesday’s hearing, Deputy District Attorney Frank Griffin asked Davis to reimpose the original sentence of 25 years in prison, with all but 15 suspended, and four years of probation.
MacLean’s court-appointed attorney, Andrew Dawson of the Capital Region Public Defenders’ office, argued for a sentence of 12 years in prison, with all but 49 months suspended, and four years of probation.
In effect, that would be a “time served” sentence, Dawson said. Arrested shortly after the 2022 fire, MacLean has already been in custody for about four years; he spent part of that time pre-trial at the state-run Dorothea Dix Psychiatric Center in Bangor.
Police and firefighters responded to the fire at 36 High St. in the early morning hours of Oct. 30, 2022. MacLean’s wife had been woken up by smoke and called 911.
Investigators later learned MacLean had been drinking alcohol that night and lit a match in a separate bedroom, attempting to set the bed and other items on fire. Firefighters had to carry him out as he refused to leave the building.
Nobody was injured, although responding police officers were treated for smoke inhalation. Firefighters extinguished the fire, contained to the bedroom, in about a half hour.
A few hours after the fire, MacLean told an Office of State Fire Marshal investigator that he set the fire to kill himself, his wife and the other residents of the apartment building.
The crimes MacLean committed were “very serious,” Davis said.
“Mr. MacLean, we are so fortunate here today that nobody was injured — seriously injured,” Davis said. “The facts of this case, in the court’s mind, are simply horrific. But for the fact that your wife was able to get up, and was able to call 911, this would have been a completely different case.”
The judge said he also considered MacLean’s criminal history, which includes several domestic violence convictions involving his wife.
On the other hand, Davis noted MacLean’s genuine remorse, military service, older age and support from family members, including his wife and daughters, were all relevant mitigating factors. He also acknowledged MacLean’s long-term struggles with post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety and short-term memory loss.
MacLean appeared to be a good candidate for probation, Davis said, imposing conditions that MacLean not use or possess alcohol or illegal drugs and participate in substance abuse and mental health counseling.
MacLean, who has grown a long, grey beard since he was last in court in Skowhegan, spoke briefly Tuesday to tell Davis that when he set the fire, he was not in a mental state to understand he was putting others in danger.
“I want to apologize for putting other people in harm’s way,” he said.
Before his trial, MacLean turned down a final plea agreement offer from prosecutors that would have dismissed the attempted murder charge and come with a sentence of nine years in prison, with all but six years suspended, and four years of probation.
MacLean has been serving his sentence at the Maine State Prison in Warren.

title: Democrat Scott Colom wins election to US Senate from Mississippi
text:
Democrat Scott Colom won election to the U.S. Senate representing Mississippi, defeating Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday. Colom will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era.
Gearing up for the loss of GOP control in Congress next year, the White House warned Democrats that planned investigations of Trump could cross into criminal conduct. House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office, though Trump and his administration have long denied any wrongdoing.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, observed Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery. His appearance there came a day after nine Kennedy family members asked a judge to block Trump’s plan to build a towering memorial arch, saying the 250-foot structure would cast a shadow over their relatives’ grave sites at the cemetery.

title: South Portland native returns to Maine with national tour of ‘Hadestown’
text:
Arman Wali has always wanted to do a big performance in his home state of Maine. Now, as the touring music director for the Tony and Grammy-winning Broadway musical “Hadestown,” Wali, a Pakistani American who grew up in South Portland, gets to make that dream a reality.
Unlike more traditional musicals, “Hadestown,” a steampunk reimagining of the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, contains no breaks in the music (save for intermission) nor an orchestra pit that hides the band. Instead, Wali and the rest of the production’s band are onstage and in direct view of the audience for the entire show.
“You have to be locked in the entire time,” said Wali.
As music director, Wali has many responsibilities on and off the stage to keep the show’s music running smoothly. For example, in addition to playing both piano and accordion in the show, Wali also conducts the performers and the seven-person band, alongside cueing the stage manager to trigger lights and sound effects.
Wali began taking piano lessons when he was around 5 years old. As a teenager, Wali became more familiar with musical theater and began playing keys for local productions at the Lyric Music Theater as well as at Stages: The Performing Arts Academy for Kids (now Stages Youth Theater).
Wali went to Boston College to study biochemistry while continuing to study classical music on the side. After a few years of working a lab job and doing music gigs, Wali decided to pursue graduate school, applying to a variety of fields and universities, in addition to Berklee College of Music. When the latter gave him a scholarship, Wali decided to take the opportunity.
Following his graduation from Berklee last December, Wali began as “Hadestown” touring music director in January.
Wali said his scientific background continues to come in handy, especially when managing the musical’s layered score and its many moving pieces.
Despite the challenges that come with a touring production, including hectic travel days and performing in theaters of varying conditions, Wali said he enjoys being able to visit cities across the U.S. and Canada. The tour will continue until at least the end of June, visiting cities such as San Francisco, Seattle, Dallas and Chicago as well as dozens of other locations.
During his visit to Portland, Wali expects to meet up with old friends as well as his dad.
“I’m excited to be back,” said Wali.
“Broadway National Tour: Hadestown,” presented by Portland Ovations, 7 p.m., Nov. 17-19, Merrill Auditorium, 20 Myrtle St., Portland. Tickets $65-$165, 150 minutes with one intermission. For more, call 207-842-0800 or go to porttix.com.
