title: Garage destroyed in Blue Hill fire, according to officials
text:
Garage destroyed in Blue Hill fire, according to officials
Several fire departments responded to a fire on Ellsworth Road and the building on fire was a total loss, no injuries were reported
Garage destroyed in Blue Hill fire, according to officials
Several fire departments responded to a fire on Ellsworth Road and the building on fire was a total loss, no injuries were reported
A garage was destroyed in a fire in Blue Hill, with several neighboring fire departments responding to help prevent flames from spreading to nearby structures.
Blue Hill Fire responded to 464 Ellsworth Road to a single-family property with two garage outbuildings, one of which was on fire.
Three campers parked nearby were also threatened by the fire, according to Blue Hill Fire.
Departments from Brooklin, Brooksville, Penobscot, Sedgewick, Surry and Orland responded, along with Peninsula Ambulance.
The fire chief said the garage is a total loss, and the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office is expected to investigate the fire on Thursday. The cause has not been determined.

title: Immigration arrests go on steadily despite Trump's misgivings after the midterms
text:
Immigration arrests go on steadily despite Trump's misgivings after the midterms
President Donald Trump's deportation offensive is continuing unabated, despite the widespread Republican defeats in the midterm elections.
Video above: Surveillance video shows ICE agents arrest Wisconsin state trooper at airport
In Los Angeles, masked immigration officers in body armor blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a heavily Latino neighborhood early Saturday. In central Alabama, twin 19-year-old brothers from Venezuela were arrested while driving back to college a day after the election.
Advocates reported arrests from California to Michigan to Massachusetts. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has not released numbers.
After Democrats trounced the GOP and won control of the next Congress, Trump said his immigration crackdown may have been “too tough” and suggested it was time to sit down with the rival party.
“I’d love to do something on immigration,” he said in an interview with CBS' “60 Minutes” recorded Friday.
Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said his orders had not changed.
“Deportations will continue,” Mullin wrote in an online post the day after the election, warning that ICE takes no days off and that “this includes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Election Day.”
María Bilbao, a campaign coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee in Miami, said she has received at least one call a day from someone detained in South Florida since the election.
“Everything remains exactly the same. The arrests have not ceased at all,” Bilbao said.
Florida Highway Patrol officers and ICE agents have detained people in their cars, as well as places including supermarkets, pharmacies and gas stations. Immigrants under supervision have also been arrested when they showed up at ICE's Miami office for their appointments.
Officers assembled outside a Los Angeles hospital
Erick Gasca, 31, got home Friday night after an evening playing board games with friends. He lives near Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles.
An “unprecedented” number of vehicles with tinted windows and no license plates were parked near the hospital's emergency room entrance, he said.
“I thought they were going to raid the hospital or something,” he recalled.
The Department of Homeland Security declined to explain the officers’ presence there, though Bill Essayli, the top Justice Department prosecutor in Los Angeles, said they were bringing a detainee for medical treatment. Essayli said two people were arrested for assaulting federal agents.
“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” DHS said in a statement.
The agents' presence attracted some 30 residents and passersby. Footage shot by Gasca’s cousin, Michelle Rivera, shows protesters shouting and officers pinning someone down.
The hospital said it wasn't involved.
“White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement,” hospital president Daniel Fontoura said in a statement, adding it would not let such activities “compromise our commitment to patient care and safety.”
A couple is arrested at the Phoenix airport
A married couple from Orlando, Florida, was arrested Saturday at the airport in Phoenix while traveling to a funeral.
Gustavo Romanello and Agustin Baccega, both from Argentina, have work permits while they seek asylum after entering the United States about six years ago, according to Jonathan Batchelor, a family friend.
Batchelor was on the phone with them at the time. A mutual friend died Friday and the couple was visiting for the funeral Saturday. As the couple left the airport, two casually dressed officers asked if one was Agustin Baccega. Batchelor heard the officer say, “Asylum seekers are not in the United States legally.”
Batchelor said he could hear Romanello walking alongside his husband during the arrest and asking the officers how to collect his things. Batchelor said they then asked what his name was, “and then the guard said, ‘Oh, do you have another set of handcuffs? This is another one.’”
The voices grew distant, and the call then ended.
Both men remain in detention centers. They worked as acrobats in Florida and had no criminal record, Batchelor said.
“This is just taking good people who have been following the rules out of their lives and out of the lives of those who rely upon them and care about them,” Batchelor said.
DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the arrests.
Twin brothers seized while driving back to college
The brothers were headed back to college after visiting their parents when they were stopped in a small city in central Alabama.
Luis and Carlos Orta-Santoro, 19-year-olds born in Venezuela and living in the U.S. for four years, are soccer players at Wallace State Community College in Hanceville, Alabama.
Relatives say they have pending asylum applications, valid work permits, and no criminal records. Both are now in an immigration detention facility.
“Our family is devastated,” said their aunt, Carolina Orta.
DHS said that while they had entered the country legally, they had “overstayed in defiance of our laws,” and their case would be heard by an immigration judge. It said pending asylum applications do not confer legal status in the U.S.
The school said in a statement, “Both young men are valued members of the Wallace State community, and our thoughts are with them during this difficult time. We sincerely hope for a positive resolution to their situation.”
A Haitian boy is taken into custody, drawing protests in San Diego
An 8-year-old Haitian boy had been living with his uncle in San Diego since his father was deported last year. The uncle, who is not a legal guardian, took him to an ICE office when the boy was summoned Nov. 4 and taken into custody.
That left the boy “without the support of their family, community and their school,” according to a letter to top administration officials from San Diego Unified School District Superintendent Fabi Bagula and school board members.
“Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” they wrote.
ICE has defended its actions.
Johny Oxeda, pastor of the Fairmount Haitian Community Church, which helped get legal representation for the boy, said he’ll ultimately benefit by going through legal channels.
Activists, though, were furious.
“This is not child protection,” said Guerline Jozef of Haitian Bridge Alliance, adding, “this is state-inflicted trauma.”

title: Ring camera with propellers: Amazon announces $250 home security drone
text:
Ring camera with propellers: Amazon announces $250 home security drone
Amazon’s Ring, known for its doorbell cameras, is branching into more at-home surveillance technology — now in the form of a drone that flies around your house.
Video above: Savannah police officer gave ICE agent husband access to Flock system
The company’s new indoor Ring Drone, listed at $250 and set to launch in late January, can fly custom, pre-set routes around your home or business, Ring said. The flights can be scheduled, or users can prompt them at any time.
“When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, Ring Drone automatically flies to previously set patrol points to investigate,” the product announcement said.
Ring describes the drone as “built from the ground up with AI at its core,” saying it can "see, think, and navigate autonomously." The company says the AI system creates a map of your house that lets the drone navigate when it’s deployed.
When powered off and docked, the drone has its camera off, Ring said. Lights tell the user when the device is recording, and the drone's propellers intentionally “aren’t quiet,” which the company says acts as a deterrent.
The company also launched the $999 rolling Rover Cam, geared toward businesses. The rover, which has a periscoping camera, streams video whenever it is moving and can “alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view,” the company said. The patrolling device allows users to activate a light tower and sirens or use two-way audio to communicate. It’s billed as “like having a guard on patrol who never clocks out.”
Both require a subscription to a Ring Protect plan, which costs $5 per month or $60 annually, Ring told NBC News.
Ring has faced criticism in the past over privacy-violation concerns. A Ring ad during last year’s Super Bowl showed how the Ring network could be used to find lost dogs — but some found the idea of using AI to scan video footage from cameras around a neighborhood worrying.
After facing backlash, Ring announced it was canceling its planned partnership with the much-beleaguered Flock Safety, a firm that operates a network of license plate readers and cameras that has been caught up in misuse scandals as stories broke of police officers using the cameras to stalk ex-partners. Ring and Flock’s agreement would have allowed agencies working with Flock to retrieve video captured on Ring devices for their investigations if allowed by customers.
Ring says video from both new devices will be handled using Ring’s “Throw Away the Key encryption,” which it calls its “strongest default encryption yet.” Ring says it is “inspired” by end-to-end encryption, generally considered a strong standard for privacy. But the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital rights advocacy group, says Ring's system is “still not even close to the privacy protections of end-to-end encryption.”
The drone is advertised as an indoor camera, and it should not be used to fly outside, per Federal Aviation Administration regulations.
For his part, Ring founder and inventor Jamie Siminoff described Ring's new robotics as "the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.”

title: Gardens Aglow 2026 opens Nov. 14
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Saturday, Nov. 14, Maine’s popular light show, Gardens Aglow, returns to Boothbay. Described by the TODAY show as one of their “unexpected destinations that are sure to get your family in the holiday spirit,” Boothbay Lights and Maine Gardens' signature light show, Gardens Aglow, light up the peninsula for six weeks through Jan. 2, 2027.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens invites guests to “Gather, Glow, and Celebrate” with this year’s “Gathered in Maine” theme. New lighted elements feature a maple tapping scene, a landscape fit for mushroom foraging, and a larger-than-life anthill with an army of ants carrying leaves and berries. Completely new every year, the in-house design and hand-strung display keep Maine Gardens' seasonal staff employed into the new year and provide vital funds for the nonprofit's mission work.
“Our team has been working hard since August on this year’s show. I say this every year, but this year might be the best,” states Gretchen Ostherr, president and CEO of Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens. “Even though I get to watch—and take part in the light hanging—I am always amazed at how we transform from a green sanctuary into a sparkling wonderland. We can’t wait to celebrate this season with families from Maine and New England.”
For the last handful of years, Maine Gardens have been nominated in the Best Botanical Garden Holiday Lights category, as part of USA TODAY 10BEST’s Readers’ Choice Awards. After landing in the top five in recent years, Maine Gardens hopes to bring the top spot to Maine this year. Event organizers hope that Gardens Aglow fans will show their Maine pride by voting daily to help Gardens Aglow bring the title home.
With price-conscious guests in mind, this year there will be three pricing tiers: Value on weekdays, Standard on Fridays and Sundays, and Premium on Saturdays, allowing guests to pick the night and price that work for them. An additional VIP add-on pass unlocks special Gardens Aglow gifts, free unlimited ticket exchanges, flexible arrival times on your selected date, and a cozy fire pit experience.
Ticket prices start at $20 for adults, $18 for seniors and veterans, and $10 for children ages 3-17. Children under the age of 3 are free. Members save 20% on all Gardens Aglow admission tickets. VIP add-on passes are $50 per ticket and are not subject to any discounts. For more information on pricing and time slots, visit GardensAglow.org.
Extend your stay and enjoy all that the region offers with Boothbay Lights. A convenient complimentary Park and Ride shuttle runs Friday, Saturday, and Sunday from Boothbay Harbor Town Office, allowing guests to experience Boothbay Harbor's shopping, dining, and lodging delights before and after the light show. For a complete calendar of regional offerings, the robust slate of Boothbay Lights events, and Park and Ride details, visit www.boothbaylights.com.
About Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens
At 325 acres, Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens is the largest public garden in New England. With two miles of hiking trails, 19 acres of ornamental and themed gardens featuring native plants of Maine and those suited to northern coastal conditions, nearly a mile of saltwater frontage, a children’s garden, a sensory garden, and so much more, there’s something for everyone. A true Maine experience, the Gardens is committed to connecting people to nature, preserving the biodiversity of the Maine coast, and continuing to be a place accessible and welcoming to all. The mission of Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens is to inspire meaningful connections between people and nature and promote plant conservation through horticulture, education, and plant science.

title: New book from Herb Sargent details practical solutions to business challenges
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The chair of Orono-based Sargent Corp. has co-written a book sharing lessons on leadership, financial discipline, culture and sustainable growth — lessons learned from decades of running his family’s heavy civil construction company.
“Field Tested: Lessons in Leading, Losing and Winning in Construction,” was co-written by Herb Sargent with Scott Peper, CEO of Mobilization Funding. The book grew out of conversations the two had while Peper was founding his financial lending platform, which works with construction subcontractors, manufacturers and small business owners.
The book addresses management structure, customer selection, financial infrastructure, pricing, partnerships, company culture, hiring and retention, negotiation, innovation and succession planning.
Each chapter is designed to give readers practical ideas they can apply within their own organizations. And while the book’s lessons are drawn largely from the construction industry, they’re also intended for business leaders managing growth, developing teams or preparing for leadership transitions.
The book’s jacket notes that “Field Tested” isn’t about construction, but about “building something that lasts.”
“A lot of the most useful lessons in business come from experience, especially the decisions you would make differently if you had the chance,” said Sargent. “We wanted to share those experiences so other business owners can recognize problems sooner, ask better questions and make stronger decisions.”
About the company
Sargent is the board chair of Sargent Corp., an ESOP now led by President and CEO Eric Ritchie.
Sargent Corp. is Maine’s third-largest construction company, according to the 2026 Mainebiz Book of Lists, based on 2024 revenue of $252.9 million.
Sargent Corp. focuses on infrastructure projects, including renewable energy, highways, airport runways and underground utilities in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic region.
“Field Tested” is available from Amazon, in paperback and e-book formats.

title: Maine author’s new children’s book embraces Christmas – and crankiness
text:
Months after the publication of his memoir, “Sigh, Gone,” Phuc Tran was contacted by the agent of kidlit author and illustrator Pete Oswald, asking if he’d consider writing picture books. “I just thought, that is a big jump — for someone who’s read my memoir to think, ‘Oh, this guy should write for kids,’” says Tran. “But I thought, sure, why not? I’m here for the adventure.”
Six years later, Tran is the author of four children’s books featuring Cranky the crane truck, most recently “A Very Cranky Christmas.” He spoke with the Portland Press Herald about normalizing crankiness, writing for both children and adults and how he really feels about Christmas.
What was the inspiration behind Cranky?
I didn’t develop the character. Pete sent me six or seven drawings and said to write whatever you want, within certain parameters. They knew they wanted the focus to be on socio-emotional learning for kids. A way to talk about your feelings, and being cranky and all that stuff. I guess my memoir really exudes crankiness!
Some themes in the Cranky series include self-acceptance, positivity and friendship. What do you hope kids will take away from these books?
As a parent, I don’t ever want my kids to feel as if the way that they feel is a problem. I don’t want to pathologize their feelings. Their feelings are their feelings and they’re valid. I hope the takeaway for kids is two-fold. One, it’s totally okay to be cranky. And two, you still have responsibilities. You still need to show up and do the things that you’re responsible for, or that people need you to do. At no point in the Cranky series does Cranky not show up to the worksite or doesn’t do his job. I think about my kids and the fight to get them to go to school sometimes — more when they were younger. They’re like, “I feel mad.” I’m like, “That’s totally valid. Tell me about why you’re mad. Also, you still need to go to school today.”
There are some French words in ‘A Very Cranky Christmas.’ What was behind your decision to include those?
It started off with Jacques Hammer — that was just kind of funny. And I have French relatives, so it’s a little bit of a funny nod to my French relatives.
How do you come up with puns? Can you talk about your writing process?
Unfortunately nobody else is responsible for the dad jokes in “Cranky” except for me. As a parent, when you’re reading books to your kids, you’re like, “Oh man, this book again?” I really wanted to write a book that would amuse me as a parent and would make me laugh but would also hopefully be entertaining to kids.
As a parent reader, I always loved doing voices and being really dramatic, so I wanted to have lots of characters and give parents the opportunity to do lots of weird voices. And then, if not that, then at least have these dumb jokes about Hall and Oates or something like that.
You’re also a Latin teacher and tattoo artist. Does this work help inspire or inform your children’s book writing?
No, God, I hope not. They’re so different. I kind of love that. We contain multitudes, to quote that Walt Whitman poem. I think culturally we just want people to be reduced to a Twitter feed or a quick bio or an elevator pitch. And I want to resist that as much as possible. I don’t want all of the parts of my personality to be congruous. I think it’s just more interesting, and I think everybody’s like that. I think the world wants to put us in a box and wants all the things to make sense, and it doesn’t have to make sense. All the different parts of my life, like being a Latin teacher, being a tattooer, writing books, being a parent and being a husband — I think those things all bring me a lot of joy, but they don’t all need to overlap.
How do you approach writing for adults versus how you approach writing picture books?
For both my memoir and the Cranky books, all I wanted to be able to do was to write the book that only I could have written. If you can write something and it’s so specifically you, I think it’s a grand success.
Publishing and writing are two very different things. Especially in this day and age, I don’t want folks who are out there aspiring to be writers to feel like, if my work didn’t get published, it’s because it wasn’t good. I think one of the things that makes good writing is: Is it original to you? Does it have a voice that only you could write?
I think every human has a distinct voice, whether it’s writing or singing or whatever. And part of that journey in writing is discovering what that voice is.
Although the hubbub around Christmas irritates Cranky, how do you personally feel about the holiday?
My feelings about Christmas have been a journey. When I first got married, I was more of a Scrooge than a Cratchit. My wife loves Christmas — it is her holiday. And my mother-in-law also loves Christmas. I don’t want to bah humbug anybody’s holiday, but it didn’t feel joyous to me. I didn’t want to decorate and do all the things. When I got together with my wife, she really won me over. So I’ve done the journey — the very stereotypical but also totally true journey — from being a Scrooge to a Cratchit. I guess Scrooge also goes on the journey to the end, so I’m Scrooge. I started off not really loving Christmas and now I love Christmas. I’m going to yell at a kid out of my window to go buy a giant goose.
Liz Iversen’s writing has appeared in The New York Times, Creative Nonfiction, and Gulf Coast. She lives with her husband and children in Maine.

title: Chick-fil-A set to more than double its footprint in Maine in early 2027
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Chick-fil-A set to more than double its footprint in Maine in early 2027
The company says three new locations being built across Southern Maine will all open early next year.
Chick-fil-A set to more than double its footprint in Maine in early 2027
The company says three new locations being built across Southern Maine will all open early next year.
For the first time in more than five years, there will soon be new options for Mainers to get their Chick-fil-A fix. Chick-fil-A announced on Tuesday that it will open three new locations in southern Maine in early 2027.
Work is well underway on the new restaurants at Biddeford Crossing in Biddeford, Auburn, and in the parking lot of the Maine Mall in South Portland. Chick-fil-A currently has locations at Rock Row in Westbrook and in Bangor. The Bangor location was the first in Maine and the one at Rock Row opened in 2021. People lined up for hours before that store opened.
The location in Auburn would be located at 65 Mount Auburn Ave., next to the Hobby Lobby in the Turner Street Center Plaza, which is adjacent to the Auburn Mall.
"Maine is an important part of Chick-fil-A's continued growth in the Northeast, and we recognize the strong sense of pride Mainers have in their communities," said Dustin Griffiths, Director of Chick-fil-A Real Estate. "As we expand our presence in Maine, we look forward to creating meaningful jobs, building lasting relationships with guests and becoming a positive part of the communities that make this state special."
The company says the new restaurants will create more than 300 jobs in Maine.
With the opening of the three new restaurants, Chick-fil-A says it will donate $25,000 per restaurant, totaling $75,000 to the Good Shepherd Food Bank.

title: Maine author’s new children’s book embraces Christmas – and crankiness
text:
Months after the publication of his memoir, “Sigh, Gone,” Phuc Tran was contacted by the agent of kidlit author and illustrator Pete Oswald, asking if he’d consider writing picture books. “I just thought, that is a big jump — for someone who’s read my memoir to think, ‘Oh, this guy should write for kids,’” says Tran. “But I thought, sure, why not? I’m here for the adventure.”
Six years later, Tran is the author of four children’s books featuring Cranky the crane truck, most recently “A Very Cranky Christmas.” He spoke with the Portland Press Herald about normalizing crankiness, writing for both children and adults and how he really feels about Christmas.
What was the inspiration behind Cranky?
I didn’t develop the character. Pete sent me six or seven drawings and said to write whatever you want, within certain parameters. They knew they wanted the focus to be on socio-emotional learning for kids. A way to talk about your feelings, and being cranky and all that stuff. I guess my memoir really exudes crankiness!
Some themes in the Cranky series include self-acceptance, positivity and friendship. What do you hope kids will take away from these books?
As a parent, I don’t ever want my kids to feel as if the way that they feel is a problem. I don’t want to pathologize their feelings. Their feelings are their feelings and they’re valid. I hope the takeaway for kids is two-fold. One, it’s totally okay to be cranky. And two, you still have responsibilities. You still need to show up and do the things that you’re responsible for, or that people need you to do. At no point in the Cranky series does Cranky not show up to the worksite or doesn’t do his job. I think about my kids and the fight to get them to go to school sometimes — more when they were younger. They’re like, “I feel mad.” I’m like, “That’s totally valid. Tell me about why you’re mad. Also, you still need to go to school today.”
There are some French words in ‘A Very Cranky Christmas.’ What was behind your decision to include those?
It started off with Jacques Hammer — that was just kind of funny. And I have French relatives, so it’s a little bit of a funny nod to my French relatives.
How do you come up with puns? Can you talk about your writing process?
Unfortunately nobody else is responsible for the dad jokes in “Cranky” except for me. As a parent, when you’re reading books to your kids, you’re like, “Oh man, this book again?” I really wanted to write a book that would amuse me as a parent and would make me laugh but would also hopefully be entertaining to kids.
As a parent reader, I always loved doing voices and being really dramatic, so I wanted to have lots of characters and give parents the opportunity to do lots of weird voices. And then, if not that, then at least have these dumb jokes about Hall and Oates or something like that.
You’re also a Latin teacher and tattoo artist. Does this work help inspire or inform your children’s book writing?
No, God, I hope not. They’re so different. I kind of love that. We contain multitudes, to quote that Walt Whitman poem. I think culturally we just want people to be reduced to a Twitter feed or a quick bio or an elevator pitch. And I want to resist that as much as possible. I don’t want all of the parts of my personality to be congruous. I think it’s just more interesting, and I think everybody’s like that. I think the world wants to put us in a box and wants all the things to make sense, and it doesn’t have to make sense. All the different parts of my life, like being a Latin teacher, being a tattooer, writing books, being a parent and being a husband — I think those things all bring me a lot of joy, but they don’t all need to overlap.
How do you approach writing for adults versus how you approach writing picture books?
For both my memoir and the Cranky books, all I wanted to be able to do was to write the book that only I could have written. If you can write something and it’s so specifically you, I think it’s a grand success.
Publishing and writing are two very different things. Especially in this day and age, I don’t want folks who are out there aspiring to be writers to feel like, if my work didn’t get published, it’s because it wasn’t good. I think one of the things that makes good writing is: Is it original to you? Does it have a voice that only you could write?
I think every human has a distinct voice, whether it’s writing or singing or whatever. And part of that journey in writing is discovering what that voice is.
Although the hubbub around Christmas irritates Cranky, how do you personally feel about the holiday?
My feelings about Christmas have been a journey. When I first got married, I was more of a Scrooge than a Cratchit. My wife loves Christmas — it is her holiday. And my mother-in-law also loves Christmas. I don’t want to bah humbug anybody’s holiday, but it didn’t feel joyous to me. I didn’t want to decorate and do all the things. When I got together with my wife, she really won me over. So I’ve done the journey — the very stereotypical but also totally true journey — from being a Scrooge to a Cratchit. I guess Scrooge also goes on the journey to the end, so I’m Scrooge. I started off not really loving Christmas and now I love Christmas. I’m going to yell at a kid out of my window to go buy a giant goose.
Liz Iversen’s writing has appeared in The New York Times, Creative Nonfiction, and Gulf Coast. She lives with her husband and children in Maine.

title: Searsmont EMS chief to return home 6 months after lumber mill explosion
text:
Searsmont EMS Chief Sarah Tompkins will return home from the hospital next week, just over six months after the fiery lumber mill explosion that killed three people and injured more than a dozen others.
Tompkins will be welcomed home during a gathering at the Searsmont Fire station on Nov. 18, according to a social media post from the town late Tuesday night.
“Sarah’s homecoming is a moment we have all been looking forward to, and we are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of love, encouragement, and support throughout her journey,” the social media post reads.
Community members and fellow first responders are welcome to join the celebration, the town said. Details about Tompkins’ escort and the timing of her arrival are expected to be released next week
The May 15 explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont killed three people, including 27-year-old Andrew Cross, of Morrill, who died at the scene. Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury, 76, died at Maine Medical Center in June, while Alden Robbins, co-owner of the lumber mill, died at Massachusetts General Hospital in July.
Several first responders, as well as members of the Robbins family, were seriously injured in the explosion. Most have returned home, most recently Lily Robbins, who was welcomed back at a community gathering on Oct. 30.
The Maine Department of Labor announced Tuesday that it cited seven emergency departments for safety violations but suspended almost all of the penalties so the towns can pay for training and new equipment.

title: White House confronts Democrats over planned probes, claiming possible 'criminality'
text:
White House confronts Democrats over planned probes, claiming possible 'criminality'
The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to “blatant criminality.”
White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.
Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to “lawyer up” as his party was on the way to stunning victories in last week's midterm election.
In response, Scharf wrote that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter’s existence was first reported by Punchbowl News.
It's just the latest shot across the bow as the White House prepares to square off against newly empowered Democrats in the House and Senate next year, a showdown with major implications for congressional authority and the balance of power between the branches of government.
Garcia pushes back on the White House letter
Outside the Capitol on Wednesday, Garcia told reporters that “Donald Trump is clearly hiding something” and that Democrats “are not going to be threatened or intimidated.”
“The truth is that he needs to understand that Congress is a coequal branch of government,” Garcia said.
He doubled down on his “lawyer up” post after the election, saying the White House was “thin-skinned” and couldn't “take any sort of heat.”
“If you have abused the American public, you should lawyer up," Garcia said. “If you're a corporate CEO and you're ripping off the American people, you should lawyer up.”
Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.
Garcia also wants to look at the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Other targets include Trump’s White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family’s role in mineral deals and Trump’s crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff.
The Republican chair of Oversight says the panel is ‘very independent’
Kentucky Republican James Comer, the current chair of the Oversight Committee who conducted a wide-ranging investigation of former President Joe Biden and his family, told The Associated Press on Wednesday that he had not yet read the letter from the White House, but stressed that the panel is "very independent.”
“Regardless of who is in the White House, there's always going to be a strong desire for the Oversight Committee to be a check and balance on the executive branch, regardless of the political scenario," Comer said.
He said he thought Garcia's “lawyer up” comments were in “bad taste” but Democrats "won the election and it's going to be his committee. So if he gets out of line, I would assume that his members will try to rein him in.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that “there could be” a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying “Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it’s through subpoenas or letters — so we’re not going to stop working with Congress.”
“Nothing I’ve said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise,” he added.
Still, Justice Department officials elsewhere were pushing back. Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Texas, wrote to Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal on Wednesday, telling him to preserve all records relevant to his investigations.
Blumenthal is poised to chair a powerful Senate investigative committee in January. Reitz called Blumenthal’s efforts an “intent to deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights,” pointing to his October letter to people who donated to the new White House ballroom.
In response, Blumenthal said he “will not be intimidated.”
“The Trump administration is so afraid of transparency and oversight that they are weaponizing the Department of Justice to baselessly target Congress in direct violation of the Constitution," he said in a statement.
Other lawmakers react to the White House's warning
Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Trump critic, said he hopes Democrats don't squander their new powers on “stupid things.”
“I hope they have real hearings about real things, not another Russia-gate,” he said, referring to a previous congressional inquiry into ties between Trump's first presidential campaign in 2016 and Russia. Trump repeatedly denounced that investigation as a “hoax.”
“I think there is some real corruption there around the fringes,” Massie said about Trump and some of those around the president. Massie lost his primary election to a Trump-backed GOP challenger.
Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., who is expected to be the next House Ethics Committee chairman, said he would not back down from any investigations because of warnings from the White House.
“If they're trying to intimidate, at least for me, it’s not going to get me,” said DeSaulnier, who was a Republican before he switched to the Democratic Party in 2000. “I don’t work for a mafia, a mob organization.”

title: Nice Thursday, Nor’easter Shifting Southwards
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) -Partly to mostly cloudy skies will continue overnight. Temperatures will be a little colder than they have been the past few nights, with lows ranging from the mid-20s to the mid-30s.
Thursday: Another Quiet Day
Thursday will be a quiet day with periods of sunshine. Afternoon highs will stay in the 40s for most of us. Clouds will thicken later in the day as a storm system approaches from the south.
Friday: Nor’easter Arrives
The Nor’easter continues to favor a more southerly track which would keep us on the outer fringes meaning this will NOT be a high impact event. No travel issues are expect either.
A mix of rain and snow could reach far southern Maine late Thursday night, then spread north and east along the coast into Friday. Areas from the Interstate toward the coast have the best chance of seeing a rain/snow mixture. The best chance of the mix will be during the morning before changing to rain and coming to an end into the afternoon.
As temperatures climb into the 40s Friday, the mix should change to rain and wash away any light snow that accumulates. Northeast winds could gust to 25 mph Friday.
Saturday: Trending Drier & Breezy
The storm will begin to move away to our southeast Saturday. Most of us will see a cloudy, breezy day, with a few isolated rain showers along the coast and snow showers in far northern Maine. North winds could gust to 30 mph.
When all said and done, snowfall totals are possible in the far north and for those from the Interstate towards the coast. It will not be much as most will see a dusting remaining to the grassy surfaces.
Next Week: Brighter & Warmer
The second half of the weekend will be drier and brighter, with highs in the 40s Sunday. Expect more sunshine and warmer temperatures (50s) into next week.

title: New quick-service salad restaurant planned for Portland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Veteran restaurateur Chad Conley announced Tuesday he’s launching a quick-service salad restaurant in the Union Station Plaza early next year.
Wild Card will be located at 252 St. John’s St., a former H&R Block office. The 2,700-square-foot space will have about 30 seats.
Conley is the owner of Rose Foods on Forest Avenue and co-owner of Palace Diner in Biddeford. He also co-founded the Philly-style sandwich shop Ramona’s on Washington Avenue. He said he’s been considering a concept like Wild Card for several years.
“We want to be able to provide food that is functional and healthy, while being delicious and interesting,” Conley said. “It can’t be salad you could get at the Whole Foods salad bar.” He also said he aims to make sure the price points stay affordable.
Wild Card’s core menu will feature about a dozen greens- and grain-based salads, along with a build-your own salad option.
Conley said Wild Card will be open seven days for lunch and early dinner.
“When I look around at the market for prepared food in Portland, I think this is something people will really benefit from,” he said.

title: InvestigateTV+: Tracing the footsteps of a WWII soldier
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ explores the power of honoring history and reclaiming legacy. We reveal how families can rebuild military records destroyed in a historic fire.
Then, we follow a community of strangers stepping up to bury a veteran from World War I.
Plus, we expose a manipulative financial scam that turns trust into a terrifying and costly trap.
Tracing a WWII soldier’s footsteps
A program at the National World War II Museum in New Orleans is helping families learn about their loved ones’ service by tracking down veterans’ official records.
Researchers can find details that include training, medical history, units, battles and promotions.
InvestigateTV’s own Tisha Powell used the program to learn more about her grandfather, Ulysses Reed Sr.
Gold courier scam
It can start with a pop-up on the computer screen and sometimes ends with the innocent victim handing over their life savings to a scammer.
The FBI reported in 2025 that the “gold courier” scam alone drained more than $300 million from victims.
A Wisconsin woman lost more than $400,000 of her retirement savings after scammers impersonated federal agencies, her investment company and the Better Business Bureau to convince her she was protecting her money.
‘The People’s House’
A collection of four Norman Rockwell paintings that spent nearly 40 years on display in the White House West Wing is now on display to the public for the first time at “The People’s House.”
Final resting place for World War I vet
On a typical day at the Vermont Veterans Memorial Cemetery, the only sound on these hallowed grounds is an American flag flapping in the gentle breeze and birds chirping from a distance.
Three men were laid to rest recently. Private Edward James Irwin was one of them. His final goodbye comes almost 45 years after his death. He served in the Army during World War I from 1917 to 1918.
You may wonder why a World War I vet who died in November 1981 is finally going to be laid to rest. Well, it goes back to Walter Ducharme’s funeral business in Rutland.

title: Firefighter suffers minor injuries at house fire in Newburgh
text:
NEWBURGH, Maine (WABI) - A firefighter suffered minor injuries putting out a fire at a Newburgh home Tuesday morning after fire crews from multiple towns responded to a fire at a house on Western Avenue.
None of the occupants of the house were injured.
Multiple departments responded to the call just before 11 A.M. Tuesday.
Officials on scene said there was some minor fire damage, but the majority of the lasting impact will be from the extensive amount of heat and water used.
Hermon Fire Chief Cody Sullivan told WABI that they were in the middle of staff training at Hermon Mountain which put them right down the road.
“In this day and age staffing matters. We were up staff today due to the training, so we were able to roll in with two fully staffed trucks, a support vehicle, and an ambulance. On a normal day, that’s not what our typical response would look like. It would’ve doubled our response time, so the fire would’ve grown twice as big before we arrived. Newburgh was shortly behind us. The quicker you can get people on scene the quicker you can extinguish the fire,” said Sullivan.
The investigation into the cause of the fire is ongoing.

title: Up and Down the Kennebec Valley: Medical history in central Kennebec Valley
text:
Augusta doctors, part two
This article will consider the remaining doctors who had cards in the July 31, 1875, issue of the Daily Kennebec Journal, and three of their predecessors. The men announcing their practices in July, 1875, included:
— W. L. Thompson, M.D., Corner State and Green Sts. Office hours 1 to 3 p.m.
— L. J. Crooker, M.D., residence and office Winthrop Street, “one door east of Baptist Church, (the church with the town clock) In rear of Court House, Augusta, Maine.” Office hours 9 a.m. to 12 m.
— Drs. Brickett & Bolan, Copartnership. Office, Cushnoc House, State St. Dr. Brickett’s office hours 9 to 12 a.m., Dr. Bolan’s 2 to 5 p.m. Dr. Brickett’s residence, Spring St. Bolan’s residence, State St., opposite Dr. H. H. Hill. Office open from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m.
* * * * * *
Henry Kingsbury, in his Kennebec County history, and the on-line site FamilySearch offer two generations of Dr. Thompsons. W. L. was William Ladd Thompson; two of his sons, William Sylvester Thompson by his first wife and Daniel Varney Thompson by his second wife, were also doctors.
William Ladd Thompson was born June 6, 1823, in Newbury, Vermont. Kingsbury said he attended Francistown (more commonly Francestown) Academy, in Francestown, New Hampshire; taught for four years in Newburyport (Massachusetts); “took medical lectures at Dartmouth”; and in 1857 graduated from the Homeopathic Medical College in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
After a few years in Dover, New Hampshire, where he married for the second time (see below for family information), Thompson came to Augusta in December, 1865, (no explanation offered for any of these moves).
In Augusta, Kingsbury wrote, Thompson “began…what is now [1892] the longest consecutive practice of any Homeopathist ever in that city.”
Thompson was also “a charter member of the State Homeopathic Medical Society, and has been its president.”
On Aug. 6, 1851, in Georgetown, Massachusetts, William Ladd Thompson married Susan Emeline Cummings, born Jan. 15, 1830. They had at least three sons, listed as Dr. William Sylvester Thompson (1853 – 1924); George Lewis Thompson (1855-1923); and Charles Cummings Thompson (1857 -1862). Susan died Dec. 25, 1858.
On June 27, 1860, in Dover, New Hampshire, Thompson married Sarah Bickford Varney.
A WikiTree summary of Sarah Thompson’s life says she was born Dec. 23, 1837, in Augusta; by 1850, the family had moved to Dover, where she married William Ladd Thompson when she was 22 and he was 37.
FamilySearch lists their seven children, all born in Augusta: a son born in 1863 who died in 1865; a son born in 1865 who died in 1868; Daniel Varney, born in 1867 and lived until 1932; another boy born in 1869 who lived until 1935; and then a daughter, born in 1872 and died in 1873; a daughter born in 1874, about whom FamilySearch says only that she lived in Augusta “for about 20 years” and is now dead; and finally a daughter born in 1875, who died in 1878.
To summarize, of Dr. W. L. Thompson’s three sons by his first wife, two grew to adulthood; of his seven children by his second wife, three grew to adulthood.
William Ladd Thompson died Sept. 30, 1894, in Augusta, and was buried in Dover, New Hampshire. WikiTree said the 1900 census listed Sarah as his widow, still living in Augusta.
WikiTree and FamilySearch agree that Sarah died Sept. 24, 1922, in Walpole, Massachusetts, and was buried in Dover, New Hampshire.
Kingsbury called the older Thompson son, William Sylvester, Will S. Thompson, and said he was born in Newburyport, Massachusetts. He graduated from Bowdoin College in 1875; “attended medical lectures at Dartmouth”; and graduated from the Homeopathic College, in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1879. Until 1892, Kingsbury said, he had been practicing in Hallowell and Gardiner.
Kingsbury’s other doctor son, Daniel Varney, born in 1867 to second wife Sarah, married Grace Brightman Randall (born Oct. 22, 1870) on Sept. 5, 1893, in Augusta. FamilySearch says nothing about his medical work. It locates him in New Jersey and later in Boston, Massachusetts, where Grace died in April, 1932, and he died Aug. 21, 1932.
* * * * * *
Dr. Leland Crooker was profiled two weeks ago, in the Oct. 29 issue of The Town Line. A local historian found that he moved to Augusta in 1870.
* * * * * *
Co-partners Drs. Brickett and Bolan were without first names on their cards in the July 31, 1875, newspaper. Brickett was without doubt Dr. George E. Brickett, who appears frequently in various sources; his son, G. Hartwell Brickett, was only 15 in 1875 (and later became a doctor).
According to miscellaneous sources, including the Maine Medical Association (a list of members from the 19th century), Dr. Wallace Bolan was born June 5, 1840, in either Weld or Phillips, “depending on the source,” son of a doctor. He earned a medical degree from Harvard in 1863, and was an assistant surgeon in the 19th Maine Infantry in 1863-1864.
Bolan had a practice in New Sharon until 1883, when he “became a physician at the Home for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers at Togus” (see the Nov. 5 issue in this series for information on this institution).
The MMA source says Dr. Bolan’s first wife, Corilla “Carrie” Brooks (Nickerson), died in 1870. His second wife, Frances E. Diggles, was born May 7, 1841, and died May 12, 1927.
The doctor died Nov. 22, 1886. He, Frances and his and Corilla’s daughter Marion (1865 -1894) are buried in Augusta’s Forest Grove Cemetery.
* * * * * *
Dr. George Edward Brickett was profiled in this subseries in the Oct. 22 issue of The Town Line. Kingsbury said that he began practicing in Augusta after his service in the Civil War. He is frequently mentioned as a mentor to young men in the area aspiring to become doctors.
* * * * * *
These doctors who chose to advertise in the local newspaper were not the only ones practicing in Augusta. One of the earliest, and most respected, was Dr. Daniel Cony (see also an earlier profile in the Feb. 23, 2023, issue of The Town Line.)
Cony was born in Shutesbury, Massachusetts, Aug. 3, 1752, and moved to the settlement at Fort Western in 1778 with his father, Deacon Samuel Cony (1718 – April 12, 1803), and older brother, Samuel (May 8, 1746 – Sept. 22, 1779).
Capt. Charles E. Nash, in his Augusta chapters in Kingsbury’s history, wrote that Cony studied medicine with Dr. Samuel Curtis, in Marlboro, Massachusetts. (Marlboro is about 60 miles east of Shutesbury.)
He was back in Shutesbury and practicing medicine when the Revolution started in April 1775. Soon afterwards, Nash wrote, he “was sent as adjutant of a regiment of infantry to join General Gates at Saratoga, and was at the surrender of Burgoyne [Oct. 17, 1777 ].” (Find a Grave says his regiment was the 6th New Hampshire.)
During his service, Cony found time to marry Dr. Curtis’s niece, Susanna Curtis (born May 4, 1752), of Sharon, Massachusetts (Sharon is about 40 miles southeast of Marlboro), on Nov. 14, 1776.
In 1778, Nash said, Cony resigned “his commission in the army” and he and his “young wife” and their first daughter (who died young; four other daughters lived to adulthood and married) came to join his father and brother in what became Augusta.
“Here he enjoyed a long and honorable career of usefulness,” Nash wrote. Nash, and Cony’s gravestone in Augusta’s Cony Cemetery, both put his medical work first in his career; but he did much else besides.
As a practicing doctor, Nash wrote, Cony was “on terms of intimacy and in correspondence with the leading medical men of Massachusetts, and was a member of the Massachusetts Medical Society.”
Laurel Thatcher Ulrich, in her book on midwife Martha Ballard’s diary, pointed out that the Society’s Boston headquarters was 150 miles from Cony’s practice, and added that he kept his membership even after he was elected president of Kennebec Medical Society, founded in 1797.
Ulrich said Cony contributed one short paper to the Massachusetts Society, on an unusual childbirth in August 1787.
Cony served in the Massachusetts General Court; was an Augusta delegate to the constitutional convention after Maine gained statehood in 1820; held judgeships; helped get Hallowell Academy and Bowdoin College chartered; and founded and cared for Augusta’s Cony Female Academy, organized in 1815 and incorporated Feb. 10, 1818.
Find a Grave quotes this inscription from his gravestone: “SOLDIER-PHYSICIAN-EXECUTIVE COUNCILLOR-LEGISLATOR-JUDGE-FOUNDER”
Susanna Curtis Cony died Oct. 25, 1833; Dr. Daniel Cony died Jan. 21, 1842. Both are buried in Cony Cemetery, with their daughter who died in infancy, Dr. Cony’s parents, his brother and a nephew who also died as an infant.
* * * * * *
Kingsbury listed two other early Augusta doctors in his chapter on the medical profession, Dr. Issachar Snell and Dr. Cyrus Briggs, who must have known each other in the 1820s.
Dr. Snell was the older, born April 16, 1775, in Bridgewater, Massachusetts. He graduated from Harvard University in 1797, studied medicine and surgery with Massachusetts doctors and practiced in Bridgewater from 1800 until he moved to Augusta in 1805.
He married Mary “Molly” Keith (1780 in 1781 – June 15, 1861) on Nov. 28, 1799, in Bridgewater. They had nine children between 1800 and 1830.
Kingsbury described Snell as a farmer, as well as a doctor. In the spring of 1806 he moved to a farm in Winthrop, where he lived until moving back to Augusta in 1828. There, Kingsbury said, he practiced medicine as a profession and “tilled the soil as a recreation.”
“His specialty was surgery, in which his skill gave him an extended reputation and practice,” according to Kingsbury.
Dr. Snell died Oct. 14, 1847, killed instantly when his sulky overturned, Kingsbury wrote. He was buried in Augusta’s Mount Vernon Cemetery, with his widow and several of their children.
FamilySearch says one of the Snell sons was a second Dr. Isachar Snell (with his first name spelled differently), born May 10, 1817, in Winthrop, and died July 13, 1877, in Augusta. Find a Grave calls him Dr. Issachar Snell III, born May 10, 1817, in Winthrop, and died July 13, 1877 (a clipping posted on the website says June 13), in Chicago (whence his body was returned for burial in Mount Vernon Cemetery).
* * * * * *
Cyrus Briggs was born in Little Compton, Rhode Island, in 1800, Kingsbury said. He graduated from Harvard in 1821; studied medicine with a prominent Boston doctor and botanist, Jacob Bigelow; and in 1826 graduated from Harvard Medical College.
“He commenced practice in Augusta in March 1827, and continued uninterruptedly for more than forty-five years,” Kingsbury wrote. An on-line source says he practiced uninterruptedly until 1870.
When Dr. Briggs started practicing, he was the only young doctor in Augusta, the on-line source says. Its writer called him “a skillful physician, industrious, prompt, remarkably attentive to his patients, and…successful in the treatment of diseases.”
“Surgery was not to his taste, and except in its simplest forms he never attempted it,” the writer said. Nor did he experiment, preferring, in this writer’s opinion, to follow “the safe and beaten track marked and worn by the leaders in the profession.”
Briggs was popular and trusted and had a large practice; but the writer thought he could have been “eminent in his profession” had he followed a “[h]abit of laborious study, with persistent effort at improvement.”
Briggs married Louisa Fisk or Fiske, of Boston, on May 27, 1827. She was born May 3, 1801, in Chelmsford, Massachusetts. They had at least two, maybe four daughters; one born in 1844 lived only six years.
The on-line writer continued: “For about a year previous to his death he was absent most of the time from his home, on visits to his friends and relations. On one of these visits, while at the house of his classmate, C.W. Upham, in Salem, Mass., he suddenly died, of heart disease, 24 June, 1871.”
Louisa died Dec. 4, 1890. She and her husband, and other family members, are buried in Augusta’s Forest Grove Cemetery.
Main sources
Kingsbury, Henry D., ed., Illustrated History of Kennebec County Maine 1625-1892 (1892)
Ulrich, Laurel Thatcher, A Midwife’s Tale The Life of Martha Ballard, Based on Her Diary, 1785-1812 (1990)

title: Presque Isle Native Competes on “The Floor”
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - A Presque Isle native is taking her love of music to national television. Callie Junkins was chosen to compete on the FOX game show “The Floor.”
100 contestants are competing in a variety of categories for $250,000 on this season of “The Floor”. Callie Junkins, a Presque Isle native, is one of this season’s contestants. In May Callie flew to Ireland to compete and says the experience was surreal.
“I was very very nervous. You can probably tell when you see the duel. I look very nervous. You really build it up in your head. Like, I’m gonna be the confident one up there but the second you actually have to go up to the podium where rob is it’s just so nerve wracking,” said Callie Junkins, a Presque Isle contestant on “The Floor”.
Between filming, Callie says she spent her time studying for whatever category might come next. “I studied relentlessly the entire time we were there. Anything you can think of that would go with a category you just relentless just go over and over it. Even if it has nothing to do with what’s gonna be on the duel because you just want to be so prepared.”
For Callie, the experience was also a chance to represent her hometown. “It’s been really cool to get to kind of showcase my small town. I feel great getting to represent such a small town and to be able to go from being there to somehow getting on this big tv show is just something you don’t see happen every day from up there.”
Callie couldn’t tell us exactly when her episode will air but says it will be soon. You can watch the next episode of “The Floor” tonight at 8 on FOX.

Veterans Day dates back to Nov. 11, 1918, when the truce between U.S. allies and Germany to end World War I was signed on the 11th day of the 11th month at the 11th hour.
President Woodrow Wilson originally proclaimed it Armistice Day, but in 1954, President Dwight Eisenhower officially renamed it Veterans Day.
Veterans Day is a federal holiday. Most banks and post offices will be closed, but grocery stores, retailers and restaurants will be open.

title: Veterans Day commemoration in Bangor honors Maine’s fallen Korean War service members
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Veterans Day ceremony in Bangor honored Mainers who died during the Korean War.
The Maine Korean War Veterans Association held the commemoration at the Maine Korean War Memorial in Mount Hope Cemetery.
About 36,000 U.S. service members died during the Korean War. 247 of them were from Maine.
The names of Mainers who died were read aloud in their memory.
Dusty Fisher of the association says it’s important to remember those who served in a conflict often called the “Forgotten War.”
“They didn’t come home. They came home, but they came home to be buried. A good number are still missing an action over there. It’s important that they and their families realize that they’re remembered,” said Fisher.
The Maine Korean War Memorial was dedicated in 1995 to honor veterans of the war.

title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state’s first Black US senator since Reconstruction
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.
Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any U.S. state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South.
“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”
The Associated Press called the race in Colom’s favor after local officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the state’s large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.
“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch.
Hyde-Smith, 67, called Colom late Wednesday afternoon to concede and released a concession speech online shortly afterward.
“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”
Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society, and he repeated that pledge after his victory.
“My commitment to you, each and every one of you, is that first I’m going to treat your children like I want my children to be treated,” Colom said. “I’m going to treat your parents the way I want my parents to be treated. I’m gonna treat your future the way I want my future to be” and “work to make every Mississippian’s life better.”
National Democrats, activists and Mississippians celebrate
Party leaders hailed the senator-elect’s triumph, with nods to the South’s emerging status as a political battleground after other victories from North Carolina and South Carolina to Georgia and Texas.
“Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online.
Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won “because you believe in the promise of your state’s people. And they believed in you right back.”
Vera Finley was among those supporters.
“I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields,” Finley said ahead of Colom’s victory speech. “Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great-grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history.”
Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state’s voters, most notably Black voters, “made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out” in a state that has seen “some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights.”
A race Washington once viewed as a long shot
The contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, finally drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia’s Raphael Warnock and Maryland’s Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see it as winnable.
The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom produced one of the year’s most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they’d “pick another senator instead.”
When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October to rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited to enter. He introduced himself and asked about their concerns.
Later, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said only nine words in six seconds before stepping away: “Is this not the best president in our lifetime?”
Colom’s appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war that drove up gas prices and tariffs that caused headaches for Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington — a critique that resonated in a state accustomed to long-serving, powerful senators.
There is some irony in Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a U.S. District Court judge. Mississippi’s senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Gov. Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.
Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom’s confirmation. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.
Colom called on Mississippi’s history
The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist.
Colom told the story of Evers’ military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction. “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”
At the lectern Wednesday night, Colom said it was appropriate that the race be called on Veterans Day, as he again paid tribute to Evers.
“He served his country, came home to Mississippi, and they wouldn’t let him vote,” Colom said. “But he had faith that Mississippi could make progress.”
Despite Republicans’ domination, the path was always there
Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi’s general elections have been closer for years than its Southern neighbors. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Gov. Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.
Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican discontent and an uptick in Democrats’ usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.
Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.
Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former U.S. agriculture secretary who’d also been Mississippi’s first Black congressman since Reconstruction.
During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of his candidacy but said he cares more about what it means for others.
“My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision and the values,” he said, “and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I’ve done that they shouldn’t get a chance.”
__
Barrow reported from Atlanta and Washington.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Watching For Snow Showers Tonight, With Another Storm Possible This Weekend
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Tuesday. We’ve been watching another round of rain and snow showers move across the region today, as a weak area of low pressure continues to influence our weather. While I don’t expect much in the way of snow accumulation from today’s activity, a few locations could still see some snowflakes flying around heading into the evening hours. Additional showers remain possible tomorrow, before we see some improvement in the forecast heading into Thursday. Beyond that, I’m keeping a close eye on the potential for a coastal storm to impact the region heading into the upcoming weekend. While there remains quite a bit of uncertainty with this system, I think it’s worth discussing the potential for accumulating snow across portions of the region.
Rain and snow showers are expected to continue across portions of Aroostook County this evening, with another round of precipitation favoring central and southern locations. Temperatures are expected to remain borderline for rain or snow, with many towns likely seeing a mixture of the two. I don’t expect much snow accumulation for most locations, although some of our higher elevation communities could manage to pick up an inch or two of accumulation. Showers should gradually become more scattered heading into the overnight hours, with most locations seeing little to no additional precipitation by tomorrow morning. Low temperatures tonight are expected to fall into the upper 20s to lower 30s, with Caribou and Presque Isle both falling to around 32 degrees. Winds are also expected to shift from the southwest to the northwest overnight, remaining fairly light around 5 to 10 mph.
Tomorrow, which is also Veterans Day, looks to feature another round of mostly cloudy skies across the region. I think we’ll have a few opportunities for breaks of sunshine, but I wouldn’t expect a completely sunny day by any means. A few additional rain and snow showers will remain possible, especially across northern and western locations and extending south toward Millinocket and Houlton. Much like today’s activity, I don’t expect these showers to produce much accumulation, with temperatures expected to remain just warm enough to prevent most snow from sticking around. High temperatures tomorrow should have no problem reaching the upper 30s to lower 40s, with Caribou expected to reach around 39 degrees, while Presque Isle and Houlton look to top out near 41 degrees. Any lingering showers should gradually come to an end heading into Wednesday evening, allowing skies to begin clearing overnight.
Thursday looks to feature some improvement in the forecast, with high pressure helping to bring more sunshine back to the region. After a colder start to the day, with temperatures falling into the lower 20s overnight Wednesday, sunshine should help temperatures rebound back closer to average heading into the midday and afternoon hours. High temperatures Thursday are expected to reach the upper 30s to lower 40s across most of Aroostook County. Caribou is expected to reach around 39 degrees, while Presque Isle and Houlton look to top out near 41 and 43 degrees respectively. Westerly winds should remain light around 5 mph, making Thursday one of our better opportunities for some outdoor activities before the weather potentially turns more active heading into the weekend.
Our attention then turns toward the potential for a coastal storm to develop heading into Friday and the upcoming weekend. The latest forecast guidance continues to show a couple of areas of low pressure developing along the Mid-Atlantic Coast, before tracking northeast toward New England. What remains unclear is exactly where these systems will track, which will ultimately determine how much precipitation we see across Aroostook County, and whether that precipitation falls as rain or snow.
The snowfall potential graphic really illustrates where I think we currently have the best opportunity for accumulating snow, with our western and higher elevation locations favored over eastern portions of the County. However, I want to emphasize that this is not a forecast for how much snow will fall, but rather a generalized look at where accumulating snow appears more likely based on the latest forecast guidance. Some solutions continue to bring the storm closer to the coast, potentially resulting in more substantial snowfall across portions of the region. Other solutions keep the system farther offshore, resulting in considerably less precipitation.
At this point, I think it’s still too early to put specific snowfall amounts on this system, especially given how much uncertainty remains regarding its eventual track. What I can say is that temperatures are expected to remain on the cooler side heading into the weekend, with highs generally reaching the mid to upper 30s across northern Aroostook County, and closer to 40 degrees farther south. I’ll continue watching how this system evolves over the next several days, as even a relatively small shift in the storm’s track could result in some fairly significant changes to our forecast.
For more details on what to expect over the next couple of days, along with the latest information on our potential weekend storm, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: SCORES OUTDOORS: The symbolism of ladybugs
text:
Last Sunday, at our usual family coffee gathering after church, the discussion centered around ladybugs, since we had just seen a couple on my daughter’s kitchen window. We debated its symbolism.
A ladybug is a small, spotted beetle that is widely viewed as a symbol of good luck, fortune, and protection.
“Ladybug” is a curious name for our common and beloved garden visitor. The word “lady” originated during the Middle Ages in Europe. The ladybug’s healthy appetite for plant-destroying pests linked it to the beneficial Virgin Mary (Our Lady). The second half of its name is an American quirk. Ladybugs are not actually true bugs, they are beetles. Outside the U.S., they are known, more accurately, as ladybird beetles.
Not all ladybugs are red with black spots. In fact, their colors range from red to yellow to black with a variety of patterns – not surprising given almost 6,000 species worldwide and almost 500 species in North America. Even within some species, color patterns vary. Most ladybugs, however, are less than 3/8 inches long, have an oval to round shape with rounded backs and flat undersides, as well as partly hidden heads and short antennae. Like all beetles, ladybugs have two sets of wings. The outer wings (often spotted), are hardened or leathery to protect the more delicate flight wings beneath.
Globally distributed, ladybugs occupy a variety of habitats, including forests, meadows, agricultural fields, and of course, your garden.
Best known for eating aphids, scale insects, and mites, most but not all ladybug species are predatory, though some species supplement their diet with pollen and nectar. A few ladybug species eat plants, and one eats fungus – a welcome help for owners of vineyards afflicted with powdery mildew.
Ladybugs fall prey to birds, small mammals, and other predatory insects, like wasps, though many ladybug species have a powerful defense. When attacked, they exude a toxic, bad tasting, yellowish alkaloid from their leg joints. The bright red coloring of many ladybugs acts as a warning to predators of this trait.
Meaning by Color and Details
• Red Ladybug: Symbolizes personal power, vitality, and – in Christian folklore – the cloak of the Virgin Mary (with the spots representing her seven sorrows).
• Yellow or Orange Ladybug: Associated with new creative energy, mental clarity, and a calming presence.
• Spot Count Superstition: According to traditional lore, the number of spots on a ladybug can represent the number of months or years of good luck ahead.
• A Landing Sign: When a ladybug lands directly on your skin or clothing, traditions treat it as a direct blessing, a “life glow-up” signal, or a reminder to practice gratitude.
Core Symbolism & Lore
• Good Luck & Fortune: It is believed that if a ladybug lands on you, good things or years of luck matching the number of spots will come your way.
• Historical Roots: During the Middle Ages, European farmers prayed to the Virgin Mary for help when pests ruined their crops. When ladybugs arrived and ate the destructive aphids, farmers called them “Our Lady’s beetles,” linking the red shell to Mary’s cloak and the black spots to her sorrows.
• True Love & Wishes: Folklore suggests making a wish when a ladybug lands on you, or viewing them as an omen that true love or positive transformation is near.
Color Meanings:
• Red: Signifies personal power, protection, and strength.
• Orange & Yellow: Relate to creativity, vitality, new beginnings, or calmness.
• Practical Value: Beyond symbolism, they are beneficial garden insects that naturally consume soft-bodied crop pests like aphids.
The ladybug is a universal symbol of good luck, protection, and positive transformation. Seeing one or having a ladybug land on you is widely viewed as a sign that worries are fading, wishes are coming true, and a lucky phase is beginning.
Core Spiritual Meanings
• Good Fortune & Wishes: Spotting a ladybug is believed to bring good luck, and folklore suggests that making a wish when one lands on you increases the chance of it coming true.
• Protection: They are seen as spiritual guards that ward off negative energies and bring emotional or physical safety.
• Transformation & Rebirth: Like many insects, their life cycle represents growth, renewal, and stepping into a new chapter of life.
• Patience and Flow: The ladybug reminds you not to force your goals or rush the process, encouraging you to let things unfold naturally.
• Love & Relationships: Their appearance can signal heart alignment, the approach of a soulmate, or a prompt to rekindle romance in a current relationship.
Fun Facts
Ladybugs breathe air through openings in their abdomen and thorax, called spiracles.
Counting spots on a ladybird’s back does not indicate its age, contrary to popular belief.
Ladybugs are the official state insect of Delaware, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, and Tennessee.
