title: Peanut the squirrel's former owner has been detained by ICE and could be deported
text:
PINE CITY, N.Y. (AP) — When New York wildlife officers euthanized a couple’s pet squirrel, Peanut, two years ago, Republicans including JD Vance seized on the critter’s killing as just another example of government overreach from meddling Democrats.
“The same government that doesn’t care about hundreds of thousands of illegal immigrant criminals coming into our country doesn’t want us to have pets. It’s the craziest, the craziest thing,” Vance said at a rally just before the 2024 election.
Now, the Department of Homeland Security under President Donald Trump has put one of the late squirrel’s owners in an immigration jail, pending possible deportation to Germany.
Daniela Bittner was arrested by immigration officers in mid-October at a small airport near New York’s border with Pennsylvania. DHS issued a statement saying Bittner was arrested because she “chose to overstay her welcome in defiance of our nation’s laws.”
Since then, Bittner has been moved through multiple immigration lockups and is now housed in Texas, according to her husband, Mark Longo, who called conditions in the lockups “deplorable.” He blamed her detention on an immigration paperwork mix-up.
“They put Peanut on a pedestal, won their election, and threw him off that pedestal immediately,” Longo said.
The arrest was the latest twist in the tale of Peanut, also known as P’nut, a once-orphaned squirrel whose fun antics made him a social media star. That is, until state officials got multiple complaints that the couple were illegally keeping wild animals in their house as pets, including the squirrel and a racoon.
During one inspection, Peanut bit the gloved thumb of a wildlife biologist and was euthanized so the squirrel could be tested for rabies.
News stories about the episode earned the family sympathy and caught the attention of Republicans on the campaign trail, who criticized the state’s response and New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul.
Longo said he tries to steer clear of politics, but that he can’t help but feel like the government keeps wading into his life.
“I’m begging the world to find an answer as to why this keeps happening to me,” he told The Associated Press by phone Wednesday. “One time, you can call it what it is. Two times, it’s now becoming a little bit more of a target.”
Longo said he and Bittner made a mistake on one of her immigration forms and didn’t catch the error while they were dealing with the dustup over Peanut’s seizure and killing.
“You know, arrest the people who deserve to be arrested. My wife is not one of them,” he said.
“You’re telling me, all of this because my wife and I forgot to do the proper form?” he added.
Longo said local officials have been looking into his wife’s case and that he’s spoken about her arrest to UFC chief Dana White, a longstanding ally of President Donald Trump whom Longo said he met after Peanut was taken.
Longo said he will have to shut down the animal sanctuary he and his wife run if she is deported.
“The only outcome that will save this place is my wife not being deported,” he said.

title: Southern Maine may see first snow of the season by week’s end
text:
Snow is on its way to southern parts of Maine for the first time this season, but whether the flakes will reach the coast is still up in the air.
The National Weather Service expects the precipitation to reach the region late Thursday and depart by early Saturday. The highest likelihood for snow to accumulate is on Friday in areas at least 1,000 feet above sea level, but lower-elevation areas could still see light snow by midmorning.
Southern Oxford County and northwestern York County stand a 30% to 40% chance of seeing at least 1 inch of snow Friday, according to the weather service. Other parts of interior southern Maine can also expect snow, whereas regions farther north are not expected to see much.
“We’re still trying to get a grasp on how continuous or showery the precipitation may be,” Greg Cornwell, a meteorologist at the weather service office in Gray, said Wednesday afternoon. “Right now, the best confidence of pretty steady precipitation is south of Augusta. … North of there, it might be quite a bit lighter.”
The southern coast stands a very slim chance of seeing snow, according to the weather service.
“I think there’s going to be enough warm air to cause most of that to be rain,” Cornwell explained.
If coastal Mainers do catch some flakes, it will most likely be when temperatures dip overnight Thursday into early Friday, he said. Still, accumulation there remains doubtful.
“There are a lot of complicating factors as to whether you get snow to stick,” Cornwell said, “but it’s something to keep an eye on.”
The meteorologist cautioned Mainers farther inland to prepare for what could be the first messy commute of the season Friday morning.
“For those traveling in the interior, it’s the first snow that may stick on the roads at points during your commute,” Cornwell said. “Just take it easy, give yourself plenty of time and remember your braking distance may be a little shorter than you think in wintry conditions.”
Parts of northern Maine, including Caribou, got measurable snow in mid-October, while light flakes fell in Rangeley and portions of western Maine over the weekend.

title: Jay data center developers amend permit application
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine data center developers amend permit application
The project is expected to be up and running by early 2029.
Maine data center developers amend permit application
The project is expected to be up and running by early 2029.
The Androscoggin Mill was once the largest paper mill in Maine, and soon it will be a data center.
Earlier this week, the developers at the mill amended its permit application. The notice updating the use of the mill to be for computer equipment, not paper machines and the parking lot that is set to be redeveloped for HVAC. There is also a change to the air license application that will cover the mill's backup generators in the event of a power outage.
"[Get] people back in the area, the stores will get busier, things will get better. There'll be reasons for people to stay in the area," Lucian Richard said.
He's worked at the mill for 35 years and remembers a time there were 1800 employees. He said it will benefit the community to get people working in the mill again.
Town leaders in Jay said the location of this project makes all the difference.
"It's a site that had industrial uses still has all of the industrial, infrastructure to support it," Jay Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere said.
That infrastructure includes the electrical grid. Tony McDonald is the developer of the mill and said he took over a Central Maine Power contract from the former owners.
"It's been around since 2009, and we're just using the power that's provided for in that contract. There's no new power here. It's just utilizing that existing contract and that existing equipment," McDonald said.
This project was the subject of a large debate during the last legislative session. The legislature passed a first-in-the-nation bill that would have put a temporary moratorium on data centers and would have required the state to create a council to ensure Maine is ready for them.
Gov. Janet Mills advocated for that measure to include an exemption for Jay, which was already in the works at the time.
The legislature failed to pass that amendment, leading to the governor to use her veto pen.
"I want to give Janet Mills credit. Janet Mills took time. She grew up here. She knows about this mill. And she took a lot of guts for her to do something by vetoing that bill," Tom Saviello, former environmental manager at the Androscoggin Mill, said.
During our Commitment 2026 Democratic gubernatorial primary debate, Governor-elect Hannah Pingree said she would have signed that bill. Just this week, she was asked about this project specifically and reiterated the call for a moratorium.
"I certainly look forward to learning more from the town and the developer," Pingree said. "That being said, I heard pretty loudly and clearly from Maine people that the development of data centers in Maine without very strong regulations in place is not something that people are interested in."
The developers are holding an open house on Dec. 10 to answer any questions community members might have.

title: REVIEW POTPOURRI: Remembering pianist Malcolm Frager
text:
Malcolm Frager
I first became aware of a very good friend from the 1980s, pianist Malcolm Frager, in 1973, because a very favorite conductor of mine, Jascha Horenstein, had collaborated in a recording for Reader’s Digest with Malcolm of the Schumann A Minor Piano Concerto as part of a set of six LPs entitled Everybody’s Favorite Concertos (And one I would find sealed 30 years later at a barn sale here in South China, the owner grudgingly charging me $3, not knowing I would have paid $20 because every single Concerto was performed by soloists and conductors of exceptional distinction.).
First, some background on Malcolm. Within a year he won first prize in not one, but two prestigious piano competitions – the Leventritt, in New York City, and the Queen Elisabeth, in Belgium, resulting in a lucrative recording contract with RCA Victor Red Seal for 25 albums, only to have the label renege and buy out for a lump sum after only one LP was released.
That one LP, LM-2465, contained very satisfying performances of Prokofiev’s knuckle busting 2nd Piano Concerto with Rene Leibowitz conducting the Paris Conservatory Orchestra and the Haydn 35th Piano Sonata. Even though RCA did Malcolm a disfavor with his contract, some bigwig at the label seemed to have had a fondness for Prokofiev’s abrasive, less than popular masterpiece because it recorded the Boston Symphony twice in the Concerto with different soloists and conductors.
Following graduation from the University of Southern Maine at Gorham in 1973, I moved to Brookline, Massachusetts, that summer and got a job running the classical record department first at Jordan Marsh and then Discount Records, in Kenmore Square.
One evening at my apartment I heard a broadcast from Tanglewood in which Malcolm performed the Brahms 2nd Piano Concerto with Michael Tilson Thomas, conducting the Boston Symphony and for some reason wasn’t very impressed.
Fast forward to 1981 – I’m teaching in Houston, Texas, and attending a concert of its Symphony Orchestra at Jones Hall led by then-principal guest conductor Sir Alexander Gibson in which Malcolm performed a lovely Mozart Rondo for Piano and Orchestra, followed by Beethoven’s Choral Fantasia for Piano, Vocalists, Choir and Orchestra.
Afterwards in the Green Room, I approached Malcolm, who suddenly beckoned me to a sofa for the friendliest one-on-one chat about music and other more personal subjects, a conversation continued the following day by phone.
During the next seven years, Malcolm appeared every year or two with the Houston Symphony and I heard him play the Beethoven 2nd and Emperor Concertos, Mozart’s 25th and Coronation Concertos and the 2nd Concerto of Karl Maria von Weber, a composer, whose large number of pieces for piano was especially dear to Malcolm’s heart.
In 1986, the Sunday Arts section of the New York Times ran an essay by Malcolm on Weber’s piano music to commemorate the 200th anniversary of the composer’s birth. He also told me that he had volunteered to record this music free of charge but there were no takers among the record labels.
Whenever Malcolm came to Houston, a local piano teacher and her husband provided hospitality, along with a piano to practice on, and a private telephone by which we had conversations lasting as long as two hours. However, we never met for dinner at a restaurant because he felt rightfully as a guest that he should take his meals with the hosts. In the course of time I mentioned Tanglewood, Brahms 2nd Concerto. He expressed dissatisfaction with it not asking my opinion.
In 1985, my former wife and I vacationed in the Berkshires where Malcolm lived in an old farmhouse with magnificent picture windows and we visited with him one evening. That house was also less than a mile down the road from the Boston Symphony’s summer home at the Tanglewood Music Center in the middle of some of the most gorgeous countryside in New England.
The last time we visited was in 1988 after a concert in which Malcolm played the Mozart 25th Piano Concerto (my personal favorite of the 27); neither of us realized that he would not return to Jones Hall because he took ill with leukemia and died in July 1991, at the age of 56.
A truly great pianist and a wonderful friend!
And his playing can be heard on YouTube.
Susan Strasberg
Actress Susan Strasberg (1938-1999) was best known for her lead role in the original Broadway production of The Diary of Anne Frank, which ran for 717 performances.
In her 1980 memoir Bitter Sweet, she described the experience:
“The day we opened on Broadway, October 5, 1955, I was in a dither. The previous night I had dreamed that I could not remember my lines. I was worried about being able to do my work in front of so many of my family and friends. I couldn’t eat, my stomach was playing strange tricks on me.
“My father said, ‘Your nervousness is a sign of your sensitivity. If you weren’t nervous, you’d be dead. Have faith in yourself. All good actors have opening-night jitters. What’s important is to use it. Make it work for you. You wouldn’t be normal if you didn’t feel the way you do.’ ”
Anne’s father Otto Frank, the only survivor in the family of the extermination camps, sent a letter to the cast:
“You will all realize that for me this play is a part of my life, and the idea that my wife and children as well as I will be presented on the stage is a painful one to me. Therefore it is impossible for me to come and see it…my thoughts are with every one of you all the time, and I hope…the play will be a success and that the message which it contains will, through you, reach as many people as possible and awaken in them a sense of responsibility to humanity….”
Susan’s father was Lee Strasberg, the fearsomely brilliant director of the Actors Studio in New York and who mentored such talents as James Dean, Marilyn Monroe, Paul Newman, Al Pacino, etc., and who portrayed Hyman Roth, in Godfather 2.
The book contains a photo from 1956 of Susan visiting with Otto Frank, in London.

title: Fort Fairfield Water Exceeds Standard Copper Level
text:
FORT FAIRFIELD, Maine (WAGM) - Copper levels in Fort Fairfield’s drinking water are above the allowed standard.
The Fort Fairfield Utilities District mailed a notice to customers and posted the notice on the town website.
The notice states that testing done by the utilities district in late August found 1.75 mg of copper per liter in the town’s drinking water.
This exceeds the allowed standard of 1.3 mg per liter. District officials say while copper is an essential nutrient, drinking water above the standard for short periods may cause gastrointestinal discomfort.
Exposure over several years can lead to liver or kidney complications.
Officials say Fort Fairfield residents using town water that have Wilson’s disease, or other specific personal health concerns, should consult their doctor.
The Utilities District General Manager Noah Bernard says the high level of copper is not an emergency and says it isn’t necessary for residents to use alternative water sources, such as bottled water.
The Fort Fairfield Utilities District is currently working to correct the problem by reviewing its corrosion control treatment plan, increasing lead and copper testing, and continuing water quality parameter testing. Officials expect the problem to be solved by March of 2027.
Anyone with questions or looking for more information on the issue should contact the Fort Fairfield Utilities District at 472-0622.

title: Bicyclist killed in Pittsfield hit-and-run crash, police say
text:
PITTSFIELD — A 56-year-old bicyclist was killed late Tuesday afternoon in a hit-and-run crash, police said.
The incident, which remained under investigation Wednesday, on Peltoma Avenue was reported around 4:30 p.m., Chief Bernie Brunette of the Pittsfield Police Department said in a statement posted to social media.
The bicyclist, identified by police as Jeffrey Cookson, of Burnham, was found dead at the scene, Brunette said.
Witnesses told Pittsfield police officers they had seen a dark-colored sedan heading south “at a very high rate of speed,” Brunette said.
“They also described the sedan as a Volkswagen Jetta with a missing headlight and windshield damage,” the chief said.
Pittsfield police requested other law enforcement agencies to be on the lookout for the vehicle. Waldo County sheriff’s deputies found a black 2003 Volkswagen Jetta with damage consistent with the witnesses’ description parked on Horseback Road, near Cookson Road, in Burnham, according to Brunette’s statement.
The Waldo County Sheriff’s Office, along with Maine State Police, seized the vehicle to preserve evidence, Brunette said.
Police did not provide information about the driver or whom they believe owns the car.
Investigators believe speed and alcohol contributed to the crash, Brunette said.

title: Vehicle crashes into people on a sidewalk in North Hollywood
text:
3 dead after vehicle crashes into people in North Hollywood
Three people are dead, and three others are in critical condition after a vehicle crashed into people on a sidewalk next to a metro station in North Hollywood on Tuesday, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department.
A white SUV hit at least five people at the busy intersection just before 6 p.m., the Los Angeles Police Department reported. At least three people were taken to the hospital, including the driver, according to officials.
Officials have not determined the cause of the crash or ruled out anything.
“We don’t know if it was done intentionally, if it was done by accident,” LAPD Captain Warner Castillo said at a news conference Tuesday night.
The driver, whose name has not been released, is in his early 60s and officials are doing an exam to check if he was under the influence, Castillo said.
Mayor Karen Bass said the victims included street vendors and pedestrians.
“I’m heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted,” she said in a post on X.
Authorities will be checking the video in the area in what will be a “prolonged but very deliberate investigation,” said LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell.
Photos and videos posted online show a white vehicle on a sidewalk next to tents for vendors, along with emergency crews. Posts show a crew moved a person away on a stretcher.

title: ‘Criminal illegal alien’ arrested after telling United flight crew he had a bomb, Homeland Security says
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A man was arrested after telling the flight crew on a United plane that he had a bomb.
According to the Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office, Rony Gomez-Alberto, 34, started acting irrationally aboard United flight 2174 around 11:20 p.m.
Authorities said he told crew members that he had a bomb on board. The Department of Homeland Security said Gomez-Alberto is a “criminal illegal alien” and that he tried to “gain entry to the cockpit” during the flight.
There were 46 passengers and six crew members aboard the United flight from Newark, New Jersey, to New Orleans.
The plane safely landed at Louis Armstrong International Airport, and all passengers got off and were taken to the terminal.
Gomez-Alberto was arrested without incident and taken to the Jefferson Parish Correctional Center, where he was booked on charges of communicating false information of planned arson and terrorizing, deputies said. Immigration and Customs Enforcement also lodged a detainer for Gomez-Alberto.
According to Homeland Security, Gomez-Alberto’s criminal history includes felony bomb threat, felony threat, terroristic state offenses and disorderly conduct.
He is from Honduras and has been removed from the country twice and was released a third time, pending removal proceedings, by a judge.

title: Mississippi fined $250K after fans threw trash on field during loss to Georgia
text:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (AP) — The University of Mississippi has been fined $250,000 by the Southeastern Conference after fans threw trash on the field and delayed the game during the first half of a blowout home loss to Georgia over the weekend.
In announcing the fine, the SEC said the objects thrown on the field during the second quarter interrupted competitive play and endangered participants. The penalty was assessed under the conference’s sportsmanship, game management and alcohol availability policies.
“The actions taken by the Conference are consistent with SEC bylaws and commissioner’s regulations related to the availability of alcoholic beverages at athletics events which state, ‘If cans or plastic bottles are used as projectiles or otherwise cause game management issues, the institution is subject to an immediate fine and suspension of the alcohol sales privilege,’” the statement said.
Ole Miss is not having alcohol sales banned for home games at this point, though the SEC reserves the right to do so in the future.
The Rebels, at the time ranked 12th, lost 42-7 on Saturday to the then-second-ranked Bulldogs. Georgia is now atop the AP Top 25, while Ole Miss fell to No. 19.

title: ICE increases security at Scarborough facility amid vandalism, armed protests
text:
SCARBOROUGH, Maine (WMTW) - Vandalism and the presence of near-daily protesters, some of them armed, have led to increased security at the Scarborough ICE facility, according to a spokesperson for the agency.
There has been a small group of protesters outside the Scarborough facility ever since ICE agent David Brouillette shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian father, when he was leaving for work in Biddeford last July.
According to the lawyer for Guerrero’s widow and members of Maine’s congressional delegation, Guerrero was not the intended target of the ICE operation and was in the U.S. under a valid federal work authorization.
Nearly four months after his death, ICE observers still have a presence outside the agency’s facility on Manson Libby Road in Scarborough. Some are monitoring the movements of agents in and out of the facility and sharing that information on social media. Others are calling for the prosecution of Brouillette and “abolishing” ICE entirely, arguing that the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown is unlawful and is spreading fear within immigrant communities in Maine.
Those fears were cited by the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition on Monday, when the organization notified community members that recent sightings of “several new vehicles” arriving at the Scarborough facility were assigned to building security, not immigration enforcement.
“We understand that any increase in immigration enforcement presence can cause fear and uncertainty,” wrote Ruben Torres, the director of advocacy and policy at the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition. “We are sharing this update to provide context and help community members distinguish this change in Scarborough ICE building security from broader enforcement activity.”
Democratic congresswoman Chellie Pingree took to Facebook to share a similar message, writing that security had increased specifically because of armed protesters.
“Mainers deserve to know what’s happening in their communities and I’m continuing to monitor the situation closely,” wrote Rep. Pingree. “Maine has endured too much chaos and violence at the hands of this rogue, unaccountable agency already.”
On Tuesday, at least one protester could be seen outside the Scarborough facility with a firearm. Open carry is legal in Maine, assuming the firearm holder is legally allowed to possess one.
A spokesperson for ICE told WMTW Tuesday that the agency’s officers are “under constant threat from violent agitators.” The spokesperson claimed that there have been six different occasions of vandalism at the Scarborough facility in the past three months.
ICE would not disclose whether the agency had plans for increased enforcement operations in Maine, citing “operational security purposes.”

title: Jaylen Brown gives Jayson Tatum cold shoulder before Celtics beat 76ers
text:
PHILADELPHIA — Jayson Tatum dapped up Jaylen Brown with a friendly tap on the shoulder and thump on the chest which his former Boston teammate ignored.
Brown gave him a cold shoulder. Tatum got the hot hand.
Brown ignored Tatum’s brief show of affection, perhaps a fitting illustration of a frosty relationship that has included radio silence between the two All-Stars since Brown was traded in the summer to the Sixers.
“No headlines about anything like that,” Tatum said. “I was just getting ready for the game. Ready for jump ball. Go out there and compete and have some fun and try and get the win.”
Tatum scored 21 points and outplayed Brown, and Paul George reminded fans he was in that blockbuster trade with six 3-pointers for 36 points in his return to Philadelphia, leading the Celtics past the 76ers 123-101 on Tuesday night.
PG flashed a reminder — both with his game and a middle finger — that he can still throw it back to his All-Star prime.
He scored 14 straight points in the fourth quarter and made six of Boston’s 22 3-pointers. George flipped off a Sixers fan in a bowling motion after he sank his fourth 3 of the game for a 100-82 lead that pushed the Celtics to their ninth win in 10 games.
“There was a fan being a (jerk),” George said. “Ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes. Dropped the ball on the ground as if I’m a dog to go fetch or got get it instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do. So I rolled him a middle finger in return.”
The Celtics had all the fun in this one.
Tatum shook hands and exchanged a big hug with LeBron James. Tatum later dunked over James and seemingly got the last laugh in the first matchup this season between the two top teams in the East.
Brown and Tatum kept their distance during pregame warmups ahead of Tuesday’s game when the Celtics played Philadelphia for the first time since the summer trade that saw Brown surprisingly switch sides.
Brown hit some jumpers on the Sixers’ end of the court. Tatum warmed up on his side with his Celtics teammates.
Neither All-Star decided to shoot his shot with the other.
Brown was traded with draft picks to the rival 76ers in July for George.
Brown ran into early foul trouble and scored only 13 points in his first game against Boston since the 2024 NBA Finals MVP was traded. He picked up two quick fouls in the first quarter and was whistled for his fourth early in the second half.
Brown declined to get into his Tatum brush off.
“I’m just focused on doing what’s best for my team,” Brown said. “Everything else was just, to be honest, I wasn’t paying attention.”
Brown got the better of Tatum early when he picked off his old teammate’s pass and fed the ball to Tyrese Maxey for a 3-pointer.
Brown said last month there was “ no beef ” between himself and Tatum, even as the dissection over the end of their relationship had dragged into the season.
The trade has been a success for both teams. The 76ers, with Brown and James aboard, are 9-3 and the Celtics now have the best record in the East at 9-2.
Joe Mazzulla coached both players when the Celtics won the 2024 NBA championship. He was ready to put the circus after the trade behind him and is proud that Tatum never had to eat crow — or any lamb chops.
“They’re just words,” Mazzulla said. “It’s not like his life’s threatened. There’s no weapons. There’s no one throwing anything at him. No one’s attacking him. It’s not really that big of a deal.”
Brown was a five-time All-Star and wound up with career-best averages of 28.7 points, 6.9 rebounds and 5.1 assists last season while Tatum missed most of last season while recovering from an Achilles tendon tear that happened during the 2025 playoffs.
With both players healthy and commanding hefty salaries that would eventually account for roughly 70% of Boston’s salary cap, the franchise faced a difficult decision about which player to keep. Boston chose Tatum.
The Sixers were happy to part with the 36-year-old George.
George shone in Philly on Tuesday after two flat seasons with the Sixers. George was poised to join Joel Embiid and Maxey to form a Philly Big Three when he left the Clippers and signed a four-year, $212 million free-agent contract ahead of the 2024 season.
George instead was ravaged by knee and adductor injuries — among others — that robbed the nine-time All-Star of his full potential that he flashed in his three previous NBA stops. He was suspended 25 games last season for violating the terms of the NBA’s anti-drug program.
George — whose 20.4 points entering the game is higher than either of his two seasons in Philadelphia — simply joined a list that included Jimmy Butler and James Harden of All-Star hired guns that failed to win a title with the Sixers.
Give this one to George and Tatum.
Let’s do it again Jan. 21 in Boston.

title: Trump administration to pursue public land sales and a decrease in federal ownership
text:
BILLINGS, Mont. (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate,” according to a new five-year plan presented by the Interior Department.
Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant” lands. They offered no details on what lands could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales.
The plan also calls for strategic land transfers and exchanges to support greater energy production, a centerpiece of the administration’s pro-fossil fuel policies. It reflects the Trump administration’s view of most public lands as assets to be used, rather than to be set aside for preservation.
The Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles (1.9 million square kilometers) of land — an area greater than Texas and California combined — along with vast underground mineral reserves. That puts the agency at the center of a contentious, decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land.
The Associated Press sent emails to Interior officials Wednesday requesting comment and further details.
Most public lands are in Western states. In some, the government controls the vast majority of land, protecting it from potential exploitation but also hindering growth.
Interior officials said that under the plan a portion of any land sale proceeds would go back to the buyer for conservation purposes elsewhere.
Yet it’s uncertain if Interior Secretary Doug Burgum can achieve the administration’s goals without cooperation from Congress.
Some conservative lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. Among the proposals, Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee suggested selling more than 2 million acres (8,000 square kilometers) to states or other entities.
Those efforts failed after amid bipartisan opposition.
The plan sets out a road map for the Interior Department’s priorities and actions between 2026 and 2030. Future administrations would not be bound by it.
The department regulates mining, drilling, grazing, recreation and other activities that many state and local officials want greater control over.
The agency’s strategic plan was last updated four years ago under former Democratic President Joe Biden.

title: Hampden Planning Board approves wastewater system expansion at Pine Tree Landfill
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - The Hampden Planning Board voted Tuesday night to approve a request to expand a wastewater management system at the Pine Tree Landfill.
Request tied to Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion
New England Waste Systems of Maine, a subsidiary of Casella Waste Management, made the request as part of a broader effort to expand the state-owned Juniper Ridge Landfill in West Old Town.
State conditions required the company to have a licensed, operating system to treat PFAS before that expansion could move forward. PFAS are often called “forever chemicals” because they break down very slowly.
Before the vote, a representative walked the Planning Board and city residents through what the proposed expansion would look like and how it would be effective.
Residents raise concerns
The decision to move forward drew concerns from a few local residents about landfill runoff.
“We’re concerned because the technologies they’re proposing, though they haven’t put in the full proposal, to remove, separate the PFAS is foam fractionation, which is not the best method. It cannot get rid of the dominant PFAS, which is short-chain PFAS. And as we know, PFAS causes cancer, teratogenic effects, effects on livers and kidneys,” environmentalist Grace Nichols said.
Hampden Director of Planning and Economic Development Amy Ryder gave an idea of what next steps would look like for the plan.
“There’s approval with conditions,” she said. “Of course, we want approval from Bangor Wastewater to make sure that they can carry this and are on board, as well as make sure they get the appropriate DEP permits. Once those are accomplished, then they will be approved to do the expansion.”
Leachate transfer
With the growth of the leachate storage tank, the amount of leachate being carried will increase as it is transferred through the Hermon sewer system to Bangor Waste Systems.

title: Immigration arrests go on unabated despite Trump's misgivings after the GOP's midterm wipeout
text:
It’s business as usual for President Donald Trump’s deportation offensive despite the Republican wipeout in the midterm elections.
In Los Angeles, masked immigration officers in body armor blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a heavily Latino neighborhood early Saturday. In central Alabama, twin 19-year-old brothers from Venezuela were arrested while driving back to college a day after the election.
Advocates reported arrests from California to Michigan to Massachusetts.
After Democrats trounced the GOP and won control of the next Congress, Trump said his immigration crackdown may have been “too tough” and suggested it was time to sit down with the rival party.
“I’d love to do something on immigration,” he said in an interview with CBS “60 Minutes” recorded Friday.
Hours later, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, said his orders had not changed.
“Deportations will continue,” Mullin wrote in an online post the day after the election, warning that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement takes no days off and that “this includes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and Election Day.”
María Bilbao, a campaign coordinator for the American Friends Service Committee in Miami, said she has received at least one call a day from someone detained in South Florida since the election.
“Everything remains exactly the same. The arrests have not ceased at all,” Bilbao said.
Florida Highway Patrol officers and ICE agents have detained people in their cars, as well as places including supermarkets, pharmacies and gas stations. Immigrants under supervision have also been arrested when they showed up at ICE’s Miami office for their appointments.
Officers assembled outside a Los Angeles hospital
Erick Gasca, 31, got home Friday night after an evening playing board games with friends. He lives near Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Los Angeles.
An “unprecedented” number of vehicles with tinted windows and no license plates were parked near the hospital’s emergency room entrance, he said.
“I thought they were going to raid the hospital or something,” he recalled.
The Department of Homeland Security declined to explain the officers’ presence there, though Bill Essayli, the top Justice Department prosecutor in Los Angeles, said they were bringing a detainee for medical treatment. Essayli said two people were arrested for assaulting federal agents.
“ICE does not target hospitals, schools, or churches,” DHS said in a statement.
The agents’ presence attracted some 30 residents and passersby. Footage shot by Gasca’s cousin, Michelle Rivera, shows protesters shouting and officers pinning someone down.
The hospital said it wasn’t involved.
“White Memorial does not participate in immigration enforcement,” hospital president Daniel Fontoura said in a statement, adding it would not let such activities “compromise our commitment to patient care and safety.”
A couple is arrested at the Phoenix airport
A married couple from Orlando, Florida, was arrested Saturday at the airport in Phoenix while traveling to a funeral.
Gustavo Romanello and Agustin Baccega, both from Argentina, have work permits while they seek asylum after entering the United States about six years ago, according to Jonathan Batchelor, a family friend.
Batchelor was on the phone with them at the time. A mutual friend died Friday and the couple was visiting for the funeral Saturday. As the couple left the airport, two casually dressed officers asked if one was Agustin Baccega. Batchelor heard the officer say, “Asylum seekers are not in the United States legally.”
Batchelor said he could hear Romanello walking alongside his husband during the arrest and asking the officers how to collect his things. Batchelor said they then asked what his name was, “and then the guard said, ‘Oh, do you have another set of handcuffs? This is another one.’”
The voices grew distant, and the call then ended.
Both men remain in detention centers. They worked as acrobats in Florida and had no criminal record, Batchelor said.
“This is just taking good people who have been following the rules out of their lives and out of the lives of those who rely upon them and care about them,” Batchelor said.
DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the arrests.
Twin brothers seized while driving back to college
The brothers were headed back to college after visiting their parents when they were stopped in a small city in central Alabama.
Luis and Carlos Orta-Santoro, 19-year-olds born in Venezuela and living in the U.S. for four years, are soccer players at Wallace State Community College in Hanceville, Alabama.
Relatives say they have pending asylum applications, valid work permits, and no criminal records. Both are now in an immigration detention facility.
“Our family is devastated,” said their aunt, Carolina Orta.
DHS said that while they had entered the country legally, they had “overstayed in defiance of our laws,” and their case would be heard by an immigration judge. It said pending asylum applications do not confer legal status in the U.S.
The school said in a statement, “Both young men are valued members of the Wallace State community, and our thoughts are with them during this difficult time. We sincerely hope for a positive resolution to their situation.”
A Haitian boy is taken into custody, drawing protests in San Diego
An 8-year-old Haitian boy had been living with his uncle in San Diego since his father was deported last year. The uncle, who is not a legal guardian, took him to an ICE office when the boy was summoned Nov. 4 and taken into custody.
That left the boy “without the support of their family, community and their school,” according to a letter to top administration officials from San Diego Unified School District Superintendent Fabi Bagula and school board members.
“Children should not lose access to education simply because of circumstances unfolding around them,” they wrote.
ICE has defended its actions.
Johny Oxeda, pastor of the Fairmount Haitian Community Church, which helped get legal representation for the boy, said he’ll ultimately benefit by going through legal channels.
Activists, though, were furious.
“This is not child protection,” said Guerline Jozef of Haitian Bridge Alliance, adding, “this is state-inflicted trauma.”
___
Associated Press reporters Gisela Salomon in Miami and Elliot Spagat in San Diego contributed.

title: Teen arrested in killing of Ghanaian student, 15, on his way to school in New York City
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A teenager was arrested Wednesday in the fatal shooting of a 15-year-old Ghanaian immigrant on his way to school, New York City police said as the victim’s family, Ghana’s government and civil rights advocates pressed for justice.
The 17-year-old male suspect was arrested on murder and other charges in the Oct. 29 death of Javits Frimpong, the New York Police Department said. The suspect’s name wasn’t released, and it wasn’t immediately clear whether he has an attorney who can respond to the allegations.
The killing has sparked protests in New York and prompted Mayor Zohran Mamdani to ask President Donald Trump to arrange a visa for Frimpong’s mother, Doris Adu Gyamfi, to travel to the U.S.
“I need justice for my child,” she said at a news conference Wednesday, then broke down in tears.
Police didn’t say what motivated the gunfire on a Bronx street as Frimpong was walking to school. The teen’s family has said he was being bullied at school, and Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said last week that officers were looking into bullying or other possible motives, such as robbery. Kenny suggested there were “three perpetrators” involved.
News of the arrest came as Frimpong’s kin, civil rights lawyer Ben Crump, the Rev. Al Sharpton and Ghana’s U.N. ambassador, Samuel Yao Kumah, gathered at Sharpton’s National Action Network headquarters for a previously planned news conference.
After leading a chant of “Justice for Javits!,” Crump noted the arrest, but added: “What we’re all wondering is: Why? Why did they kill this young man, this person with such a bright future?”
As Crump spoke, the teen’s mother wept on Sharpton’s shoulder.
Frimpong’s death has shocked Ghanaians, Kumah said, calling the arrest “a step in the right direction.”
Frimpong joined his father in the U.S. a year ago, seeking better educational opportunities, his relatives said. His father, Thomas Frimpong, said his son “was living the dream.”
The teen’s sister, Millicent Frimpong, said he aimed to become a physician and to follow in family footsteps by joining the military.
“He was so ready that he made me save my uniform for him,” she recalled.
She said he wrote in his journal that he was proud to be in the U.S. and that school was going well.
Thomas Frimpong has said that school bullies were bothering his son, a quiet teen who spent much of his time on his cellphone, but that Javits told him: “Dad, I’m OK.” Two students were suspended because of the bullying, the father said.
A message seeking information about the matter was sent Wednesday to the city Department of Education.

title: Driver in deadly crash in Los Angeles arrested on 3 murder counts, police say
text:
Driver in deadly crash in Los Angeles arrested on 3 murder counts, police say
The 61-year-old driver of a minivan that killed three people when it crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station during rush hour was arrested on three counts of murder, a police spokesperson said Wednesday.
Police have said the driver was taken out of the vehicle and was able to talk, but he appeared in shock after Tuesday's crash. Officials were not immediately able to determine the cause or whether he acted intentionally.
Police identified the driver as Ihor Demianenko, a resident of the Valley Village neighborhood of Los Angeles, Officer Norma Eisenman said. He was booked on three counts of murder, although the police spokesperson said she didn’t know whether he was still at a hospital early Wednesday.
It was not immediately clear if Demianenko had a lawyer who could respond to the allegations.
The crash at a busy intersection in the North Hollywood neighborhood also critically injured two women. The vehicle ended up under a food vendor’s tent, and Mayor Karen Bass said the victims included street vendors and pedestrians.
Investigators will go through video of the crash frame by frame, LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said.
“It will be probably a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here,” he said.
Luis Luna-Guzman was working at a burger stand nearby when he heard a loud boom and saw people on the ground along with food and cups. People nearby started running toward the crash.
As he moved closer, he found an injured woman lying near the bike racks, her face, arms and legs bloody, he said, recalling her eyes were closed as she moaned in pain.
“I told her, ‘Don’t move, help is coming,’” Luna-Guzman said, adding that he saw a woman’s body nearby, while another woman was lying unmoving on the stairs leading to the station.
Adrin Nazarian, a Los Angeles City Council member whose district includes North Hollywood, described the area as a close-knit community where there is always commotion and activity.
The minivan was on the sidewalk surrounded by debris Tuesday night with its driver’s side door left open and an air bag deployed. Fire engines and emergency crews worked nearby as a helicopter flew overhead.
One entrance to the metro remained closed Tuesday night, but otherwise the property wasn’t impacted and the stations for the bus and subway were open, according to Jose Ubaldo, spokesperson for the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority.

title: Augusta council approves preliminary deal to process Hatch Hill trash in Hampden
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Augusta City Council approved a preliminary agreement with Municipal Waste Solutions to change how trash is handled at Hatch Hill, the regional landfill serving the city and seven surrounding communities.
Municipal Waste Solutions would process Augusta’s waste at a facility in Hampden.
How the proposal would work
Under the proposal, most household waste brought to Hatch Hill would be hauled to Hampden. Recyclable materials would be recovered there without residents having to separate them from their trash.
Recycling goals
City Manager Jared Mills said the plan could improve Augusta’s recycling rates and contribute to Maine’s goal of recycling 50% of the state’s municipal waste.
“What we’re doing now in Augusta, we recycle even with the bins that we have. When we had two bins that were open, we’re at like 3-5% recycling rate in Augusta,” Mills said. “This is going to boost us whether people want to recycle or not to like upwards of 30-50%.”
Landfill life and next steps
Mills said the plan could extend Hatch Hill’s life and avoid an expansion of the landfill that would cost millions of dollars.
A final contract is now being developed.

title: China TIF committee weighs in on new laws
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
China Tax Increment Financing (TIF) Committee members spent the first hour of their Nov. 9 meeting discussing with consultant Raegan LaRochelle recent changes in state law.
LaRochelle, attending virtually, said the changes are intended to expand the kinds of projects for which municipalities can use TIF funds, instead of tax dollars.
China’s TIF money comes from Central Maine Power Company’s tax payments on its power line through the town and its South China substation. The money goes into a TIF fund that is to be used to promote economic development.
The newest law changes, LaRochelle said, extend TIF uses to cover construction, renovation or operation of public safety structures and shelters; and construction or renovation – but not operation – of municipal services facilities.
Committee members discussed the fact that China’s fire stations are all owned by the private fire departments, not by the town. Committee member Joann Austin wondered if the departments being non-profit organizations would make a difference.
They listed multiple structures that should qualify as municipal services facilities, from the buildings in the town office complex and at the transfer station to the former Weeks Mills schoolhouse.
Discussion touched on China’s TIF districts, in China Village and on Route 3, and on how well the districts relate to China’s comprehensive plan – not well, Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood said.
From the audience, China Four Seasons Club President Thomas Rumpf reported on how his organization has used its TIF funds in the past year: almost two miles of new trails, and several repaired or improved trails, including a 7.7 mile loop now suitable for horses.
Many of China’s trails are now multi-use, not just for ATVs and snowmobiles, thanks to TIF funds, he said.
LaRochelle and Hapgood plan to continue discussing what effects the updated TIF could have on projects in China, and to bring more information to the next TIF committee meeting. Rumpf had two suggestions: developing the portable building into an emergency shelter, and replacing the bridge in Weeks Mills Village.
TIF plan revisions and expenditures need voters’ approval. Hapgood suggested the committee aim to have proposed warrant articles for the June 2027 annual town business meeting ready by March 1, 2027.
The next TIF committee meeting is tentatively scheduled for 6 p.m., Monday, Dec. 7. Alternate date is Monday, Dec. 21. Monday, Jan. 4, 2027, is either another alternate, or a potential follow-up date if a prior meeting is held.

title: ICE agent in deadly Biddeford shooting had history of anti-immigrant rhetoric, New York Times reports
text:
BIDDEFORD, Maine (WMTW) - The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent involved in the fatal shooting of a Colombian man that happened in Maine nearly four months ago expressed anti-immigrant sentiments in emails sent to his family members, according to a report from The New York Times.
David Brouillette had been identified by The Associated Press as the ICE officer who shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13. Both Brouillette’s first ex-wife and his daughter told the AP that Brouillette told them he was the one who shot and killed Guerrero. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has declined to identify Brouillette as the ICE agent involved in the shooting.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that Brouillette’s sister, Elizabeth Emen, shared a series of emails with The Times from 2021 in which Brouillette berated Emen and their relatives and criticized her for her longtime relationship with a Colombian man, with whom she had two children.
The report from The Times also goes into detail about Brouillette’s recruiting history, citing an anonymous source who said Brouillette was sped through the vetting process and that he was cleared to work for ICE in December 2025.
WMTW contacted Homeland Security with a request for comment about the report from The New York Times, but has yet to receive a reply.
Ben Gideon, an attorney representing Guerrero’s wife and his estate, has issued a statement in response to The Times’ report on Brouillette.
“David Brouillette is the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training,” Gideon said in his statement. “Johan Sebastian’s death was not an inevitable accident. It was a natural and predictable choice of the policies of our government and its political leadership.”
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat who represents Maine’s 1st Congressional District, said that she demanded answers from Homeland Security about training and background checks in the days following Guerrero’s death, and that Wednesday’s report from The New York Times makes a full, independent investigation even more urgent.
“DHS must release Brouillette’s hiring, vetting, training, and deployment records and cooperate fully with independent investigators,” Pingree said in a statement. “Responsibility reaches beyond the officer who pulled the trigger. It extends to the leadership that armed and deployed him, and to an administration that put its deportation agenda ahead of human life. Every official responsible must be held accountable. Johan Sebastián’s family deserves justice, and I will keep fighting until they get it.”
Pingree and U.S. Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, have said Guerrero was not the target of the ICE operation that ultimately resulted in his death. King and Pingree also said that Guerrero, the father of a 3-year-old girl, had no criminal history.
In September, another attorney representing Guerrero’s family testified before members of Congress. The testimony was part of a public forum examining several deadly shootings involving federal immigration agents.

title: Gardens Aglow: One of Maine's most popular holiday attractions is set to open
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gardens Aglow: One of Maine's most popular holiday attractions is set to open
The theme for this year's display is "Gathered in Maine" and there are three different pricing tiers this year, depending on the day of the week.
Gardens Aglow: One of Maine's most popular holiday attractions is set to open
The theme for this year's display is "Gathered in Maine" and there are three different pricing tiers this year, depending on the day of the week.
One of Maine's most popular holiday season attractions opens this weekend.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens in Boothbay announced on Tuesday that Gardens Aglow will open on Saturday, Nov. 14. The huge light display will be open through Jan. 2, 2027.
The theme for this year's display is "Gathered in Maine," and new features include a maple tapping scene, a landscape fit for mushroom foraging, and a larger-than-life anthill with an army of ants carrying leaves and berries.
“Our team has been working hard since August on this year’s show. I say this every year, but this year might be the best,” said Gretchen Ostherr, President and CEO of Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens. “Even though I get to watch—and take part in the light hanging—I am always amazed at how we transform from a green sanctuary into a sparkling wonderland. We can’t wait to celebrate this season with families from Maine and New England.”
This is the 12th year for the holiday lights display at the gardens, featuring hundreds of thousands of lights. People come from all over New England and beyond to see Gardens Aglow, which has been named one of the Top 5 Best Botanical Garden Holiday Lights in the country by USA TODAY several times. About 1 million people have visited the display since the gardens started the experience.
Tickets for Gardens Aglow start at $20 for adults, $18 for seniors and veterans, and $10 for children ages 3 to 17. Children under the age of 3 are free. Tickets are cheapest on weekdays and most expensive on Saturdays.
For more information on pricing and time slots, visit GardensAglow.org.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens covers 325 acres, making it the largest public garden in New England. The gardens feature two miles of hiking trails, 19 acres of ornamental and themed gardens featuring native plants of Maine and those suited to northern coastal conditions, nearly a mile of saltwater frontage, a children’s garden, a sensory garden, and more.

title: Buxton elected a charter commission. What will it do?
text:
Buxton voters on Election Day elected six members to a charter commission. Joined by three appointed members, they are responsible for revising the town’s charter, a document that acts as a constitution for the town.
The town’s charter must be updated at least every seven years, but members say they expect this revision will be more substantial than previous adjustments made since it was adopted in 2000. Town Clerk John Myers said the commission could choose to draft the charter entirely anew. If approved by voters, their work will shape how Buxton is governed going forward.
The elected members of the commission are Debra Bickford, former Board of Selectmen member Clifford Emery, town Treasurer William Hall, Mary MacLeod, board member Beverly Young, and Kevin Young.
The Board of Selectmen appointed appeals board member and former planning board member Henry Huntley, and former Board of Selectmen member Jean Harmon to the commission. It also tapped Mark Blier, a former Board of Selectmen member, current appeals board member and state representative for Maine House District 138 whose term ends on Dec. 1.
Most commission members said they are open to many ideas on how to change the charter, but a few topics are top of mind.
According to Myers, Buxton is the largest community in Maine that does not have a town manager, which is a frequent point of discussion among town residents and employees. The charter commission could choose to add that position.
“I think (adding a town manager) does need to be explored, because we do need to consider it as the town grows,” Harmon said. “But it’s up to the voters in the town to decide, because there is a cost associated with that.”
Some members also say they are interested in changing the town clerk role from an elected position to an appointed one to ensure someone with experience takes over when Myers retires.
“I think that a qualified person, put in that position, appointed, would be of importance to the community,” Blier said.
Blier and Huntley both said they would also like to change the way Buxton sells surplus equipment from a bidding system to an auction system because they think it would make the town more money.
MacLeod, a Buxton resident of 20 years, said she ran for the commission because she has found local politics are more effective than state and national politics. She started attending public meetings recently to advocate for data center restrictions before Buxton voters passed a 180-day moratorium on the facilities last month.
She believes the charter could be changed to make certain processes easier and language clearer.
“There seems to be a consensus to some degree that, those who serve as selectmen need to have more accountability, but also more latitude to make important decisions when they need to be made,” MacLeod said. “The way it is right now, it’s created a little bit of tension with the community, but it’s certainly nothing that couldn’t be fixed.”
Voters at a special town meeting in October rejected an article to use $6,351 of unassigned surplus funds toward a detective vehicle to replace one that was ruined in an accident in June. The item was controversial because the Board of Selectmen had already approved the expenditure over the summer as an emergency, allowing the town to buy the vehicle before sending the article for funding to voters.
Bickford, a retired teacher who became interested in local government through volunteering with the organization Aging in Buxton, believes that ethics for town officials should be more clearly defined in the charter. She also says Buxton should switch from an annual town meeting system for voting on the budget to a ballot system so that more people can vote without attending a meeting.
Emery was a Board of Selectmen member for 23 years. He declined to specify which aspects of the charter he is interested in changing before the commission begins meeting, but he hopes to bring his knowledge of the town’s history and politics to the group.
“I think it’s going to be something that somebody’s going to need to kind of guide a little bit,” Emery said. “When people come in with an extreme thing, maybe somebody can kind of explain why it’s the way that it is.”
All the commission members who responded to requests for interviews said they are looking forward to hearing input from the other members. The first meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. on Nov. 30 at Buxton Town Hall.
Myers said the commission has nine months to provide a preliminary report on its changes and can request an extension from the board of up to 24 months.
“(The charter commission) isn’t a compilation of people that were just appointed by the Select Board because they think they’re going to favor what they decide,” Huntley said. “There’s some pretty disparate views there.”

title: Veterans should not be going hungry as we thank them for their service
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
William Lambers, a historian, is the author of “The Road to Peace” and partnered with the UN World Food Program on the book “Ending World Hunger.”
Lt. Col. Will Brown was on a mission during World War I that took an unexpected turn. Brown was in southern France with the U.S. Army. He was checking out road conditions as the U.S. and Allies looked to finally defeat Germany and the Central Powers.
But his mission changed very quickly. Brown got official word that the Armistice of Nov. 11, 1918 had taken effect. The war was over and Brown suddenly became a messenger of peace.
Brown went town to town in southern France, sharing the wonderful news with the French people. He cried out in French the words “Finis la guerre” which meant the war’s over. Families would run to greet Brown. Children and their parents were waving flags in the streets celebrating the joyous news.
Brown’s peace mission was reported in his hometown newspaper, the Indianapolis Star, including parts of a letter he wrote: “I can not express my gratitude at being able to perform such a mission, nor can I describe the relief in my own mind and heart at the thoughts that hostilities have ceased and we no longer have to stand up as targets to an enemy’s shellfire, gas attacks or other barbarous methods by which this horrible war has been conducted ….”
Brown was so thankful for the end to the war and prayed that a lasting peace was in sight. After being in the horror that was supposed to be “The war to end all wars,” peace was the great hope. Armistice Day, November 11, celebrates the end of World War I and the hope for peace.
But we are still searching for a lasting world peace.
On Armistice Day, we must keep up the quest for an end to all wars and a forever peace. That is a mission we must never abandon. In fact one of the lessons of World War I is that conflict gives rise to another powerful enemy, hunger. The war had destroyed agriculture and food supplies.
Millions of civilians in Europe faced starvation after the Armistice and were saved by food from the American people. Many veterans were part of the American Relief Administration that delivered this life-saving aid.
We must never forget that where there is war there is hunger and famine. We should bring food for peace to those in need around the world. This is a peace mission we all can advocate for and support.
Armistice Day is today known as Veterans Day to honor all those who have served in the military. We should also remember to help those service members who are struggling in hunger. During World War II, America started a food stamp program to help families in need on the homefront. Military veterans were among those able to purchase groceries thanks to the food stamps.
Today, the modern day version of food stamps is the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Over a million military veterans use SNAP to buy groceries. However a law passed by Congress last year makes it harder for veterans to keep these SNAP benefits beyond three months. Veterans are now required to fill out paperwork after three months demonstrating work and volunteer hours so they can keep receiving SNAP benefits. Previously veterans were exempt from these rules.
There is now the danger that some veterans could lose their SNAP benefits if they fail to complete the complex paperwork or get enough work or volunteer hours. Congress should take action to make sure veterans who need SNAP don’t have to jump through hoops to retain these benefits. Military veterans who need SNAP should get an exemption from the time limit and work rules.
On this Veterans Day let’s thank our soldiers for their service and give them a helping hand. We must continue searching for that lasting peace that the Armistice of 1918 gave us hope could be achieved.

title: Southern Maine may see first snow of the season by week’s end
text:
Snow is on its way to southern parts of Maine for the first time this season, but whether the flakes will reach the coast is still up in the air.
The National Weather Service expects the precipitation to reach the region late Thursday and depart by early Saturday. The highest likelihood for snow to accumulate is on Friday in areas at least 1,000 feet above sea level, but lower-elevation areas could still see light snow by midmorning.
Southern Oxford County and northwestern York County stand a 30% to 40% chance of seeing at least 1 inch of snow Friday, according to the weather service. Other parts of interior southern Maine can also expect snow, whereas regions farther north are not expected to see much.
“We’re still trying to get a grasp on how continuous or showery the precipitation may be,” Greg Cornwell, a meteorologist at the weather service office in Gray, said Wednesday afternoon. “Right now, the best confidence of pretty steady precipitation is south of Augusta. … North of there, it might be quite a bit lighter.”
The southern coast stands a very slim chance of seeing snow, according to the weather service.
“I think there’s going to be enough warm air to cause most of that to be rain,” Cornwell explained.
If coastal Mainers do catch some flakes, it will most likely be when temperatures dip overnight Thursday into early Friday, he said. Still, accumulation there remains doubtful.
“There are a lot of complicating factors as to whether you get snow to stick,” Cornwell said, “but it’s something to keep an eye on.”
The meteorologist cautioned Mainers farther inland to prepare for what could be the first messy commute of the season Friday morning.
“For those traveling in the interior, it’s the first snow that may stick on the roads at points during your commute,” Cornwell said. “Just take it easy, give yourself plenty of time and remember your braking distance may be a little shorter than you think in wintry conditions.”
Parts of northern Maine, including Caribou, got measurable snow in mid-October, while light flakes fell in Rangeley and portions of western Maine over the weekend.

title: Portland City Council could soon pursue cruise ship scrubber wash ban
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Portland City Council will consider a resolution Monday that would recommend banning cruise ships from using exhaust gas cleaning systems — known as “scrubbers” — or from discharging scrubber wash water while berthed at city-owned piers.
If approved, Portland would become the first port in Maine to ban their use.
The resolution, which would request that city staff amend Portland’s tariff structure for regulating cruise ships, has been a long time coming for environmental advocates, who have pointed to evidence that scrubber wash discharge contains acidic pollutants that are harmful to marine wildlife and the ocean.
Forwarded by councilors Regina Phillips and Pious Ali, the resolution states that a ban would protect Portland’s coastal ecosystem and points to similar measures implemented elsewhere that have not disrupted “maritime trade or port competitiveness.”
Open-loop scrubbers use seawater to wash exhaust gases, after which the untreated or minimally treated wash water is discharged into surrounding waters.
JoAnn Locktov, co-founder of Portland Cruise Control, said Wednesday that the resolution would stop an estimated 32 million gallons of toxic scrubber wash water from being dumped into Casco Bay per season.
“Cruise ships shouldn’t be allowed to turn their air pollution into our water pollution,” she said. “This is about protecting the bay, not reducing cruise visits.”
Locktov said Seattle bans scrubber wash at berths through its port tariff, and just had its biggest cruise season ever.
The proposed resolution in Portland states that viable alternatives exist to open-loop scrubbers, including the use of low-sulfur marine gas oil, as well as closed-loop or hybrid scrubbers that retain wash water in holding tanks.
This spring, city staff proposed a cruise ship tariff structure that provided a $2 per passenger discount for ships using low-sulfur fuels such as marine gas oil. However, the proposal never made it through budget discussions because of pushback from Portland Cruise Control and city councilors.
Councilor Wes Pelletier, who made the motion to remove the proposed discount, said Wednesday that he did so because he preferred an outright ban.
“It’s something that’s doable and keeps Casco Bay cleaner, and I’m happy to see us getting to a place where it’s on the tariff,” he said.
Roughly 85 ships — some of them visiting several times — were scheduled to dock in Portland harbor in 2026.

title: Augusta woman issued a disorderly conduct summons after August Quarry Tap Room incident
text:
The woman involved in a physical altercation in August at the Quarry Tap Room in Hallowell has been issued a summons to appear in court on a charge of disorderly conduct.
That decision was announced Wednesday in a news release from police Chief Zachary Kindelan, following a review by the Aroostook County District Attorney’s Office.
A video of a physical altercation outside the Quarry Tap Room at 122 Water St. involving Kirsten Hinkley, of Augusta, who was a patron at the bar, and a staff security member went viral on social media. The video shows the security member holding Hinkley in a headlock.
Hinkley later posted photos on Facebook documenting several deep scrapes and bruises on her neck. She also claimed to have suffered a concussion during the altercation and went to the emergency room for treatment.
The video of the incident provoked discussion online about bar safety and security practices. In a post on Facebook at the time, Kindelan said the Hallowell Police Department would conduct a comprehensive, neutral investigation.
The investigation was referred to Kennebec County District Attorney Maeghan Maloney to decide whether formal charges would be brought against either party.
On Monday, Maloney said she passed the case to Aroostook County District Attorney Todd Collins for review.
Maloney serves on the board of a local nonprofit with one of the owners of the Quarry Tap Room. While she said she did not have a conflict, she said she asked Collins to review the case and make a decision on charges out of an abundance of caution.
Hinkley was issued a summons to appear in court on Jan. 4.
The Quarry Tap Room has been at the center of numerous controversies.
The Hallowell City Council just voted to renew the Quarry Tap Room’s liquor license Monday, a decision that drew crowds to the council meeting for a public hearing.
Kindelan had originally written a letter last week stating he would not support the license renewal for the restaurant until significant improvements and policies were implemented about safety.
After a meeting with the bar and restaurant staff, Kindelan reversed his position and said he was in support of renewing the license. He said it was not his intention to prohibit the license from being renewed, but to provide context to his recommendation that the bar make improvements before renewing the license.
In his original letter to the licensing board, Kindelan, who was sworn in as chief in July, wrote that in his short tenure on the job, his department had been called to the restaurant and taproom 15 times, resulting in 11 arrests or summonses. Many were for people accused of drunken driving after leaving the bar.
Matthew Clancy, the former chief of Maine Capitol Police, stepped down from his position after he was arrested for allegedly assaulting a Hallowell police officer at the Quarry Tap Room in August 2025.
Despite the controversies surrounding the establishment, when Mayor George Lapointe asked the crowd at the Monday city council meeting to raise their hands if they supported renewing the liquor license for the business, nearly every hand in the room went up.

title: 10-year-old wrestler’s Halloween costume gets incredible reaction from ‘The Rock’ himself
text:
EDWARDSVILLE, Ill. (KMOV/Gray News) - A 10-year-old wrestler who dressed as Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson for Halloween never expected to get the attention of the man himself.
Brooklyn Kepler, a 10-year-old girl from Illinois, wrestles with the Edwardsville Wrestling Club. Johnson is her hero, and her 10th birthday had a “The Rock” theme.
“I’ve always liked ‘The Rock.’ I thought he was just fun and big,” Brooklyn said. “I want to be a bodybuilder when I’m older, and he’s a bodybuilder.”
The 10-year-old wanted to be Johnson for Halloween, specifically his old-school wrestling look. Her mother, Michelle Kepler, made the costume, which included a bald cap, wrestling briefs and fake muscles.
Michelle posted her progress on social media. When she finished, she and her daughter were pleased with the result.
“I’m mind-blown. It looks so good,” Brooklyn recalled.
Brooklyn’s costume won second place in a local costume contest. For most people, that would be pretty good, but it wasn’t enough for one person who saw the family’s video: Johnson himself.
“This is Brooklyn,” wrote Johnson in a social media post. “She’s an awesome 10yr old and took Halloween this year to the next level - by going as (wrestling) ROCK - bald head, tattoos, wrestling gear, and mic skills that kills… IF YA SMELLLL…"
To make up for Brooklyn not winning the costume contest, Johnson said he would fly the 10-year-old and her family to California to be his guests at the red carpet premiere of “Jumanji: Open World” in December.
“Can’t wait to meet you, and your family and can’t wait for you guys to enjoy our movie, JUMANJI,” he wrote. “thanks for being such a cool fan.”
Brooklyn said she was in her mother’s lap crying when the family found out about Johnson’s invitation.
“I was so happy,” Brooklyn said.
“I was in tears,” her mother added.
Michelle said the family is grateful to Johnson and his team for noticing the video and inviting them. Both the video and Johnson’s response have gone viral.
“We’re kind of living the dream right now,” Michelle said.
