title: Biden says he would not have proceeded with campaign had he known he had cancer
text:
Biden says he would not have proceeded with campaign had he known he had cancer
Former President Joe Biden said in an interview released on Wednesday that his debate performance with Donald Trump in 2024 “was not very consequential” and that he would not have tried to seek a second term had he known he had cancer.
The interview with PEOPLE comes ahead of the release of Biden’s presidential memoir, “Promise Me, America,” next week.
The July 2024 debate, in which Biden appeared confused and had difficulty articulating his case for another term, eventually led to the president dropping out of the race and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, just 107 days before the 2024 election.
His debate performance also prompted his wife, first lady Jill Biden, to think the president was having a stroke. But Biden downplayed its influence in the new interview.
“Look, I don’t know anybody who hasn’t made a mistake in a debate,” Biden said in the PEOPLE interview. “To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”
A planned second debate took place in September, but between Harris and Trump.
Biden would have 'resigned' if he had known about the cancer
The former president was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer just four months after leaving office.
He conceded to having felt “lousy” before knowing about the cancer, and added he would not have attempted to mount another campaign for the White House had he known he was sick.
“If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I would’ve not gone forward, because I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for (president),” he said. “But that wasn’t the case … I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job.”
He said he let the public know of his diagnosis “when we found out” and denied having hid the truth about his health during his presidency.
“I didn’t do that,” Biden said. “We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on. I think it’s important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through.”
Biden’s book will be released next Tuesday. He has said his cancer will limit his ability to promote it.

title: Jaylen Brown gives Jayson Tatum cold shoulder before Celtics beat 76ers
text:
PHILADELPHIA — Jayson Tatum dapped up Jaylen Brown with a friendly tap on the shoulder and thump on the chest which his former Boston teammate ignored.
Brown gave him a cold shoulder. Tatum got the hot hand.
Brown ignored Tatum’s brief show of affection, perhaps a fitting illustration of a frosty relationship that has included radio silence between the two All-Stars since Brown was traded in the summer to the Sixers.
“No headlines about anything like that,” Tatum said. “I was just getting ready for the game. Ready for jump ball. Go out there and compete and have some fun and try and get the win.”
Tatum scored 21 points and outplayed Brown, and Paul George reminded fans he was in that blockbuster trade with six 3-pointers for 36 points in his return to Philadelphia, leading the Celtics past the 76ers 123-101 on Tuesday night.
PG flashed a reminder — both with his game and a middle finger — that he can still throw it back to his All-Star prime.
He scored 14 straight points in the fourth quarter and made six of Boston’s 22 3-pointers. George flipped off a Sixers fan in a bowling motion after he sank his fourth 3 of the game for a 100-82 lead that pushed the Celtics to their ninth win in 10 games.
“There was a fan being a (jerk),” George said. “Ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes. Dropped the ball on the ground as if I’m a dog to go fetch or got get it instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do. So I rolled him a middle finger in return.”
The Celtics had all the fun in this one.
Tatum shook hands and exchanged a big hug with LeBron James. Tatum later dunked over James and seemingly got the last laugh in the first matchup this season between the two top teams in the East.
Brown and Tatum kept their distance during pregame warmups ahead of Tuesday’s game when the Celtics played Philadelphia for the first time since the summer trade that saw Brown surprisingly switch sides.
Brown hit some jumpers on the Sixers’ end of the court. Tatum warmed up on his side with his Celtics teammates.
Neither All-Star decided to shoot his shot with the other.
Brown was traded with draft picks to the rival 76ers in July for George.
Brown ran into early foul trouble and scored only 13 points in his first game against Boston since the 2024 NBA Finals MVP was traded. He picked up two quick fouls in the first quarter and was whistled for his fourth early in the second half.
Brown declined to get into his Tatum brush off.
“I’m just focused on doing what’s best for my team,” Brown said. “Everything else was just, to be honest, I wasn’t paying attention.”
Brown got the better of Tatum early when he picked off his old teammate’s pass and fed the ball to Tyrese Maxey for a 3-pointer.
Brown said last month there was “ no beef ” between himself and Tatum, even as the dissection over the end of their relationship had dragged into the season.
The trade has been a success for both teams. The 76ers, with Brown and James aboard, are 9-3 and the Celtics now have the best record in the East at 9-2.
Joe Mazzulla coached both players when the Celtics won the 2024 NBA championship. He was ready to put the circus after the trade behind him and is proud that Tatum never had to eat crow — or any lamb chops.
“They’re just words,” Mazzulla said. “It’s not like his life’s threatened. There’s no weapons. There’s no one throwing anything at him. No one’s attacking him. It’s not really that big of a deal.”
Brown was a five-time All-Star and wound up with career-best averages of 28.7 points, 6.9 rebounds and 5.1 assists last season while Tatum missed most of last season while recovering from an Achilles tendon tear that happened during the 2025 playoffs.
With both players healthy and commanding hefty salaries that would eventually account for roughly 70% of Boston’s salary cap, the franchise faced a difficult decision about which player to keep. Boston chose Tatum.
The Sixers were happy to part with the 36-year-old George.
George shone in Philly on Tuesday after two flat seasons with the Sixers. George was poised to join Joel Embiid and Maxey to form a Philly Big Three when he left the Clippers and signed a four-year, $212 million free-agent contract ahead of the 2024 season.
George instead was ravaged by knee and adductor injuries — among others — that robbed the nine-time All-Star of his full potential that he flashed in his three previous NBA stops. He was suspended 25 games last season for violating the terms of the NBA’s anti-drug program.
George — whose 20.4 points entering the game is higher than either of his two seasons in Philadelphia — simply joined a list that included Jimmy Butler and James Harden of All-Star hired guns that failed to win a title with the Sixers.
Give this one to George and Tatum.
Let’s do it again Jan. 21 in Boston.

title: Why Tom Petty Stopped His Daughter From Listening to Aerosmith
text:
Why Tom Petty Stopped His Daughter From Listening to Aerosmith
Adria Petty, the oldest daughter of the late Tom Petty, says that "my dad used music to raise me." And he didn't hesitate to exercise some fatherly intervention when she felt she was on the wrong path.
Adria describes the experience as something like a father-daughter master class. "My dad would always walk in the room and throw a CD on the bed, a piece of vinyl on the bed, 'Tell me what you think of this,'" Petty, who helped curate the new Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers' Origins 1971-78, tells UCR.
Read More: Every Tom Petty Album Closing Song Ranked
"We would sit down after I listened to it a lot and discuss it, and I would listen to every record with my liner notes out, look at all the lyrics, look at who played on it, look at everything the artist intended, and then talk about it with him.
"So there was a long love of music between us -- just sort of, ‘Why is something good?"
They did not always agree, however. "There were a lot of things I liked in my teens that he was really upset by," Petty recalls.
"In particular Aerosmith's Pump was very concerning to him. When I was listening to, like, 'Janie's Got a Gun,' he was like, 'I need to intervene here' and he went and bought me a bunch of records -- Jimi Hendrix Experience, and I got (Bob Dylan's) Highway 61 Revisited. I got essential things to listen to because he was getting a little worried."
Those experiences with her father have served Petty well in her role as a principal of Petty Legacy LLC, the company established with her sister Annakim and their stepmother Dana Petty during 2019 to manage Tom Petty's catalog and copyrights.
In addition to her ownership role, Adria has stepped up to curate and co-produce posthumous archival sets such as An American Treasure in 2018, the following year's The Best of Everything, 2020's Wildflowers & All the Rest, Live at the Fillmore 1997 in 2022 and a variety of other projects.
For Origins, which coincides with the 50th anniversary of Petty and the Heartbreakers' self-titled debut album, she worked with longtime Petty engineer Ryan Ulyate and managers Will Botwin and Scott Greer for a box set celebrating the Heartbreakers' first two albums and the road the band took to get there.
It contains remastered editions of the first album and 1978's You're Gonna Get It!, including extended versions of several tracks, and both audio and video live performances.
The centerpiece, however, is No Sleep Til L.A., which plucks a diverse collection of early Petty, Mudcrutch and Heartbreakers recordings -- some of which are new mixes of songs included on the 1995 compilation Playback -- as well as an EP dubbed The Cut Out Bin with five tracks Petty recorded on his own, before settling in with the Heartbreakers.
No Sleep Til L.A. is also available separately on vinyl and CD.
"We sequenced No Sleep...thinking two things," Petty says. "One side is the Troubadour, the other side the Whisky (A Go Go). So Side A is the Whisky, a little more New Wave edge, punk. Then we go into a country-rock, Laurel Canyon, Troubadour vibe on side two.
The unreleased material was drawn from a significantly larger universe of songs Ulyate found in the vaults, Petty says, and she's confident that, "I know what my father would want to come out, and not come out. I don't want people in the streaming era to be playing songs that aren't good."
The surviving Heartbreakers -- particularly Mike Campbell and Benmont Tench, who have worked on some of the other projects -- were consulted for Origins as well. "Adria has been wonderful with curating the estate; I think she's doing a fantastic job, as is (Ulyate), just terrific," Tench tells us. "They're pretty much hitting it out of the park, and I appreciate the fact I'm consulted and I'm heard...and I'm glad people are getting to hear how we got to what we sounded like on those first two records."

title: This Maine Schoolteacher Became One of the Greatest Heroes of the Civil War
text:
This Maine Schoolteacher Became One of the Greatest Heroes of the Civil War
Did you suck at history in school like I did? Because, same. However, despite my inability to do a good job reciting the constitutional amendments in 7th grade, it didn't stop me from being fascinated by history- especially Maine history.
And with today being Veteran's Day (unless you're reading this on a day other than 11-11) I thought it pertinent (can't believe I spelled that right on the first try) to share with you the story of Joshua Chamberlain.
You see, Joshua Chamberlain was just a humble school teacher in the Pine Tree State, however, he actually became one of the most celebrated heroes of the Civil War. Wild, eh?
According to the National Park Service, Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain grew up with a strong interest in the military and it actually ran in the family. His ancestors had served in the American Revolution, the War of 1812, and even the Aroostook War right here in Maine (Yes, there was a war in Maine, no it wasn't over potatoes). But Chamberlain initially took a different path. He graduated from Bowdoin College in 1852 and returned a few years later, in 1855, to become a professor, teaching languages and rhetoric.
Here's where it gets wild though. Back in 1863 at the Battle of Gettysburg, he and his men were told to defend Little Round Top. If you don't know what Little Round Top is, that's a story for another time.
Long story short, Chamberlain and his fellow soldiers eventually ran out of ammo. At that point, a normal person would probably order a retreat and start running for their lives. But Chamberlain, being the true blooded Mainer he was, ordered a 'bayonet charge' and they stormed the enemies with the knives on the end of their rifles.
As crazy as that sounds, he actually survived and ended up making it back home to Maine. He even served 4 terms as Maine Governor. Additionally (because that wasn't enough) he was awarded the prestigious Medal of Honor for his bravery at Little Round Top.
Not too shabby for a schoolteacher from Brewer, eh?

title: A piece of Mars in Maine: Rare meteorite goes on display
text:
A piece of Mars in Maine: Rare meteorite goes on display
A professor from the University of Maine helped determine how old the meteorite is, and a museum in Maine has more of the sample than any other location in the world
A piece of Mars in Maine: Rare meteorite goes on display
A professor from the University of Maine helped determine how old the meteorite is, and a museum in Maine has more of the sample than any other location in the world
A unique piece of Mars is going on display in Maine on Wednesday.
The Maine Mineral & Gem Museum in Bethel acquired most of Teghaza 001 (TEG 001), an extraordinarily rare Martian meteorite that scientists believe offers a glimpse into a much wetter, more Earth-like Mars billions of years ago.
The largest known specimen of the meteorite is now on display at the museum, next to the single largest piece of the Moon on Earth. With a total known weight of just 1.75 pounds worldwide, TEG 001 is the second-oldest known Martian meteorite and comes from a region of Mars that scientists have never sampled before. The Maine Mineral & Gem Museum has multiple pieces of the meteorite.
Only two other known Martian meteorites are older than 4 billion years: Allan Hills 84001 and NWA 7034, also known as Black Beauty.
TEG 001 is mineralogically unique and contains hydrous minerals. Because the water alteration on Mars occurred 4.1 billion years ago, the meteorite itself is likely even older.
Science, one of the world's foremost scientific journals, recently published an article on the TEG 001 meteorite.
"One of the paper's reviewers called TEG 001 a Rosetta Stone for Mars … and, indeed, we've only begun to scratch the surface," said Yang Liu, a scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California.
University of Maine professor Alicia Cruz-Uribe and her colleagues were analyzing a box of rock samples from Mars when they confirmed the age of the meteorite.
In a lab at the California Institute of Technology in the summer of 2025, Cruz-Uribe and her colleagues measured isotopes showing that Teghaza 001 is 4.1 billion years old.
“I think we actually jumped up and down; full-on dance party in the lab,” said Cruz-Uribe.
Sahrawi meteorite hunters found TEG 001 in Mali's Sahara Desert in 2022, near an ancient salt mine that was a major North African source of rock salt until the late 1500s. After learning of the find, MMGM's Meteorite Chair Darryl Pitt advised MMGM co-founder Lawrence Stifler to acquire TEG 001 for the Museum.
TEG 001 reached Earth after an ancient asteroid struck Mars, launching Martian surface material into space. Some of those fragments entered an Earth-crossing orbit. Martian meteorites are exceedingly rare: together, their documented total weight is less than 500 kilograms (about 1,100 pounds).
"Before sending a sample to Yang Liu, I wondered whether TEG 001 might represent a new type of Martian meteorite," said Carl Agee, director of the Institute of Meteoritics at the University of New Mexico. "Among the fascinating revelations is evidence of an early Mars that is more Earth-like. The scientific community is fortunate that much of this extraordinary meteorite will be preserved for posterity at the MMGM."
The Maine Mineral & Gem Museum houses more than 80,000 specimens, features 22 exhibits, a scientific research laboratory, and more of the Moon than all of the natural history museums in the world combined.

title: Jay data center could create up to 1,000 construction jobs, 150 permanent positions, developer says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — A data center proposed for the former Androscoggin Mill, which appears to have new life after the developer pulled out in June, could create as many as 1,000 construction jobs and 150 permanent positions, a partner in the project said Tuesday.
In addition, a redesigned cooling system would limit water usage — often a concern in data center projects — to a one-time fill rather than the substantial daily replacement water previously anticipated, said Tony McDonald, a partner in JGT2 Redevelopment LLC.
McDonald confirmed that Sentinel Data Centers remains involved in the project and that the company is moving forward with an amendment to its state environmental permit.
“We never walked away from this project or this town,” McDonald said in written responses provided through Dan Cashman, public relations director at Sutherland Weston Marketing Communications.
The proposal earlier this year drew the attention of Gov. Janet Mills, who vetoed a bill that would have temporarily banned data centers in Maine because it did not include an exemption for the Jay project.
Still, the project stalled after Sentinel announced in June it was stepping away.
The news that Sentinel’s project was back on reached Augusta as well, with Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree saying Jay should not be a “testing ground” for data centers and that Maine needs “strong regulations in place.”
Residents in a number of communities, including Lewiston, have come out fiercely against data center construction, raising concerns about environmental impact and energy usage. On Nov. 3, eight Maine municipalities passed permanent or temporary bans on data centers.
“We have seen the damage in Virginia and Texas: higher electric bills, strained grids, pollution, and communities not getting promised benefits,” Pingree said in a statement.
“Jay deserves good jobs and investment at the mill site, but not at the cost of ratepayers, neighbors or the environment.”
PROJECT UPDATE
The updated plans offer a clearer picture of the proposed redevelopment. McDonald said the project would reuse about 1 million square feet of former mill buildings and the property’s existing electrical connection, with no grid upgrades anticipated.
The most significant change involves water consumption.
During a March 23 presentation to the Jay Select Board, McDonald described a closed-loop cooling system requiring about 300,000 gallons of water daily to replace evaporation losses. The latest concept calls for a one-time permanent fill with no discharge into the Androscoggin River, he said.
“Our water system concept has changed since the spring; we are looking at a closed-loop, one-time permanent fill with no discharge to the river,” McDonald said.
He estimated the initial fill would require less than 1% of the 35 million to 45 million gallons of water the paper mill previously used each day. The estimated total fill is 260,000 gallons, with no additional water required during operation, he said.
The developer also revised its employment projections, anticipating 800 to 1,000 construction jobs and 125 to 150 permanent positions across three shifts. Earlier estimates called for about 800 construction jobs and more than 100 permanent positions.
The proposed development was previously valued at $550 million. McDonald did not provide an updated investment estimate or anticipated construction start date.
The project’s electrical demand drew statewide attention earlier this year when lawmakers considered legislation temporarily restricting permits for large data centers. McDonald previously estimated the facility would initially require about 82 megawatts of electricity.
In his latest responses, McDonald said the project would use the mill’s existing electrical contract and grid connection, eliminating the need for upgrades. He also maintained that the development would not negatively affect local electricity bills, although no independent assessment of potential ratepayer impacts was provided.
McDonald said discussions with Sentinel continued despite the company’s decision in June not to proceed at that time.
“Our discussions never stopped,” he said. “Yes, Sentinel is involved in the project.”
Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere told the Select Board on Monday that the companies were moving forward again but had not reached a final agreement.
McDonald emphasized that the latest permitting activity involves the original development rather than a replacement proposal.
“This isn’t a new project or a new application,” he said. “It’s the same project, the same owner, the same site, moving forward through the state’s public review with DEP.”
AMENDMENTS AND OPEN HOUSE
According to a public notice, JGT2 is seeking a minor amendment under Maine’s Site Location of Development Act and a new minor source air emission license. The proposal includes reusing existing buildings for computing equipment and converting former parking and rail yard areas to accommodate heating, ventilation and air conditioning equipment.
The permitting schedule remains uncertain, and McDonald said the company is prioritizing regulatory review and assembling the appropriate construction team over committing to a specific timeline.
The redevelopment could also increase municipal tax revenue, although updated estimates of the property’s anticipated taxable value have not been provided.
JGT2 plans next month to hold a public open house at the former mill, where residents can ask questions about the proposal, including its electricity and water requirements. LaFreniere said Dec. 10 is under consideration, but the date has not been confirmed.
McDonald said the company will announce the date and time at www.TheJayMill.com, where residents can also submit questions as plans develop.

JoBe Cerny, who voiced the Pillsbury Doughboy, has died
JoBe Cerny, who voiced the Pillsbury Doughboy for years, including the animated character's iconic giggle, has died. He was 78 years old.
The voice actor died in Illinois on Oct. 30.
Related video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
The actor's career spanned several decades in commercials, movies, and TV shows, but his role as the voice of the Pillsbury Doughboy, also known by the name Poppin' Fresh, was the most widely recognized.
"I get to be somebody different every day, and in the end, I'm glad I stuck with my irresponsible decision to have fun," Cerny once said of his career, according to his obituary.
He stepped back from the Pillsbury Doughboy voice role around 2020, according to reports.
Cerny also had other acting credits in "Legally Blonde 2: Red, White & Blonde" and "My Best Friend's Wedding," according to IMDb.
He is survived by his wife of 56 years, Eileen, two sons, and two grandchildren.

title: Firefighters dig through rubble after NYC building collapse kills 1 and traps people in wreckage
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-story building in Brooklyn on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least one person and trapping others beneath the wreckage.
Firefighters were called to the scene in the borough’s Flatbush section around 4 p.m. News helicopter footage showed dozens of firefighters scouring the debris, with a group homing in on one area and appearing to use a saw to cut through the wreckage.
One person died, and four others were rushed to a hospital in critical condition, according to the New York City Fire Department. Six additional people were taken to hospitals with minor injuries.
The aerial videos showed firefighters digging at least one person out of the rubble and removing them on a stretcher.
The building that collapsed had been perched at the edge of a lot where another one-story building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated, and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.
Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.
A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked.
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.

title: Low-cost home fixes and age tech can help older adults stay safe at home
text:
(Aging Untold) — Small changes around the house can make the difference between staying home safely and a fall that changes everything.
Tara Ballman, executive director of the National Aging in Place Council, joined Aging Untold to talk through low-cost fixes, signs that long-distance caregivers should watch for and technology that can help.
Evaluate your home for trip hazards
Ballman said two low-cost areas have a high impact.
The first is trip hazards.
“You probably don’t remember where your throw rugs are, how long they’ve been there, and it might be coming up on the sides,” Ballman said.
She said the hazards go beyond rugs. Electrical cords that run to a lamp, shoes piled by the front door and clutter from pets or robot vacuums can also be trip hazards.
“I would love for everyone to go take a fresh look at their homes from new eyes, and see where those trip hazards are,” Ballman said. “That’s free for you to evaluate your own home.”
Check the lighting
Lighting is the second area.
“As you age, your eyes are affected by the light,” she said. “So you might need more light in some areas. Or if the light is too bright and creating a glare, that can be dangerous as well.”
What long-distance caregivers can look for
Ballman said some signs that a home is no longer working for a parent or loved one are small and easy to miss until you visit in person.
She suggested asking:
- Is your loved one sleeping in the bed, or on a sofa or chair in the living room?
- Are they able to use their shower, or are they using a sink to sponge bathe?
Age tech: a safety net without surveillance
Ballman described “age tech” as technology that helps people stay in their homes longer and more safely. She said the options are not expensive.
Examples she gave include:
- A sensor on a door that shows whether it opened three or four times for someone who lets dogs in and out each day.
- A countertop system that brings you your medicine every day, so you don’t have to wonder whether you took it.
- Smart toilet seats that, based on how a person sits and stands, can measure blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen levels.
- Pressure-sensitive grab bars that can sense extra weight.
- Pressure-sensitive floor mats that alert a loved one if someone falls in the bathroom.
“There’s a way that you can make sure they’re safe without putting cameras in their homes,” Ballman said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said the goal is to preserve dignity and longevity at home while keeping safety nets in place.
Automatic lighting for nighttime and entryways
Ballman said automatic lights matter most on the path from the bed to the bathroom at night. She also recommended automatic sensors outside, at the door and on multiple levels, including ceiling fixtures, floor lamps and lights that come up from below.
“The automatic sensors for lights are something that every home should have, whether you have an older adult in it or not,” Ballman said.
Start the conversation now
Ballman encouraged families to begin conversations before a crisis.
“Get comfortable with being uncomfortable, because knowledge is power,” she said. “The more that you know and the more research you can do ahead of time, it’s just going to give you more options when you’re not in a crisis situation than when it’s a crisis, and there’s this many options and you don’t know how to pay for it.”
Six easy things you can do
- Look for trip hazards. Check rugs, electrical cords, shoes by the door and clutter from pets or robot vacuums.
- Review the lighting. Older eyes may need more light in some areas, and glare from light that is too bright can also be dangerous. Upgrade and balance lighting if necessary.
- Watch for changes in routine. Where a loved one sleeps and how they bathe can show the home is no longer working for them.
- Consider age tech. Door sensors, medication systems, pressure-sensitive grab bars and floor mats can help without cameras in the home.
- Add automatic lights. Ballman said sensors from the bed to the bathroom, and at entrances, are something every home should have.
- Talk early. Researching options before a crisis gives families more choices.

title: With Democrats in power, will Congress stop ICE raids in Maine?
text:
Democrats dominated local and federal races in Maine and across the country by galvanizing anger with President Donald Trump and his administration. Immigration was one of the top issues that fueled their gains.
The topic came to the forefront of Maine’s race for U.S. Senate several times over the last year: First in January when Immigration and Customs Enforcement sent a surge of agents to the state for what was dubbed “Operation Catch of the Day,” and again in July when ICE agents shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian man, outside his home in Biddeford.
Now that Democrats are set to control both houses of Congress, it’s likely that they will look to exert more control over ICE, which has acted with near-impunity for months by investigating itself, stymieing local inquiries and rejecting oversight from Democratic legislators in the wake of fatal shootings and detainee deaths.
Maine immigrant advocacy groups are cautiously optimistic in light of last week’s election results. But how much power Congress can or will exert over an agency housed under the executive branch remains an open question.
“Just because there’s this majority in Congress doesn’t mean raids are going to stop. It doesn’t mean arrests are going to stop,” said Ruben Torres, policy director at the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition. “This tension will still be there and we need to be prepared for that.”
Immigration was the third most important issue to Maine voters, according to a September poll conducted by The New York Times, the Portland Press Herald and the Siena Research Institute — trailing only inflation and the economy.
Sen.-elect Troy Jackson has described ICE as a “rogue agency” and said the country needs immigration reform, “not masked raids and fear.” Abolishing ICE was a position central to his campaign.
“It’s time that ICE is disbanded and we go back to putting that money into Customs and Border Patrol,” Jackson said during an October debate. “They have training, they’re law enforcement, people respect them — we don’t respect ICE.”
Jackson isn’t the only Democratic senator-elect who campaigned on abolishing ICE. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota have both called to dismantle the agency. Many other Democrats elected this year campaigned on the more moderate position of reforming it.
Jackson’s transition team did not respond to questions about whether he still seeks to abolish ICE or how feasible that goal ultimately is.
It’s unlikely there’s enough political appetite to abolish ICE, according to Marcela Escobari, a senior fellow at the nonpartisan Brookings Institution and a former immigration adviser on the National Security Council. What’s more probable is for Congress to investigate ICE’s alleged abuses and reform some of its recently employed enforcement tactics, she said.
“Congress is likely to shed light on how ICE and CBP operate,” Escobari said. “Who are they stopping? How are agents being trained? Are they following the law?”
Though only the president and ICE’s directors have authority over its operations, which have grown increasingly aggressive during Trump’s second term, Congress can attempt to control how much money the agency receives and how it is allocated.
“It’s likely they bring transparency to how the money is spent and how enforcement is being delivered,” Escobari said.
To do so would involve clawing back some of the $70 billion in funding for immigration enforcement that Congress passed in June.
Some federal officials have signaled a willingness to shift their hardline stances on immigration in the wake of the midterms. Vice President JD Vance said in a lengthy post-election X post that “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance.”
Even Trump said his immigration policies “might be too tough” in a “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday. He also expressed willingness to compromise with Democrats in Congress moving forward.
But Trump also signaled that more of the same is coming in his second term when he elevated Stephen Miller, a staunchly anti-immigration figure in his administration, to the post of chief of staff last week.
Maine immigrant rights organizations are hoping for the best while bracing for the worst.
“I take (Trump’s comments) with a grain of salt and a shot of whiskey,” said Torres, with the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition.
Torres and other Maine immigrant advocates expressed a desire for Jackson and the new congressional majority to focus not just on reversing the changes to ICE’s tactics in recent years, but to reform America’s broader immigration system and widen pathways to citizenship.
Lisa Parisio, policy director of the Maine Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project, said the election results in Maine and around the country signal a “clear and powerful rejection” of the Trump administration’s immigration agenda.
“The new Congress must reflect the short- and long-term will of the people through robust oversight and investigation and an uncompromised legislative agenda that takes strategic steps to protect people now while building towards citizenship for all who call the United States home,” Parisio said.
But while Congress can scrutinize budget priorities and line items, Parisio noted the huge amount of new funding that ICE has been apportioned through 2029. And much of that spending is at ICE and Trump’s discretion.

title: Bass Harbor resident donates 100 pints of blood over 30 years
text:
BASS HARBOR — For nearly 30 years, Bass Harbor resident Bill Weir has quietly helped people across New England one pint at a time. Last week, he hit a milestone with the 100th pint of blood he has donated.
Weir had just relocated from Camden to Mount Desert Island to work at a union trust company and shortly thereafter the local Rotary Club sponsored a mobile blood drive; it began his almost 30-year journey to 100 pints.
“The first time I gave blood, I almost fainted. I had to lie down.”
Weir jumped up, though, and pushed through it. He got involved with Rotary and ran blood drives, and these acts snowballed into the creation of annual drives with the high school, realtors, and other organizations.
“I got really enthused and started to give more than once a year, a couple of times a year, and then I started giving four and five times a year and sometimes six times a year.”
Weir felt it was important to help and wanted to encourage the community to take part too. Then, when working for Bar Harbor Savings and Loan, he got the bank involved and turned his blood donation experience into a community event.
“I started getting a lot of feedback, and our bank decided that it would be one of our major volunteer situations at the Bar Harbor Savings and Loan. So we started sponsoring blood drives about every two months.”
Over the next three decades, he donated every 56 days and up to six times a year, eventually giving 53 pints in a single decade.
Recently, Weir rolled up his sleeve in Bangor for his 100th pint, representing 12.5 gallons of blood.
For Weir, though, reaching triple digits was never about personal recognition; he just wanted to help.
“I don’t want to make it so much about me as it is how important it is for people to give, I’m not the hero. I didn’t have to do anything for it. I just happened to have the luck of the draw.”
Five years ago, the American Red Cross notified Weir that he had been selected to participate in a special program, which looks for donors with rare blood types.
“I was notified by the Red Cross that I had been selected in a program called “Heroes for Babies” and I said, ‘well, what the heck is that?’”
Weir explained that routine testing revealed his blood was absent of “cytomegalovirus” (CMV), a virus that is carried dormant by roughly 85% of adults. According to Weir, CMV is harmless to adults, but if transfused into infants or newborns with fragile immune systems, it can be fatal.
Because of that negative status, Weir’s donations are tracked and rushed directly to neonatal intensive care units across New England, including facilities in Bangor, Rockport, Portland, Boston and New York City.
“If a newborn baby has it and they need a blood transfusion because of a medical issue, if the blood they get has that (CMV) in it, it can kill them,” Weir explained.
Once the blood is donated, Weir said that after a few weeks he gets a notification telling him where it went around New England.
At age 77, Weir said that in order to keep his donation levels up, his body demands strict physical maintenance. He explained that donating regularly draws on iron reserves and depletes vitamin B12, so he takes iron supplements, receives regular B12 shots, and carefully manages his blood pressure.
“I’ve been giving blood a long time, but as you get older, it starts to tax you,” said Weir.
Weir said that to keep his body in shape, he gets out on the water to kayak or paddleboard every day. As of March 3, he said he had not missed a day and has logged 382 trips out on the water. His goal for the year is 400.
“You have to stay in pretty good shape, which I do. I’m always out walking or hiking. But because of this, it sort of dovetails with what I like to do. I think a healthy lifestyle is important. Particularly as you get older.”
Weir hopes his 100-pint milestone encourages others to overcome the initial hesitation and begin their own routine.
“It’s just like an athlete training for sports, you’ve got to make up your mind what you’re going to do,” Weir said. “I want people to know that anybody can do it. But it takes a lot of work.”

title: Aging Untold: The hidden risks of denial in caregiving
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address caregiver denial and explore why recognizing when an aging loved one needs more help leads to better, safer care.
Plus, we share practical ways to make a home safer for aging in place, from quick, low-cost fixes to knowing when to get a full home assessment, as well as costs and resources to help pay for modifications.
Finally, we introduce you to an inspiring Vermont “super ager” approaching 90 who is proving it is never too late to build strength through Pilates.
One of the hardest hurdles that families face is admitting when a loved one starts to need extra support.
Being in denial can protect us in a time of grief, but avoiding reality for too long can contribute to caregiver burnout and compromise care.
There are several facets to denial. The Aging Untold experts are sharing the signs to look for and tips for meeting loved ones where they are.
There are some small changes that you can make in a home to allow you or a loved one to age in place safely.
Tara Ballman, executive director of the National Aging in Place Council, said two low-cost areas have a high impact. The first is trip hazards, and the second is lighting.
Ballman provided additional tips on what long-distance caregivers can look for and recommendations for “age tech,” technology that helps people stay in their homes longer and more safely.
It can be difficult to think clearly when you or a loved one are going through a medical crisis.
But advocating for yourself or a loved one entails paying attention, asking questions and being vocal, aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
She is sharing a personal story, and the Aging Untold experts explain how to build a team to help you navigate a crisis and share relevant information with the care team.
Sue Talmage is sure that she is the oldest student at Essential Physical Therapy and Pilates in Montpelier, Vermont.
The 88-year-old drives there twice a week to take the classes she has been attending for close to two decades.
“It’s an important part of my life,” Talmage said.
Instructor Willow Wonder leads Talmage’s class, which runs 45 minutes with no breaks. She said Talmage serves as an inspiration for others who come to the studio.

text:
President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to make it harder to get food aid through the federal government’s big grocery assistance program that serves about 1 in 10 Americans.
The administration says the proposed rule would close a loophole by no longer allowing some people who receive benefits under the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program to automatically qualify for the separate Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program too.
About 6.3 million people could lose eligibility for SNAP by the 2029 fiscal year if the proposed change takes effect, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which administers the program. That is on top of 5.5 million people who already have lost SNAP benefits over the past year.
The plan is laid out in a proposed rule published Tuesday on how to run SNAP, and the government is seeking public comment until next month. If it is accepted, the rule would not take full effect for about two years.
The proposal addresses the link between 2 federal programs
At issue are two separate federal programs. The TANF program provides federal grants to states, which set their own eligibility rules for distributing cash and other benefits to low-income families with children. The incomes of recipients vary by program and state.
Federal guidelines generally limit SNAP food benefits to those earning less than 130% of the poverty level, a little over $1,700 monthly for an individual or nearly $3,600 for a family of four. To reduce duplicative paperwork, the federal government allows people who already receive TANF benefits to automatically qualify for SNAP — though they still have to apply.
Some states have used that automatic eligibility to expand SNAP benefits to people who might not otherwise qualify. In 2009, President Barack Obama’s administration encouraged states to provide people a minimal TANF-funded benefit, such as an informational pamphlet or telephone hotline, as a way of qualifying them for the food program.
Forty-one states and the District of Columbia have some form of broad-based categorical eligibility for SNAP, according to a USDA report from last year.
The first Trump administration proposed to clamp down on such tactics in 2019. But that proposal was withdrawn by President Joe Biden’s administration in 2021.
The latest proposal is more sweeping and could prevent states from basing SNAP eligibility on TANF-funded benefits such as job-related counseling or one-time vouchers for vehicle repairs so that people can get to work, said David Super, a law professor at Georgetown University who has studied the food aid program.
“The administration here is basically proposing to eliminate the flexibility that Congress gave the states to serve working poor people,” Super said.
SNAP is also connected to other programs for low-income people
Being in a household that receives SNAP benefits also makes school children eligible for free meals. The Agriculture Department says that nearly 1.8 million children would lose eligibility with their family losing SNAP — but that 97% of them would still qualify for free or reduced price school meals through another process.
But the government says some of the children would not get the lunches, even if they are eligible, if their families don’t apply.
The proposal comes at a time when the number of people receiving the aid has fallen sharply — and on the heels of sweeping election gains for Democrats across the country.
“The public indicated they want their elected officials to focus on making life affordable,” the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning policy research institute, said in an analysis of the proposal. “Yet the Trump Administration is doubling down on making it harder for people to feed their families.”
It has been a period of flux for the food aid program
As of July, the Department of Agriculture, which runs SNAP, said 36 million people were receiving the aid. That was down by 13% from a year earlier. Over that time, another federal requirement expanded a work requirement to more enrollees, including those ages 55 to 64 and to parents whose youngest children are at least 14.
Trump’s big 2025 tax and policy law that broadened the work requirement also requires states to start shouldering about three-fourths of the cost of running it, up from half. And they will also have to pay some of the costs of the benefits if their error rates exceed certain thresholds. Congressional Democrats are pushing for a delay in implementation of that change.
The newly proposed rule from the Trump administration “is just one of many things right now that states are grappling with that would reduce access to SNAP,” said Carolyn Vega, director of policy analysis for the advocacy group Share Our Strength.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities is concerned that the eligibility change may result in higher error rates for states — making them have to pay for more of the cost of benefits.
Patricia Anderson, an economics professor at Dartmouth College, said that out of the various administration efforts to reduce SNAP, “this one seems the most reasonable” because some people with higher incomes qualify through categorical eligibility.
But she said there is a different conversation that can be had about whether the SNAP eligibility guidelines are too strict.

title: Here's Why Maine Ranks Among the 5 Worst States for Drivers
text:
Here’s Why Maine Ranks Among the 5 Worst States for Drivers in The Nation
If you've ever driven down I95, sat behind someone doing 45 in the passing lane, or watched somebody try a three-point turn in the middle of an intersection, you might not be surprised by this one.
I feel like both of those things happened just last week for me.. But I may have been the one doing the 3 point turn because I forgot my airpods at home. Whoops.
But listen to this, Maine has officially ended up among the states with the worst drivers in America, according to a new LendingTree study. And before anyone gets defensive, we have the numbers to back it up.
Maine has now sadly ranked 5th worst in the country, with 42.3 driving incidents per 1,000 drivers.
Maine's Drivers Have Been Ranked for 2026
The study looked at accidents, DUIs, speeding-related incidents and other driving citations between January and August 2026.
This is what got me, Maine ranked 4th in the country for accidents, with 28 crashes per 1,000 drivers. Massachusetts came in third, which means our sweet and very friendly drivers next door aren't exactly helping our reputation either.
New Jersey took the unfortunate crown as the state with the worst drivers overall, while Michigan had the best driving record in the study.
Now, I'm not saying every Maine driver is bad. Some of us are super lovely and responsible people who use our blinkers and understand how rotaries work.
But, we all know that ONE person, who does treat there blinker like an accessory. And let's talk about winter driving. I know, right? We haven't even gotten through another Maine winter yet! But still, put that ONE person with ice, and snow and you've got an issue.
Read More: Christmas Car in Augusta, Maine Spreads Holiday Cheer
So, the next time somebody cuts you off, just remember: apparently, we've got a national reputation to maintain. Yikes.
What do you think, Maine? Are we really that bad behind the wheel, or is this study completely missing the mark?

title: 10-year-old wrestler’s Halloween costume gets incredible reaction from ‘The Rock’ himself
text:
EDWARDSVILLE, Ill. (KMOV/Gray News) - A 10-year-old wrestler who dressed as Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson for Halloween never expected to get the attention of the man himself.
Brooklyn Kepler, a 10-year-old girl from Illinois, wrestles with the Edwardsville Wrestling Club. Johnson is her hero, and her 10th birthday had a “The Rock” theme.
“I’ve always liked ‘The Rock.’ I thought he was just fun and big,” Brooklyn said. “I want to be a bodybuilder when I’m older, and he’s a bodybuilder.”
The 10-year-old wanted to be Johnson for Halloween, specifically his old-school wrestling look. Her mother, Michelle Kepler, made the costume, which included a bald cap, wrestling briefs and fake muscles.
Michelle posted her progress on social media. When she finished, she and her daughter were pleased with the result.
“I’m mind-blown. It looks so good,” Brooklyn recalled.
Brooklyn’s costume won second place in a local costume contest. For most people, that would be pretty good, but it wasn’t enough for one person who saw the family’s video: Johnson himself.
“This is Brooklyn,” wrote Johnson in a social media post. “She’s an awesome 10yr old and took Halloween this year to the next level - by going as (wrestling) ROCK - bald head, tattoos, wrestling gear, and mic skills that kills… IF YA SMELLLL…"
To make up for Brooklyn not winning the costume contest, Johnson said he would fly the 10-year-old and her family to California to be his guests at the red carpet premiere of “Jumanji: Open World” in December.
“Can’t wait to meet you, and your family and can’t wait for you guys to enjoy our movie, JUMANJI,” he wrote. “thanks for being such a cool fan.”
Brooklyn said she was in her mother’s lap crying when the family found out about Johnson’s invitation.
“I was so happy,” Brooklyn said.
“I was in tears,” her mother added.
Michelle said the family is grateful to Johnson and his team for noticing the video and inviting them. Both the video and Johnson’s response have gone viral.
“We’re kind of living the dream right now,” Michelle said.

title: Pillsbury Doughboy voice actor JoBe Cerny dead at 78
text:
(Gray Media) – JoBe Cerny, who was the iconic voice behind the Pillsbury Doughboy, has died. He was 78.
Born on Dec. 5, 1947, Cerny died Oct. 30, 2026, his family said in his obituary online.
While arguably best remembered for his roles in advertising projects, he also appeared in films including “My Best Friend’s Wedding” and “Road to Perdition.”
He was also the high-pitched voice of the Pillsbury Doughboy, who giggled when he was poked in the belly until about 2020, according to The Hollywood Reporter.
Cerny joined The Second City in 1970 as part of the Mainstage and National Touring Company, according to his obituary.
“Well known for his friendly and gregarious personality, he had the extraordinary ability to coincidentally run into someone he knew almost everywhere he went,” his family wrote.
Cerny is survived by his wife, two sons and grandchildren.

title: Maine deregulated electricity 26 years ago. Time for a rigorous review.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bill Webster of Georgetown is a former superintendent of schools in Lewiston. He was also controller for Hannaford Bros. and owned and operated Haven’s Candies. He is now an active SCORE mentor, providing free mentoring to existing and aspiring entrepreneurs.
Would most Maine residential customers pay 20 cents per kilowatt hour if they knew that a 12-cent option was available? Probably not. Do most Mainers know who supplies their electricity and what their rate is per kilowatt hour?
Most Mainers know who delivers it to them: Central Maine Power or Versant Power, depending upon where you live. These distributors also send you the bill, maintain the power lines and restore service after storms. But the company that actually supplies your electricity is an entirely different business.
I suspect many Mainers couldn’t identify their electricity supplier without searching through their monthly bill. Until recently, I thought I knew mine.
In 1997, Maine enacted legislation restructuring the state’s electricity industry. Beginning in March 2000, consumers could choose among competing electricity suppliers, while utilities such as CMP continued to deliver the electricity. The premise was straightforward: Competition would provide more choices and encourage lower prices.
For customers who didn’t choose a supplier, the state established the Standard Offer, with rates determined through competitive bidding overseen by the Maine Public Utilities Commission.
More than a quarter-century later, it’s worth asking whether that experiment has delivered the promised benefits. Consider my recent experience.
Earlier this summer, I contacted CMP and confirmed that I was receiving electricity through the Standard Offer. My June bill clearly identifies it as my supplier. Imagine my surprise when I discovered that my supplier had subsequently changed to SmartEnergy, at a rate of 20.4 cents per kilowatt-hour, approximately 60% higher than the Standard Offer rate of 12.721 cents. The price difference certainly helps fund the rebates that SmartEnergy offers.
When I contacted SmartEnergy, I was told that my wife had authorized the change during a telephone conversation in May. She recalls responding to a solicitation concerning a rebate but says she never knowingly agreed to change our electricity supplier.
The solicitation itself was intriguing. Prominently displayed were the words, “Please choose a payout option for your rebate.” It also identified us as CMP customers. Was this an offer from our electricity provider, a refund we were entitled to receive, or a marketing promotion designed to attract new customers?
Apparently, we didn’t understand what was being offered.
Whether the record of the phone call establishes that proper authorization was obtained remains to be determined. But the experience illustrates how difficult it can be for consumers to understand the choices they are making.
And there’s more. Like many Mainers, I also participate in a community solar program. That arrangement involves credits against my CMP bill and a separate monthly statement from another company. Between the delivery company, the electricity supplier and the solar program, understanding my household’s electricity costs has become surprisingly complicated.
Does all this competition actually save us money?
According to a January 2026 report presented by Maine’s Office of the Public Advocate, Maine residential customers purchasing electricity from competitive suppliers paid an estimated $156 million more between 2016 and 2024 than they would have paid under the Standard Offer.
The report also found that low-income customers were disproportionately affected. These results were also similar to a study done in Massachusetts. That is a disturbing finding for a system intended to benefit consumers through competition.
Competition can be valuable. Some suppliers offer renewable energy options or fixed-rate contracts that may appeal to certain customers. But competition only works well when consumers understand what they are purchasing and can compare prices and terms.
At a minimum, every electricity supplier should be required to disclose prominently its rate alongside the current Standard Offer, the length of the contract, what happens when it expires and exactly what a consumer is authorizing. Solicitation materials should make unmistakably clear that accepting an incentive may involve changing electricity suppliers.
Perhaps Maine should go further and reconsider whether its current system of residential
electricity competition is delivering sufficient benefits to justify its complexity. I hope this becomes a priority of the next Legislature.
Electricity is an essential service, not a discretionary purchase. Mainers deserve reasonable prices, understandable bills and informed choices. After 26 years of deregulation, shouldn’t we be asking whether the system is working for the people who pay for it?

title: FOR YOUR HEALTH: Alzheimer's patients deserve answers sooner
text:
by Kenneth E. Thorpe
Nearly half of American voters have a loved one who has been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. And Alzheimer’s will touch even more families in the years ahead, as the number of Americans living with the fatal disease nearly doubles by 2050.
Thankfully, scientists are developing new tools to help diagnose and manage Alzheimer’s. Among the most promising are blood tests that could help millions of Americans receive diagnoses earlier — so they can start treatment sooner.
But it’s not enough for these tools to exist. Patients need access to these promising tests as soon as they’re approved. For that to happen, Congress will need to pass legislation ensuring Medicare can cover new screening tests – and cut the red tape that currently risks preventing Alzheimer’s patients from getting the care they need.
A bipartisan bill, the Alzheimer’s Screening and Prevention (ASAP) Act, would do precisely that. The bill offers lawmakers an opportunity to remove a barrier standing between patients and earlier diagnosis, potentially allowing patients to get valuable time back.
Historically, Alzheimer’s was difficult to diagnose. Initial symptoms can be hard to recognize, particularly among older adults experiencing general cognitive decline. Doctors had to rely on a combination of medical history, physical exams, brain scans, and cerebrospinal fluid testing.
As a result, it can take patients over three years after symptoms first emerge to receive an official diagnosis.
Now, new tools are emerging that could dramatically speed up this timeline. Last year, the FDA cleared the first blood test used to help diagnose Alzheimer’s. The test detects biological markers in the blood associated with the disease, offering an easier and less invasive testing option. In the future, doctors could use similar blood tests as screening tools to identify Alzheimer’s far earlier — long before symptoms worsen.
That kind of earlier diagnosis can make an enormous difference.
For one, it gives families more time to plan and prepare for the financial and caregiving burdens that come with Alzheimer’s. Long-term care services can cost $72,800 to $115,000 annually. Many family members of patients with Alzheimer’s and other dementias become caregivers themselves, collectively providing more than 19 billion hours of unpaid care worth over $446 billion.
Alzheimer’s damages the connections between brain cells. Once those neurons are lost, they can’t be repaired or regenerated. Alzheimer’s treatments therefore generally focus on preventing damage and slowing the disease’s progression. And after a certain point, patients simply aren’t eligible for treatment anymore.
Yet for patients to benefit from recent diagnostic advances, Medicare needs to cover them.
Policymakers shouldn’t stop there, though. As Alzheimer’s science continues to advance, Medicare needs to keep pace by removing unnecessary barriers and ensuring that patients can actually access the new diagnostics and treatments that researchers develop.
We increasingly have the tools to change the trajectory of early-stage Alzheimer’s. But first, we must ensure that patients can access those tools in time. Doing so would create wide ripple effects of positive impact on millions of individuals and families facing this staggering diagnosis.
Kenneth E. Thorpe, PhD, is the Robert W. Woodruff Professor of Health Policy at the Rollins School of Public Health at Emory University and the honorary Chair of the Partnership to Fight Chronic Disease. This piece originally ran in DCJournal.com.

title: Meteorite found in the Sahara shows what Mars was like 4.1 billion years ago
text:
Meteorite found in the Sahara shows what Mars was like 4.1 billion years ago
Scientists have identified one of the oldest Martian rocks ever found on Earth — and it’s revealing new clues about the red planet’s earliest history, including evidence that water altered its crust at least 4.1 billion years ago.
The rose-colored meteorite, known as Teghaza 001, has a unique chemical composition that sets it apart from previously studied samples from Mars, scientists say.
Related video above: New space mission set to explore Mars' moons
"This is a very rare, ancient Martian meteorite, and it gives us a chance to look at the early crust and mantle of Mars, at a time when life was just starting on Earth," said Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, and lead author of a study on the sample published Oct. 29 in the journal Science.
This meteorite is believed to have formed from magma derived from the mantle — a planet’s inner layer of hot rock — which later became part of the outer crust. "The chemistry of this sample shows it comes from a Martian crustal area we have not sampled before," Liu added.
Teghaza 001 is named after a salt plain in the West African country of Mali, where meteorite hunters discovered it in 2022. The meteorite consists of eight fragments weighing 798.5 grams (1.76 pounds) in total, with the largest weighing 442 grams (0.97 pounds).
The impact of an asteroid or comet that struck Mars blasted Teghaza 001 out of the red planet’s relatively weak gravity and into space. The meteoroid then started orbiting the sun, potentially for several million years before being captured by Earth’s gravity and entering our planet’s atmosphere. It’s hard to determine when the impact on Mars originally occurred, or even when the meteorite landed on Earth, but the sample’s surface features reveal that it might have spent some time in the desert before its discovery, according to Liu.
"It is always nice to see a new visitor from Mars, and this one is ancient — one of the oldest from the planet, and older than any home-grown Earth rock," said Matthew Genge, an associate professor of Earth and planetary science at Imperial College London, who was not involved with the study.
"That alone is fascinating," Genge said in an email. "It gives a window into the earliest stages of Mars' history, a time when water is expected to have been present on the planet."
A lucky gamble
An initial analysis didn’t immediately reveal that the rock was particularly old, and Liu almost passed on studying it.
"When I was first offered it," she said. "The sample was classified as a shergottite, the most abundant type of Martian meteorite we have on Earth."
Liu had previously analyzed several shergottites, which make up almost 90% of the known Martian meteorite collection and are usually less than 600 million years old, but she ultimately agreed to investigate the sample.
She noticed Teghaza 001 contained zircon, a type of crystal that forms when molten rock cools. "Zircons are like a time capsule that allows us to precisely date the formation age of a rock," she said.
Dating of the crystals indicated an age of at least 4.1 billion years, which means the meteorite formed roughly within the first 400 million years of Mars’s existence. To confirm this estimate, the sample was also processed via a new aging method developed by study coauthor Hayward Melton, a doctoral student at the California Institute of Technology.
"This method uses a laser to vaporize very small regions of a sample, instead of dissolving larger pieces of it," Melton said in an email. "Using a laser means that we can measure samples like Teghaza 001 significantly faster than traditional techniques."
The team used a small laser beam — about one-tenth the diameter of a human hair — to analyze the tiny grains and crystals inside the samples. This new technique reduced the time required to date a sample from a month to a day, Melton added, and left more of the original material available for further studies.
The meteorite is a basalt, similar to rocks that cover the floor of Earth’s oceans and erupt from volcanoes in places such as Iceland and Hawaii, according to Genge.
Teghaza 001 has a unique composition that indicates it interacted with water in the ancient Martian crust, the new analysis has shown. This may give scientists "a deeper understanding of not only early Mars, but also Earth, and help us learn why Mars became dry while the Earth did not," Melton said. "This, in turn, would have implications for understanding the habitability of planets."
Other peculiar features make Teghaza 001 stand out from Martian meteorites. It’s made mostly of two calcium-rich minerals, but in proportions that have never been seen before in any other samples, Liu said. The specimen also contains isotopes of oxygen in relative abundance that are unlike other known rocks from the red planet, according to Liu.
The mineral and chemical composition of a meteorite can help scientists ascertain its Martian origin by comparing it with data gathered on the planet’s surface by NASA missions to Mars, including the Viking landers and the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.
For Teghaza 001, the researchers went one step further and identified 13 locations on Mars’ southern highlands from where the rock could have originated.
"I think the science community will be very interested in this sample, and there will be many more discoveries to come," Liu said. "I am still very interested in resolving some questions I couldn’t answer with our paper, which is only in the beginning."
‘A possible feast of discovery’
After its discovery in 2022, the meteorite caught the attention of Darryl Pitt, a meteorite collector and chair of the meteorite division at the Maine Mineral & Gem Museum in Bethel, Maine.
"What drew me most to Teghaza 001 was a mineralogy that was unlike that of any previously studied Martian sample, combined with its age," Pitt said. "This set the table for a possible feast of discovery."
Video below: NASA animation shows ancient, wet Mars transtion to a present-day desert world
He eventually brokered a deal for the museum to acquire the rock for an undisclosed amount.
"What is truly remarkable about Teghaza 001 is that it allows us not only to be able to study another planet," said Genge, of Imperial College London, "but also to peer deep under its surface to see what the planet was like only 500 million years after it formed."

title: Maine Girls Should Use Their Voices, The Best Asset They Have
text:
Deciding what I wanted to say at a Girl Scout conference over the weekend made me think about what I wish I'd known early in my personal and professional journey.
In a World Where Women are Often Overlooked, Maine Women Need to Speak Up
On Saturday, I sat on a panel with two intelligent young women at the Transforming Leadership conference at the University of Maine in Orono.
We talked about how we got to where we are now, and how we overcame the personal challenges we faced.
For me, that was self-confidence.
READ MORE: Maine's Job Market Named 7th Best in the Nation
I was a painfully shy kid who often avoided personal interactions because I was afraid the other person wouldn't like me.
I never raised my hand in class, even when I knew the right answer.
Oh, if I could have known then how much richer my life would be with less self-doubt.
Maine Girls Can Grow Into Strong Women Who Can Do Anything
When I began working in radio, I had to grow into an extrovert who loved interacting with people and talking in front of crowds.
I found that people care about what I have to say, and that being wrong once in a while is just a new opportunity to learn.
Radio is a male-dominated field, and the 'girl announcers,' as we were known in my early days, were often quietly pushed to the side.
My advice to young women? Don't let this happen to you.
Maine Girls: Learn to Use Your Voice Because It's Your Best Asset
Speak up when you feel ignored and make them listen, because what you say matters.
Don't be afraid to say hello, answer a question in class, or share what you're thinking, because your opinion is as valid as everyone else's.
Fear will creep in, as it still does for me, and that's okay.
Speaking in front of a group of Girl Scouts was intimidating, and part of me wanted to run, but I'm glad I overcame those doubts and got to share some of what I've learned.
Don't let fear stop you from doing what you want in life.
Be confident, stand tall, and let the world see you.
Use your voice. It's the best asset you have.

title: This Maine Schoolteacher Became One of the Greatest Heroes of the Civil War
text:
This Maine Schoolteacher Became One of the Greatest Heroes of the Civil War
Did you suck at history in school like I did? Because, same. However, despite my inability to do a good job reciting the constitutional amendments in 7th grade, it didn't stop me from being fascinated by history- especially Maine history.
And with today being Veteran's Day (unless you're reading this on a day other than 11-11) I thought it pertinent (can't believe I spelled that right on the first try) to share with you the story of Joshua Chamberlain.
You see, Joshua Chamberlain was just a humble school teacher in the Pine Tree State, however, he actually became one of the most celebrated heroes of the Civil War. Wild, eh?
According to the National Park Service, Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain grew up with a strong interest in the military and it actually ran in the family. His ancestors had served in the American Revolution, the War of 1812, and even the Aroostook War right here in Maine (Yes, there was a war in Maine, no it wasn't over potatoes). But Chamberlain initially took a different path. He graduated from Bowdoin College in 1852 and returned a few years later, in 1855, to become a professor, teaching languages and rhetoric.
Here's where it gets wild though. Back in 1863 at the Battle of Gettysburg, he and his men were told to defend Little Round Top. If you don't know what Little Round Top is, that's a story for another time.
Long story short, Chamberlain and his fellow soldiers eventually ran out of ammo. At that point, a normal person would probably order a retreat and start running for their lives. But Chamberlain, being the true blooded Mainer he was, ordered a 'bayonet charge' and they stormed the enemies with the knives on the end of their rifles.
As crazy as that sounds, he actually survived and ended up making it back home to Maine. He even served 4 terms as Maine Governor. Additionally (because that wasn't enough) he was awarded the prestigious Medal of Honor for his bravery at Little Round Top.
Not too shabby for a schoolteacher from Brewer, eh?

title: USDA warns consumers not to eat these frozen meat products
text:
(Gray News) - The U.S. Department of Agriculture is warning consumers not to eat certain frozen meat products because they may contain undeclared allergens.
The products were made by BetterBallen Foods. The USDA said the beef, pork and chicken products contain sesame. The beef products also contain anchovy.
Neither allergen is listed on the appropriate labels.
Where the products were sold
The BetterBallen products were sold online by Lowlands House for nationwide shipping. They may have also been sold at events in South Carolina.
Why no recall was issued
A recall was not issued because the products are no longer available for purchase. The products, however, may still be in consumers’ freezers.
What consumers should do
Customers should throw the products away or return them to the place of purchase.

title: Father charged with attempted murder after 11-month-old son found buried alive in dog crate
text:
LEXINGTON COUNTY, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - The father of a baby found buried alive this week has been charged with attempted murder.
According to the Lexington County Sheriff’s Department, 25-year-old Michael Comer’s charges also include unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary.
Lexington County authorities said the 11-month-old baby, Koah Sharp, miraculously survived after Comer buried him in a dog crate.
The boy’s father was arrested Monday night.
Koah was found alive Tuesday afternoon just over 24 hours after he was last seen with his father.
Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said Koah was found buried in a dog crate wrapped in a towel.
“By the grace of God, [it] probably provided enough air for him to survive an estimated 24 hours under that dirt,” Koon said.
The sheriff said Comer’s mother was caring for the child when Comer arrived at the home on Monday. She then left Koah in Comer’s care while another caregiver was on the way.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone and Koah was gone with him,” Koon said.
Other members of Koah’s family filed a missing persons report Monday afternoon.
Koon said authorities went to the nearby home of Comer’s father, where they found both doors open and Koah’s belongings, but no sign of them.
Authorities arrested Comer after finding him in a shed in Batesburg.
It wasn’t until later that investigators were able to locate Koah at Comer’s father’s house. They noted finding a pine straw and “freshly disturbed dirt.” Once they started digging, they heard him crying.
“So, as you imagine, the race was on,” Koon said. “Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out.”
Koon said it’s believed that Koah was buried for around 24 hours.
The sheriff said Koah was treated at an area hospital.
Comer’s arrest comes just over a month after he was placed on probation following a guilty plea for aggravated breach of peace, according to public court and state records.
Court records also show Comer had previous arrests earlier this year for domestic violence, as well as a weapons-related charge.

title: Authorities looking for Eddington woman wanted on active arrest warrant
text:
EDDINGTON, Maine (WABI) - An Eddington woman who is out on bail in an infant overdose case is once again wanted by authorities.
During a traffic stop Sunday, authorities say they seized illegal drugs and stopped Brittany Wood, 36, from destroying potential evidence.
In the two days since, officials with the Penobscot County Sheriff’s Office say they tried several times to get Wood to surrender voluntarily, but she did not.
Wood faces charges of unlawful possession of scheduled drugs, falsifying physical evidence and violating conditions of release.
Earlier case
The Sheriff’s Office was searching for Wood in July on separate charges connected to an infant overdose. Wood was taken into custody several days later while leaving a home in Eddington.
Her attorney said in court that Wood had been on vacation and did not know about the warrant until she saw news reports online. The defense also said Wood was on her way to turn herself in when she was arrested.
Officials said Wood’s 9-month-old child overdosed in May, with Wood and the baby testing positive for cocaine and fentanyl. A grand jury indicted Wood in October on charges related to the incident.
Wood is a member of the RSU 63 School Board, representing Eddington.
Town Manager Shawna Hinkley said earlier this year that there is no recall process for RSU 63 school board members. Under an absenteeism policy, a member who misses three consecutive meetings is removed from the board.
Wood missed two consecutive meetings after the July warrant. She was released on bail in time to attend the third and kept her seat.
WABI reached out to RSU 63 School Board chair Rachel Downs for comment. She confirmed Wood is still an elected member of the board. “The district will continue to follow applicable district policies and Maine law, including 20-A M.R.S. § 1474 which outlines the circumstances under which a vacancy on a regional school unit board may be declared," Downs said. “Since this is a matter involving an elected official and pending law enforcement matters, the School Board does not have further comments at this time.”
We have contacted the town of Eddington for more information.
Anyone with information about Wood’s whereabouts is asked to call the Sheriff’s Office at 947-4585.
