title: Irma P. Hall, ‘Soul Food’ and ‘The Ladykillers’ actor who found fame at 60, dies at 91
text:
(AP) - Irma P. Hall, the veteran actor who brought warmth and authority to matriarchal roles in “Soul Food” and “The Ladykillers,” and whose acting career took off after decades as a teacher, died Tuesday in Dallas. She was 91.
Her family announced her death Wednesday. No cause was given.
Hall was best known to many viewers as Big Mama, the family’s steadying force in the 1997 film “Soul Food.” The role earned her an NAACP Image Award and led to a return as the character in the television series based on the film.
She received a Cannes Film Festival Jury Prize for her performance as Marva Munson, a Bible-reading landlady opposite Tom Hanks in the Coen brothers’ 2004 comedy “The Ladykillers.” Hall also appeared in “A Family Thing,” “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil,” “Beloved,” “Patch Adams,” “Collateral” and Tyler Perry’s “Meet the Browns.”
Hall was 60 when “A Family Thing” brought her a major film role. She played Aunt T., a blind woman whose counsel helps guide two half brothers, played by James Earl Jones and Robert Duvall. The part drew attention to an actor who had spent years developing her craft onstage and in smaller screen roles.
“I was just concentrating on developing this craft,” Hall said in a 1996 interview with The Associated Press. “I guess you really never know where you are, you probably think you are on a lower rung than you really are.”
Hall had not set out to become an actor. Born Irma Dolores Player on June 3, 1935, in Beaumont, Texas, she was raised in Chicago and later returned to Texas for college. She taught English and foreign languages in Dallas public schools for more than two decades.
Her path to the screen began when actor and director Raymond St. Jacques heard her recite poetry in Dallas and cast her in his 1973 film “Book of Numbers.” Hall continued teaching as she took acting roles, then made performance her full-time work in the 1980s. She also helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre and remained involved in developing young artists.
Hall’s career included theater, television and film. Her credits ranged from the 1997 Clint Eastwood drama “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil” to the 1998 films “Beloved” and “Patch Adams.” She also voiced Great Aunt T. in the 2001 “Rugrats” Kwanzaa special.
In 2004, Hall was recovering from serious injuries suffered in a car crash, including open-heart surgery, a broken arm and a crushed ankle, when she traveled from a Chicago convalescent center to attend a private screening of “The Ladykillers.”
“I loved the whole thing,” she told The Associated Press. “You never really know until you see it on the screen.”
Hall said she had heard from Hanks and the Coen brothers while recuperating. They had signed her pillow, she said. “Whenever I miss them, I hug it.”
In Dallas, Hall was also a longtime member and Church Mother at Inspiring Body of Christ Church. Her family remembered her as a woman of faith who read to children at the church’s school and stayed active in its theater ministry.
“She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said in the family’s announcement.

title: Kennedy family joins lawsuit to block Trump’s arch
text:
Kennedy family joins lawsuit to block Trump’s arch
Kennedy family joins lawsuit to block Trump’s arch
One of America’s most storied political dynasties — the Kennedy family — is suing the Trump administration to block construction of the president’s 250-foot triumphal arch.
Nine members of the Kennedy family filed a motion Tuesday in federal court in Washington, D.C., to stop the arch from being built, arguing that it obstructs views of the family’s gravesites in Arlington National Cemetery as well as “the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes.”
“President Donald J. Trump is attempting to unlawfully erect a massive arch that will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family’s honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes,” the family wrote in the filing.
Related video above: Post-midterms, President Trump focuses on D.C. beautification projects
The Kennedys argue the design and location of the massive arch would obstruct the clear sightline of the family’s gravesites, including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame from the vantage point of the Arlington Memorial Bridge, ultimately “destroying an essential element” of the gravesite’s design.
The Kennedys are joining a lawsuit filed last month by Washington, D.C., and Virginia. Veterans and preservationists, as well as Arlington County, have also sued to block the project.
Opponents say the enormous scale of the arch and the location would also disrupt the sightline of the row of national landmarks that includes the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington House and the Robert E. Lee Memorial, and that the towering monument will break the solemnity of funerals of Arlington National Cemetery.
The plaintiffs in the new filing include the children and grandchildren of President John F. Kennedy’s brothers – Sens. Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy – who are among the six family members buried at Arlington National Cemetery.
The family is arguing they have particularly good standing to challenge the arch, because courts in the past have recognized families’ interests in protecting their relatives’ gravesites.
“The gigantic proposed arch is an illegal interference with Arlington National Cemetery and the heroes remembered there, including at the gravesites and memorials of the Kennedy brothers and Ethel Kennedy. Only Congress has the constitutional power to authorize an intrusion of this magnitude,” said Norman Eisen and Steve Jonas of Democracy Defenders Fund, who are representing the Kennedy family members. “Today, members of the Kennedy family are joining with the other litigants in this case to protect this historic site – and to defend the rule of law and separation of powers.”
A federal judge last week blocked construction of the arch for 14 days after a final vote approving the structure passed late Thursday despite fierce opposition from citizens who voiced concern during a marathon public hearing.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, an Obama appointee who is overseeing one of the high profile lawsuits to stop construction, ruled that the Trump administration would be prohibited from “initiating, making or otherwise effectuating” any “construction-related activity” near the proposed site of the arch.
President Donald Trump has previously said he intends to complete the arch before he leaves office in two years, but the aggressive timeline has been complicated by the ongoing legal challenges.
In a review released by the National Park Service in August, the administration acknowledged that the arch would have “adverse” effects on as many as 42 historic sites.
The arch is just one example of the president’s efforts to reshape the nation’s capital to his own liking. Construction and renovation projects around Washington, from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the Kennedy Center, have figured heavily in his second term — something his critics have labeled “vanity projects.”
Members of the Kennedy family who are buried at Arlington National Cemetery include President John F. Kennedy; first lady Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis; Sen. Robert F. Kennedy and his wife, Ethel Kennedy; Sen. Edward M. Kennedy; and Lt. Joseph P. Kennedy Jr.

title: Farmington voters to revisit mobile home rent protections Nov. 19
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — Residents will be asked to reconsider key provisions of the town’s voter-approved mobile home lot rent ordinance at a special town meeting Thursday, Nov. 19.
It comes after the Select Board advanced proposed amendments that would alter rent increase limits, eliminate retroactive protections and ease some requirements for park owners.
The ordinance passed by a wide margin Nov. 3, but Town Manager Erica LaCroix told selectmen Tuesday, Nov. 10, that changes recommended by the town attorney are needed to clarify its language and make it manageable for the town to administer. The proposed revisions drew objections from a resident involved in organizing the original petition, who argued that the changes go beyond administrative corrections and undermine protections voters approved.
The original ordinance limited annual lot rent increases to the lesser of the Consumer Price Index plus 1 percentage point or 3%. The proposed amendments would change that formula, although the precise replacement was not established during the meeting discussion.
LaCroix said the existing cap could prevent park owners from recovering rising operating costs, potentially discouraging maintenance or threatening the continued operation of some parks.
She also recommended eliminating a provision that would apply the ordinance retroactively to July 14. Although some Maine communities have adopted similar provisions, LaCroix said retroactive enforcement would be difficult for Farmington to administer and is not legally required.
Other proposed changes would reduce the financial documentation park owners must provide when seeking rent increases above the standard limit. Owners would still need to demonstrate an actual, immediate financial need and disclose revenues, expenses and proposed capital improvements, but would no longer be required to provide amortization calculations.
The revisions also require all five members of the proposed rent stabilization hearing board to be Farmington residents, rather than allowing a minority of members to live elsewhere.
LaCroix recommended that the hearing board be independent, with neither mobile home park owners nor tenants serving as members. The board would meet only when appeals are filed and would have 30 days to respond to a petition.
The ordinance provides for hearings beginning Jan. 1. If the town has not appointed a hearing board by then, the Select Board would handle appeals.
During public discussion, a resident involved in the petition effort challenged the proposed changes, particularly the rent cap revision. She argued that comparable limits exist in other municipalities and that voters had already expressed strong support for the ordinance.
She asked the board to consider an emergency working group involving residents and town officials before scheduling another vote, saying the revised proposal had been developed without direct public involvement.
The board proceeded with the warrant for the Nov. 19 meeting, where residents will have an opportunity to consider the amendments.
LaCroix also acknowledged the possibility of litigation over the ordinance, regardless of whether the amendments are adopted.
The special town meeting will be held at the Farmington Community Center, 127 Middle St. The Select Board’s action Tuesday authorized the proposed changes to go before voters; it did not enact them.

title: WKRP to Replicate Classic 'Turkey Drop' Stunt for a Good Cause
text:
WKRP to Replicate Classic ‘Turkey Drop’ Stunt for a Good Cause
Ever thought turkeys could fly? Then you'll love what real-life Ohio radio station WKRP is planning for Thanksgiving.
The Cincinnati-based oldies station, named after the beloved sitcom, will pay homage to one of the series' most famous episodes, holding their first annual Turkey Drop the day before Thanksgiving.
Of course, this event will be markedly different from the unintentional offscreen massacre: the station will sell 3,000 small, numbered rubber turkeys, to drop from the top of a fire truck down to a target below. The closest to the center of the target will win a cash prize.
The drop will take place at 7:30 p.m. on Wednesday, November 25 outside the Casual Pint taproom in Hamilton. Proceeds from the turkey sale will benefit the Open Door Food Pantry, which serves residents in the Butler County area. Fans can also purchase t-shirts commemorating the event.
Read More: The Day 'WKRP' Taught Us That Turkeys Can't Fly
The Turkey Drop pays homage to "Turkeys Away," the legendary early episode of WKRP in which the station's Thanksgiving publicity stunt gone wrong. The enduring hilarity of hapless newscaster Les Nessman (Richard Sanders) reporting live on the carnage of turkeys thrown from a helicopter onto a shopping mall — as well as station manager Arthur Carlson (Gordon Jump)'s closing declaration "As God is my witness...I thought turkeys could fly" — helped the fledgling show find an audience. The episode (based on a real radio promotion) was ranked as one of the 100 greatest episodes of all time by TV Guide.
While this particular Turkey Drop has taken place in the Hamilton County area before, the forthcoming event has the first-time sponsorship of the oldies station located at 97.7 FM on the dial, which obtained the rights to the call sign earlier this year and went live this past May.

title: Letter: Money in Bangor City Council race sets wrong priorities
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Money, misinformation and moral panic. I think these are the real city council winners in Bangor. Bangor has seen a meteoric rise in moneyed interests attempting to influence our city: real estate interests, conservative-funded media, anonymous Facebook pages, and a wealthy, connected Cape Elizabeth citizen. One group alone spent $15,000 on this race.
It’s fair to say that Bangor needs change, but this is not the way. We should prioritize people over property and evidence-based solutions over feelings. In a city where more than half of households rent, and where the city’s own housing study says we lost 2,000 households earning under $75,000 in a decade, citizens should be concerned that real estate interests are able to put their bottom line ahead of our needs.
The problems that Bangor faces today are not isolated. Homelessness, addiction, and the choice between food and medicine are symptoms of a broken system, and they are showing up across the nation. The anonymous pages claiming addicts are pouring in from elsewhere never cite a source; according to MaineHousing, nearly half of the people in our shelters are from Bangor.
We should be looking at solutions that are already working in other towns. Affordable housing works. If allowing real estate and other special interests to run things actually worked, we would be living in a utopia.
It’s time to put people first and invest in policies that will empower our citizens rather than lining landlords’ pockets.
Mitchell Cooper
Bangor

title: Gardens Aglow 2026 opens Nov. 14
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Saturday, Nov. 14, Maine’s popular light show, Gardens Aglow, returns to Boothbay. Described by the TODAY show as one of their “unexpected destinations that are sure to get your family in the holiday spirit,” Boothbay Lights and Maine Gardens' signature light show, Gardens Aglow, light up the peninsula for six weeks through Jan. 2, 2027.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens invites guests to “Gather, Glow, and Celebrate” with this year’s “Gathered in Maine” theme. New lighted elements feature a maple tapping scene, a landscape fit for mushroom foraging, and a larger-than-life anthill with an army of ants carrying leaves and berries. Completely new every year, the in-house design and hand-strung display keep Maine Gardens' seasonal staff employed into the new year and provide vital funds for the nonprofit's mission work.
“Our team has been working hard since August on this year’s show. I say this every year, but this year might be the best,” states Gretchen Ostherr, president and CEO of Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens. “Even though I get to watch—and take part in the light hanging—I am always amazed at how we transform from a green sanctuary into a sparkling wonderland. We can’t wait to celebrate this season with families from Maine and New England.”
For the last handful of years, Maine Gardens have been nominated in the Best Botanical Garden Holiday Lights category, as part of USA TODAY 10BEST’s Readers’ Choice Awards. After landing in the top five in recent years, Maine Gardens hopes to bring the top spot to Maine this year. Event organizers hope that Gardens Aglow fans will show their Maine pride by voting daily to help Gardens Aglow bring the title home.
With price-conscious guests in mind, this year there will be three pricing tiers: Value on weekdays, Standard on Fridays and Sundays, and Premium on Saturdays, allowing guests to pick the night and price that work for them. An additional VIP add-on pass unlocks special Gardens Aglow gifts, free unlimited ticket exchanges, flexible arrival times on your selected date, and a cozy fire pit experience.
Ticket prices start at $20 for adults, $18 for seniors and veterans, and $10 for children ages 3-17. Children under the age of 3 are free. Members save 20% on all Gardens Aglow admission tickets. VIP add-on passes are $50 per ticket and are not subject to any discounts. For more information on pricing and time slots, visit GardensAglow.org.
Extend your stay and enjoy all that the region offers with Boothbay Lights. A convenient complimentary Park and Ride shuttle runs Friday, Saturday, and Sunday from Boothbay Harbor Town Office, allowing guests to experience Boothbay Harbor's shopping, dining, and lodging delights before and after the light show. For a complete calendar of regional offerings, the robust slate of Boothbay Lights events, and Park and Ride details, visit www.boothbaylights.com.
About Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens
At 325 acres, Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens is the largest public garden in New England. With two miles of hiking trails, 19 acres of ornamental and themed gardens featuring native plants of Maine and those suited to northern coastal conditions, nearly a mile of saltwater frontage, a children’s garden, a sensory garden, and so much more, there’s something for everyone. A true Maine experience, the Gardens is committed to connecting people to nature, preserving the biodiversity of the Maine coast, and continuing to be a place accessible and welcoming to all. The mission of Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens is to inspire meaningful connections between people and nature and promote plant conservation through horticulture, education, and plant science.

title: Veterans honored with new Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial in DC
text:
Veterans honored with new Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial in DC
This Veterans Day and for countless Veterans Days to come, the work by a sculptor from Vermont will be a major place to honor military service and sacrifice in the Gulf War
Veterans honored with new Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial in DC
This Veterans Day and for countless Veterans Days to come, the work by a sculptor from Vermont will be a major place to honor military service and sacrifice in the Gulf War
As the nation pauses to observe Veterans Day, a new memorial in Washington, D.C., will honor service and sacrifice in the Gulf War in 1990 and 1991. The Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial has been in the works for more than a decade, and an artist raised in Vermont made major contributions to the finished product.
"One of our goals, overall, was to first create a beautiful place that people want to come to," explained sculptor Emily Bedard. "Once they're here and having that experience, then they can think deeper about the artwork. What is this representing? Who is this honoring? And then they can go back and learn more about Desert Storm and the veterans."
Bedard grew up in the Chittenden County town of Milton and now has a studio in New York. She was on a team of artists who collaborated on the new memorial, which is located near the Lincoln Memorial and Vietnam Veterans Memorial on the National Mall.
Bedard designed a curving stone wall with bas-relief sculptures that tell the story of the U.S.-led coalition of forces that liberated Kuwait from Iraq's invasion. The new addition to the National Mall honors the roughly 700,000 U.S. military personnel who served in Operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm and remembers the nearly 400 who made the ultimate sacrifice.
"It's an incredibly humbling experience," Bedard said in late October when she was in Washington, D.C., for the dedication of the memorial. "It's really wonderful to see it public today and mostly to have veterans come and see this work and to receive this sense of closure after 35 years of waiting to be recognized for their service."
Bedard said she hopes people will experience the new memorial at different times of day, explaining that the angle of the sun changes the experience of walking past the curving wall. The figures on it reflect the surge of international forces that came to Kuwait's aid with precise planning and swift action, Bedard explained.
"To the American people, to all those who answered the call to serve, your place in Kuwait's national memory and in our hearts will never be forgotten," said Sheikha Al-Zain Al-Sabah, Kuwait's ambassador to the United States.
The new landmark will be open to visitors 24/7, according to the National Park Service. It was paid for with private funds, not taxpayer dollars, according to the National Desert Storm Memorial Association.
"The National Park Service tells me that literally 5 to 6 million people are going to come through this memorial every year," said Scott Stump, a Desert Storm veteran who also served as the president of the organization that worked to make the memorial a reality. "It's very humbling to know that that story is going to live on long after all of us are gone."

title: Bicyclist Recovering, Hit-and-Run Driver Facing Felony Charges
text:
A 65-year-old woman is recovering after being seriously injured in a hit-and-run crash at the intersection of Main Street and Biscay Road in Damariscotta on the morning of Wednesday, Nov. 4.
Jaja Martin, of Bremen, was struck by a vehicle while riding her bicycle in Damariscotta, according to a press release from the Damariscotta Police Department. The driver, John Barczak, 67, of Rockland, was later arrested and now faces three felony charges.
Lincoln County Communications Center received the call around 5:26 a.m. that a woman on a bicycle had been struck by a vehicle and the vehicle had left the scene. When emergency responders arrived, the vehicle and the operator were not present, according to the police department.
Martin was transported by Central Lincoln County Ambulance Service to MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta for treatment. Due to the severity of her injuries, she was later transported Maine Medical Center in Portland for further treatment, according to the Damariscotta Police Department.
In a Monday, Nov. 8 phone interview, Martin said she was awake and being well cared for by hospital staff.
“She had severe injuries requiring multiple surgeries,” said Lauri Boxer-Naconder, a lawyer representing Martin and her husband, Dave.
During the investigation involving review of physical evidence, surveillance footage, and vehicle-related information, Damariscotta Police Officer William Smith identified a red Toyota Tacoma that he believed to be involved in the crash. The vehicle was subsequently located at a local business and Smith was able to identify Barczak as its driver.
Barczak was arrested without incident at 4 p.m. on Nov. 4 and transported to Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset. As of Tuesday, Nov. 10, Barczak was still at the Wiscasset jail.
He was charged with elevated aggravated assault, a Class A felony; reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon, a Class C felony; and leaving the scene of an accident involving serious bodily injury, a Class C felony.
In addition to CLC Ambulance Service, the Damariscotta Police Department was assisted by the Damariscotta Fire Department, the district attorney’s office, and Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, according to the press release.
The Martins said the outpouring of support and concern they were receiving from everyone had been almost overwhelming. Jaja Martin added the response has made her love the community even more.
“Every note and every text means so much to me,” she said.
Martin said she does not know what the next steps are for her recovery, but she looks forward to when she is able to get back on her bike.

title: Driver in deadly Los Angeles metro station crash is arrested on DUI and murder counts
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The 61-year-old driver of a minivan that killed three people when it crashed outside a Los Angeles metro station during rush hour was arrested on suspicion of driving under the influence and three counts of murder, a police spokesperson said Wednesday.
Police have said the driver was taken out of the vehicle and was able to talk, but he appeared in shock after Tuesday’s crash. Officials were not immediately able to determine the cause or whether he acted intentionally.
Police identified the driver as Ihor Demianenko, a resident of the Valley Village neighborhood of Los Angeles, Officer Norma Eisenman said. She didn’t know whether he was still at a hospital early Wednesday.
It was not immediately clear if Demianenko had a lawyer who could respond to the allegations.
The crash at a busy intersection in the North Hollywood neighborhood also critically injured two women. The vehicle ended up under a food vendor’s tent, and Mayor Karen Bass said the victims included street vendors and pedestrians.
Investigators will go through video of the crash frame by frame, LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said.
“It will be probably a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here,” he said.
Luis Luna-Guzman was working at a burger stand nearby when he heard a loud boom and saw people on the ground along with food and cups. People nearby started running toward the crash.
As he moved closer, he found an injured woman lying near the bike racks, her face, arms and legs bloody, he said, recalling her eyes were closed as she moaned in pain.
“I told her, ‘Don’t move, help is coming,’” Luna-Guzman said, adding that he saw a woman’s body nearby, while another woman was lying unmoving on the stairs leading to the station.
Adrin Nazarian, a Los Angeles City Council member whose district includes North Hollywood, described the area as a close-knit community where there is always commotion and activity.
The minivan was on the sidewalk surrounded by debris Tuesday night with its driver’s side door open and an air bag deployed. Fire engines and emergency crews worked nearby as a helicopter flew overhead.
One entrance to the metro remained closed Tuesday night, but otherwise the property wasn’t impacted and the stations for the bus and subway were open, according to Jose Ubaldo, spokesperson for the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority.
___
Thanawala reported from Atlanta.

title: New Vinalhaven hybrid ferry touted for saving fuel
Family of ICE agent in Biddeford shooting accuses him of immigrant bias, New York Times reports
text:
New interviews with family members of the federal immigration agent who shot and killed a man in Biddeford this summer show they had growing concerns about his mental health and anti-immigrant bias.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that David Brouillette, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who shot and killed a 25-year-old Colombian man in July, sent a series of racist emails to his sister in 2021, criticizing her relationship with a Colombian man who is the father of her two children.
“He can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries,” Brouillette wrote in one email, according to the Times, which noted that the emails contained several typos. He also said that the man’s “bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”
The Department of Homeland Security issued a lengthy statement on Wednesday morning, declining to identify its agents and defending its hiring practices. The agency also said it “does not comment on matters regarding personnel who are no longer with the agency,” although a spokesperson did not clarify if that applied to Brouillette.
Brouillette was identified by those who know him as the agent who shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 during an enforcement operation in Biddeford.
Durán Guerrero was a Colombian citizen with work authorization and no criminal history, according to his family’s attorneys. Sen. Angus King said in July that a DHS official told him that Durán Guerrero was not the target of the agents’ operation that morning.
Brouillette has not responded to repeated requests for comment from the Portland Press Herald and his phone number was still out of service when a reporter called Wednesday. The Times reported that Brouillette declined to speak with them after a reporter left a letter at his home. DHS has declined to name the agent involved.
The Times report also provides new details about Brouillette’s training to become an ICE agent, and his work history, citing anonymous sources who were briefed on his work history. Two people told the Times that Brouillette skipped ICE’s full training course in Georgia.
Another source reported that officials had not looked into Brouillette’s background at the time of the shooting, because the federal agency had “a gigantic backlog” of reports. Brouillette could not access some computer systems because he didn’t have full clearance, the Times reported.
“The agency restricted his access to certain computer systems because he had not been fully cleared, yet apparently saw no problem trusting him with the power to take someone’s life,” U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, said Wednesday.
A DHS spokesperson, responding through a media email without names, said that the agency refuses to “dox” employees, citing safety concerns, and defended its “rigorous standards” for ICE agents and vetting procedures.
“Incoming ICE officers, many already with years of law enforcement experience, are onboarded in accordance with applicable policies and standards. Any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE,” the spokesperson wrote. “This administration is preserving ICE’s reputation as one of the most elite law enforcement agencies not only in the U.S., but the entire world.”
Benjamin Gideon, an attorney for Durán Guerrero’s family said in a statement that the Times’ reporting “adds to the long list of Mr. Brouillette’s disqualifying conduct” and hostility toward immigrants.
“Johan Sebastián’s death was not an inevitable accident,” Gideon said in the statement.
Gideon urged newly-elected members of Congress to investigate. Pingree said the Times’ reporting revealed an “unconscionable betrayal of the public’s trust” by ICE, and she called for the agency to be abolished.
The Press Herald previously reported that a Hallowell official saw “too many red flags” in Brouillette’s background to hire him at the local police department, despite his experience working as a child support enforcement officer for the state, and as a corrections officer in Windham.
Brouillette and his second ex-wife had filed a total of eight protection from abuse order requests against each other that detailed allegations of verbal and physical abuse.
Ashley Brouillette, David Brouillette’s first ex-wife, who has also accused him of being abusive, was one of the first people to tell reporters that he was the shooter. She said he told her so when he called her on July 15. She said Wednesday that she spoke about her ex-husband about a week later, in an interview with members of DHS and the Office of the Maine Attorney General.
Both agencies have announced investigations into the July 13 shooting, although none have shared updates since then.
Sean Murphy, another attorney for Durán Guerrero’s family, said that state prosecutors told his clients earlier this summer that Attorney General Aaron Frey wanted to make a decision on the investigation before he leaves office. Lawmakers will elect a new attorney general next month.
A spokesperson for the Maine attorney general referred a reporter to what’s been publicly released and said they don’t comment on pending investigations.
According to the Times, Brouillette declined to speak with them after a reporter left the letter at his home in Maine. Brouillette also called the sheriff’s office and said he was under “executive protection,” according to the Times.
This echoes what the father of Brouillette’s young stepdaughter wrote in court records for a protection from abuse order earlier this summer. Brouillette and his wife reportedly told the father that they were entering “protective custody” due to threats Brouillette received, following the shooting.

title: Kennedy family members ask a judge to block Trump’s Arlington memorial arch
text:
(AP) - Nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty asked a judge Tuesday to block President Donald Trump’s plan to build a towering memorial arch, saying the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would cast a shadow over their relatives’ gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery.
The shadow would “fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites,” the relatives argued. They filed a motion to intervene in two existing lawsuits seeking to block construction of the arch.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan last week prohibited the Trump administration from breaking ground on the structure for 14 days.
The nine Kennedy family members who filed suit are children and grandchildren of Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, brothers of the slain U.S. president John F. Kennedy, both of whom served in the U.S. Senate. They are buried close to the eternal flame that marks JFK’s gravesite, a trio of memorials that are a major draw for the millions of people who visit the Arlington cemetery each year.
Building the arch would be a “permanent denigration” of the gravesites, and the Kennedy offspring “would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended,” lawyers for the relatives wrote. They are represented by veteran Washington lawyer Norm Eisen and Democracy Defenders Fund.
“It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery,” said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle. “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation.”
Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s health and human services secretary who has a fractured relationship with many of his relatives, did not join the lawsuit.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections.
The White House last week unveiled a glitzy new website to showcase the arch, which is slated to rise in a mass of gold ornamentation and stately gray granite between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

title: CHRISTIAN VIEWS: The empty chair at the community table
text:
Every community has a table, even when it is not made of wood. Sometimes it is a church supper, a library gathering, a volunteer meeting, or a conversation after a school event. We recognize the people who return each week. We notice who brings the casserole, who pours the coffee, and who stays to stack chairs.
But how often do we notice the person who never comes?
In Maine’s small towns, distance is measured not only in miles. For someone who no longer drives, a meeting a few miles away may feel impossibly far. For a parent working irregular hours, the familiar invitation to “stop by anytime” may not feel like an invitation at all. And for a newcomer, walking into a room where everyone seems to know everyone else can require extraordinary courage.
Jesus once told a host not to fill a banquet only with friends and people able to repay the invitation. Instead, he urged the host to welcome those who were ordinarily left out. It was a challenge to the habit of treating hospitality as a comfortable exchange among people already connected.
That teaching asks something of us now. A community can be friendly without being accessible. It can be proud of its traditions while overlooking those who cannot easily participate in them. True hospitality begins when we ask who is missing, why they are missing, and what we might change.
Perhaps a neighbor needs a ride. Perhaps a gathering could begin a little earlier. Perhaps the person standing quietly by the door needs someone to make introductions rather than another cheerful instruction to “make yourself at home.”
None of this requires a large budget or a new committee. It requires attention. It requires us to believe that a person’s absence matters, even when that person is not someone we already know.
The best traditions are not preserved by keeping the same people around the same table forever. They survive when a new generation and a new neighbor discover that there is a place for them, too.
Jesus described a kingdom in which welcome is not reserved for those who can return the favor. Our towns can practice a little of that kingdom whenever we make space for someone who has been standing outside the circle.
The next time the chairs are set out, count them carefully. Then ask whether there is one more person who ought to be there.
Douglas Vandergraph is a Christian writer and teacher based in Fort Collins, Colorado.

title: US charges 3 men with plotting terror attacks, including planned assault on UK air base
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A man jailed on terrorism charges in New York was able to pass secret messages to Iranian operatives planning an attack on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force, according to an indictment unsealed Tuesday.
The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode shrouded in mystery since Sept. 27, when a group of men were detained on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward a British air base where U.S. bombers were stationed.
The new charges accuse Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national jailed at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, of a role in plotting to attack the Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, in western England, even though he’d been arrested last spring.
According to prosecutors, al-Saadi used coded language in phone and video calls to his mother and sister in Iraq to pass messages encouraging associates to carry out the air base bombing.
Two other men have been charged in the case, which accuses Iran-backed operatives of plotting nearly 20 terror strikes on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S.
Neither of those men, Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national, and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, are in U.S. custody.
US attorney says men sought to unleash a ‘campaign of terror’
“These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche said: “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American service members will be prosecuted by the United States government.”
Seven men arrested in the United Kingdom in connection with the incident at the RAF base in Fairford were all released on bail. One of those men was subsequently rearrested on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service and charged, along with another man, under the National Security Act, British authorities said.
British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to the United States.
RAF Fairford, 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
Man accused of fueling plots from jail with coded messages
U.S. prosecutors said in the indictment that while speaking to his family from the Brooklyn jail, al-Saadi told them he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass messages to him about “work,” a term al-Saadi used to describe terrorist activity.
“What are they doing about all our old work?” al-Saadi asked his sister on a July 30 call, according to the indictment. It said he asked her whether it had been canceled or just put on pause, to which she responded that “it isn’t canceled.”
On a Sept. 24 call, al-Saadi asked about al-Hassani, whom he was told had been transferred to the “International Section,” and instructed his family to “give him money so we can do it,” it said.
Since his May arrest, al-Saadi had been held in solitary confinement. The Justice Department said he was dangerous because of his desire to attack U.S. and Israeli interests.
New charges come amid court battle over al-Saadi’s phone access
Al-Saadi was permitted phone and video calls with his family, but each call was monitored and recorded by the FBI, according to court filings.
In September, al-Saadi’s lawyer complained that some of his calls were repeatedly interrupted and cut off without explanation. Citing concerns that he was using coded language, including “work” and “a job,” the government later said it was limiting him just to a single hourlong call each month.
Still, from June through September, al-Saadi participated in nine phone or video teleconference calls from jail, according to a court filing by prosecutors. In one, al-Saadi’s mother told him to stop talking about a topic because “they may end the call,” according to a court filing that said the FBI then terminated the call.
The indictment alleged the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terror attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.
In one instance in mid-April, the indictment said, al-Saadi, al-Hassani and Mohajeri directed an individual to carry out an arson attack on a Jewish charity organization in London in real time as they watched it on video that was projected from a laptop computer onto a large screen. The next day, they directed another attack on a synagogue in London, with al-Hassani directing the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree,” the indictment said.
In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a “prisoner of war.” He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday.
Both Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hizballah commander.
___
This story was first published Nov. 10, 2026. It was updated Nov. 11, 2026, to correct that only one of the two individuals charged under the National Security Act was previously arrested in Britain in connection with the suspected plot.
___
Tucker reported from Washington. Associated Press Writer Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington also contributed.

title: MAINE-LY GARDENING: How did your garden grow?
text:
As the growing season comes to an end Maine gardeners have been harvesting the last of this year’s crops and thinking ahead to 2027.
There have been successes and disappointments as with every gardening year. Many people I know had a poor cucumber year in 2026. Was this year better for them? The drought has continued, although there has been recent rainfall, even thunder showers in some spots. We can only hope for a more generous amount, and better distribution, of rain next year, while still wary of planting certain plants that have been most affected in recent years.
The temperatures have been fairly warm this fall. We may have taken advantage of the nice weather as we’ve done our fall gardening and yard work over a longer stretch of time. We’re relieved to have needed less firewood or oil to heat the house, but the times still have been hard on the wallet.
While some people home for a mild winter, others recognize that our region is home to trees and other perennial plants have evolved to require cold winters. We may recall a year when one unseasonably warm February day followed by a normal freezing night killed the flower buds on peaches and other plants. And folks with a sugar bush, or even one or two trees to tap, are hoping that 2027 will be a good year for that delicious first harvest.
As we survey the yard, woodshed, and pantry, we can’t help but look back on previous years and compare, hoping that our plans and work will be enough. Perhaps there are a few plants on the windowsill that were potted up to spend another winter indoors will provide some greenery and thoughts of spring.
Before long we’ll be looking over the seed catalogs. The very organized gardeners among us will have been keeping notes. Some years ago, we had a particularly organized neighbor who had kept notes for a decade: how many pounds of beans and how many of each variety of tomatoes he’d gotten from his back yard garden. A garden designer friend was quick to realize that the advent of the cellphone camera made it so much easier to keep records for her clients and her own garden. A lot of us are more easy going, or just so busy with work and family, that we find ourselves unsure which variety of lettuce did best and wonder if that container of early summer flowers should have more sun or more shade. Once again, we vow to keep better notes next year!
But there can be rewards for letting Nature reclaim some space in what we call Our Gardens. In June we spotted a squash plant among the tomatoes, and a little bean plant in the asparagus bed. Instead of pulling them, we decided to see what seeds may have survived in the compost pile.
The squash turned out to be a butternut and outperformed those we planted on purpose. We harvested a dozen nice big squashes from that one plant, and the tomatoes didn’t seem to mind. The surprise bean also grew happily, supported by a couple of the asparagus “trees.” It was a Cherokee Trail of Tears descended from a handful of seeds given to me about 10 years ago. We grow several types of beans each year to eat fresh, freeze, or dry, but I always save and plant some of the Cherokees for their purple pods, pretty pink flowers and shiny black beans. For allowing it to remain in the garden, that one plant gave us 1.3 pounds of beans which I weighed and recorded with each picking, remembering our old neighbor.
 © Judith Chute Hsiang
Jude Hsiang is a retired University Extension Master Gardener Program instructor and a member of the China Community Garden.

title: Father charged with attempted murder after 11-month-old son found buried alive in dog crate
text:
LEXINGTON COUNTY, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - The father of a baby found buried alive this week has been charged with attempted murder.
According to the Lexington County Sheriff’s Department, 25-year-old Michael Comer’s charges also include unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary.
Lexington County authorities said the 11-month-old baby, Koah Sharp, miraculously survived after Comer buried him in a dog crate.
The boy’s father was arrested Monday night.
Koah was found alive Tuesday afternoon just over 24 hours after he was last seen with his father.
Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said Koah was found buried in a dog crate wrapped in a towel.
“By the grace of God, [it] probably provided enough air for him to survive an estimated 24 hours under that dirt,” Koon said.
The sheriff said Comer’s mother was caring for the child when Comer arrived at the home on Monday. She then left Koah in Comer’s care while another caregiver was on the way.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone and Koah was gone with him,” Koon said.
Other members of Koah’s family filed a missing persons report Monday afternoon.
Koon said authorities went to the nearby home of Comer’s father, where they found both doors open and Koah’s belongings, but no sign of them.
Authorities arrested Comer after finding him in a shed in Batesburg.
It wasn’t until later that investigators were able to locate Koah at Comer’s father’s house. They noted finding a pine straw and “freshly disturbed dirt.” Once they started digging, they heard him crying.
“So, as you imagine, the race was on,” Koon said. “Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out.”
Koon said it’s believed that Koah was buried for around 24 hours.
The sheriff said Koah was treated at an area hospital.
Comer’s arrest comes just over a month after he was placed on probation following a guilty plea for aggravated breach of peace, according to public court and state records.
Court records also show Comer had previous arrests earlier this year for domestic violence, as well as a weapons-related charge.

title: VETERANS CORNER: Remembering sacrifices made by veterans on Veterans Day
text:
Veterans Day, originally known as Armistice Day, was created to end major hostilities in World War I. It has a very significant beginning as it was enacted on the 11th hour of the 11th day on the 11th month in 1918. It didn’t become a legal federal holiday until 1938, and was renamed Veterans Day after World War II and the Korean War, in 1954, in honor of those who served. This is in fact to honor all Veterans who served their country honorably during the times of war or those ready in time of peace.
Some people confuse Veterans Day with Memorial Day which are in fact two separate and distinct holidays. Memorial Day is celebrated to honor those who gave the supreme sacrifice. I for one has a hard time with the word celebrate for events such as this. There are those who argue this point as a celebration does take place in honor of the dead. My argument has always been that it’s difficult to celebrate a time of mourning. But in any case we set a day aside in honor of their service.
Although some of us do join in the festivities we do so solemnly coupled with prayer and thankful appreciation of those who gave their lives. Although they are separate we must remember that hundreds of thousands of men and women did die during times of unrest and war. Veterans Day honors both the living and the dead. Like it is written, “Freedom Isn’t Free”. Those reading my very humble words are alive, here, and free because of the Veteran, both deceased and alive.
We often forget when we see that bent and sometimes grouchy old man or woman that once he or she was young, strong and perhaps handsome or beautiful. If you get the chance take a look at the photo of a friend or family member when they were young and now that they are old. The comparison should tell you something which is also in your future, if you’re fortunate enough to last as long. Give it some thought and it should change some perspectives and cause a trail of realistic thought. Also, while you are at it, don’t ignore the limp, gait or wheelchair. Also, the sacrifice for some is greater than dying with those they served with. Lost love and opportunity can be very devastating for many who served their country, with dignity and honor.
Is it really too much to help in anyway, those who have given so much for their families, friends and country. I am a veteran, yet I always find myself thanking others and treating some to a meal or a couple of dollars for whatever. Some veterans never recover from their military experience. All should be respected but those are the ones who may need a little bit more. I personally have spent many years helping veterans that I feel are in need all over the world. Also, when you think of veterans, don’t forget their families. They often times need help also. Don’t turn your back on a veteran who has left this world by avoiding his family. Sometimes there is great need to be found there. I personally belong to several organizations that make it a very serious point to remember widows and orphans. You don’t need to be a Christian to show compassion. However, you do have to believe in a higher power. For me all things beautiful have a veteran’s name written on it.
One day while walking through a graveyard as many of us do on Veterans Day, I passed by a grave that was very old but for some reason I stopped at that grave to read that which had been carved in the marble. It said, “Look at me now and remember, where you stand now looking down, I once stood”. That kind of caught my breath. It was as if he was talking to me. I put my hand on that stone and offered a very humble prayer, which included, “ I think I understand old friend”. I didn’t know him, can’t even remember his name but I never forgot the wisdom in his message; even big guys can shed a tear. I guess Veterans Day means different things to different people and perhaps to some, they mean nothing at all. Perhaps they should be the ones included in the next draft. Some people have to learn the hard way, what is important and what to be thankful for. Someone once said, “Love your neighbor as yourself”. Some of you will get the message and be forever thankful for the Veteran. Pray for the day that it will be no longer necessary and military graveyards will cease to exist except in old history books.
God bless you all and especially every Veteran both here and beyond. Hope you had a happy Veterans day.

title: More than a dozen key races remain too early to call one week after Election Day
text:
More than a dozen key races remain too early to call one week after Election Day
The strength of Democrats’ majorities in the House and Senate remains undetermined one week after Election Day as more than a dozen races are still too early to call.
Democrats are on track to hold 54 Senate seats in January, but could pick up one or two more from Republicans as votes are counted in Alaska and Mississippi. With 255 seats in the House, Democrats will have their largest majority elected to the chamber since 2008, with the potential to pick up several more seats as the remaining races are called.
Here’s a look at where things stand in some of the uncalled races:
Mississippi's Senate seat remains too early to call
Late in the afternoon Tuesday, Democrat Scott Colom was about 2,600 votes ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for Senate in Mississippi.
There are two key deadlines in the vote-counting process in Mississippi this week: Mail-in absentee ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday.
It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count.
Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, Associated Press journalists and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.
The state will certify its results on Dec. 3.
On Monday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said about 14,200 provisional ballots had been processed, of which about 80% were accepted, and about 2,700 mail-in absentee ballots had not yet been returned.
Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is eligible for a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
The vote count is ongoing in Alaska's Senate race
Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 votes in Alaska's Senate race on Tuesday afternoon, with an estimated 76% of the vote counted. The results of some absentee ballots are expected to be released late Tuesday, though the final absentee ballots mailed back from outside the U.S. are accepted as late as Nov. 18, 15 days after Election Day.
Ranked choice voting could also affect the timeline. Peltola is just over 1 percentage point short of the majority needed to win outright. If neither candidate wins a majority, the race will proceed to ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18. The state's “target date” for certifying the election results is Nov. 25.
Recounts in Alaska are automatic only in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request a recount within five days of the state's certification.
More than a dozen House races are still up in the air
In most of the House races that have not been called, the margin between the leading candidates was less than 1 percentage point among votes counted as of late Tuesday afternoon.
In North Carolina, four races remain undecided, the most of any state, and Republican incumbents were being challenged in all. There are no automatic recounts in North Carolina, but candidates may request a recount if the margin between candidates is 1% or less of the total votes. The state must receive the recount request by noon Eastern time Nov. 17, two business days after the county canvass in the state. The state is scheduled to certify its results Nov. 24.
In California, only one of the remaining House races, in the 23rd District, will affect the chamber's balance of power. The other uncalled race is between two Democrats. Mail ballots must be received by Tuesday and counties must certify their results Dec. 3. The state will certify its results Dec. 11.
In South Carolina's 2nd District, a recount is ongoing in the race between Republican incumbent Joe Wilson and Democrat Zyon Khalia. Wilson led Khalia by only about 3,000 votes in the original tally by late Tuesday afternoon, when 99% of the votes had been counted.
In Minnesota's 1st District, the race was still undecided late in the afternoon Tuesday, with about 300 votes separating the top two candidates and an estimated 99% of votes counted. Recounts are not automatic in Minnesota, but a candidate can request a publicly-funded recount if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is less than 0.25% of the vote.
In Tennessee’s 4th District, about 300 votes lay between Democrat Victoria Broderick and Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais as of late afternoon Tuesday. In that state, recounts are held only as part of a legal challenge in the courts. There are no automatic recounts, and losing candidates may not request recounts.
Two governorships remain undecided
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher led state Republican Senate President Ty Masterson in the race for governor of Kansas by less than 1 percentage point late Tuesday afternoon. On Nov. 4, the state announced that a close-race audit of election results requiring a hand count of selected ballots had been triggered in six close Kansas races, including the gubernatorial race. The audit must be completed before Nov. 16, the day by which counties must certify their results.
In the race for governor of Alaska, only about 76% of votes were estimated to have been counted late Tuesday afternoon, and the Democratic candidate, Jonathan S. Kreiss‑Tomkins was leading Bernadette M. Wilson by about 45,000 votes, 49.6% to 28.9%. The race will advance to ranked choice tabulation if no candidate receives more than 50% of votes.

title: Bessent moves to a military base over safety concerns, an AP source says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was recently forced to relocate to a military base over concerns for his safety.
The move comes as Bessent has spent the last several months executing a massive economic campaign against Iran aimed at severing all of Tehran’s remaining financial ties around the world.
A person familiar with the matter, who spoke to The Associated Press on Wednesday on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive details, said the relocation was partly due to media reports that helped identify Bessent’s home address. The relocation was earlier reported by The New York Times.
Recent U.S. intelligence showed that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel in the Middle East and elsewhere, which contributed to the State Department last month reducing staffing at four U.S. embassies in the region.
President Donald Trump said this week that the more than 8-month-old Iran war “militarily is effectively over,” but his administration has kept up the financial warfare in a bid to get Iran to capitulate to U.S. demands over Tehran’s nuclear program.
The Treasury Department in August pledged an “economic D-Day” against Tehran, and it has become a massive sanctions and influence campaign.
U.S. officials have spent the past few months traveling from Europe to the Middle East and meeting behind closed doors on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly to make the case to some of Tehran’s closest and most vital trading partners: Sever those financial ties or face retaliation from the United States.
And it appears some have followed suit. The United Arab Emirates and Turkey — key trading partners and regional neighbors — halted Iran’s top commercial bank from issuing transactions in their countries, while some of the country’s top airlines were cut off from critical regional routes from Istanbul to Muscat, Oman.
Other top Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, also live on military bases.

title: Veterans Day Parade in Bangor and Brewer honors those who served
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Crowds gathered in Bangor and Brewer for the annual Veterans Day parade, bringing the community together to honor those who have served and those who are currently serving in the military.
Sponsored by the Bangor High School Army JROTC, the parade began on Vista Way in Brewer, where active and retired military members marched alongside local organizations into downtown Bangor.
For United States Air Force Brigadier General Byron Newell, participating in the event was a way to connect with currently active veterans.
“Every year that I’m out here still in uniform, I’m just incredibly grateful to have this purpose in my life,” said Newell, “I know that my fellow veterans feel the same way. While I look forward someday to that retirement, it’s just for me, it’s just to get out here and march with those of us who are still serving actively in the Guard, the Army, the Air Force here in the state. It’s just a lot of pride.”
For veterans in the parade, it was a chance to connect with the community and hear its appreciation.
“What’s nice being in the parade is that you get to experience everybody appreciating what you’ve done and what you did, to get a thank you for your service, especially from little kids. It’s nice. It’s heartwarming,” said Kevin O’Connell who served in the Maine Air National Guard.
“It’s the least we can do. People can’t relate unless they’ve done it and to honor those folks and especially when it hasn’t always been the way, unfortunately. I think back to the Vietnam veterans and how they were treated,” said Retired Chief Master Sergeant Andrew MacDonald who had served in the Maine Air National Guard.
Among those watching the parade was Bill Dean, who served in both the Navy and the Air Force for a total of 42 years. He says the parade was a chance to reconnect with friends and to admire those who served.
“Anybody that’s willing to give up that time and potentially their life for their country. It’s an honor to meet anybody that’s done that,” said Dean.
Participants in the parade also emphasized the importance of recognizing veterans going through everyday struggles.
“Just the importance of doing what we can for our veterans, not just on the holidays, but throughout the year. Keeping that present in our minds, whether it’s heating oil in the winter or just to support when they’re on hard times. It’s important for us to always be cognizant of that,” said Newell.
Governor elect Hannah Pingree also made an appearance at the parade.

title: InvestigateTV+: Tracing the footsteps of a WWII soldier
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ explores the power of honoring history and reclaiming legacy. We reveal how families can rebuild military records destroyed in a historic fire.
Then, we follow a community of strangers stepping up to bury a veteran from World War I.
Plus, we expose a manipulative financial scam that turns trust into a terrifying and costly trap.
Tracing a WWII soldier’s footsteps
A program at the National World War II Museum in New Orleans is helping families learn about their loved ones’ service by tracking down veterans’ official records.
Researchers can find details that include training, medical history, units, battles and promotions.
InvestigateTV’s own Tisha Powell used the program to learn more about her grandfather, Ulysses Reed Sr.
Gold courier scam
It can start with a pop-up on the computer screen and sometimes ends with the innocent victim handing over their life savings to a scammer.
The FBI reported in 2025 that the “gold courier” scam alone drained more than $300 million from victims.
A Wisconsin woman lost more than $400,000 of her retirement savings after scammers impersonated federal agencies, her investment company and the Better Business Bureau to convince her she was protecting her money.
‘The People’s House’
A collection of four Norman Rockwell paintings that spent nearly 40 years on display in the White House West Wing is now on display to the public for the first time at “The People’s House.”
Final resting place for World War I vet
On a typical day at the Vermont Veterans Memorial Cemetery, the only sound on these hallowed grounds is an American flag flapping in the gentle breeze and birds chirping from a distance.
Three men were laid to rest recently. Private Edward James Irwin was one of them. His final goodbye comes almost 45 years after his death. He served in the Army during World War I from 1917 to 1918.
You may wonder why a World War I vet who died in November 1981 is finally going to be laid to rest. Well, it goes back to Walter Ducharme’s funeral business in Rutland.

title: Aging Untold: The hidden risks of denial in caregiving
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address caregiver denial and explore why recognizing when an aging loved one needs more help leads to better, safer care.
Plus, we share practical ways to make a home safer for aging in place, from quick, low-cost fixes to knowing when to get a full home assessment, as well as costs and resources to help pay for modifications.
Finally, we introduce you to an inspiring Vermont “super ager” approaching 90 who is proving it is never too late to build strength through Pilates.
One of the hardest hurdles that families face is admitting when a loved one starts to need extra support.
Being in denial can protect us in a time of grief, but avoiding reality for too long can contribute to caregiver burnout and compromise care.
There are several facets to denial. The Aging Untold experts are sharing the signs to look for and tips for meeting loved ones where they are.
There are some small changes that you can make in a home to allow you or a loved one to age in place safely.
Tara Ballman, executive director of the National Aging in Place Council, said two low-cost areas have a high impact. The first is trip hazards, and the second is lighting.
Ballman provided additional tips on what long-distance caregivers can look for and recommendations for “age tech,” technology that helps people stay in their homes longer and more safely.
It can be difficult to think clearly when you or a loved one are going through a medical crisis.
But advocating for yourself or a loved one entails paying attention, asking questions and being vocal, aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
She is sharing a personal story, and the Aging Untold experts explain how to build a team to help you navigate a crisis and share relevant information with the care team.
Sue Talmage is sure that she is the oldest student at Essential Physical Therapy and Pilates in Montpelier, Vermont.
The 88-year-old drives there twice a week to take the classes she has been attending for close to two decades.
“It’s an important part of my life,” Talmage said.
Instructor Willow Wonder leads Talmage’s class, which runs 45 minutes with no breaks. She said Talmage serves as an inspiration for others who come to the studio.

title: Former NFL coach Rex Ryan accused of hitting 2 pedestrians with truck in Nashville, leaving scene
text:
Former NFL coach Rex Ryan accused of hitting 2 pedestrians with truck in Nashville, leaving scene
Former NFL coach Rex Ryan surrendered on Wednesday for booking on six misdemeanor warrants stemming from a Nashville crash last week in which police said two pedestrians were struck by his pickup truck and suffered minor injuries.
According to the Metropolitan Nashville Police Department, the pedestrians were crossing Broadway from 4th Avenue with a walk sign before midnight last Thursday when Ryan's pickup truck turned from 4th Avenue and ran over both pedestrians' feet and made contact with one of the victims' legs.
See the report in the video above
The victims told police that the vehicle kept going, but stopped for a red light at Broadway and Representative John Lewis Way, and they waved down Ryan.
According to the news release, the victims stated Ryan got out of the truck and argued with them before getting back in and driving away. The victims were able to take pictures of Ryan and the truck's license plate, which is registered to him, police said.
Ryan is facing two counts of leaving the scene of an accident, two counts of failure to give information/render aid, and two counts of failure to obey a traffic control signal. His bond was set at $6,000, and the victims suffered minor injuries, according to police.
The former New York Jets and Buffalo Bills head coach coached in the NFL for more than two decades. Ryan worked as a defensive line and linebackers coach for the Arizona Cardinals (1994-1995), spent 10 seasons with the Baltimore Ravens from 1999 to 2008, before making a leap to become the head coach of the Jets from 2009 to 2014 and head coach of the Bills from 2015 to 2016.
During his tenure with the Jets, he coached his team to two AFC Championship appearances in the 2009 and 2010 NFL seasons. Since his last season coaching in 2016, he has worked as an NFL analyst for ESPN.

title: Guard reprimands group with Hegseth at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier after laughter was heard
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.
Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that “all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s top spokesman, said that “while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”
“The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe,” he added.
The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from World War I, World War II and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army’s 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as “The Old Guard,” since 1948.
Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that also was attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.
The effort was led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth’s critics were not successful in Tuesday’s vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach the defense secretary. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.
A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes.
“On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime,” Hegseth said Tuesday.
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth argued. “This is sabotage.”
Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.
Rep. Gwen Moore, D-Wis., said Hegseth demonstrated “his utter lack of fitness for his office.”
“One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier,” she wrote in a social media post.
It was not the first time members of Trump’s team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.
During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honor U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.
Trump, who had been invited by troops’ families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the “disaster” of the Afghanistan withdrawal.
U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

title: Did You Know the U.S. Military Uses Silly String in Combat?
text:
Did You Know the U.S. Military Uses Silly String in Combat?
Who didn't have a blast with Silly String growing up? Even as adults, it can be a blast at parties and fun to enjoy with your kids, nieces, and nephews. It truly is silly and makes you smile and laugh.
It wasn't meant to be a toy, though. Originally, it was invented to help with broken bones as a cast.
According to the Interesting Facts website, two guys, an inventor and a chemist, tried to create something that a doctor could spray onto your arm or leg that would instantly harden while your bones healed.
But Leonard A. Fish and Robert P. Cox found themselves laughing after testing some 500 nozzles on pressurized cans, searching for the best method to spray their invention.
When one nozzle propelled a stream 30 feet across the room, Fish and Cox had another idea — maybe this stringy goo would work better as a plaything. After tweaking their recipe, the duo arranged a meeting with an executive at Wham-O, the company behind such popular toys as the Frisbee and Hula Hoop.
In 1972, Silly String hit the stores, and the rest is history in the entertainment world, where good times are guaranteed for kids and adults of all ages.
Enter 1993.
According to Interesting Facts, even though the seriousness of helping to heal broken bones didn't make the list of Silly String uses, the United States military did find a way to use it.
LEARN MORE: THE POST-IT NOTE WAS INVENTED BY ACCIDENT
You've heard of IEDs, right? Improvised explosive devices in hostile areas are all too common for our ground troops. One way to help locate these dangers is with Silly String. According to Wikipedia, an Army instructor discovered how spraying it could help detect tripwires.
A spritz of the stringy stuff is light enough to drape across nearly invisible trip wires without setting them off, calling attention to these deadly traps often nestled in doorways and gates.
According to Interesting Facts, if you've never heard this, that's okay. It's not like the military advertises it, and no one really knew about this until 2007.
The revelation of its effectiveness prompted one mother, whose son was stationed in Iraq in the early 2000s, to collect 80,000 cans of Silly String and nearly identical products to send overseas to aid the war effort and save a few more lives.
According to NBC News, soldiers would spray the substance, which shot out around 10 feet. If it hung in the air, they knew the doorways or areas were booby-trapped with trip wires.

title: Chick-fil-A to open 3 new restaurants in Maine
