text:
BIDDEFORD, Maine (WABI) - Chick-fil-A will open three new restaurants in Maine, adding an estimated 300 jobs, the company said.
The chain plans to open locations in Biddeford, South Portland, and Auburn in early 2027.
Right now, Chick-fil-A has locations in Bangor and Westbrook.
Dustin Griffiths, director of Chick-fil-A real estate, said Maine is an important part of the company’s growth in the Northeast.
“Maine is an important part of Chick-fil-A’s continued growth in the Northeast, and we recognize the strong sense of pride Mainers have in their communities,” Griffiths said. “That commitment to community aligns closely with our approach to growth, which centers on local Owner-Operators who are invested in the places they serve. As we expand our presence in Maine, we look forward to creating meaningful jobs, building lasting relationships with Guests and becoming a positive part of the communities that make this state special.”
Jobs and scholarships
Chick-fil-A said the expansion will bring an estimated 300 jobs. The company said the jobs offer hands-on training, pay, benefits, scholarship opportunities and flexible work schedules.
Team Members can apply for Chick-fil-A Remarkable Futures Scholarships, which are awarded twice per year. The company has awarded more than $212,000 in scholarships to Maine-based Team Members to support continued education.
Nonprofit grants and donations
In January, Chick-fil-A, Inc. will open the True Inspiration Awards for the 2028 grant cycle. Local Owner-Operators can submit Maine nonprofits.
The company has awarded $75,000 to the Good Shepherd Food Bank following a nomination by Brad Terrell, the local Owner-Operator of Chick-fil-A Rock Row.
With the opening of the three new restaurants, Chick-fil-A will donate $25,000 per restaurant, for a total of $75,000, to the Good Shepherd Food Bank. The food bank is a Feeding America partner food bank.
Surplus food program
Through the Chick-fil-A Shared Table program, two existing Maine Chick-fil-A restaurants have helped create more than 66,000 meals across Maine by redirecting surplus food.

title: Meet the 22 people helping Hannah Pingree choose her government
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree’s transition committee is a roadmap to her agenda, and most of its members helped get her elected.
The 22 people introduced Tuesday to help pick her Cabinet span business, labor, tribal leaders and a former Republican senator, but their political giving is overwhelmingly Democratic. Thirteen gave to her campaign, and some backed her through groups they lead.
The volunteer panel has little time. Pingree wants to name every commissioner before her Jan. 6 inauguration, and she must send lawmakers a plan to close a $1 billion budget gap by early February.
“I said throughout this campaign that I was running to deliver results, and the results start with the right people making leadership decisions,” Pingree said.
The committee tracks her biggest promises. Co-chair Maulian Bryant leads the Wabanaki Alliance, which endorsed Pingree after she pledged a tribal sovereignty bill in her first 100 days. Gov. Janet Mills generally resisted the push from tribes, although she made piecemeal reforms.
Education is well represented, too. Co-chair Roger Katz, a former centrist Republican state senator, chairs the University of Maine System board of trustees, and Vicky Cohen sits on the State Board of Education. Pingree, who has promised more teacher training, named education commissioner as one of her most important picks.
Other members bring deep policy portfolios. Ken Colburn, a Bar Harbor consultant who co-chairs the Maine Climate Council’s energy working group, has long pushed to tie utility profits to performance. Pingree’s energy plan promises to “tie utility profits to lower bills.”
Maureen Drouin leads Maine Conservation Voters, which spent about $850,000 to help Pingree win the June primary. Her group broke with Mills after the governor vetoed a ban on large data centers in April to save a project at the former paper mill in Jay. Pingree backed a ban on the campaign trail, and the developer filed for state permits on Monday.
“Jay should not be the testing ground for a data center project before Maine has strong regulations in place to protect communities,” Pingree said in a statement.
Liza Fleming-Ives runs a lender that finances the kind of affordable housing Pingree wants to fund with $100 million a year. Sen. Peggy Rotundo, D-Lewiston, the outgoing budget committee chair, knows the gap better than anyone on the panel. Two doctors, former state Rep. Richard Evans and Barbara Crowley, are on board as Pingree pushes a public insurance option.
The panel also mirrors the coalition Pingree built to win a crowded primary. She drew support from Mills, other establishment Democrats and environmental groups, then won over unions that had backed former Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Graham Platner and his successor, former Senate President Troy Jackson.
Former L.L Bean CEO Steve Smith and Luke Holden, the founder of Luke’s Lobster, sit alongside Grant Provost of Ironworkers Local 7 and Ben Waxman, a former AFL-CIO aide who runs a union apparel company in Westbrook.
Fleming-Ives and Waxman were Pingree’s biggest donors on the committee, at about $3,000 each, and Katz gave $2,500. Not everyone was with her from the start. Waxman gave matching amounts to Jackson in the primary, and Provost backed Jackson before the Maine AFL-CIO endorsed Pingree in August. Holden also gave $250 to former gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Bush, the only gift to a Republican by a committee member this cycle.
Pingree said Tuesday that her Cabinet could include independents and Republicans. She said committee members were not being eyed as candidates, though she did not know how the process would play out.
“I think we did ask people to join this committee with the understanding that they were not applying for jobs,” she said.

title: Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed says he would vote for ‘Trumpcare’ for all
text:
(Gray News) - Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, said Tuesday that he supports “cradle-to-grave” healthcare and would vote for “Trumpcare” for all.
El-Sayed made the comments in an interview with CNN anchor and chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins.
“Donald, if you’re watching, we can put your name on it. I know you like to put your name on stuff. You can finally meet the unmet promise in America to guarantee everybody healthcare, so it’s on the table if you want to do it,” he said.
El-Sayed said he wants everyone to have healthcare in America and what it is called is a secondary issue.
“If we’re able to guarantee everybody cradle-to-grave coverage without a co-pay, a premium, or deductible ... I think that would be a win. So if he wants to call it Trumpcare for all, like, I’m game,” he said.

title: High school football parent caught on camera pooping in rival school’s hallway, police say
text:
GROSSE POINTE FARMS, Mich. (WWJ) - Police in Michigan say the father of a high school student was caught on camera defecating in the hallway at a rival school during a district championship football game.
Officials with Grosse Pointe Public Schools say the father of a Bedford High School student entered Grosse Pointe South High School without permission Friday night during a football game between the two schools and took a bowel movement in the middle of a hallway.
“It seems very immature for a parent to act that way,” resident Christina Dzul said.
Officers with Grosse Pointe Farms Police are investigating the incident, which was caught on camera. They say the father got into the school through a door that had been left open for a scheduled band concert.
Police say the school’s security footage shows the man walk past multiple bathrooms before allegedly defecating on the hallway floor.
Police used the video to identify the father. During the investigation, he reportedly said he had experienced a medical emergency. However, police say they are still looking into the incident.
“This behavior is wholly unacceptable and is inconsistent with the standards of conduct and respect that the District expects of anyone entering its school facilities. The District has filed a police report regarding this incident and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate,” said Grosse Pointe Public Schools in a statement released Monday.
Bedford Public Schools Superintendent Carl Shultz also released a statement that said, “At Bedford Public Schools, we hold our students, staff, and community to high standards of safety, respect, and sportsmanship, both on and off the field. We are fully cooperating with the host district and local law enforcement.”
One resident named Andrew says he isn’t surprised by the incident, given the current state of youth sports.
“Honestly, these days with youth sports and parents and the way people get into their feelings, nothing surprises me,” he said. “People are animals.”
Grosse Pointe South beat Bedford 42-0 in Friday night’s football game.

title: WSDG transforms sound at Bar Harbor’s historic The 1932 Criterion Theatre
text:
BAR HARBOR — WSDG has completed the first phase of a major technical upgrade at The 1932 Criterion Theatre, a press release said. Working alongside systems integrator Stone Mountain Systems, WSDG designed a new sound reinforcement system and supporting AV infrastructure that significantly improved the audience experience while respecting the character of this historic Art Deco venue.
The theater’s sound system had required a comprehensive upgrade for many years. Its previous configuration could not provide the coverage, output or consistency needed for contemporary productions, with the most significant limitations experienced on the balcony. The former main loudspeaker system was ground-stacked on the elevated stage, making it difficult to direct sound effectively toward every part of the audience.

title: ‘Huge inspiration’: 88-year-old Vermont woman keeps moving with Pilates
text:
BARRE, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Nearly every day, Sue Talmage walks on the land in Barre that she owns with Bruce, her husband of more than 40 years. Twice a week, she drives to Montpelier for something else entirely.
At 88, Talmage is sure she is the oldest student at Essential Physical Therapy and Pilates — and she has been taking classes there for close to two decades.
“It’s an important part of my life,” Talmage said.
What is Pilates?
Pilates is a combination of repetitive exercises focused on building balance, flexibility and core strength.
Studies show older adults are prone to losing muscle mass, which can lead to falls and other complications.
Instructor Willow Wonder leads Talmage’s class, which runs 45 minutes with no breaks.
‘Huge inspiration’
Wonder said Talmage’s physical ability stands out.
“If you think old people have balance issues, this is not the case,” Wonder said. “I think she’s very unique to have such ability, strength, balance, flexibility — all of the things at that age. I just have not seen much of.”
Wonder also said Talmage serves as an inspiration for others who come to the studio.
“Absolutely — huge inspiration to everyone that comes here,” Wonder said.
Talmage said she does not see herself that way. For her, staying fit is a personal goal.
“Eighty-eight is a long time,” she said.
After class, Talmage said she feels no soreness and returns home to her daily walk.
“I feel great and I can still do just about everything I want to,” she said.

title: These key races remain too early to call one week after Election Day
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The size of Democrats’ majorities in the House and Senate remained undetermined one week after Election Day as more than a dozen races were still too early to call Tuesday.
Democrats are on track to hold 54 Senate seats in January, but could pick up one or two more from Republicans as votes are counted in Alaska and Mississippi. With 255 seats in the House, Democrats will have their largest majority elected to the chamber since 2008, with the potential to pick up several more seats as the remaining races are called.
Here’s a look at where things stand in some of the uncalled races:
Mississippi’s Senate seat remains too early to call
Late in the afternoon Tuesday, Democrat Scott Colom was about 2,600 votes ahead of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for Senate in Mississippi.
There are two key deadlines in the vote-counting process in Mississippi this week: Mail-in absentee ballots must be received by Tuesday, and counties are required to submit their certified election results — including tallies of provisional ballots — to the state by Friday.
It is unclear exactly how many ballots are left to count.
Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, Associated Press journalists and analysts communicate with each of the state’s 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.
The state will certify its results on Dec. 3.
On Monday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said about 14,200 provisional ballots had been processed, of which about 80% were accepted, and about 2,700 mail-in absentee ballots had not yet been returned.
Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is eligible for a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
The vote count is ongoing in Alaska’s Senate race
Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 2,500 votes in Alaska’s Senate race on Tuesday afternoon, with an estimated 76% of the vote counted. The results of some absentee ballots are expected to be released late Tuesday, though the final absentee ballots mailed back from outside the U.S. are accepted as late as Nov. 18, 15 days after Election Day.
Ranked choice voting could also affect the timeline. Peltola is just over 1 percentage point short of the majority needed to win outright. If neither candidate wins a majority, the race will proceed to ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18. The state’s “target date” for certifying the election results is Nov. 25.
Recounts in Alaska are automatic only in the event of a tie vote. Candidates may also request a recount within five days of the state’s certification.
More than a dozen House races are still up in the air
In most of the House races that have not been called, the margin between the leading candidates was less than 1 percentage point among votes counted as of late Tuesday afternoon.
In North Carolina, four races remain undecided, the most of any state, and Republican incumbents were being challenged in all. There are no automatic recounts in North Carolina, but candidates may request a recount if the margin between candidates is 1% or less of the total votes. The state must receive the recount request by noon Eastern time Nov. 17, two business days after the county canvass in the state. The state is scheduled to certify its results Nov. 24.
In California, only one of the remaining House races, in the 23rd District, will affect the chamber’s balance of power. The other uncalled race is between two Democrats. Mail ballots must be received by Tuesday and counties must certify their results Dec. 3. The state will certify its results Dec. 11.
In South Carolina’s 2nd District, a recount is ongoing in the race between Republican incumbent Joe Wilson and Democrat Zyon Khalia. Wilson led Khalia by only about 3,000 votes in the original tally by late Tuesday afternoon, when 99% of the votes had been counted.
In Minnesota’s 1st District, the race was still undecided late in the afternoon Tuesday, with about 300 votes separating the top two candidates and an estimated 99% of votes counted. Recounts are not automatic in Minnesota, but a candidate can request a publicly-funded recount if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is less than 0.25% of the vote.
In Tennessee’s 4th District, about 300 votes lay between Democrat Victoria Broderick and Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais as of late afternoon Tuesday. In that state, recounts are held only as part of a legal challenge in the courts. There are no automatic recounts, and losing candidates may not request recounts.
Two governorships remain undecided
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher led state Republican Senate President Ty Masterson in the race for governor of Kansas by less than 1 percentage point late Tuesday afternoon. On Nov. 4, the state announced that a close-race audit of election results requiring a hand count of selected ballots had been triggered in six close Kansas races, including the gubernatorial race. The audit must be completed before Nov. 16, the day by which counties must certify their results.
In the race for governor of Alaska, only about 76% of votes were estimated to had been counted late Tuesday afternoon, and the Democratic candidate, Jonathan S. Kreiss‑Tomkins, was leading Bernadette M. Wilson by about 45,000 votes, 49.6% to 28.9%. The race will advance to ranked choice tabulation if no candidate receives more than 50% of votes.

title: Frontier Airlines opens first-class bookings, plans more legroom and in-seat power
text:
(Gray News) – A major airline is announcing plans to offer more legroom in seats.
Frontier Airlines opened reservations Tuesday for new first-class seats and shared plans to bring in-seat power to select passengers.
First-class and extra-legroom seats
First-class seats with up to 37 inches of pitch will be configured in the first two rows of the aircraft. Additional extra-legroom seats will also be in rows three through eight with up to 34 inches of pitch, the company described.
The in-seat power connections will be limited to the first eight rows.
Booking and travel dates
The first-class seats can be booked now, but will not be available for travel until March 5, 2027.
Other onboard changes
The changes are part of Frontier’s push to improve the experience onboard planes; other enhancements include Starlink Wi-Fi.
“We’re transforming what customers can expect when they fly Frontier,” chief marketing officer Bobby Schroeter said. “First Class seating, more room to stretch out, in-seat power and fast, reliable Starlink Wi-Fi will bring a new level of comfort and convenience to flying with us.”

title: Veterans tour Washington war memorials using AI glasses
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A group of veterans from across the country toured the nation’s war memorials in Washington on Tuesday, using special sets of AI glasses to help them find fallen service members.
The group was flown into the capital as part of an honor flight trip that was sponsored by Meta.
Many of the veterans that were on the three-day trip, were blind or visually impaired. And each of them were given a pair of the Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to help them navigate the war memorials that were built in their honor.
“We were able to work with the veterans, who are able to use their glasses to, even those who are blind or low vision... explain to them what they’re looking at, and tell them more information about the memorials,” said John Bockstanz, an Innovation Policy Manager at Meta, who is also an Iraq War veteran.
The glasses use built-in cameras, microphones and AI to perceive wearers’ surroundings then can describe them.
Victor Dunham, a Vietnam veteran from Texas, said he used the glasses to try to find out more about a friend named Anthony, or Tony as he knew him, who died while serving alongside him.
“I was trying to to locate him, and I kept coming up with a major that died on that day,” Dunham said. “Well, when I came here, I had an opportunity to use my Meta glasses and learn a little bit further, and we explored the possibility of trying to find this guy.”
The glasses helped Dunham find Anthony on the Vietnam Memorial wall.
“I didn’t know him well, but I felt like I did, and I was with him obviously, when he died,” Dunham said. “But I closed that loop today.”
Bockstanz said Meta has committed to donating 130,000 pairs of the glasses to visually impaired and blinded veterans across the nation.
“They’re already sharing how these AI glasses are transforming their daily lives,” he said. “Restoring their independence, helping them navigate busy airports, read menus at restaurants, or even matching clothing. And that’s why Meta is supporting our veterans. It is not just a single flight. It’s an ongoing, year-round commitment to giving back.”
Dunham said the the trip was incredible for him and his son Mark, an Iraq War veteran, who also came.
“This experience here has been wonderful for me, and I appreciate it beyond belief,” he said.
The trip was also moving for Bockstanz.
“It’s the most meaningful thing I’ve ever done at this company,” he said.

NASHVILLE (WSMV/Gray News) - Former NFL coach Rex Ryan is accused of running over the feet of two pedestrians while driving a pickup truck in Nashville.
Police said the 63-year-old former Jets coach was driving just before midnight last Thursday when he made a right turn and ran over the feet of two people crossing the street, according to a press release.
The pedestrians told police Ryan allegedly kept driving, but they caught up to him at a red light. After an argument, Ryan got out of his vehicle.

title: Longer waits for migrant children raise questions about safety, cost and care
text:
Longer waits for migrant children raise questions about safety, cost and care
In 2021, brothers John and Maxwell left Guatemala with their mother, seeking refuge in the United States. Their father had been murdered — shot dozens of times — while working at their convenience store, and their family faced continued threats. They hoped to reach their sister and uncle in Florida.
When they made it to the U.S.-Mexico border, John said their mother wasn’t allowed to enter. It was 2021, and pandemic-era restrictions were, in effect, making it difficult for adults to come through. So their mother made a tough decision.
"My mom said, 'You need to continue,'" John said.
The boys crossed on their own and entered federal custody as unaccompanied children.
The agency responsible for children’s care after they are transferred from border authorities is the Office of Refugee Resettlement, or ORR. John and Maxwell spent about three weeks in its care.
But children entering the system today can face a very different wait: a stay that was once counted in days or weeks is now counted in months.
Hearst Television’s National Investigative Unit and Get the Facts Data Team worked for months to review several years of ORR data and records. The review found average stays grew from about one month to nearly four months in 2025. Currently, children are waiting more than six months on average — the longest average the teams found.
So, what changed?
New sponsor requirements
"There was criticism of the entire system, saying that it was broken," said John Barry, an attorney who represents John and Maxwell.
Barry said ORR tightened its vetting process after a 2024 Office of the Inspector General report found gaps in sponsor screening that could leave children vulnerable to exploitation.
The inspector general recommended that ORR ensure required safety checks are completed and documented before a child is released, improve guidance for evaluating sponsor identity, and strengthen home-study and post-release follow-up procedures.
In March 2025, ORR changed which identity documents sponsors could use. The agency added stricter proof-of-income requirements the following month. ORR’s current process also includes background and address checks, fingerprints, in-person interviews and DNA analysis to verify claimed family relationships. Depending on the case, the agency may conduct a home study and post-release monitoring.
On June 26, 2026, HHS proposed incorporating many of those recommendations into ORR federal regulations. The proposal would put specific sponsor identity documents, proof-of-income requirements and updated background checks into regulation.
ORR’s proposal acknowledges that the new document requirements could cause "disruption and/or delay" in releasing children to sponsors. The agency says it weighed that possibility against the safety risks it identified. In its written response to the National Investigative Unit, ORR said it does not comment on proposed rulemaking.
ORR cites risks but has not quantified the results
ORR told the National Investigative Unit that enhanced screening has identified "numerous sponsors with child abuse and/or sex offense criminal history" who, the agency said, likely would have been approved under prior policies.
But when asked how many unsafe placements or trafficking risks the new requirements had prevented, ORR said: "We do not have an exact number, as that is not something that has previously been readily tracked."
In the same written response, ORR said it had prevented "hundreds, if not thousands" of unsafe placements. It did not provide a count or data showing how it reached that estimate.
ORR also said it had spent the previous year and a half locating 157,000 children it described as having been released to poorly vetted sponsors under the Biden administration. The agency said it continues to search for more than 85,000 children to confirm their safety.
The agency did not provide a count of sponsors it identified with criminal histories, the number of applications denied for that reason, or a comparison of safety outcomes under the previous and current processes.
ORR said the most significant delays happen when sponsors complete applications and when the agency verifies documents, backgrounds and family relationships. The process can take longer, the agency said, when a sponsor comes from a country that does not share identity records with the United States. ORR did not break down what portion of the increase it attributes to the identity-document changes, income requirements or other factors.
Advocates say fear can keep sponsors away
Neha Desai, managing director of children’s human rights and dignity at the National Center for Youth Law, said multiple changes have contributed to longer stays, including new sponsor requirements, changes to information-sharing protections and enforcement actions that may discourage relatives from coming forward.
"There are multiple factors that have led to that massive increase of time that kids are spending in custody," Desai said.
Asked whether children are staying longer because relatives fear being detained, Desai said: "Yes, I think it's fair to assume that that's what's happening. There's no way to quantify that."
Desai claims that since November 2025, more than 3,000 parents, guardians and other potential caretakers had been arrested through a government initiative to detain potential caregivers who are in the U.S. without legal authorization and potentially deport them. ORR’s written responses did not address Desai’s claim.
"There is no doubt in my mind that children are being used as bait to go after the families that are coming forward to care for them," Desai said.
Desai said the agency should restore information-sharing protections and remove requirements she says make it harder for sponsors to come forward without improving children’s safety.
A pediatrician describes the potential harm
Dr. Raul Gutierrez, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco, has worked with unaccompanied children since 2010. He said children’s experiences in federal custody vary, but prolonged uncertainty and separation can compound trauma.
"When you put these kids in an environment of toxic stress over a prolonged period of time, those brains go into survival mode," Gutierrez said.
He said the effects vary by child and can include depression, anxiety, difficulty sleeping and withdrawal. Prolonged stays can also disrupt education, play and social development, he said.
"For me, it just feels like, think about what your child needs and what you want to give them in order for them to thrive. That's exactly what these kids need," Gutierrez said.
ORR said children in its care can receive legal services, case managers, child advocates, medical care and mental-health support. The agency said its responsibility is to ensure children are placed safely.
The financial cost of longer stays
Aside from the health and safety priorities, ORR told the National Investigative Unit that daily care costs range from $375 to $600 per child.
At the time of this report, about 1,860 children were in ORR care. Applying the agency’s range to that reported population produces an estimated daily cost of roughly $700,000 to $1.1 million.
The brothers' experience
John and Maxwell spent five days at a border facility in Texas when they entered the U.S. in 2021 before being transferred to an ORR shelter. "We got food, we got a bed, we've got clothes," John said.
Their sponsor review moved quickly because their uncle and older siblings were already established in the United States and could provide the necessary credentials. The boys were released to their sister in Florida after about three weeks.
"ORR was really great. That's how ORR is supposed to work," Barry said.
Still, the boys said the wait felt exceptionally long, and no one explained the entire process or when they would be released.
"Everyone’s talking about their family and what’s happening with my family," John said. "It’s a lot of anxiety. We were pretty anxious."
Two days after they reached Florida, their uncle told them their mother had died in Mexico from untreated diabetes while trying to bring them to safety.
Today, John and Maxwell said they are glad to be in Florida, where they have more opportunities. Maxwell hopes other children waiting in federal care will have a chance to build a life outside a shelter.
"This place is made of opportunities, so if they can make the people our age come, maybe they got opportunities to grow up, to have a nice job, to a nice future," he said.
The 'Get the Facts Behind the Reporting' and data was done by Data Visualization Journalist Katrina Ventura and edited by David Hurlburt, Executive Director of Editorial Strategies.

title: UMA to cut funding for East Millinocket education center
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The University of Maine at Augusta will stop funding a learning center in East Millinocket next year.
The decision is part of a broader set of moves the University of Maine System is making to cut its budget in the wake of years of multimillion-dollar shortfalls. It also reflects how the path to earning a degree at any university within the UMaine System is changing.
UMA administrators have not announced any looming budget gaps, but the cuts will save the university tens of thousands of dollars, said Samantha Warren, a spokesperson for the system. Other centers in Saco, Rockland, Rumford, South Paris, Houlton and Belfast are either being closed or their budgets are being cut, Warren said.
UMA and Eastern Maine Community College have jointly run the Katahdin Higher Education Center in East Millinocket since 1987.
The center will remain open until the end of the academic year, partially because of $100,000 Gov. Janet Mills directed toward it in June. The center’s future beyond that hasn’t been decided, EMCC spokesperson Michael Hambrock said.
In the 2024-25 academic year, UMA paid EMCC nearly $150,000 to run the center with 14 students enrolled in the university’s programs, Warren said. Funding was then reduced the next year to roughly $57,000, which covered part of the center’s operating budget and a portion of two employees’ salaries and benefits, according to a memorandum of understanding between EMCC and UMA.
That funding dropped to $10,000 for the current academic year.
Although funding has drastically decreased, 82 students have attended short-term workforce training programs this fall, Hambrock said. Those programs, which are not part of UMA’s curriculum, will not change this spring, Hambrock said.
In recent years, there’s been a push toward online learning inside the UMaine system, such as the University of Maine at Presque Isle’s YourPace program. The system has continued to examine the role of physical learning locations as online programs increasingly make up a growing share of academic credits earned, Warren said.
“As we work to right-size our footprint for the future, we are more committed than ever to advancing innovative, cost-effective approaches to meeting the needs of all Maine learners, who we know depend on access to our public universities for education and upward mobility,” Warren said.
By cutting funding to the Katahdin Higher Education Center, the UMaine System is vacating the Katahdin region. The nearest campus to the Millinocket area is now the University of Maine Orono campus.
While no decisions about the center’s future have been made, conversations with community partners about what the next steps for the center have been productive, Hambrock said.

title: They longed to hold their fragile NICU babies. A new device made it possible
text:
They longed to hold their fragile NICU babies. A new device made it possible
Imahri Simington imagined the birth experience she would have with her first child the way many mothers do: her water breaking, contractions starting, naturally dilating and going to the hospital for a vaginal birth. Then: resting her son, who she already knew would be named Jhosiah, for the very young king in the Bible, against the skin of her chest and feeling the oxytocin wash through her body.
The pregnancy had been smooth — until more than two months before he was due. Her feet had swollen worryingly, and Jhosiah didn’t seem to be kicking as much as normal. She drove herself to the hospital, just in case.
After an emergency C-section in July for severe preeclampsia at 30 weeks, she and Jhosiah’s dad saw staff holding up their son, who weighed a little over 2 pounds. Then she passed out.
The next time she saw him, Jhosiah wore a mask that delivered pressurized air into his lungs. There were cords everywhere. And she couldn’t hold him the way she’d imagined so many times, which filled her with sadness.
Then, a doctor approached. The hospital was facilitating a new research trial. She could be the first in the United States to try a new device that would let her hold Jhosiah against her skin for as long as she wanted. She could even fall asleep with him on her chest.
An hour later, Simington and Jhosiah were nestled together using the Skincubator. It allows parents to hold premature and fragile newborns who need intensive care. Studies have shown skin-to-skin contact has myriad benefits that help newborns grow, such as regulating heart rate and strengthening the immune system. It’s also been shown to reduce stress for parents and help them form deeper connections with their children, said Dr. Jaclyn Ruggiero, a neonatologist at Children’s Memorial Hermann.
Medical staff took out what looked like a parachute or jetpack and strapped it to Simington. Then they put Jhosiah inside. He was warm against her skin. She felt a surge of emotion — happiness and surprise “that this was something that would be possible,” tempering the difficulty of adjusting to the fact that her baby was in the neonatal intensive care unit.
“The way I see it,” Ruggiero said of the hospital’s use of the Skincubator, “our goal is, ‘How do we help baby and family find each other again?’… It’s in that relationship that healing happens. It’s in connection that we survive.”
Helping parents during 'a journey of emotion'
Skin-to-skin contact, or kangaroo care, plays a vital role in newborns’ development. But many hospitals, especially in the United States, hesitate to allow parents to hold premature babies because doing so could dislodge breathing tubes and IV lines connected to lifesaving medical equipment. Premature babies also need incubators to keep them warm.
Children’s Memorial Hermann is the first hospital in the U.S. to use the Skincubator, which was invented in Israel. It’s already helped put parents' and doctors’ minds at ease, Ruggiero said.
“The smaller you get, and the tinier you get, and the earlier you get, the more anxious and scared a family will be,” she said.
Dorian Ojemen and Tiffany Ikwuagwu understand that fear all too well. The Houston couple were thrilled when they learned they were expecting twins. Everything changed when Ikwuagwu, herself an OB-GYN, started to feel something was off with the pregnancy.
An ultrasound showed her cervix was dilated, so she went to Children’s Memorial Hermann for a stitch to keep it closed. She was expecting to go home. Then, early the next morning, her water broke for one of the twins when she was only 23 weeks pregnant.
Ikwuagwu spent nearly a month in the hospital, celebrating her birthday there with family and friends. Doctors hoped to delay the births as long as possible because outcomes improve dramatically when premature babies are delivered closer to full term.
“I’ve seen other patients in similar situations, and I’ve seen both good outcomes and bad outcomes,” Ikwuagwu said. “Now I was the patient. It was a journey of emotion.”
Doctors determined the twins needed to be delivered when Ikwuagwu developed an infection at 26 weeks. Ojemen left the hospital that morning to go to work as a lawyer. He raced back in time for the births of his daughter, Simone, and son, Silas, but the NICU team quickly whisked them away for the lifesaving care they needed.
Silas was only 1 pound, 10 ounces, and Simone was slightly bigger at 2 pounds, 6 ounces. They needed to stay in a specialized, high-humidity environment for the first 10 days of their lives while their skin barriers developed. Ikwuagwu and Ojemen could only touch their children through an incubator, using their fingers.
So they were intrigued when Ruggiero came to them with the idea of using the Skincubator. At the same time, Ojemen was nervous he might inadvertently harm them while holding them.
Those worries dissipated quickly when the NICU team secured a pair of Skincubator devices on the couple’s chests. Ikwuagwu held Simone, and Ojemen held Silas.
Until that moment, the new father felt like he’d been “tagging along” for the pregnancy and first days of his twins’ lives, offering support but unable to do anything more to help. That changed the moment he became the first father in the world to use the Skincubator to feel his baby’s skin on his chest.
“When this was offered, I was like, ‘I’ll try it, but I don’t know if I’m doing anything.’ And then I did it, and I thought, ‘OK, I have some benefit,’” Ojemen said. “I can have a benefit and contribution that doesn’t have to be the same as (their mother’s). But it’s still valuable.”
Looking forward
A handful of families have used the Skincubator at Children’s Memorial Hermann as part of the hospital’s preparation for a clinical trial that will study its effectiveness. The first phase of the clinical trial will focus on safety and will involve 60 babies born prematurely, between 25 and 30 weeks, Ruggiero said.
Later stages of the trial will focus on its effectiveness in improving skin-to-skin contact during a premature baby’s first week of life. It will also measure whether using the device can reduce rates of stress, anxiety and depression in parents, Ruggiero said.
Simington loved the skin-to-skin contact the device allowed because she felt it was a way she could help her son’s health. The first day she used it, she held him for eight hours, unclipping him only when she needed the restroom.
She did the same the second day. Jhosiah was growing noticeably stronger. Medical staff decided he no longer needed the pressurized air.
Within two weeks, he’d outgrown the Skincubator, which is designed only for the smallest babies — under 4.4 pounds.
One day, she may help others use the device. She recently completed her nursing degree and had already planned to work in either labor and delivery or the NICU.
Now, Jhosiah’s at home in Cypress and weighs more than 9 pounds. His mother loves the size of his appetite, comparing it to that of a football player, if a football player were 20 inches tall. She proudly watches him hold up his head and try to roll over. He’s already a good sleeper, she notes, only waking maybe twice to eat.
“He’s come a long way, but he’s strong like his mom and dad,” she said. “So he definitely was going to overcome everything that transpired in the hospital.”

title: Celtics storm back to beat Raptors for 5th straight win
text:
TORONTO — Jayson Tatum made the tying and go-ahead free throws with 25.2 seconds remaining and the Boston Celtics overcame a 22-point deficit to beat the Toronto Raptors 98-93 on Wednesday night, extending their winning streak to five.
Tatum scored 24 points, Derrick White had 19 and Payton Pritchard added 14. Neemias Queta had 11 points and 13 rebounds as the Celtics improved to 4-0 against Atlantic Division opponents.
Boston’s Paul George sat out because of an illness a night after he scored 36 points in a winning return to Philadelphia.
Tatum shot 6 for 21 and finished 2 for 11 from 3-point range. He was 10 for 12 at the free throw line.
Toronto’s Ja’Kobe Walter scored 17 points and rookie Allen Graves added a career-high 13, but the Raptors fell below .500 for the first time at 5-6.
Raptors forward Kawhi Leonard (left knee) missed his ninth straight game but is “progressing well” with individual conditioning, coach Darko Rajakovic said before the game. On Tuesday, the Raptors said they’d update Leonard’s status in a week.
Scottie Barnes (left groin) missed his third straight game but Immanuel Quickley returned after missing the past two because of a sore right hamstring. Collin Murray-Boyles started for the fourth time after sitting out a loss to Memphis on Monday because of illness.
Walter scored all 12 of his points from long-range as the Raptors tied a franchise record for 3-pointers in a quarter by shooting 10 for 18 from distance in the first.
Toronto shot 6 for 25 from distance the rest of the way.
The Raptors led 59-37 after Jamal Shead’s free throw with 5:24 remaining in the second, but the Celtics answered with 16 straight points. Tatum scored the first 10 by himself as Boston cut the deficit to 61-54 at halftime.
Up next
Celtics: Host Dallas on Sunday.
Raptors: At Philadelphia on Thursday.

title: Presque Isle rings Bells of Peace on Veterans Day
text:
In the ninth year since their launch, the Bells of Peace rang out at Presque Isle’s Veterans Memorial Park at 11 a.m. Wednesday.
The tolling of a bell 21 times honors those who lost their lives serving the country, and is offered in the spirit of a 21-gun salute.
The Doughboy Foundation founded the initiative in 2018 to commemorate 100 years since the end of the First World War. Armistice was declared in 1918 and countries worldwide rang bells in jubilation. President Woodrow Wilson launched Armistice Day, which decades later became Veterans Day to honor all who have served.
“The ringing of the bells, the Bells of Peace initiative, all has to do with Veterans Day itself and the fact that we ended the war on the 11th day at the 11th hour in the 11th month,” said Kim Smith, Presque Isle’s resource development and public information officer.
Presque Isle played a significant role in the nation’s defense from 1940 to 1961, when its air base served as the last U.S. point for servicemen and women bound for Europe, she said — a fact noted by President John F. Kennedy during a 1960 visit.
The city also housed the nation’s first nuclear missile, the Snark, Smith said.
Tayliegh Lopez of Caribou, a member of the Disabled American Veterans, rang the bell.
Lopez returned to northern Maine two years ago, having grown up in the area while her father served at the former Loring Air Force Base.
“It was the only place I remember being happy. It was the only home I ever knew,” she said. “Dad was stationed at Loring … from 1979 to 1983.”
Lopez attended Caribou schools and then served 10 years in the U.S. Army, followed by a two-year stint in the U.S. Navy.
She joined a group of around 20 local veterans for the ceremony.
Adjutant Jasper Lee of Smart-Ricker Unit 10, Disabled American Veterans, encouraged everyone to remember service members’ commitment to defend the freedom Americans enjoy. He also spoke of the nation’s need to honor its commitments to care for service members.
“I believe veterans deserve more than a medal and deeper cuts to programs and services,” Lee said. “The nation’s best and most effective resource is a veteran.”
After the playing of taps by DAV member Rod Cameron, veterans laid a wreath at the park’s monument.
Members of The County Composite Squadron of Civil Air Patrol marched solemnly in front of the park’s veterans monument, calling to mind the constant, silent patrol at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery.
“The freedoms we enjoy come with a cost, and today we pause to remember those who paid it,” City Manager Sonja Eyler said. “Thank you for being here and for helping us ensure that they are never forgotten.”

title: Boy who helped first responders better comfort children with autism named TIME’s Kid of the Year
text:
HENRICO, Va. (WWBT/Gray News) - A Virginia boy has been named TIME’s Kid of the Year thanks to his role in helping first responders better comfort children with autism.
Nine-year-old Ledger is getting honored for his work, which has included working alongside Henrico County firefighters, paramedics and police officers.
First responders in Henrico have been deploying a new set of specialized tools designed to comfort and improve communication with patients on the autism spectrum during emergency calls with the help of Ledger.
Known as “LGM Bags,” the clear backpacks are filled with sensory-friendly items, communication boards and therapeutic tools.
The program began with a crisis in Prince George County, where Ledger’s father, Sergeant J.T. Mann, a 28-year veteran of county emergency services, was dispatched to search for a missing child with autism.
After several hours of searching, the child was found safely, hiding under a grill cover behind a residence.
Knowing that individuals on the spectrum are often drawn to water or wooded areas to escape loud noises and strangers, Mann said he asked his son Ledger, who was diagnosed with autism at age 2, what would make him feel safe if he were ever lost and found by a first responder.
Ledger immediately began brainstorming comfort items, including stuffed animals, noise-canceling headphones and fidget spinners.
The 9-year-old also insisted that the backpack holding the items must be completely clear so that non-verbal children could easily see inside and point to what they need.
Ledger then emptied $100 from his piggy bank to fund the very first prototypes.
“He said, ‘Dad, I want to do this myself initially,’” Mann recalled. “He took a hundred dollars out of his piggy bank and made the first bags himself and didn’t want the money back or anything. And those were the first bags we distributed, actually out of his own money.”
To date, the “LGM” program, named after Ledger’s initials, has distributed over 432 bags across Virginia, West Virginia, North Carolina and Florida.
The initiative has garnered national and international attention, including being featured in TIME and People and even billboard recognition as far away as Australia.
The program’s expansion into Henrico County was championed by Lakeside Station 5 Firefighter Courtney Koppelman.
Koppelman, who recently joined the Henrico Division of Fire after serving in Hanover County, grew up with a brother who had spina bifida and a learning disability.
“It’s really close to my heart with having a brother who was special needs growing up, and the world not always meeting him where he was at,” Koppelman said. “So it’s great to meet people where they are and make them feel safe and heard and helped.”
Koppelman had previously created her own personal sensory bags to carry on calls.
She knew from experience that emergency scenes can be terrifyingly loud and visually overwhelming, especially inside an ambulance.
“Ambulances are very overwhelming, with the engine revving, monitors beeping and other loud sounds,” Koppelman said. “The noise-canceling headphones alone provide a much more comfortable ride for our patients.”
Koppelman saw that sensory tools were valuable not just for children on the spectrum, but also for elderly patients experiencing dementia and adults suffering from severe anxiety or trauma.
She requested that Henrico County leadership explore a department-wide program.
Henrico leaders quickly embraced the idea.
Dr. Anjali Ferguson, who spent nearly a decade as deputy medical director before taking the OMD role full-time two years ago, noted that these bags fill a critical void in pre-hospital care.
“When I’m in the hospital, we have child life specialists that come in with these toys and distracting agents or even iPads,” Ferguson said. “But we don’t have that in the field. So this sort of bridges that gap between what we have available to us in the field and what we have in the hospital.”
According to Ferguson, the bags do more than just soothe anxious minds; they directly enable first responders to provide safer and more efficient medical treatment.
“Everyone in Henrico County is passionate about providing the most elite service for citizens,” Koppelman said. “And I feel like this is just a small component to upping that service provided on a daily basis. It makes my heart happy. I’m glad we’re able to provide that service for people.”
The donated bags have since been placed on all frontline Henrico ambulances, EMS captain vehicles, and with police crisis intervention officers.

title: ‘They’re doing it somehow’: Washington County parents find their way to financial stability
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This is the third story in the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham reported this story as a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.
MACHIAS — A week before fall classes started, Donielle Fields got a call from a new student.
A mother, enrolling at the University of Maine at Machias through Family Futures Downeast, was panicked. Her power was about to be turned off, her baby was out of diapers and there was no gas in her car. Fields, who coaches first-year students in the program, told the mother to take a breath.
They’d figure it out together.
Situations like these are common among parents in the program, which is designed to help them attend college and achieve financial stability. In Washington County, nearly half of households live in poverty or just above it.
Fields said financial hardships seem to be getting worse and that many of the newly enrolled parents in the program struggle to feed their families and find jobs. She said the challenges they face — including finding housing and childcare — are daunting. Some rely solely on government assistance programs.
“How in the hell are our families surviving?” Fields said. “Our families have no income or very little income, but they’re doing it somehow.”
The county, in far Down East Maine, is known for its rugged coastline and traditions of blueberry harvesting, lobstering and commercial fishing. The locals here are known for their work ethic and resilience despite limited opportunities for high-paying careers. Many people work multiple seasonal jobs to piece together a living.
Data released in June by the United Ways of Maine shows that 45% of households in Washington County are in poverty or below the threshold known as ALICE — Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed — where people don’t always qualify for assistance but often struggle to cover basic expenses. Nearly three-quarters of households with children led by single women are below the threshold.
For the past 11 years, Family Futures Downeast has been addressing some of the most common obstacles, said director Marsha Sloan. About 225 families have participated in the program.
“It’s one person, one family, at a time moving out of poverty,” Sloan said.
Through the nonprofit program, parents enroll at Washington County Community College or the University of Maine at Machias and are assigned a coach. They all take the same classes together during the first year, then focus on earning certifications or degrees. Their children are also supported through the program, which often pays for activities, sports equipment and summer camps.
The program’s coaches have all experienced poverty or financial instability and understand the challenges the students face, Sloan said.
Fields said when students come to her
Those solutions, she said, can prevent the barriers
MOVING OUT OF POVERTY
It wasn’t until Ambrosia Ross was an adult and read a book about poverty that she realized how poor her family had been.
“I was like, ‘Oh my goodness, other people don’t go dumpster diving for food,’” she said.
But even during the most desperate times,
“My mother was determined that we were never going to look at ourselves as worse off than other people, and we were never going to think less of ourselves because of where we were in life,” said Ross, a 34-year-old mother of four.
Ross wanted to go to college, but couldn’t see a path to get there. After marrying at 18 and starting a family, she said she and her husband lived in a 450-square-foot cabin with no running water or electricity on her in-laws’ property. They relied on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and MaineCare while her husband worked at a local bank and saved for a house.
When Ross heard Family Futures Downeast was accepting people into the first cohort of students, she jumped at the chance to finally go to college. When she graduated with a bachelor’s degree, she said her mother cried.
The degree didn’t have a significant immediate impact on the family’s financial situation. After school, Ross worked as a breastfeeding coach and started a small business running Dungeons & Dragons games.
She said they saved enough to buy a house in Pembroke that had been in foreclosure.
This summer, Ross was hired as a coach at Family Futures Downeast, which more than doubled the family’s household
“I know in the long run it’s worthwhile, but in the short-term it’s scary,” she said. “We’re still trying to stay in penny-pinching mode.”
‘IT’S GETTING HARDER’
In September, just a few weeks into the semester, Ashley Crowley arrived
The 39-year-old single mother from Addison needed help from Fields to add citations to an essay and navigate the school’s online portal. So far classes were going well, Crowley told her coach, but she was still adjusting to life as a college student.
Crowley grew up on Beals Island and has spent most of her life working multiple jobs at a time, including digging for sandworms in tidal mudflats. She said she has spent
She said she dreams of a
Unable to find consistent childcare so she can work, Crowley said her monthly income is about $700 from Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. She also gets $540 a month in SNAP benefits. Most days, she said, she eats only one meal.
As winter approaches, she said she is concerned
“I wake up every morning at 2 wondering if I’m going to make this work,” she said.
Fields, who lives in East Machias with her fiancé and their five children, knows the struggle well. Growing up in the area, she said she knew people who lived without running water or enough food. Her father was a woodcutter and they always had what they needed, but she said as an adult she has had to rely at times on assistance programs to support her family.
Fields said she now makes a good wage and her fiancé is a self-employed diesel mechanic. They live in a 54-year-old mobile home he found at a junkyard and fixed up. With the help of a local nonprofit, they were able to build an addition to make more space for the kids.
A couple of years ago, they were finally able to afford a vacation in a rented cabin and started building up a savings account. Fields said they had to drain it this year to pay for equipment repairs and are now living paycheck to paycheck.
During the summer, Fields brought her two youngest kids to their school everyday for free breakfast and lunch.
“We figured it out, but now figuring it out isn’t good enough,” she said. “It’s getting harder and it shouldn’t be getting harder.”
FEEDING MACHIAS
On a warm Wednesday morning in August, Nancy Lewis and Ken Warner moved efficiently through the main room of the Machias Area Food Pantry, unloading food donated from the local grocery store and freshly harvested produce.
They lined long tables draped in royal blue tablecloths with bins of summer squash, cucumber, cabbage and berries. Warner stacked loaves of bread in a neat display and Lewis put a bucket with long stems of fragrant dill near the open door. Shelves of beans, rice, pasta and canned goods were already stocked and labeled.
The food pantry opened 40 years ago, serving a dozen families from a space in the basement of the Centre Street Congregational Church. Warner and Lewis took over as directors in 2022, gained nonprofit status and moved the pantry to a new building three years ago.
It’s been busy ever since.
“If we weren’t here, there are some folks that would be in desperate trouble. The incomes are not that high here, but expenses are high,” Warner said. “Food purchasing and gas are high. It’s difficult for them to make ends meet without some kind of safety net.”
The pantry, open two days a week, serves people from 11 communities around Machias, a town of about 2,000 people known for its annual wild blueberry festival. Some families drive nearly an hour to get
In an average week, around 175 families come in for groceries, Lewis said. Lately, five or six new people have been registering each week.
“A lot of our clients are working and just can’t make ends meet,” Lewis said.
Programs like this are critical in Washington County, where, according to Feeding America, the overall food insecurity rate in 2024 was at nearly 19% and the rate for children was about 26%. Three-quarters of Washington County’s food insecure residents qualified for SNAP, according to the organization.
Maine was one of the first states to implement universal free school meals, a move designed to reduce childhood hunger and the stigma around food assistance. Research by Michele Polacsek, a University of New England professor, shows the critical role those meals play as a reliable source of nutrition, particularly in rural communities.
Polacsek said
“Rural poverty creates barriers to food security and nutrition security that go beyond what other families in poverty experience,” she said.
At the food pantry in Machias on that day in August, the first few patrons of the day arrived before it officially opened. After checking in, they pushed small grocery carts through the building, choosing the items they wanted. Some said the food helps them make ends meet, especially at the end of the month when their SNAP benefits are tapped out.
Gina Rackliff stopped by to pick up food for her family of six, and another family who
Marga James, who retired to Machias 15 years ago, came in to get food for herself and three others unable to
“It would be a crisis,” she said.
The pantry relies on the community to make it all work. Hannaford donates food a few times a week and during summer local gardeners drop off green beans, garlic, beets and loads of yellow squash and zucchini.
Lewis and Warner believe that every person who comes to the pantry deserves high quality food and the dignity of choosing for themselves what to take home.
“It’s a basic right,”
‘OVERCOMING EVERYTHING’
As a kid, Chelsey Megquier was always up early and ready to get to school for breakfast, especially when there hadn’t been any food for dinner the night before. As an adult, she said, she
Megquire, 36, said she wanted to create a more stable life for herself and her daughter.
“This doesn’t have to be the story of my life,” she said.
Megquire, who lives in Calais with her wife and 14-year-old daughter, went back to school several years ago with support from Family Futures Downeast, which helped pay for an expensive car repair and sports equipment for her daughter.
After earning her associate’s degree from Washington County Community College, Megquire was hired as a bookkeeper at a nonprofit. She’s now working on her bachelor’s degree with plans to become an accountant.
Megquire said her family is now more financially stable,
A few years ago, Megquire was able to buy her first home. After she was handed the keys, she and her daughter pulled the for sale sign out of the ground and, together, threw it into a trash can.
“That was part of overcoming everything,” she said. “This was ours.”

title: Whitefield Lions Club celebrates young artists in peace poster contest
text:
The Whitefield Lions Club announced the winners of their annual Lions Clubs International Peace Poster Contest during their October meeting. This year’s theme, “Harmony in Humanity,” drew 69 talented students to share their vision of peace through art from five area schools: Whitefield, Palermo, Chelsea, Windsor, and Jefferson.
“Our club really appreciates our connection to our area schools and promoting youth through Community, Kindness and Peace. We are so grateful to all the teachers and all that they do!” said this year’s club contest organizer, Lion Lynda Despard.
The Whitefield Lions Club thanks all participants and their art teachers, whose guidance made the contest possible. The first-place posters will now advance to the state level of competition.

title: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications.
The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of gray hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That’s landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry.
But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businessperson who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. Alice Huang is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.
It’s a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The Department of Justice has opened its own investigation. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review.
Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that “whoever wins AI, wins.” Nvidia is the backbone of America’s plans for dominating the field.
When asked about Jensen Huang’s affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew.
“I think he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said, adding that ”he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question.
“They could have been mentioned,” he said. ”Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”
Authorities are investigating Megaspeed and Alice Huang
With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing.
That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the United States.
Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times.
The Commerce Department’s investigation was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement inquiry.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang.
Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn’t address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation.
Beijing has said the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated” and called it “nothing but smears.”
Trump has been close with Jensen Huang
After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Jensen Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president’s own promises of an economic renaissance.
The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth.
Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future.
“From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he’s ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, reindustrializing the United States, of protection, of national security,” Jensen Huang told AP in an interview this summer. “He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs.”
Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang’s Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science.
The president called him “a man whose determination laid the foundations for the explosion of super intelligence and put America at the front of the race, an amazing man, gotten to know him so well.”
Nvidia also donated $25 million to help fund the construction of Trump’s White House ballroom.
Multiple estimates suggest that more than half of the stock market gains during Trump’s second term came from the growth of the AI industry and the construction of data centers.
Without that growth, consumer spending could slump, delivering another economic setback to a president who has already failed to deliver on his campaign promise of stopping inflation. Rising prices were among the reasons that voters delivered a harsh rebuke to Republicans in last week’s midterm elections, returning control of Congress to the Democrats.
Nvidia CEO pushed to sell some chips to China, faces congressional scrutiny
While Huang said his interests were in helping America succeed, he also expressed a strong view that Nvidia should be able to sell some of its less advanced chips such as the H200 to China. Nvidia long argued that the sales would help ensure that the broader AI ecosystem was tied to America, boxing out Chinese chipmakers that are developing semiconductors and systems to compete with his company.
Those arguments previously came under scrutiny, including from Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who wanted him to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions about his desire to loosen export restrictions.
Huang has so far refused to appear, and Democrats responded angrily when his infidelity came to light, raising concerns that a bulwark of American technology may have been compromised by the Chinese government.
Warren said in a statement Monday that Nvidia had reportedly gotten approvals to export “hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military.”
And Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, Warren continued, “raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related.”
___
Chan reported from Hong Kong and Ng from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Associated Press journalists Wu Jia in Beijing, Didi Tang in Washington and Russ Bynum in Savannah, Ga., contributed to this report.
