title: Former LA Player Named as Boys First-Year Basketball Coach
text:
Lincoln Academy has named 2025 graduate Tyson Ball as the new basketball coach for the Eagles first-year team, otherwise known as the freshman boys basketball team. Ball will take over for Cody Tozier, who moved into the JV coach position that was vacated when Rand Maker retired after the 2025-2026 season. Ball’s father, Ryan Ball, is the head coach for the boys varsity team.
Although this will be Tyson Ball’s first regular season role as an official coach at Lincoln Academy, the Nobleboro resident said he is ready, in part because he has been building up his coaching experience over the past several years.
“I’ve been helping my father coach youth basketball since around seventh grade, but I’ve been around the gym attending practices since I was in second grade,” said Ball, who is 19 years old. “Last year, I coached basketball at the high school level including the Bar Harbor tournament and several other tournaments throughout the state. Having grown up around the program and knowing some of the players coming in from junior high should definitely help me build relationships with the first year team.”
For fans of Lincoln Academy basketball, it may come as no surprise that Ball has become a high school basketball coach at a young age. When Ball suffered a sustained leg injury as a junior during the 2023-2024 season, he could not play and instead took on an unofficial role helping out with all the levels of the Lincoln Academy program. His leadership and coaching talent caught the attention of then-JV coach Maker, who singled out Ball as a key mentor that helped his JV team to an undefeated season.
“Tyson Ball has the mind of a coach and has always been positive when working with the JV kids and younger players,” said Maker in an article published in the Feb. 22, 2024 edition of The Lincoln County News.
Ball said that he is honored to have the opportunity to coach a team for LA at a young age and thinks he can use his youth as an advantage.
“I always figured I would eventually help my father on the bench as a volunteer,” said Ball. “I never imagined I’d have the opportunity to coach at the high school level this young. When I played at LA (2021-2025), we only had a JV team, and I moved between JV and varsity. Being a former player and a younger coach, I think I can relate to the first-year players and connect with them through both my (JV) playing experience and understanding of today’s culture.”
Ball will be working alongside the entire LA basketball coaching staff on a daily basis, including Ryan Ball, Tozier, and assistant coach Kevin Feltis. In the previously cited LCN article about the 2023-2024 JV team, Maker emphasized how important it is that the LA high school boys basketball program is fully integrated as a single program despite the three separate teams.
“We run the same systems as the varsity, which helps the swing players and reduces the transition when players go from one team to the other,” said Maker back in 2024.
LA’s “one program” concept still rings true as Tyson Ball begins his first season as a LA coach.
“I believe having a coaching staff that works together is important for the success of the entire program,” said Ball.
Ball was quick to point out that coaching is about interacting with people more than winning basketball games.
“One of my favorite things about coaching is the relationships you build with players, families, and people throughout the community” said Ball. “It’s given me the opportunity to connect with people I might not otherwise have met. My coaching philosophy is built around developing life skills, encouraging high performance, and getting the most out of every player. I want to teach more than basketball and help each kid develop into a better athlete, teammate, and person.”
For now, Ball’s biggest role with the program and as the first-year team coach is in player development.
“My biggest goal for coaching the first-year team is to make every player better and help them become more confident and prepared for the varsity level,” said Ball. “I want each player to leave the season as a better basketball player and teammate.”
While his dad helped inspire him to become a coach, Ball said being the son of a basketball coach was not always as easy as it may seem.
“I’ve talked with a lot of other coach’s sons throughout my life, and they say it is hard because you have to live and talk basketball all the time,” said Ball. “But it makes you a better player, and in the end, a better coach, and I wouldn’t have wanted it any other way.”

title: ‘They’re doing it somehow’: Washington County parents find their way to financial stability
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This is the third story in the series Stretched Thin: The cost of getting by in Maine, which looks at the financial hardships Mainers face. Social services reporter Gillian Graham reported this story as a USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism 2026 National Fellow and a participant in the Center’s engagement initiative.
MACHIAS — A week before fall classes started, Donielle Fields got a call from a new student.
A mother, enrolling at the University of Maine at Machias through Family Futures Downeast, was panicked. Her power was about to be turned off, her baby was out of diapers and there was no gas in her car. Fields, who coaches first-year students in the program, told the mother to take a breath.
They’d figure it out together.
Situations like these are common among parents in the program, which is designed to help them attend college and achieve financial stability. In Washington County, nearly half of households live in poverty or just above it.
Fields said financial hardships seem to be getting worse and that many of the newly enrolled parents in the program struggle to feed their families and find jobs. She said the challenges they face — including finding housing and childcare — are daunting. Some rely solely on government assistance programs.
“How in the hell are our families surviving?” Fields said. “Our families have no income or very little income, but they’re doing it somehow.”
The county, in far Down East Maine, is known for its rugged coastline and traditions of blueberry harvesting, lobstering and commercial fishing. The locals here are known for their work ethic and resilience despite limited opportunities for high-paying careers. Many people work multiple seasonal jobs to piece together a living.
Data released in June by the United Ways of Maine shows that 45% of households in Washington County are in poverty or below the threshold known as ALICE — Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed — where people don’t always qualify for assistance but often struggle to cover basic expenses. Nearly three-quarters of households with children led by single women are below the threshold.
For the past 11 years, Family Futures Downeast has been addressing some of the most common obstacles, said director Marsha Sloan. About 225 families have participated in the program.
“It’s one person, one family, at a time moving out of poverty,” Sloan said.
Through the nonprofit program, parents enroll at Washington County Community College or the University of Maine at Machias and are assigned a coach. They all take the same classes together during the first year, then focus on earning certifications or degrees. Their children are also supported through the program, which often pays for activities, sports equipment and summer camps.
The program’s coaches have all experienced poverty or financial instability and understand the challenges the students face, Sloan said.
Fields said when students come to her
Those solutions, she said, can prevent the barriers
MOVING OUT OF POVERTY
It wasn’t until Ambrosia Ross was an adult and read a book about poverty that she realized how poor her family had been.
“I was like, ‘Oh my goodness, other people don’t go dumpster diving for food,’” she said.
But even during the most desperate times,
“My mother was determined that we were never going to look at ourselves as worse off than other people, and we were never going to think less of ourselves because of where we were in life,” said Ross, a 34-year-old mother of four.
Ross wanted to go to college, but couldn’t see a path to get there. After marrying at 18 and starting a family, she said she and her husband lived in a 450-square-foot cabin with no running water or electricity on her in-laws’ property. They relied on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and MaineCare while her husband worked at a local bank and saved for a house.
When Ross heard Family Futures Downeast was accepting people into the first cohort of students, she jumped at the chance to finally go to college. When she graduated with a bachelor’s degree, she said her mother cried.
The degree didn’t have a significant immediate impact on the family’s financial situation. After school, Ross worked as a breastfeeding coach and started a small business running Dungeons & Dragons games.
She said they saved enough to buy a house in Pembroke that had been in foreclosure.
This summer, Ross was hired as a coach at Family Futures Downeast, which more than doubled the family’s household
“I know in the long run it’s worthwhile, but in the short-term it’s scary,” she said. “We’re still trying to stay in penny-pinching mode.”
‘IT’S GETTING HARDER’
In September, just a few weeks into the semester, Ashley Crowley arrived
The 39-year-old single mother from Addison needed help from Fields to add citations to an essay and navigate the school’s online portal. So far classes were going well, Crowley told her coach, but she was still adjusting to life as a college student.
Crowley grew up on Beals Island and has spent most of her life working multiple jobs at a time, including digging for sandworms in tidal mudflats. She said she has spent
She said she dreams of a
Unable to find consistent childcare so she can work, Crowley said her monthly income is about $700 from Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. She also gets $540 a month in SNAP benefits. Most days, she said, she eats only one meal.
As winter approaches, she said she is concerned
“I wake up every morning at 2 wondering if I’m going to make this work,” she said.
Fields, who lives in East Machias with her fiancé and their five children, knows the struggle well. Growing up in the area, she said she knew people who lived without running water or enough food. Her father was a woodcutter and they always had what they needed, but she said as an adult she has had to rely at times on assistance programs to support her family.
Fields said she now makes a good wage and her fiancé is a self-employed diesel mechanic. They live in a 54-year-old mobile home he found at a junkyard and fixed up. With the help of a local nonprofit, they were able to build an addition to make more space for the kids.
A couple of years ago, they were finally able to afford a vacation in a rented cabin and started building up a savings account. Fields said they had to drain it this year to pay for equipment repairs and are now living paycheck to paycheck.
During the summer, Fields brought her two youngest kids to their school everyday for free breakfast and lunch.
“We figured it out, but now figuring it out isn’t good enough,” she said. “It’s getting harder and it shouldn’t be getting harder.”
FEEDING MACHIAS
On a warm Wednesday morning in August, Nancy Lewis and Ken Warner moved efficiently through the main room of the Machias Area Food Pantry, unloading food donated from the local grocery store and freshly harvested produce.
They lined long tables draped in royal blue tablecloths with bins of summer squash, cucumber, cabbage and berries. Warner stacked loaves of bread in a neat display and Lewis put a bucket with long stems of fragrant dill near the open door. Shelves of beans, rice, pasta and canned goods were already stocked and labeled.
The food pantry opened 40 years ago, serving a dozen families from a space in the basement of the Centre Street Congregational Church. Warner and Lewis took over as directors in 2022, gained nonprofit status and moved the pantry to a new building three years ago.
It’s been busy ever since.
“If we weren’t here, there are some folks that would be in desperate trouble. The incomes are not that high here, but expenses are high,” Warner said. “Food purchasing and gas are high. It’s difficult for them to make ends meet without some kind of safety net.”
The pantry, open two days a week, serves people from 11 communities around Machias, a town of about 2,000 people known for its annual wild blueberry festival. Some families drive nearly an hour to get
In an average week, around 175 families come in for groceries, Lewis said. Lately, five or six new people have been registering each week.
“A lot of our clients are working and just can’t make ends meet,” Lewis said.
Programs like this are critical in Washington County, where, according to Feeding America, the overall food insecurity rate in 2024 was at nearly 19% and the rate for children was about 26%. Three-quarters of Washington County’s food insecure residents qualified for SNAP, according to the organization.
Maine was one of the first states to implement universal free school meals, a move designed to reduce childhood hunger and the stigma around food assistance. Research by Michele Polacsek, a University of New England professor, shows the critical role those meals play as a reliable source of nutrition, particularly in rural communities.
Polacsek said
“Rural poverty creates barriers to food security and nutrition security that go beyond what other families in poverty experience,” she said.
At the food pantry in Machias on that day in August, the first few patrons of the day arrived before it officially opened. After checking in, they pushed small grocery carts through the building, choosing the items they wanted. Some said the food helps them make ends meet, especially at the end of the month when their SNAP benefits are tapped out.
Gina Rackliff stopped by to pick up food for her family of six, and another family who
Marga James, who retired to Machias 15 years ago, came in to get food for herself and three others unable to
“It would be a crisis,” she said.
The pantry relies on the community to make it all work. Hannaford donates food a few times a week and during summer local gardeners drop off green beans, garlic, beets and loads of yellow squash and zucchini.
Lewis and Warner believe that every person who comes to the pantry deserves high quality food and the dignity of choosing for themselves what to take home.
“It’s a basic right,”
‘OVERCOMING EVERYTHING’
As a kid, Chelsey Megquier was always up early and ready to get to school for breakfast, especially when there hadn’t been any food for dinner the night before. As an adult, she said, she
Megquire, 36, said she wanted to create a more stable life for herself and her daughter.
“This doesn’t have to be the story of my life,” she said.
Megquire, who lives in Calais with her wife and 14-year-old daughter, went back to school several years ago with support from Family Futures Downeast, which helped pay for an expensive car repair and sports equipment for her daughter.
After earning her associate’s degree from Washington County Community College, Megquire was hired as a bookkeeper at a nonprofit. She’s now working on her bachelor’s degree with plans to become an accountant.
Megquire said her family is now more financially stable,
A few years ago, Megquire was able to buy her first home. After she was handed the keys, she and her daughter pulled the for sale sign out of the ground and, together, threw it into a trash can.
“That was part of overcoming everything,” she said. “This was ours.”

title: Camden to remove street paid parking kiosks in wake of voter poll
text:
After a little more than a year of heated debate, Camden Public Works will soon be removing the paid parking kiosks from streets downtown and storing them at the Wastewater Treatment Plant.
The Select Board voted 5-0 on Tuesday, Nov. 10 to take that action in response to the votes from townspeople in the November election on the non-binding questions about parking. The town will be retaining paid parking kiosks on the Public Landing.
Townspeople voted 2,583-845 to remove metered parking from the streets in a non-binding question Nov. 3. On the second question, they voted 1,976-1,423 to keep metered parking on the Public Landing.
The issue of parking has been a matter of fierce debate in the community for more than a year. The town kiosks were installed in September 2025 and most of them were immediately vandalized.
In June, Chris Nolan was reelected to the Select Board and Bobbi Oxton Blake was elected, giving those who oppose paid parking a majority on the Select Board. But when the vote came in July on whether to pause the parking program, Susan Dorr joined Blake and Nolan in approving the pause, while Ken Gross argued the issue should be decided by townspeople at the polls in November.
Dorr said at the Select Board meeting Tuesday night that she was an advocate of paid parking originally, but she was moved to change her position by a letter presented by Camden business owners speaking out against the paid parking program.
“They’re the folks keeping the lights on,” she said.
She added that she felt some of the rhetoric around the issue when petitions were being circulated in town opposing paid parking involved a lot of overblown and emotional reactions to the program.
Dorr said the rollout of the paid parking program was clumsy and confusing and could have been more elegant.
She also said it might be a good idea to recharge the town Parking Committee to look at the options for the future.
Acting Town Manager Jodi Hanson said the vote impacts 32 kiosks with 31 on the streets of Camden and one for demonstration purposes at the Town Office.
Select Board member Christopher Rheault said there was research that went into the paid parking program which outlined benefits that included addressing traffic issues as well as the issue of parking itself.
The issue was originally on the agenda as a discussion item, but the board voted to move it to an action item, in part because it would be good to have the Public Works Department remove the kiosks and store them before the weather gets too cold.
Rheault also argued the town should go ahead and sell the kiosks if possible to recoup some money, noting that even if the town decides to dust off the paid parking idea two years in the future, by then the technology will likely have moved on to something better. Hanson said she had reached out to Butts Ticket Systems, the company that sold the kiosks to Camden, and it was possible the company might buy back some of the main boards and screens. She said it may also be possible to sell them in the open marketplace.
The town also has in storage signs explaining the parking program, which for the most part were never put up.
Rheault said that if the parking committee is restarted it needs to have a more cohesive structure. He said the committee in the past has been more of an ad hoc situation with people showing up and voting rather than a formal process.
Chair Chris Nolan said the town traffic ordinance would need to be updated, but Rheault did not see that as a priority since the plan was basically to maintain the status quo.
“I’ll take a look at it,” Nolan said.

title: Fire departments, state officials make changes in the wake of a deadly lumber mill fire in Searsmont
text:
Fire departments, state officials evolve in the wake of a deadly lumber mill fire in Searsmont
The Maine Department of Labor is bringing safety training to rural communities after issuing citations to fire and rescue departments that responded to the deadly fire at Robbins Lumber
Fire departments, state officials evolve in the wake of a deadly lumber mill fire in Searsmont
The Maine Department of Labor is bringing safety training to rural communities after issuing citations to fire and rescue departments that responded to the deadly fire at Robbins Lumber
The Maine Department of Labor is bringing safety training to rural communities after issuing citations to fire and rescue departments that responded to the deadly Robbins Lumber fire in Searsmont this spring.
Forty-six agencies responded to the fire. Two firefighters died and eight first responders were injured.
The Maine Department of Labor opened investigations into every department that reported an injury or fatality, which is standard practice. Each department received at least one citation. The cited departments were Appleton, Belmont, Lincolnville, Montville, Morrill and Searsmont fire departments, as well as the Searsmont Rescue Department.
The Maine Occupational Safety and Health program oversees health and safety standards in the public sector. MEOSH investigates followed complaints and reports of fatalities or serious workplace injuries. The program also aims to conduct proactive workplace inspections, but investigative resources are dedicated to complaints and incidents first.
Collectively, the departments were fined $108,000 for 24 citations. The Labor Department waived nearly all penalties on the condition that the departments address the safety concerns.
"We would rather see communities spend those resources on actual change rather than paying a fine," said Kate Burkhart, director of the Bureau of Labor Standards at the Maine Department of Labor.
The settlements also require safety training, but many of the departments are primarily staffed by volunteers who also work full-time jobs.
"Free is not enough because asking someone to take a day away from work and lose that pay in order to come to Augusta for training means it's not really accessible," said Burkhart. "So, we are restructuring."
The department plans to offer targeted safety training in Waldo and Knox counties on nights and weekends.
"I don't think that folks in rural communities that rely on volunteers care any less or don't want to keep their folks safe, but there is a disparity in resources that I think needs to be addressed," Burkhart said.
The Searsmont Rescue Department was cited for setting up a rehabilitation station for injured firefighters just feet from the silo where the fire started. Other citations involved improper use of protective gear. The most common issue was that departments lacked an accountability system to track firefighters’ whereabouts.
"Whether you responded to that fire that day or not, there are lessons that can be learned, and moving forward, thinking about how to ensure that firefighters and emergency responders are safe," Burkhart said.
The departments have already resolved the most urgent issues. Trainings are scheduled for the next few months, and all changes are expected to be implemented by the end of February 2027.

title: Video captures heroic police officer helping pull driver out of burning car following crash
text:
DAVIS, Calif. (KXTV) — Davis police Cpl. Pheng Ly broke the driver’s window of a burning car and pulled the man inside to safety in the early morning hours of Nov. 1, according to the Davis Police Department.
Ly arrived at the scene of a car fire and was met with people screaming. His body-worn camera video shows him breaking the window to reach the driver.
Corporal describes the rescue
The incident happened after Halloween night. Ly was in the Davis area when the call came out.
The crash technically fell under California Highway Patrol jurisdiction, but Ly said he was nearby and wanted to help.
“I tried to pull the door to open the door to get him out, but the door was locked,” Ly said. “So I took out my pocket knife, which has a window punch on it, and I was able to smash out the driver’s window, reach inside, unlock the door, open the door and yank the driver out of the vehicle after undoing his seatbelt.”
Ly said he was the first to arrive at the scene and the fire was spreading toward where the driver was seated.
“I remember when I reached in to undo his seat belt and grab him out, the wall of fire was right there in front of him through that clear windshield, so I’m glad I got there when I did,” Ly said.
Driver arrested after treatment
Davis police said CHP investigated the collision. The driver was arrested on suspicion of DUI after being treated for his injuries.
The department commended Ly for actions it said may have saved the driver’s life.
Similar rescue about six years ago
Davis police also recalled a separate incident about six years ago, when Ly rescued a woman in Solano County.
“A woman had driven her car off the roadway, and the vehicle had overturned and caught fire,” Ly said. “Once again, I was nearby. I heard it on the police radio. I got there first and I was able to pull her out of the vehicle.”
Ly: ‘I just move’
Ly said he was doing his job. He is a father of four, and said the driver he rescued was a few years older than his oldest son.
“I see a situation where someone’s life is in danger. Of course I’m scared. I’m very scared, but I’m not scared for me. I’m scared for the person that’s trapped in the car,” Ly said. “I’m afraid that I might fail him or let him down, and so I just move and let my experience take over, and you know, everything worked out right.”
Ly has been with the Davis Police Department for 25 years. He plans to retire in a year and a half.

title: Woman loses more than $400K of retirement savings to gold courier scam
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WINNEBAGO COUNTY, Wis. (InvestigateTV) — It can start with a pop-up on the computer screen and sometimes ends with the innocent victim handing over their life savings to a scammer.
The FBI reported in 2025 that the “gold courier” scam alone drained more than $300 million from victims.
Criminals trick victims, often retirees, that their personal information has been compromised. The scammer then convinces them that in order to secure their assets, they need to convert cash into gold bars or coins.
Then the fraudsters send a fake courier to collect the gold in person.
A Wisconsin woman lost more than $400,000 of her retirement savings after scammers impersonated federal agencies, her investment company and the Better Business Bureau to convince her she was protecting her money.
“Forty years’ worth of savings, and it’s gone,” said the woman, who we will call Mary.
How it began
Mary said the scheme started when she clicked a pop-up on her computer while scheduling an appointment with her financial advisor. “With their logo on it,” she noted.
“They locked my computer to the point where I couldn’t even shut it off manually,” Mary said.
She then received a call from someone claiming to represent her investment company, who told her the account had been hacked and that she was a suspect in weapons dealing and money laundering.
“Someone just took out a high-interest loan in your name for $35,000,” Mary said, recounting what she was told.
“And they showed me eight places where my Social Security number was being used,” she said. “So now I’m terrified. I’m absolutely terrified.”
The callers told Mary her financial advisor was also a suspect and that she should not speak to anyone. They sent a non-disclosure agreement directly to her printer.
Impersonators and gold purchases
Calls continued from people impersonating the sheriff’s office, the FBI and the Federal Trade Commission, making her believe they were working to restore her account. “That’s the trick is to get your confidence.”
Mary said the callers told her she needed to purchase gold to protect her money.
Mary spent $131,208 on 24 gold coins.
Then came a twist: A call from the Better Business Bureau, telling her she’s been scammed.
“He said, ‘You’ve been working with the scammers. You need to stop right now. And I’m going to help you,’” Mary said.
But it was an imposter. The caller arranged for a courier to collect the gold coins from Mary in a fast food parking lot. Mary said she was given only a first name and a password to identify the courier — the courier had a description of her car and clothing, but she had no description of them.
Months of continued fraud
Mary said people at her bank and at the business where she purchased the gold questioned her about the large cash withdrawals.
“I had to keep making excuses why I wanted these large amounts of cash,” she said.
She continued because she believed her money was being recovered and could see it appearing to be restored in her account. She was also instructed to purchase Bitcoin and thousands of dollars in gift cards.
“I put 600 miles on my car just running all over town, buying gift cards,” Mary said. “But you see it put back into your account. It’s all there.”
The fraud continued for three months. It ended when Mary tried to call the person she believed was her BBB contact and found the number had been disconnected.
“I grabbed everything, and I went right down to the police station,” she said.
‘Unprecedented’ loss, officials warn
Mary also contacted the Wisconsin Better Business Bureau to report that imposters had stolen more than $400,000 in her name.
“The extent was unprecedented. I mean, this is probably the largest amount of money loss that we’ve had reported in one single scam,” said Lisa Schiller of the Wisconsin Better Business Bureau.
The Wisconsin Department of Financial Institutions said the scam is surging and frequently targets seniors, using gold as part of the ruse to convince victims they are protecting or recovering their money. Officials said the operations are often run by international crime networks that use couriers for pickups.
- Related link: Real government agents aren’t asking you to buy and deliver gold bars (FTC)
“Hang up your phone or shut down your computer, because once you engage with them, you go down the rabbit hole with them and it’s very hard to disengage at that point, psychologically,” said Robin Jacobs of the Wisconsin Department of Financial Institutions.
Investigation ongoing, no arrests
Local police investigating Mary’s case said in a statement: “We are looking at all aspects of this investigation to try and identify suspects; that would include trying to find video, if any is available. This investigation is still ongoing, and at this time we are not sure if it is connected with other crimes.”
No arrests have been made.
Mary said she does not know whether she will recover any of her savings.
“There’s no guarantee that any of it will come back,” she said. “The banks aren’t responsible, you’re responsible, because you did it.”
Mary is bravely sharing her story to prevent others from becoming victims.
“I don’t want this to happen to anybody else, because this is a nightmare,” Mary said. “I’m freaking out. Am I going to have to file bankruptcy? Am I going to lose my house? I mean, I’m terrified.”
Officials advise the public to never trust anyone who calls and instructs them to move money to protect it or to hand over gold.
They also warn against allowing people they do not know to access their computer or personal information. If you receive a call from an unknown number you’re advised to hang up, call someone you’re familiar with, or call the police.
Any suspected fraudulent activity to the FBI at ic3.gov

title: ‘Criminal illegal alien’ arrested after telling United flight crew he had a bomb, Homeland Security says
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A man was arrested after telling the flight crew on a United plane that he had a bomb.
According to the Jefferson Parish Sheriff’s Office, Rony Gomez-Alberto, 34, started acting irrationally aboard United flight 2174 around 11:20 p.m.
Authorities said he told crew members that he had a bomb on board. The Department of Homeland Security said Gomez-Alberto is a “criminal illegal alien” and that he tried to “gain entry to the cockpit” during the flight.
There were 46 passengers and six crew members aboard the United flight from Newark, New Jersey, to New Orleans.
The plane safely landed at Louis Armstrong International Airport, and all passengers got off and were taken to the terminal.
Gomez-Alberto was arrested without incident and taken to the Jefferson Parish Correctional Center, where he was booked on charges of communicating false information of planned arson and terrorizing, deputies said. Immigration and Customs Enforcement also lodged a detainer for Gomez-Alberto.
According to Homeland Security, Gomez-Alberto’s criminal history includes felony bomb threat, felony threat, terroristic state offenses and disorderly conduct.
He is from Honduras and has been removed from the country twice and was released a third time, pending removal proceedings, by a judge.

Meet Claire, our Adoptable Pet of the Week
text:
Meet Claire, our Adoptable Pet of the Week in Greater Portland
This week's featured adoptable pet from the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland is Claire, an 8-month-old puppy who has love and energy to spare.
Claire has learned how to sit for treats, but she still has a lot of training to do. Since Claire is still a puppy, the Animal Refuge League is looking for a family who is ready to help her become the best dog she can be.
"Claire, we think, is a real sweetheart," said Matt Blanchard of the Animal Refuge League. "She's really adorable. She does well with dogs. She's done well with kids, and we just ask that if you have dogs or kids at home, you bring them by the shelter for the adoption counsel and they all get to know each other there."
More information about Claire is available on the Animal Refuge League's website, as long as she is still looking for her forever home.
Anyone who is interested in meeting Claire or other adoptable pets can visit the Animal Refuge League's shelter at 217 Landing Road in Westbrook between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., except on Wednesdays, when the shelter is closed for adoptions.
The Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland does adoptions on a first-come, first-served basis. On the days the shelter is open, sign-in sheets will be placed on the front door at 9 a.m. to track the order of arrival of adopters who show up early. People who arrive early are asked to remain on the campus once they sign in.
Dog owners who are interested in adopting dogs that are older than 6 months, including Claire, are required to have their dogs meet the adoptable pet before a new pet can be brought home.

title: Sanford approves plan to reopen Heritage Crossing once security cameras are installed
text:
The city of Sanford plans to reopen Heritage Crossing after a newly approved, 24/7 security camera system is installed along the street.
The cameras are one possible solution to ongoing safety and trespassing concerns at the International Woolen Mill complex. Heritage Crossing has been shut down to vehicles and pedestrians since an emergency declaration was issued last month.
At Tuesday’s City Council meeting, members heard a presentation from a representative of LiveView Technologies Mobile Security, a company that owns and operates solar-powered security cameras.
The cameras utilize “advanced human and vehicle geofencing analytics,” aimed at detecting motion and unauthorized visitors in closed-off areas in and around the mill, company representative Mike Santoro told councilors.
Santoro emphasized that the cameras are different from controversial Flock cameras. (Late last year, the City Council revoked its initial approval to bring that company’s automated license plate reading cameras to Sanford.)
“I’m sure folks are familiar with everything going on in the news with Flock and how it feeds into a national database with shared information, and a bunch more,” Santoro said. “We do not feed into a national database of information. You, Sanford, owns 100% of that data.”
Santoro also added that the analytics attached to the camera are not associated with artificial intelligence and do not utilize any sort of license plate reading technology.
“We had Flock come in here and lie straight to our face about privacy concerns,” council member Jonathan Martell said. He asked that the contract with LVT include provisions to protect the city in the event of a privacy breach. Santoro said that could be done.
According to the proposal, the plan would include three LVT camera systems, costing $84,600.
The council approved the proposal unanimously.
The cameras are expected to be delivered and installed within the next two weeks. Once they’re are up and running, Heritage Crossing will be reopened, though access to the mill itself remains restricted.

title: Searsmont EMS chief to return home 6 months after lumber mill explosion
text:
Searsmont EMS Chief Sarah Tompkins will return home from the hospital next week, just over six months after the fiery lumber mill explosion that killed three people and injured more than a dozen others.
Tompkins will be welcomed home during a gathering at the Searsmont Fire station on Nov. 18, according to a social media post from the town late Tuesday night.
“Sarah’s homecoming is a moment we have all been looking forward to, and we are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of love, encouragement, and support throughout her journey,” the social media post reads.
Community members and fellow first responders are welcome to join the celebration, the town said. Details about Tompkins’ escort and the timing of her arrival are expected to be released next week
The May 15 explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont killed three people, including 27-year-old Andrew Cross, of Morrill, who died at the scene. Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury, 76, died at Maine Medical Center in June, while Alden Robbins, co-owner of the lumber mill, died at Massachusetts General Hospital in July.
Several first responders, as well as members of the Robbins family, were seriously injured in the explosion. Most have returned home, most recently Lily Robbins, who was welcomed back at a community gathering on Oct. 30.
The Maine Department of Labor announced Tuesday that it cited seven emergency departments for safety violations but suspended almost all of the penalties so the towns can pay for training and new equipment.

title: ‘The help they deserve’: Buckfield veteran tells story of trauma in an effort to aid those who can’t
text:
There is a particular song that can take Jamison McAlister to a safe place, and it might surprise some to hear that it’s “Highway to Hell,” from the 1980 AC/DC album “Back in Black.”
When you hear the 23-year Army combat veteran of two Middle East wars talk about it, though, it all makes sense.
His recall is of a Black Hawk helicopter in the Middle East, where he heard “Highway to Hell” and other rock ‘n’ roll songs played repeatedly. Another is “You Shook Me All Night Long,” from the same album.
“Every day, you’d have to go up in a helicopter,” he said, “and they’d play rock and roll music.”
One day he asked the pilot, a Vietnam veteran, why tunes were always blasting. The answer?
“He said, ‘because it calms the infantry guys down,’” McAlister said. “He said, ‘they were so nervous … they would hear something, or something would trigger them. They’d click their safety off, and next thing you know, we’d hit a bump or air pocket and they’d start shooting holes in the floor. Or the top.’”
That pilot continued the practice through his years of service, and by the time McAlister found himself in Iraq in 1990, the two AC/DC songs had become mainstays.
“That’s how long it took us to get to the battlefield,” he said. “By the end of the second song, we’d be on the ground. Two songs and we’re on the ground and moving.
“To this day, if I hear these songs, which I do a lot, my mindset clicks. I’m no longer scared. You could put me in the worst scenario and I’m fine. I’m as cool as a cucumber.”
McAlister, who is 56, carried that coolness for years, all through his 23-year career and into his post-service years.
He never gave serious thought to post traumatic stress disorder. He did not believe in it, even as friends would later talk about the effects it had on them.
That concept was drilled into him and fellow recruits 35 years ago by platoon commanders with years of experience, and possibly the knowledge that repression can be the strongest survival skill they might teach.
“These guys were the A Shau Valley guys. Mekong Delta. Hamburger Hill. To privates, recruits — they’d say PTSD was a bunch of bull—-. And no one had the right to claim PTSD. They hadn’t earned it,” McAlister described.
‘I WASN’T HERE’
One of McAlister’s buddies, who finished his military service at the same time he did, started having problems. He told him he was having flashbacks, but McAlister brushed it off.
His friend was put on a prescription regimen, which included medical marijuana.
“The thing was, if you claim you have it (PTSD), you’re weak,” he said. “So, I’d listen to him, but you know, I just thought it was bull.”
Whatever care the man was receiving, it didn’t help. He became over medicated and would get so stoned he would take even more.
“He’d say, ‘hey Mac, what’s the day?’ On Monday he wouldn’t remember taking his pills and then he’d call the next day and say ‘what day is this’ and wouldn’t remember taking them the day before, even if I told him he had.
“He just kept taking them,” McAlister said. “And then he finally overdosed and died.”
Despite what McAlister had been trained to think, it was learning that his friend was gone that triggered his own PTSD incident, the first of many.
One minute he was in his bedroom, sitting on a waterbed. The next thing he knew was he was no longer there.
“I’m not sitting on my bed,” he said. “I’m sitting on a helicopter that’s full of body bags. … I was there. I wasn’t here.”
Other suppressed memories began popping up. By that time he had returned to live on the family farm in Buckfield and care for his 90-year-old father.
For years after retiring from the military he had lived a nomadic lifestyle, following jobs offered by friends who continued to work in the field.
Once he found himself in the familiar environment he had once limited to brief visits, though, McAlister’s PTSD finally caught up with him.
He planned his return to be a visit. He would help his father, get the farm’s affairs in order and then go. But this time he was not able to leave. His family needed him to stay.
“It had been my coping mechanism, to cycle through short 30-day stays before redeploying,” he said. “That cycle prevented me from confronting my trauma.”
‘WE STICK TOGETHER’
Now, McAlister was the one in need of help — help he had never used because he did not believe he needed it and had never been told was available.
It did not occur to him when he got a toothache that he could have a $3,500 dental treatment taken care of by Veterans Affairs … until his civilian dentist told him.
“I was out 12 years before I ever went to the VA,” he said. “And the people there, they’re great.”
The experience of seeing combat veterans wait for services behind others who never saw battle became a new trigger for him.
“We were told we didn’t earn the right,” he repeated. He did not know he deserved it.
Finally, McAlister sought counseling for his PTSD. It was at a session that his sister accompanied him to when he had a breakthrough.
“The therapist asked me, why hadn’t I come home before,” he said. “At first I said it was because my dad didn’t need me until now. But she pushed it and I just said it — ‘I haven’t earned the right to.’”
Pressed to consider why he felt he had not earned the right, he had another realization. “I didn’t feel I had the right because we didn’t win the war,” he said.
Using cognitive recall, McAlister’s counselor helped him draw out and face old traumas. He shared a few of his past experiences while being interviewed. “Stuff that I didn’t think was still there,” he said. “Combat veterans have a switch in them.”
One other key part of coming to terms with his condition was a return to school and writing it out. It has helped to validate and give form to his voice.
Recognizing his own PTSD and finally taking care of himself through VA medical and behavioral health services, McAlister noticed something else about veterans. Something he feels is not right.
“I was at the VA clinic,” he said, “either Lewiston or Rumford. I’m waiting and this woman comes in, and her husband comes in. He is shaking. I could see his tattoos were military unit symbols, and he was old enough he had to be a Vietnam vet. I concluded he was probably in a PTSD moment.”
McAlister approached the older man and asked if he was OK. He said he was, but his shaking and demeanor told a different story. He wanted to know who McAlister was and why did he care?
“I told him I was infantry. That we stick together,” he said. “And all of a sudden he calmed down and was able to have a normal conversation. He said he needed to talk to someone right then.”
McAlister checked to see what the man’s wait would be.
“There were four veterans sitting there. I asked if any served in combat, had served in Vietnam, or anything. Nope. One did four years, one did 15, one did 11, and whatever. I asked if they minded if this guy went ahead of us,” McAlister said.
“One guy looked me in the eye and said, ‘I’ve waited two and a half months to get this appointment and I’m not about to miss it, so no.”
Before McAlister had a chance to bristle at the other veteran’s callousness, a counselor intervened, took the Vietnam veteran into an office and left the five men standing there. He told the four veterans what he thought of their responses.
After the words were said, the wife accompanying her husband made a point to call out McAlister, too.
“She told me I was the first person who he could talk calmly with in more than a week. ‘I didn’t know how to get to him,’ she said.
“For me, it goes back (to my counseling). Deserve or earn. Most of us combat veterans that went outside the wire, we still don’t believe we’ve earned the right for these benefits,” McAlister said. “While one who served for 30 seconds knows they deserve every one.”
McAlister knows that civilians and even noncombat veterans might not understand his frustration, since he is entitled to the same benefits and it is a choice to exercise them or not.
He went through years of denial and hell before getting to where he found his voice. He reached out to tell his story because he knows there are others like him, in the shadows, hiding the depth of their struggles. He wants them to ask for what they deserve.
“They should go first. They should not have to wait,” he said. “A disabled combat veteran, someone who got their arms blown off. They should go first.
“The reason I’m telling my story, is because of our deserve/earn mentality. You can tell by looking them in the eye if a veteran is combat.
“For that one person out there in the same boat — I want them to get help. I had a toothache and I saw that people out there really do care. And still so many have never ever gone for the help they deserve.”

title: Family of ICE agent in Biddeford shooting accuses him of immigrant bias, New York Times reports
text:
New interviews with family members of the federal immigration agent who shot and killed a man in Biddeford this summer show they had growing concerns about his mental health and anti-immigrant bias.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that David Brouillette, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who shot and killed a 25-year-old Colombian man in July, sent a series of racist emails to his sister in 2021, criticizing her relationship with a Colombian man who is the father of her two children.
“He can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries,” Brouillette wrote in one email, according to the Times, which noted that the emails contained several typos. He also said that the man’s “bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”
The Department of Homeland Security issued a lengthy statement on Wednesday morning, declining to identify its agents and defending its hiring practices. The agency also said it “does not comment on matters regarding personnel who are no longer with the agency,” although a spokesperson did not clarify if that applied to Brouillette.
Brouillette was identified by those who know him as the agent who shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 during an enforcement operation in Biddeford.
Durán Guerrero was a Colombian citizen with work authorization and no criminal history, according to his family’s attorneys. Sen. Angus King said in July that a DHS official told him that Durán Guerrero was not the target of the agents’ operation that morning.
Brouillette has not responded to repeated requests for comment from the Portland Press Herald and his phone number was still out of service when a reporter called Wednesday. The Times reported that Brouillette declined to speak with them after a reporter left a letter at his home. DHS has declined to name the agent involved.
The Times report also provides new details about Brouillette’s training to become an ICE agent, and his work history, citing anonymous sources who were briefed on his work history. Two people told the Times that Brouillette skipped ICE’s full training course in Georgia.
Another source reported that officials had not looked into Brouillette’s background at the time of the shooting, because the federal agency had “a gigantic backlog” of reports. Brouillette could not access some computer systems because he didn’t have full clearance, the Times reported.
“The agency restricted his access to certain computer systems because he had not been fully cleared, yet apparently saw no problem trusting him with the power to take someone’s life,” U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, said Wednesday.
A DHS spokesperson, responding through a media email without names, said that the agency refuses to “dox” employees, citing safety concerns, and defended its “rigorous standards” for ICE agents and vetting procedures.
“Incoming ICE officers, many already with years of law enforcement experience, are onboarded in accordance with applicable policies and standards. Any claims of substandard training or vetting are FALSE,” the spokesperson wrote. “This administration is preserving ICE’s reputation as one of the most elite law enforcement agencies not only in the U.S., but the entire world.”
Benjamin Gideon, an attorney for Durán Guerrero’s family said in a statement that the Times’ reporting “adds to the long list of Mr. Brouillette’s disqualifying conduct” and hostility toward immigrants.
“Johan Sebastián’s death was not an inevitable accident,” Gideon said in the statement.
Gideon urged newly-elected members of Congress to investigate. Pingree said the Times’ reporting revealed an “unconscionable betrayal of the public’s trust” by ICE, and she called for the agency to be abolished.
The Press Herald previously reported that a Hallowell official saw “too many red flags” in Brouillette’s background to hire him at the local police department, despite his experience working as a child support enforcement officer for the state, and as a corrections officer in Windham.
Brouillette and his second ex-wife had filed a total of eight protection from abuse order requests against each other that detailed allegations of verbal and physical abuse.
Ashley Brouillette, David Brouillette’s first ex-wife, who has also accused him of being abusive, was one of the first people to tell reporters that he was the shooter. She said he told her so when he called her on July 15. She said Wednesday that she spoke about her ex-husband about a week later, in an interview with members of DHS and the Office of the Maine Attorney General.
Both agencies have announced investigations into the July 13 shooting, although none have shared updates since then.
Sean Murphy, another attorney for Durán Guerrero’s family, said that state prosecutors told his clients earlier this summer that Attorney General Aaron Frey wanted to make a decision on the investigation before he leaves office. Lawmakers will elect a new attorney general next month.
A spokesperson for the Maine attorney general referred a reporter to what’s been publicly released and said they don’t comment on pending investigations.
According to the Times, Brouillette declined to speak with them after a reporter left the letter at his home in Maine. Brouillette also called the sheriff’s office and said he was under “executive protection,” according to the Times.
This echoes what the father of Brouillette’s young stepdaughter wrote in court records for a protection from abuse order earlier this summer. Brouillette and his wife reportedly told the father that they were entering “protective custody” due to threats Brouillette received, following the shooting.

title: Goodwill gets $100K to expand workforce services in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Goodwill Northern New England will receive $100,000 over two years from Bank of America’s Neighborhood Builders program to expand workforce support and employment services across Maine.
The investment will support Goodwill’s Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Employment and Training program, operated in partnership with the Maine Department of Health and Human Services.
“A strong workforce is essential to a strong economy, yet too many Mainers still face barriers to employment and career advancement,” said Brian King, president of Bank of America Maine.
“Goodwill Northern New England is helping connect people to the training, support and opportunities they need to succeed in the workforce,” he continued. “Through Neighborhood Builders, we’re investing in an organization that is expanding economic opportunity and helping strengthen Maine’s workforce for the future.”
‘Investing in programs and people’
As Maine’s largest employment and training provider for SNAP recipients, Goodwill Northern New England helps participants develop individualized career plans while addressing barriers such as transportation, housing, childcare and health needs.
More than 23,000 Maine SNAP recipients currently qualify as work registrants, underscoring the need for employment and training support statewide, BofA said in its funding announcement.
“We know there are thousands of Mainers who could benefit from the right employment support, and reaching more people requires investing in both our programs and our people,” said Tripp Harrison, president and CEO of Goodwill Northern New England.
“Bank of America’s investment will help us open doors to new possibilities through the power of work, while developing the leadership capacity to sustain and grow this impact,” he added.
